resulting in functional bugs [6]. Automatically evaluating this align-
ment is difficult. Metrics designed primarily for code similarity, such 
as CodeBLEU [8], CodeBERTScore [9] and CodeScore [10], measure 
structural or semantic resemblance to reference code. However, they 
cannot inherently verify behavioral equivalence or guarantee that the 
code accurately fulfills the promptâ€™s specific functional goals. This gap 
highlights the ongoing challenge of automatically validating the true 
functional correctness and prompt fidelity of LLM-generated code.
To comprehensively address these multifaceted issues, this paper 
proposes a novel two-stage framework named CodeEnhancer that im-
proves the security, correctness, and quality of LLM-generated Python 
code. The framework integrates automated validation with targeted 
model improvement through fine-tuning. As a contribution to the re-
search community, we provide the full implementation of the CodeEn-
hancer framework on GitHub.1
The first stage of CodeEnhancer consists of an iterative validation 
and refinement pipeline. This pipeline couples the LLMâ€™s code gener-
ation capabilities with established Static Application Security Testing 
(SAST) tools. Specifically, it uses Pylint [11] to check for syntax is-
sues, and Bandit [12] to detect security vulnerabilities. When the LLM 
generates an initial code snippet based on a natural language prompt, 
these SAST tools are used to analyze it. Any detected issues trigger 
a structured feedback mechanism that provides the LLM with specific 
details, such as the type, location, and severity of the issue, which are 
necessary to revise the code. The generate-validate-refine loop then 
iterates, progressively improving the code until it passes all checks or 
reaches a predefined iteration limit.
While this iterative validation pipeline is effective for post-generation 
correction, it has limitations when relied on solely. The process can be 
computationally intensive and may struggle with complex vulnerabil-
ities that require a deeper understanding of security. Additionally, it 
does not improve the LLMâ€™s inherent ability to proactively generate 
secure code. The LLM remains reactive, depending entirely on external 
tool feedback.
Therefore, the second stage of our framework introduces a targeted 
fine-tuning methodology to enhance the LLMâ€™s intrinsic security aware-
ness and code generation capabilities. This stage adapts the base LLM 
(GPT-4o) using specialized datasets containing secure coding exam-
ples. In particular, fine-tuning is done with one of the following: (1) 
an existing dataset comprising expert-written secure code examples, 
representing best practices and an idealized security standard [13], 
and (2) a novel dataset curated from the framework-refined code 
outputs produced by the first stage (the validation pipeline) of our 
own framework. Thus, we can explore whether LLMs benefit more 
from learning idealized secure patterns or from learning the practical 
process of transforming potentially flawed code into secure, validated 
code via automated feedback loops. We hypothesize that fine-tuning 
on framework-refined data will better prepare the LLM to handle real-
world coding scenarios and generate more robust, secure code from the 
beginning.
The synergy between these two stages is crucial. The fine-tuned LLM 
produces better initial code, reducing the workload and the number of 
iterations required in the validation pipeline. At the same time, the 
validation pipeline can generate better, more refined code examples 
that could be used for further stage of model improvement, creating 
a virtuous cycle.
The primary contributions of this paper are:
1. The design and implementation of a comprehensive, two-stage 
CodeEnhancer framework integrating an iterative LLM-SAST 
validation pipeline and a subsequent targeted LLM fine-tuning 
methodology to enhance Python code security.
1 https://github.com/cyb3rlab/CodeEnhancer
2. A rigorous evaluation demonstrating the frameworkâ€™s effective-
ness using the LLMSecEval benchmark [13] to validate the first 
stage and the LLMSecEval and SecurityEval benchmarks [14] to 
assess the performance of the fine-tuned models in the second 
stage. In particular, the evaluation compares the effectiveness 
of fine-tuning with datasets derived from expert-written secure 
examples and those generated by the automated refinement pro-
cess. The results highlight the benefits of the integrated approach 
and the superiority of leveraging framework-refined data for 
fine-tuning. Notably, this approach outperformed expert-written 
examples in terms of model performance and proved to be more 
cost-effective.
3. An analysis provides insights into the synergistic benefits of 
combining automated validation with model adaptation. This 
contributes to the development of more trustworthy and secure 
AI-assisted coding practices.
The remainder of this paper is structured as follows: Section 2 
provides a background and motivation for the research, and Section 3 
reviews related work in LLM-based code generation, security vulnera-
bility detection, static analysis, and fine-tuning approaches. Section 4 
details the proposed methodology, elaborating on both the real-time 
validation pipeline and the fine-tuning extension. Section 5 outlines the 
experiment setup, including datasets, models, and evaluation metrics. 
Section 6 presents and analyzes the experimental results, comparing the 
performance of the baseline and fine-tuned models. Section 7 discusses 
the limitations of the current work and suggests directions for future 
research. Finally, Section 8 concludes the paper by summarizing the 
key findings and contributions.
2. Background and motivation
The advent of LLMs is a significant milestone in artificial intelli-
gence that has had a profound impact on various domains, including 
software engineering. Models such as Mistral [15], GPT-4 [1], and 
DeepSeek-R1 [16] are trained on vast datasets containing billions of 
lines of code and natural language text. This extensive training en-
ables these models to discern complex patterns, syntax, and common 
programming idioms across multiple languages. Consequently, these 
models can generate code directly from natural language prompts, 
offering substantial potential to accelerate software development [17]. 
Integrated tools, such as GitHub Copilot, leverage these capabilities 
by automating routine coding tasks, allowing developers to focus on 
higher-level system design and problem-solving and boosting produc-
tivity [4].
Alongside the rise of AI-driven code generation, Static Application 
Security Testing (SAST) has become integral to modern secure software 
development practices. SAST tools analyze application source code, 
bytecode, or binary code without executing it, aiming to detect po-
tential bugs, style inconsistencies, and security vulnerabilities early in 
the development lifecycle [18]. SAST tools employ techniques such 
as pattern matching, data flow analysis, and control flow analysis to 
identify deviations from coding standards, such as using Pylint [11] 
to check for compliance with Pythonâ€™s PEP 8, and common security 
pitfalls such as those cataloged by OWASP or MITRE. Security-focused 
SAST tools like Bandit [12] for Python or the more general-purpose 
CodeQL [19] specifically target known vulnerability patterns, including 
SQL injection, cross-site scripting (XSS), hardcoded secrets, and inse-
cure API usage. Early detection through SAST is crucial for reducing 
the cost and effort required for remediation compared to finding flaws 
later in testing or after deployment.
Despite their impressive code generation capabilities, LLMs are 
not infallible. A growing body of evidence highlights significant con-
cerns about the quality and security of the code LLMs produce [4â€“6]. 
LLM-generated code frequently contains:
Knowledge-Based Systems 342 (2026) 115925 
2 
J. Lee et al.
1. Syntax Errors: Recent work [20] has revealed that syntax er-
rors account for most faults in LLM-generated Verilog code. 
Addressing these errors alone achieved a 98.5% fix rate using 
retrieval-based prompting in the study, highlighting syntax cor-
rection as a critical step toward improving the reliability of 
machine-generated code.
2. Security Vulnerabilities: LLMs often replicate insecure coding 
patterns that are present in their vast training data, generating 
code susceptible to exploits such as command injection, path 
traversal, and improper cryptographic function handling [6,7].
3. Functional Correctness Issues: Ensuring that the generated 
code accurately reflects the userâ€™s intent, as specified in the 
prompt, remains a critical challenge [6]. LLMs may misinter-
pret requirements, overlook edge cases, or produce code with 
subtle logical flaws, leading to incorrect behavior even if it is 
syntactically valid [21].
These shortcomings necessitate robust mechanisms to validate and 
improve LLM-generated code before integrating it into software projects. 
However, relying solely on LLMs to iteratively fix or refine their own 
code often yields suboptimal results. This approach suffers from a 
form of model bias, wherein the same reasoning flaws that led to the 
initial issues may persist or compound during self-revision. A recent 
study [22] has demonstrated that LLMs frequently struggle to detect 
or correct nuanced logical or security flaws in their own outputs, espe-
cially in the absence of structured external feedback. Previous research 
found that LLMs often fail to self-correct reasoning errors without 
external input, and in some cases, their performance degrades after 
self-correction. Similarly, another study highlighted that self-correction 
without external guidance can lead to overfitting to syntactic patterns, 
which limits the modelâ€™s ability to ensure functional correctness or 
robust security guarantees [23].
Other researchers also have shown that fine-tuning large language 
models on carefully constructed code datasets can improve their ability 
to generate more secure and functional code. Training on examples that 
reflect secure coding practices reduces the likelihood of introducing 
vulnerabilities while improving the syntactic and semantic quality of 
the outputs. These findings suggest that fine-tuning is an effective 
mechanism for aligning LLMs with practical coding standards and 
expectations in real-world development settings [24,25].
Therefore, this paper addresses the limitations of relying solely on 
LLM code generation, post-hoc SAST analysis, or isolated fine-tuning 
efforts. There is a clear need for a more holistic approach. We propose 
and evaluate a comprehensive, integrated framework that combines 
the strengths of LLMs and SAST tools synergistically. Our framework 
establishes a virtuous cycle in which an iterative validation pipeline 
integrates SAST feedback to refine generated code. Simultaneously, a 
targeted fine-tuning methodology leverages these refined outputs to 
enhance the LLMâ€™s ability to generate secure, functionally correct code 
from the outset. The overarching goal is to create a more robust and 
trustworthy pathway for leveraging LLMs in software development by 
addressing syntax, security, and functional correctness in a unified, 
multi-stage process.
3. Related work
Research efforts to improve the quality and security of LLM-genera
ted code span several areas, including direct code generation im-
provements, automated code repair, the use of SAST tools, specific 
evaluation methodologies, and fine-tuning techniques. Table 1 provides 
a comparative overview of representative approaches based on their 
primary focus and the specific aspects of code quality they address, 
contextualizing our proposed integrated framework.
3.1. LLM-based frameworks for code generation, validation, and repair
Recent advances in LLM-based code generation have led to a diverse 
array of frameworks that aim to improve the quality, correctness, 
and security of generated code. As summarized in Table 1, these 
approaches differ in their primary focus, tool integration, and treatment 
of validation or repair tasks.
Early work by Chen et al. [3] introduced Codex, a fine-tuned 
GPT-3 model trained on code data, which was demonstrated to be 
capable of generating functional code from natural language prompts. 
However, Codex did not explicitly address code repair or security 
validation, despite achieving high pass rates on benchmark tasks such 
as HumanEval.
In contrast, Alrashedy et al. [26] presented a framework that in-
tegrates LLMs with SAST tools to automatically patch security vul-
nerabilities in source code. Their system leverages SAST tool output 
to generate prompts for LLM-based repair and is one of the earliest 
pipelines to combine static analysis and generation in an automated 
feedback loop.
Pearce et al. [27] further investigated the zero-shot repair capabil-
ities of Codex on vulnerable code snippets. Although no fine-tuning or 
external validation tools were used, the study revealed the potential 
and limitations of prompting alone in addressing security-related issues.
More recent work has shifted toward improving the intrinsic ability 
of LLMs to produce secure code through fine-tuning. For example, Li 
et al. [24] conducted an empirical study on fine-tuning models using 
security patch commits and demonstrated measurable improvements 
in vulnerability reduction. Similarly, Weyssow et al. [25] explored 
parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) methods for code generation, 
however, their study focused more on syntax and structural quality 
than on vulnerability mitigation.
Separately, Keltek et al. [28] proposed LSAST, a hybrid system in 
which SAST tools, such as Bearer, are paired with LLMs to enhance vul-
nerability detection coverage. Although LSAST is not explicitly aimed 
at code generation or repair, it exemplifies the complementary use of 
LLMs for security analysis and code validation.
Building on these advancements, research published in 2024 and 
2025 has scrutinized the efficacy of autonomous self-correction in 
LLMs. For example, Olausson et al. [30] demonstrated that relying 
solely on an LLMâ€™s intrinsic self-repair capabilities without robust ex-
ternal feedback often yields diminishing returns or introduces new 
errors. To overcome this limitation, the field is rapidly shifting toward 
iterative optimization frameworks. Ridnik et al. [29] introduced flow 
engineering approaches that use test-driven validation to refine code 
iteratively, while Kumar et al. [31] explored reinforcement learning 
methods to train models specifically for self-correction.
Unlike prior studies that intentionally prompt the model to generate 
insecure code by using artificial inputs, focus on isolated aspects such 
as generation and repair, or struggle with the limitations of intrinsic 
self-correction, our framework integrates all these components into a 
unified pipeline that employs natural, real-world prompts. By combin-
ing iterative static validation with fine-tuning on both expert-written 
and framework-refined code, our approach systematically bypasses the 
unreliability of autonomous self-repair highlighted in recent literature. 
It addresses syntax errors, functional correctness, and security vulner-
abilities cohesively, firmly positioning our work within the rapidly 
evolving domain of automated, feedback-driven code optimization.
3.2. Code evaluation using SAST tools
SAST tools are standard instruments for security assessment. For 
Python, Bandit [12] targets common security flaws, and Pylint [11] 
checks for code smells, style issues, and syntax errors. More sophis-
ticated tools like GitHubâ€™s CodeQL adopt semantic analysis to detect 
complex vulnerabilities across multiple languages [19]. Researchers

Enterprise tools, such as SonarQube [34] and Checkmarx [35] also 
exist. These tools offer broader capabilities and integrations, but they 
come with different complexities and costs.
3.3. Functional correctness evaluation
Validating that generated code behaves according to the intention 
expressed in the prompt is crucial yet challenging. Metrics such as 
CodeBLEU [8] and CodeBERTScore [9] measure code similarity by 
directly comparing the reference code and the target code. Execution-
based testing using benchmarks such as HumanEval [3] or The Mostly 
Basic Programming Problems (MBPP) [36] measures functional correct-
ness by checking pass rates against predefined unit tests [37]. While 
valuable, this approach might not fully cover the promptâ€™s specification. 
To address this issue, newer metrics aim for better alignment without 
relying solely on reference code. CodeScore [10] trains a model to 
predict execution outcomes. ICE-Score [38] uses an LLM itself to assess 
LLM-generated code against the given input prompt. SBC-Score [39] 
employs a novel reverse-generation technique, inferring requirements 
from the generated code and comparing them back to the original 
prompt using semantic similarity, lexical overlap, and completeness 
measures. Our framework incorporates a functional validation step 
using LLM reasoning based on prompt-derived specifications.
4. CodeEnhancer methodology
CodeEnhancer improves the security and quality of LLM-generated 
Python code with a two-stage approach: (1) a code generation & valida-
tion and refinement pipeline that integrates LLMs with SAST tools, and 
(2) a fine-tuning methodology that improves the LLMâ€™s secure coding 
capabilities. Fig. 1 provides an overview of this integrated architecture.
4.1. Stage 1: Code generation & validation and refinement pipeline
The first stage focuses on generating code and iteratively improving 
it based on immediate feedback from SAST tools. This pipeline con-
sists of several key steps designed to address syntactic, security, and 
functional correctness progressively, thus being in alignment with a 
structured quality assurance process.
4.1.1. Code generation with structured prompt template
LLMs often produce syntactically correct yet structurally inconsis-
tent or incomplete code when prompted with free-form instructions. 
To address this, our framework adopts a structured prompt template 
that demonstrates the desired output format and enforces a consistent 
generation template across diverse tasks.
The process begins with a natural language prompt provided by the 
user that describes the desired code functionality. To enhance clarity 
and facilitate subsequent validation, we employ a structured prompt 
template. This template instructs the LLM to generate functional code 
and a detailed docstring that restates the userâ€™s request, specifies the 
codeâ€™s purpose, and describes the steps to achieve the intended func-
tionality. The LLM then processes this structured input to generate an 
initial Python code snippet with an embedded docstring that serves as 
a functional specification.
The core idea is to guide the LLM to include a module-level doc-
string with three required fields at the top of each Python file.
1. Input Prompt â€” a restatement of the original user request.
2. Intention â€” the purpose or goal of the function.
3. Functionality â€” a precise description of how the function
achieves that goal.
This docstring improves the code and enables automated down-
stream evaluation. For example, our functional correctness validation 
leverages LLM reasoning to compare the functionality described in the 
docstring with the actual code logic.
4.1.2. Multi-faceted code validation
The Code Validation component iteratively improves the quality 
and security of LLM-generated code by detecting and correcting errors 
across multiple dimensions. This process integrates LLMs with SAST 
tools using three validation components, as follows:
1. Syntax Error Validation: The framework incorporates Pylint to 
validate the syntactic correctness and structure of the generated 
code. This includes identifying missing or misplaced elements 
such as parentheses, indentation inconsistencies and improper 
use of reserved keywords. Identified issues are logged, and cor-
rective prompts are sent to the LLM, which iteratively refines 
the code to align with these standards. This ensures that the 
generated code is both executable and adheres to basic syntac-
tic conventions. Fig. 2 provides an example of a syntax issue 
detected by Pylint, illustrating the type of feedback used for 
iterative correction.
2. Vulnerability Validation: To ensure security, the framework 
integrates Bandit, a SAST tool specifically designed for Python. 
Bandit scans the code for vulnerabilities, such as command 
Knowledge-Based Systems 342 (2026) 115925 
4 
J. Lee et al.
Fig. 1. Overall architecture of CodeEnhancer, illustrating the relationship between the code generation & validation refinement pipeline (Stage 1) and the 
fine-tuning methodology (Stage 2).
Fig. 2. Example of a code syntax issue detected via Pylint.
Fig. 3. Example of a code vulnerability issue detected via Bandit.
injections, insecure data storage, or improper use of sensitive 
configurations such as hardcoded passwords. Each detected vul-
nerability is linked to a specific CWE identifier for precise cate-
gorization and tracking. When vulnerabilities are detected, they 
are logged with detailed descriptions, including CWE identifiers 
and severity levels. The framework then prompts the LLM to 
revise the code accordingly, aiming to eliminate the detected 
issues while preserving the original functionality. By leveraging 
the functionality of Bandit, the system proactively reduces the 
risk of having security vulnerabilities. Fig. 3 shows an example 
of a security issue identified by Bandit, which serves as a basis 
for the targeted code correction through iterative refinement.
3. Functional Correctness Validation: Ensuring that the code 
performs as intended is crucial for practical deployment. For 
this purpose, the LLM compares the logic of the generated 
code against its associated docstring. The docstring serves as 
a functional specification, and the LLM identifies discrepan-
cies by parsing the described behavior and matching it with 
the implemented logic. To avoid conflicts between functional 
correctness and security, the validation does not enforce exact 
implementation details. Rather, it considers the code correct as 
long as it achieves the same intended behavior, even if different 
libraries or algorithms are used to improve security or perfor-
mance. For instance, if the docstring indicates that the function 
Knowledge-Based Systems 342 (2026) 115925 
5 
J. Lee et al.
retrieves user data from a database, but the implemented code 
contains only a placeholder and no actual database queries, the 
framework will flag this discrepancy during validation. Then, 
the LLM autonomously modifies the code to align it with the 
specified requirements. This step validates functional correctness 
and improves adherence to the intended design and usability 
standards.
4.1.3. Feedback aggregation and formatting
If any issues are detected during the validation stage, the findings 
from Pylint, Bandit, and the functional correctness check are collected 
and formatted into a structured feedback report. To ensure clarity, this 
feedback report is formatted as a structured natural language prompt 
using XML-like markup tags, such as <Code>, <PylintIssues>. This 
report typically includes:
1. The specific tool that flagged the issue.
2. The code snippet containing the issue.
3. An explanation of the issue, as provided by the tool or the LLM.
This structured markup explicitly separates the current code im-
plementation from the raw error messages. This provides the LLM 
with unambiguous context and strict formatting rules. This approach 
is crucial for effectively guiding the LLM in the refinement step.
4.1.4. Iterative code refinement
If any issues are identified, the aggregated feedback is sent back to 
the LLM along with the original prompt and the current (flawed) code 
version. The LLM is then instructed to revise the code to specifically 
address the reported issues while preserving the original docstring 
and intended functionality. This generate-validate-refine cycle repeats 
iteratively. The loop terminates under one of the following conditions:
1. All the validation steps (syntax, security, and functional correct-
ness) are passed successfully.
2. A predefined maximum number of iterations is reached.
This iterative process enables the framework to improve the code 
progressively. The final output of this stage is either a validated code 
snippet or the best version achieved within the iteration limit.
In our experiments, the maximum number of iterations was em-
pirically set to five. This is because preliminary tests showed that 
most correctable syntax errors and security vulnerabilities were re-
solved within three to four iterations. Our experiment results that 
are presented later in the paper further support this statement, since 
we observed no changes in the cumulative percentage of secure code 
snippets between four and five iterations (see Fig. 8). Consequently, 
setting the iteration limit to five is enough to accommodate functional 
corrections, while ensuring the LLM does not enter an infinite loop. This 
decision also ensures the frameworkâ€™s overall efficiency and minimizes 
LLM API costs.
4.2. Stage 2: LLM fine-tuning
Although the validation pipeline effectively corrects issues, the 
second stage of the framework proactively enhances the LLMâ€™s ability 
to generate secure code snippets through fine-tuning. This process 
involves dataset preparation, model training, and integration.
4.2.1. Dataset preparation and model training
A key innovation of our framework is that the fine-tuning dataset is 
constructed without expert intervention using the outputs from Stage 
1. Thus, rather than relying on manual dataset construction, our frame-
work automatically generates the fine-tuning dataset by pairing each 
input prompt with the code produced after a comprehensive validation 
and refinement pipeline. Only code that passes all automated checks is 
included in the final dataset for supervised fine-tuning. This approach 
Fig. 4. Example of a natural language prompt from the LLMSecEval dataset.
greatly reduces the manual effort typically required, and also improves 
the quality and reproducibility of dataset preparation.
The general supervised fine-tuning approach utilizes prompt and 
code pairs. To evaluate different fine-tuning strategies, we constructed 
two distinct datasets with input prompts from the LLMSecEval dataset. 
These prompts were paired with two types of target source code: (1) 
framework-refined code, which is automatically generated optimized 
code produced after our Stage 1 validation pipeline with docstrings 
excluded, and (2) expert-written secure code, consisting of manually 
written secure code examples provided in the dataset.
4.2.2. Integration and evaluation
The fine-tuned models can then be integrated back into Stage 1, 
replacing the baseline LLM. We hypothesize that the fine-tuned models 
will generate higher-quality initial code, improving the efficiency and 
effectiveness of the overall framework. The evaluation of the com-
parative performance of the baseline and fine-tuned models will be 
presented in Section 6.
5. Experiment setup
This section introduces the experiment setup, including the datasets 
and LLMs used, as well as the evaluation metrics. Specifically, we 
evaluated Stage 1 of the framework using Experiment #1, and Stage 
2 using Experiment #2.
5.1. Datasets
In our experiments, we utilized two datasets, which are described 
below.
LLMSecEval:. The LLMSecEval dataset [13] is used in both experi-
ments. This dataset is specifically designed to evaluate the security 
and robustness of LLM-generated code. This dataset is based on the 
MITRE CWE Top 25 Most Dangerous Software Weaknesses and covers 
21 distinct CWE categories. These categories include common issues, 
such as buffer overflows (CWE-120), command injection (CWE-77), 
and improper input validation (CWE-20). The dataset contains 150 
carefully designed natural language prompts, each of which is crafted 
to induce specific coding vulnerabilities in Python when processed by 
LLMs. These prompts simulate real-world development scenarios in 
which insecure code may be generated inadvertently.
Each prompt is accompanied by multiple secure reference imple-
mentations written by domain experts to provide ground truth ex-
amples as a reference. The dataset enables precise benchmarking of 
code quality in terms of vulnerability presence, syntax correctness, 
and functional behavior. This makes it a comprehensive resource for 
evaluating security-oriented LLM applications (see Fig. 4).
SecurityEval:. For Experiment #2, we used the SecurityEval dataset
[14], which covers a broader and more diverse set of security-sensitive 
tasks. Unlike LLMSecEval, SecurityEval targets various vulnerability 
types beyond the MITRE Top 25 and is designed to challenge the 
generalization capabilities of LLMs. The dataset consists of 121 natural 
language prompts that span 69 distinct CWE categories, offering wide 
coverage across both common and less frequently addressed vulnerabil-
ities. We adopted SecurityEval for Experiment #2 because the models 
Knowledge-Based Systems 342 (2026) 115925 
6 
J. Lee et al.
Fig. 5. Example of a natural language prompt from the SecurityEval dataset.
being evaluated were fine-tuned based on the output of Experiment 
#1, and a new dataset was necessary to avoid overfitting and assess 
generalization performance (see Fig. 5).
5.2. LLM configurations
We used different LLM models in each experiment, as explained 
next.
Baseline Model (Experiment #1):. In this research, we adopted GPT-
4o for both code generation and validation tasks. Although the LLM-
SecEval dataset was originally evaluated using a GPT-3 based model 
(code-davinci-002, now discontinued), we upgraded to GPT-4o to lever-
age its performance and versatility. Its contextual understanding and 
iterative refinement capabilities make it exceptionally well-suited for 
our framework, enabling the generation of secure, functional, and high-
quality Python code that robustly addresses diverse vulnerabilities.
Baseline and Fine-Tuned Models (Experiment #2):. In Experiment 
#2, we evaluated three model variants:
1. Baseline: A basic GPT-4o model, used as a baseline for compar-
ison.
2. Fine-Tuned Model Using Expert Examples: GPT-4o that has 
been fine-tuned using expert-written secure code examples from 
the LLMSecEval dataset.
3. Fine-Tuned Model Using Framework Output: GPT-4o is fine-
tuned using the framework-refined code produced through our 
validation pipeline in Experiment #1 using LLMSecEval.
We executed our full framework five times for each model, produc-
ing five sets of code outputs before and after refinement.
5.3. SAST tool version
To ensure the reproducibility of our results, we report here the 
version of each SAST tool used in our experiments. Thus, Pylint v3.3.7 
was employed for syntax validation, and Bandit v1.8.3 for security 
vulnerability detection throughout all our experiments. We note that 
these were the latest stable releases available for the two tools at the 
time the experiments were conducted.
5.4. Evaluation metrics
We used multiple evaluation criteria to assess the models compre-
hensively. In all cases, the iterative refinement process was performed 
with a maximum limit of five iterations.
Syntax Errors:. We adopted Pylint to detect syntax errors in the 
generated code, not for PEP-8 style checks.
Vulnerabilities:. We chose Bandit to identify security vulnerabilities 
according to CWE categories. We focus on the number of detected 
vulnerabilities and their resolution rates after refinement.
Functional Correctness:. First, we manually evaluated functional cor-
rectness by inspecting whether the code accurately implements the 
intended functionality described in the prompt and the embedded 
docstring.
Additionally, we evaluated the quality of the generated code using 
three advanced metrics:
1. CodeBLEU: This metric measures syntactic and semantic simi-
larity based on n-gram matching, AST structure similarity, and 
data flow consistency [8].
2. CodeBERTScore: It uses transformer-based contextual embed-
dings to assess semantic alignment between the generated code 
and the Ref. [9].
3. ICE-SCORE: It evaluates how well the generated code com-
plies with the given instructions and its likelihood of being 
executable, using an LLM-based review system. It uses two sep-
arate 0â€“4 scales to independently assess usefulness (how helpful 
the code is for solving the task) and functional correctness 
(how accurately the code implements the intended behavior) 
independently [38].
6. Experiment results and analysis
This section presents the results of our experiments, analyzing the 
performance of the three model configurations in generating secure 
Python code. We examined vulnerability detection and resolution, code 
quality metrics, and the effectiveness of our fine-tuning methodology.
6.1. Experiment #1: Code generation & validation and refinement results
The Experiment #1 was evaluated using 150 Python code snippets, 
each of which was generated using prompts from the LLMSecEval 
dataset. These prompts are designed to test an LLMâ€™s ability to handle 
security-sensitive tasks aligned with CWE categories.
6.1.1. Syntax error validation
No syntax errors were detected in any of the 150 Python code 
snippets generated during Experiment #1 of our framework evaluation. 
While preliminary experiments using earlier versions of LLMs had 
occasionally resulted in syntax issues such as indentation errors or 
missing delimiters, all code generated using the GPT-4o model in this 
study passed syntax validation on the first attempt. This suggests that 
GPT-4o is capable of producing syntactically correct Python code when 
guided by a well-structured prompt and docstring.
6.1.2. Vulnerability validation
During the vulnerability validation phase, a total of 64 code snippets 
with vulnerabilities were detected in the initial code generated from 
the LLMSecEval dataset. After the iterative refinement process, this 
number decreased to 11, corresponding to an 82.8% resolution rate, 
as shown in Fig. 6(a). This result highlights the effectiveness of our 
validation framework in addressing the majority of security issues 
through automated feedback and code correction.
Our analysis showed that the unresolved CWE-78 vulnerabilities 
after iterative refinement were primarily caused by the use of the 
subprocess module in Python. This module is often used to execute 
shell commands and introduces risks when user inputs are directly 
concatenated into commands. Although Bandit flagged the use of the 
subprocess module with warnings, the framework failed to effectively 
address these vulnerabilities effectively by enforcing strict validation of 
user inputs. The lack of input sanitization allowed these security issues 
to persist, underscoring the critical importance of incorporating com-
prehensive input validation mechanisms to mitigate risks associated 
with shell command execution.
Banditâ€™s analysis of secure code examples written by experts from 
LLMSecEval revealed similar CWE-78 issues when the subprocess mod-
ule was used. In these instances, the same errors were flagged in the

limitations of current strategies in addressing CWE-78 issues involving 
the subprocess module.
6.1.3. Functional correctness validation
As shown in Fig. 6(b), among the 150 code snippets generated 
and evaluated, the LLM itself identified 7 cases with potential func-
tional correctness issues during the iterative validation process due to 
inconsistencies between the implemented logic and the correspond-
ing docstring. This represents 4.7% of the total. This self-diagnosis 
mechanism demonstrates the modelâ€™s ability to reason about its own 
outputs through prompt-guided validation. Notably, codes with issues 
were successfully resolved through iterative refinement within several 
feedback iterations. This demonstrates that the framework effectively 
detects subtle discrepancies and autonomously resolves most of them 
without external feedback.
The types of issues detected by the LLM included missing essential 
module imports, the need for improved input handling to enhance func-
tionality, and using more appropriate modules instead of suboptimal 
choices. In each case, the LLM attempted to revise the implementation 
to better align with the requirements stated in the docstring. These 
findings underscore the effectiveness of our approach in identifying 
and incrementally improving code quality based on explicit functional 
specifications.
6.1.4. Quantitative results using code-level metrics
Additionally, we conducted a quantitative evaluation using three 
code-level metrics.
CodeBLEU Evaluation:. To evaluate the impact of the code validation 
& refinement stage further, we compared the CodeBLEU scores of 
code snippets. We conducted the comparison across three categories: 
initial code generated before the iterative refinement process, refined 
code after completing the iterative refinement process, and secure code 
examples from the LLMSecEval dataset, which served as benchmarks.
As shown in Table 2, the CodeBLEU score improved slightly after 
the iterative refinement process. A notable increase was observed in

Although the overall CodeBLEU scores were relatively low, this can

resulting in high-quality reference implementations. In contrast, our 
framework generates code based on GPT-4o, which may introduce 
architectural and stylistic differences, including library choices and 
error-handling patterns. Therefore, it is difficult for framework gener-
ated code to achieve a high overlap with these expert-crafted samples, 
especially under reference-based metrics such as CodeBLEU that reward 
superficial form similarity.
Therefore, fine-tuning the model directly on expert-written code 
that follows different structural conventions than the target modelâ€™s 
native generation distribution may limit the modelâ€™s ability to adapt 
effectively and may result in unexpected behaviors, such as incomplete 
outputs or inconsistencies in the generated code.

the refinement process enhances certain aspects of code quality, it 
primarily preserves the original structure, making only minor, targeted

Furthermore, a manual review comparing the refined and initial

functionalities, such as enhanced validation mechanisms, improved 
robustness, and more comprehensive input handling. Importantly, even 
after the code validation experiment, the refined code snippets retained 
a level of functional and semantic consistency comparable to that 
of expert-designed secure code examples while offering capabilities 
beyond those included in the examples.
While this finding underscores the strength of LLMs in applying 
precise and minimal edits during refinement, it also aligns with the 
limitations discussed in Section 6.1.2. Specifically, the frameworkâ€™s 
tendency to preserve the original code structure may contribute to its 
inability to resolve deeply embedded or architectural security issues, 
such as those observed in unresolved CWE-78 cases. These results 
highlight a key trade-off in the refinement process: balancing minimal 
intervention with the need for comprehensive structural transformation 
when necessary.
ICE-SCORE evaluation:. To assess how well each code variant fulfilled 
the instructional intent conveyed through the input prompts, ICE-
SCORE metrics were employed on both the initial and final codes across 
the full set of 150 code snippets.
As shown in Table 4, both the initial and final codes achieved 
nearly perfect scores, with only a very slight decrease observed after 
refinement. This suggests that, although iterative refinement involved 
additional actions, such as patching vulnerabilities or adding exception 
handling, these modifications did not adversely affect the codeâ€™s overall 
alignment with the original prompt or its usefulness.
Overall, our quantitative results demonstrate that the refinement 
process addressed security concerns and enhanced robustness without 
compromising the intended functionality or instructional fidelity of the 
code outputs.
However, these results also highlight an important limitation: exist-
ing evaluation metrics alone cannot fully capture the effectiveness of 
our framework. While improvements are observable in standard code-
level metrics, current quantitative measures may not fully reflect some 
nuanced aspects of security, code robustness, and instruction align-
ment. Therefore, more comprehensive or specialized evaluation metrics 
are needed to accurately assess the broader benefits and subtleties of 
our approach.
6.2. Experiment #2: Fine-tuning results
Experiment #2 investigates the effectiveness of fine-tuned LLMs 
that use different training sources to improve the intrinsic security and 
quality of generated Python code. While Experiment #1 validated the 
performance of an unmodified GPT-4o model using the LLMSecEval 
dataset, Experiment #2 employs both the LLMSecEval and SecurityEval 
datasets for evaluation. The LLMSecEval dataset continues to play a key 
role because the outputs generated from it in Experiment #1 also serve 
as one of the fine-tuning sources.
To mitigate the potential overfitting to the LLMSecEval dataset, 
SecurityEval is also utilized. SecurityEval provides a broader and more 
diverse set of prompts designed to expose security flaws across a 
wide range of vulnerability types. This ensures that the evaluation 
results reflect the modelsâ€™ ability to generalize beyond the patterns 
present in the fine-tuning data. For each dataset, code generation and 
iterative validation refinement were performed up to five times, in 
accordance with the methodology of our framework. This approach 
enables a systematic and fair comparison of model performance across 
both benchmarks.
Three models are compared: the baseline GPT-4o model, a variant 
fine-tuned on expert-written secure code examples, and a model fine-
tuned on the outputs of our own validation framework. Through this 
evaluation, we aim to determine which training strategy better equips 
LLMs to produce secure, functional, and high-quality code without 
relying solely on post-generation refinement mechanisms.
6.2.1. Syntax error validation
Across the LLMSecEval and SecurityEval datasets, each prompt was 
subjected to up to five rounds of iterative validation and refinement af-
ter code generation. As discussed in Section 6.1.1, modern LLMs rarely 
produce syntactically invalid Python code. In our evaluation, only two 
code snippets with syntax errors were identified among the initial 
outputs of the SecurityEval dataset. These errors were promptly de-
tected and corrected by the frameworkâ€™s integrated validation pipeline. 
Incorporating systematic syntax checking as an initial step ensures that 
our framework preemptively addresses even rare or minor syntactic 
mistakes, thus enhancing the reliability of downstream security and 
functional validation. This approach further reduces the likelihood that 
such issues will propagate in automated code-generation workflows.
6.2.2. Vulnerability validation
The vulnerability validation experiment assessed the number and 
proportion of code snippets containing security flaws before and after 
iterative refinement, as detected by Bandit. Fig. 7 summarizes the 
results for both the LLMSecEval (150 code snippets) and SecurityEval 
(121 code snippets) datasets.
For LLMSecEval, the baseline GPT-4o model initially generated code 
with security vulnerabilities in an average of 65.4 out of 150 snippets 
(43.6%), while the expert-tuned model produced 82.0 vulnerable snip-
pets (54.7%). The framework-tuned model produced an average of only 
27.6 (18.4%) vulnerable code snippets. After five refinement cycles, 
these numbers decreased substantially: the baseline GPT-4o model 
averaged 11.4 (7.6%) residual vulnerable code snippets; the expert-
tuned model averaged 22.0 (14.7%) residual vulnerable code snippets; 
and the framework-tuned model averaged 10.0 (6.7%) residual vulner-
able code snippets. Notably, the framework-tuned model produced the 
fewest security flaws before and after the iterative validation process.

A similar trend was observed with the SecurityEval dataset. Initially, 
the baseline GPT-4o, expert-tuned, and framework-tuned models pro-
duced an average of 74.0 (61.2%), 41.2 (34.1%), and 42.6 (35.2%) vul-
nerable code snippets, respectively, out of 121 total samples. After re-
finement, these numbers decreased to 5.0 (4.1%) for the baseline GPT-
4o model, 11.0 (9.1%) for the expert-tuned model, and 4.2 (3.5%) for 
the framework-tuned model. Once again, the framework-tuned model 
produced the fewest residual vulnerable code snippets, demonstrat-
ing the self-refinement approachâ€™s effectiveness in minimizing security 
issues.
Fig. 8 shows, for each model, the cumulative percentage of code 
snippets that are free of vulnerabilities after each refinement iteration. 
At iteration 0, the percentage represents the proportion of secure code 
in the initial code generation. With each refinement, this percentage in-
creases as more vulnerabilities are resolved, until it eventually plateaus 
when no further improvements can be made.
For example, the framework-finetuned model in SecurityEval starts 
with 64.9% secure code snippets at iteration 0 and quickly rises to 
95.2% after one refinement. It reaches 96.2% by iteration 2 and re-
mains stable thereafter. The baseline model begins with a lower pro-
portion of secure code (38.6%), but it also reaches a similar final 
level (96.7%) after five iterations. The expert-fine-tuned model begins 
with 63.6% secure code snippets and gradually climbs to 92.0%. These 
results demonstrate that the framework-fine-tuned model generates 
more secure code from the beginning and achieves a high level of 
security with fewer refinement iterations than the other models. This 
highlights the efficiency and effectiveness of our framework.
Overall, the validation framework is an effective fine-tuning strat-
egy that enables LLMs to generate more secure code with fewer it-
erations without relying on expert-written examples. Although the 
expert-tuned model was trained on curated data from security pro-
fessionals, it required more revisions and left more vulnerabilities 
unresolved. In contrast, the framework-fine-tuned model learns from 
its own refinement process, proactively reducing vulnerabilities before 
validation.
This approach simplifies fine-tuning, making it a scalable, low-cost 
process that minimizes human involvement. The results suggest that 
self-refinement via automated validation is a practical, competitive 
alternative to expert-guided fine-tuning. It achieves comparable or 
superior outcomes without manual dataset construction.
6.2.3. Functional correctness validation
Fig. 9 presents the number and percentage of code snippets with 
functional correctness issues at any point during the initial or re-
finement stages (â€˜â€˜Initial/Refined Codeâ€™â€™), as well as those with such 
issues in the final output (â€˜â€˜Final Codeâ€™â€™), for both LLMSecEval and 
SecurityEval datasets, for each model.
For LLMSecEval (150 code snippets), the baseline model exhibited 
functional correctness errors in 8.2 cases (5.5%) during the initial or 
refinement stages, with only 1.2 cases (0.8%) remaining in the final 
output. The framework-tuned model triggered functional correctness 
errors in 21.8 cases (14.5%) during validation and refinement, however 
this number was decreased to just 0.4 cases (0.3%) in the final output, 
demonstrating strong self-correction capability. In contrast, the expert-
tuned model exhibited a much higher number of functional correctness 
failures during validation and refinement (126.8 cases, 84.5%), and 
118.4 cases (78.9%) still had errors in the final output, indicating little 
improvement.
Manual review revealed that the high number of incorrect code 
snippets for the expert-tuned model was largely due to its tendency 
to generate incomplete or partially implemented code. This resulted 
in frequent detection of functional errors throughout the validation 
process, with many issues persisting in the final output.
For LLMSecEval, we found that 14 of the initial/refined code snip-
pets generated by the framework-tuned model (9.3% of the total 150 
samples) had functional correctness issues due to missing import state-
ments for required libraries or modules. This issue frequently arose 
when the fine-tuned model employed distinct or more secure libraries 
than the GPT-4o model yet neglected to incorporate the requisite 
import statements. These cases represented a significant proportion of 
the overall functional correctness issues identified during the initial 
and refinement stages. Fortunately, these errors were easily resolved 
during the refinement process by automatically adding the missing 
import lines. We suspect that this pattern may be related to overfitting

on code outputs from prior LLMs, repeatedly generated incomplete 
or underspecified solutions. This resulted in persistent errors, even 
after several feedback cycles. Manual inspection suggests that, with 
validation-guided refinement, the framework-tuned model can reliably 
address prompt requirements, quickly correcting errors as they arise 
and converging on correct outputs with fewer remaining failures.
7. Discussion
This section summarizes the main limitations of our framework and 
outlines directions for future work.
7.1. Limitations in functional correctness evaluation
Current metrics like CodeBLEU, CodeBERTScore, and ICE-Score 
mainly measure similarity to reference code, so they do not always 
capture true functional correctness. These metrics may penalize useful 
improvements that are not specified in the prompt. Thus, these scores 
do not accurately reflect the actual quality of LLM-generated code.
Our evaluation relies on static analysis and similarity rather than 
comprehensive test cases. While creating exhaustive tests would be 
more accurate, it is time-consuming and difficult to scale. Current 
methods also miss some semantic correctness issues, especially when

there are multiple valid solutions. Advanced methods, such as formal 
verification, could help but are difficult to apply broadly. Improved 
evaluation approaches combining static analysis, dynamic testing, and 
semantic checks are needed.
7.2. Static analysis limitations
Our framework uses SAST tools to detect errors and security is-
sues. This is an improvement over typical LLM-only approaches [26]. 
However, these tools do not always consider the entire code context, 
which can result in false positives and false negatives during analysis, 
as discussed in [40,41]. In practice, it is generally observed that static 
analysis tools can trigger unnecessary code modifications, while still 
missing certain vulnerabilities due to false positives and negatives. 
Previous research [42] has demonstrated that using multiple SAST tools 
can enhance detection accuracy and coverage, thereby reducing false 
positives and negatives. To address these issues, we plan to incorporate 
a broader range of SAST tools in the future.
7.3. Scalability beyond benchmarks and generalizability
The effectiveness of fine-tuning depends on the diversity and cov-
erage of the training dataset. Although LLMSecEval and SecurityEval 
provide a wide variety of security-related programming tasks, they 
do not fully represent all real-world or domain-specific scenarios. To 
ensure robustness as new security threats emerge, it will be essential 
to continuously expand the training and evaluation data with relevant, 
up-to-date examples. In addition, the availability of large, high-quality 
security datasets remains limited; therefore, we also plan to build more 
diverse, custom datasets for future LLM training.
Moreover, the current implementation and evaluation of CodeEn-
hancer are limited to standalone Python snippets. In practice, software 
systems are often substantially more complex than isolated code snip-
pets and may involve larger codebases, richer dependencies, and other 
programming languages. As a result, the generalizability of our frame-
work to more complex real-world projects and other languages remains 
unproven. Future work will focus on extending the framework to 
handle such complexity and language-specific integrations of SAST 
tools.
7.4. Fine-tuning data issues
As discussed in Section 6.2.3, the expert-tuned model exhibited 
substantially lower functional correctness and frequently generated 
incomplete implementations. We acknowledge that this outcome raises 
a potential concern about comparison bias: expert-written secure ref-
erence implementations may not always align with the structural con-
ventions and output style that the target base model (GPT-4o) naturally 
tends to generate. Even when both solutions are correct and secure, 
they may differ in aspects such as library usage, abstraction level, and 
error-handling granularity.
This mismatch can be amplified during supervised fine-tuning and 
may lead to degraded behaviors, including incomplete or underspeci-
fied code generation, as observed in our experiments. While this repre-
sents a limitation in directly leveraging static expert corpora for fine-
tuning rapidly evolving foundation models, it also motivates a practical 
strength of our approach. In CodeEnhancer, the framework-refined 
fine-tuning data is automatically derived from the target modelâ€™s own 
outputs after iterative validation, producing training targets that are 
more consistent with the target modelâ€™s preferred output format, while 
still satisfying the security and functional checks. As a result, the 
framework-refined data provides a scalable and adaptable fine-tuning 
pathway that reduces reliance on distribution-sensitive external refer-
ence implementations.
Nevertheless, we observed occasional behavioral anomalies in the 
intermediate outputs of the framework-tuned model that were intro-
duced during fine-tuning. These anomalies included missing import 
statements, which compromised executability even when the intended 
logic was correct. These anomalies underscore the influence of fine-
tuning data on generation behavior and suggest that, in practical 
deployments, fully autonomous code generation may still benefit from 
a lightweight human-in-the-loop review.
As a solution, in future work we will attempt to resolve these 
anomalies by integrating static dependency checks into the fine-tuning 
data preparation pipeline.
8. Conclusion
In this paper, we introduced CodeEnhancer, a unified framework 
for enhancing the security and quality of Python code generated by 
Knowledge-Based Systems 342 (2026) 115925 
12 
J. Lee et al.
LLMs. Our two-stage approach combines real-time validation with tar-
geted fine-tuning to address syntax errors, security vulnerabilities, and 
functional correctness within a single pipeline.
The validation pipeline applied to the baseline GPT-4o model re-
moved 82.8% of vulnerabilities and resolved all functional correctness 
issues in the first stage.
In the second stage, we fine-tuned the LLM using both expert-
written and framework-refined code. The framework-tuned model
achieved the lowest vulnerability rates consistently among all models. 
For instance, on the LLMSecEval dataset, the proportion of vulnerable 
code was decreased from 43.6% for baseline GPT-4o-generated code to 
18.4% before refinement and further to 6.7% after refinement. On the 
SecurityEval dataset, vulnerability rates decreased from 61.2% for the 
GPT-4o baseline model to 35.2% before refinement and to 3.5% after 
refinement. Similar trends were observed for functional correctness.
Importantly, the framework-tuned model consistently outperformed 
the expert-tuned model in Experiment #2, achieving lower vulner-
ability rates and higher functional correctness on both benchmark 
datasets. These results highlight the effectiveness of automated self-
refinement and suggest that high-quality self-generated data may be 
more beneficial for fine-tuning than relying solely on expert-written 
code.
Despite these improvements, limitations remain. Current metrics do 
not fully capture functional equivalence, static analysis cannot assess 
semantic correctness, and datasets may not cover all programming do-
mains or new security threats. Addressing these challenges will require 
broader, continually updated datasets and better evaluation methods.
As future work, we plan to integrate more static and dynamic analy-
sis tools, adopt advanced fine-tuning strategies, and test the framework 
in real-world development settings. These steps are necessary to in-
crease coverage further, keep pace with evolving security practices, and 
better assess the practical reliability of AI-generated code.
As LLMs become central to software development workflows, gen-
erating secure and correct code is critical. Our proposed framework is 
a significant step toward that objective. It demonstrates that combin-
ing LLMs with static analysis and purpose-driven fine-tuning substan-
tially increases the trustworthiness and reliability of AI-assisted coding 
systems.

Enhancing Software Code Vulnerability Detection Using GPT-4o
and Claude-3.5 Sonnet: A Study on Prompt
Engineering Techniques
Jaehyeon Bae â€ 
, Seoryeong Kwon â€ 
and Seunghwan Myeong *
Department of Industrial Security Governance, Inha University, Michuhol-gu, Incheon 22212, Republic of Korea;
qhrtnddkzos@inha.edu (J.B.); w.dynamic14@inha.edu (S.K.)
* Correspondence: shmyeong@inha.ac.kr
â€  These authors contributed equally to this work.
Abstract: This study investigates the efficacy of advanced large language models, specifically
GPT-4o, Claude-3.5 Sonnet, and GPT-3.5 Turbo, in detecting software vulnerabilities. Our exper-
iment utilized vulnerable and secure code samples from the NIST Software Assurance Reference
Dataset (SARD), focusing on C++, Java, and Python. We employed three distinct prompting tech-
niques as follows: Concise, Tip Setting, and Step-by-Step. The results demonstrate that GPT-4o
and Claude-3.5 Sonnet significantly outperform GPT-3.5 Turbo in vulnerability detection. GPT-4o
showed the highest improvement with the Step-by-Step prompt, achieving an F1 score of 0.9072.
Claude-3.5 Sonnet exhibited consistent high performance across all prompt types, with its Step-by-
Step prompt yielding the best overall results (F1 score: 0.8933, AUC: 0.74). In contrast, GPT-3.5 Turbo
showed minimal performance changes across prompts, with the Tip Setting prompt performing best
(AUC: 0.65, F1 score: 0.6772), yet significantly lower than the other models. Our findings highlight
the potential of advanced models in enhancing software security and underscore the importance of
prompt engineering in optimizing their performance.
Keywords: GPT; prompt learning; prompt engineering; software security; information security;
vulnerability detection; Claude-3.5
1. Introduction
The Fourth Industrial Revolution has brought various opportunities and increased con-
cerns about cyberattacks [1]. The convergence of physical and cyberspace through Industry
4.0 has created many vulnerabilities, making us more susceptible to cyberattacks [2]. While
big data and IoT technologies have brought many conveniences, they have also introduced
numerous challenges [3,4]. As a result, the Fourth Industrial Revolution has increased
access to cyberspace, leading to an exponential rise in internet usage [5]. Furthermore,
COVID-19 has accelerated the growth of internet usage by shifting academic, professional,
and personal activities to cyberspace [6â€“8], which has also heightened security concerns
in cyberspace [5]. This trend is confirmed by the Internet Crime Complaint Centerâ€™s 2023
Internet Crime Report [9]. The number of reported cybercrime incidents and associated
losses have steadily increased from 2018 to 2023, with a significant spike in reports in 2020
following the surge in internet usage due to COVID-19. This trend is illustrated in Figure 1.
Various information security technologies have emerged to address the increasing
threats in cyberspace [10]. New technologies such as machine learning and blockchain
have also begun to be applied to information security [11,12]. ChatGPT has recently gained
attention and brought about a significant technological change. The role of ChatGPT has
evolved to the point where it can assist information security officers [13,14].
The automated detection of software vulnerabilities is a fundamental issue in software
security. It has recently become a major topic due to the growing interest in deep learning-
Electronics 2024, 13, 2657. https://doi.org/10.3390/electronics13132657
https://www.mdpi.com/journal/electronics
Electronics 2024, 13, 2657
2 of 16
based vulnerability detection techniques [15]. Therefore, in this study, we explore the
feasibility of detecting vulnerabilities in software code using GPT-3.5 Turbo, GPT-4o, and
Claude-3.5 Sonnet. The primary goal is to examine how GPT-4o improves detection capabil-
ities over GPT-3.5 Turbo and how Claude-3.5 Sonnet compares with GPT-4o. Additionally,
based on the work of Bsharat, Myrzakhan, and Shen (2023) [16], we investigate whether
simple prompting tweaks can enhance detection performance. We aim to demonstrate that
if GPT and Claude models can detect vulnerabilities in code, they can be used to identify
and rectify vulnerabilities without relying on time-consuming and expensive vulnerability
detection tools. Furthermore, GPT-4o has a faster processing time than GPT-4 Turbo, the
latest version of GPT-4, while delivering performance as good as or better than GPT-4
Turbo [17,18]. Given that the cost of using GPT-4o is half that of GPT-4 Turbo, if GPT-4o
demonstrates superior performance in detecting code vulnerabilities, it could be utilized as
a cost-effective vulnerability detection tool. Claude-3.5 Sonnet also has a faster processing
time and better performance than GPT-4 Turbo, with costs half those of GPT-4 Turbo [19,20].
Therefore, if GPT-4o and Claude-3.5 Sonnet both demonstrate superior performance in de-
tecting code vulnerabilities, they could be utilized as cost-effective vulnerability detection
tools. The API costs and context windows of GPT-4o, GPT-4 Turbo, GPT-3.5 Turbo, and
Claude-3.5 Sonnet are summarized in Table 1.

2. Theoretical Background
2.1. Large Language Models and GPT
Vaswani et al. (2017) proposed the Transformer, a novel AI learning model architecture
that relies entirely on attention mechanisms [21]. It enables more parallelization, achieving
new highs in translation quality with only 12 h of training on 8 P100 GPUs. Super-scale lan-
guage models, which are language models with large parameter sizes, are generated based
on the Transformer [22]. These large-scale language models have produced revolutionary
results in solving a wide range of natural language understanding and generation tasks.
They are now the de facto standard for most natural language processing tasks.
Electronics 2024, 13, 2657
3 of 16
The first large-scale language model developed by OpenAI was GPT-3. GPT-4 is
the fourth model in the GPT language model series developed by OpenAI, following
GPT-3.5, which was a fine-tuning of GPT-3. GPT-4 can handle 32,768 tokens, eight times the
4096 tokens of GPT-3.5. To put this in perspective, GPT-4 can process about 25,000 English
words. The GPT model is based on the Transformer architecture. This architecture has
several weights and biases used to process text and generate a prediction of the next
word. These weights and biases are the parameters of the GPT model. The number of
parameters in a GPT model represents its ability to learn more complex language patterns
and structures.
For this reason, the number of parameters is an important indicator of a modelâ€™s
performance and learning ability. GPT-3 models have 175 billion parameters. The number of
parameters in GPT-4 models is a trade secret and is not publicly available. Instead, OpenAI
has published evaluation results from running benchmarks based on GPT-4 and GPT-
3.5 [17]. On 9 April 2024, OpenAI announced GPT-4 Turbo, which increased the number
of tokens that can be processed at once to 128k, and, on May 13, 2024, OpenAI released
GPT-4o, an improved version of GPT-4. GPT-4o improved the response time to 0.23 s by
switching to speech-to-speech instead of text-to-speech, and improved tokenization for
languages other than English, reducing the number of tokens used from about 1.1x to about
4.4x, significantly speeding up the processing of languages [18]. The reduction in tokens
allows GPT-4o to be about twice as fast as GPT-4 Turbo but at half the price, and the speed
limit can be improved by a factor of five. GPT-4o can now recognize and describe images
and videos in real time, with appropriate changes in the tone of voice. The benchmark
results for GPT-4o are published on OpenAIâ€™s website [18], and a reconstructed table of the
benchmark results for GPT-3.5, GPT-4, GPT-4 Turbo, and GPT-4o is shown in Table 2.

The shots at the bottom of the evaluation results refer to examples given to the model
before performing a specific task. A 0-SHOT means that the model is not given an example
of a questionâ€“answer pair, and is asked to generate an answer to the question based on its
previously learned knowledge. For one or more shots, the model is provided with that
number of questionâ€“answer pairs and asked to generate answers to new questions based
on them. When we look at the benchmark results for GPT-4, we see improvements over
GPT-3.5 in all areas. In particular, we see a significant improvement in handling math
questions. OpenAI translated the MMLU benchmarks into various languages using Azure
Translate and found that most of the languages tested, including low-resource languages
like Swahili and Welsh, outperformed GPT-3.5â€™s English performance [17]. For GPT-4o, we
achieved GPT-4 Turbo-level performance in text, inference, and coding intelligence, while
reaching new highs in multilingual, audio, and vision capabilities.

2.2. Comparison of Claude-3.5 Sonnet and GPT-4o
Claude-3.5 Sonnet, developed by Anthropic, is a state-of-the-art large language model
that competes directly with OpenAIâ€™s GPT-4o. Anthropicâ€™s first conversational AI, Claude-
1, included 52 billion parameters. Alongside this, they released a lightweight version called
Claude-1 Instant, which charged USD 1.63 per million tokens. In July 2023, they introduced
Claude-2, a new model priced at USD 8 per million tokens, which showed strengths in
coding, complex reasoning, and creative tasks when compared to Claude-1 Instant. In
February 2024, Anthropic announced Claude-3, which outperformed GPT-4, with Claude-3
Opus being superior in writing and multilingual understanding at the time of its release.
The Claude-3 series is divided into Haiku, Sonnet, and Opus, with Haiku having the fastest
output speed, and Opus having the highest output quality.
Claude-3.5 Sonnet, released on 20 June 2024, improved the operational speed and cost
efficiency when compared to Claude-3, operating at twice the speed and at a lower cost than
Claude-3 Opus [19,20]. According to Anthropicâ€™s model description, it has been trained
on data up to April 2024 and outperforms GPT-4o and Gemini 1.5 Pro in various domains.
Notably, in LiveBench, an LLM evaluation sponsored by Abacus.AI and conducted by
teams from New York University, Nvidia, the University of Maryland, and the University of
Southern California, Claude-3.5 Sonnet is rated as the top-performing model [23]. It shows
approximately a 25% better coding performance than GPT-4o, indicating strong potential
in static code analysis for vulnerability detection. Based on the benchmark results released

2.3. Previous Studies on Detecting Code Vulnerabilities through Large Language Models
Recent research has highlighted the potential and limitations of using large language
models (LLMs) like GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 in software vulnerability detection tasks. According
to Fu et al. (2023), while large models such as GPT-4 exhibit significant advancements
with 1.7 trillion parameters, they still face challenges in vulnerability detection tasks when
compared to specialized models like CodeBERT and GraphCodeBERT. Their study showed
that fine-tuned models on specific tasks performed better, indicating that general models
like GPT-4 require fine-tuning to reach optimal performance levels [24].
Another study by LÃ³pez Espejel et al. (2023) focused on GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 perfor-
mance in various tasks, providing insights into how prompt engineering can influence
model performance. The study found that slight modifications to prompts significantly
impacted the quality of the generated outputs, underscoring the importance of an effective
prompt design. It is particularly relevant to vulnerability detection, where precise prompts
could enhance the modelâ€™s ability to identify vulnerabilities accurately [25].
Furthermore, the performance of GPT-4 in various NLP tasks, including vulnerability
detection, has been explored extensively in technical reports. These reports indicate that,
Electronics 2024, 13, 2657
5 of 16
while GPT-4 outperforms its predecessors in many areas, its effectiveness in specialized
tasks like vulnerability detection still depends heavily on the prompt design and fine-
tuning [25]. The research by Bsharat, Myrzakhan, and Shen (2023) demonstrated that
simple prompting strategies could significantly enhance the performance of GPT models
in detecting vulnerabilities. Their work suggests that tailored prompts can leverage the
extensive knowledge embedded in models like GPT-4, making them more effective for
specific tasks [25].
In addition, a study by Ranaldi and Pucci (2024) examined the sycophantic behavior
of LLMs like GPT-4 [26]. Their investigation revealed that LLMs often align their responses
with usersâ€™ beliefs, which can lead to inaccuracies if the user provides misleading prompts.
They highlighted that LLMs perform well in objective tasks, but are susceptible to human
influence in subjective contexts. This finding underscores the importance of fine-tuning
and precise prompt engineering to mitigate biases and improve the reliability of LLMs in
tasks like vulnerability detection.
Sosa et al. (2023) explored the use of NLP models to detect contradictory claims
about COVID-19 drug efficacy in the biomedical literature [27]. They introduced a new
NLI dataset annotated by domain experts and demonstrated the effectiveness of these
models in identifying contradictory claims. The study highlighted the importance of fine-
tuning and curriculum learning, showing that models like PubMedBERT, fine-tuned with a
forward curriculum, achieved the best performance. Their case study on remdesivir and
hydroxychloroquine showcased the modelsâ€™ ability to assist domain experts in managing
large volumes of research and identifying significant contradictions.
The exploration of recent and older LLMs for software vulnerability detection reveals
both these modelsâ€™ potential and limitations. The latest LLMs like GPT-4o and Claude-
3.5 Sonnet show improved capabilities over older versions such as GPT-3.5 and Claude-
3. This study aims to investigate these aspects further, focusing on how GPT-4o and
Claude-3.5 Sonnet can be optimized for cost-effective and efficient vulnerability detection
in software code. These insights form the basis of the current research, which aims to
evaluate the performance of GPT-4o and Claude-3.5 Sonnet and explore the benefits of
prompt engineering in enhancing vulnerability detection capabilities.
3. Experimental Design
3.1. Collection of Vulnerable Code
To experiment, we collected test cases containing vulnerabilities in the code. We specifi-
cally selected cases with vulnerabilities recognized by the Common Weakness Enumeration
(CWE) [28]. The vulnerable code cases used in our experiments are publicly available from
the Software Assurance Reference Dataset (SARD) provided by NIST [29]. In the study,
we prioritized collecting test cases from the SARD with a status of â€˜acceptedâ€™ (thorough
documentation, correct representation of weaknesses, and high quality). For test cases with
a status of â€˜candidateâ€™ (not yet reviewed for completeness and quality), we reviewed the
secure coding guidebook [30,31] before including them in our collection. The collected test
cases were limited to those designated as â€˜badâ€™ (test cases containing clear vulnerabilities
or errors, with detailed documentation on the flaws, including the Common Weakness
Enumeration (CWE) ID, name, file name, and line number where the flaw is located) in the
SARD. We limited the programming languages of the cases collected from SARD to C++,
Java, and Python. A total of 43 cases were collected, and the results are shown in Table 4.

3.3. Data Preprocessing
The code collected from NISTâ€™s SARD was saved in CSV format using Visual Studio
Code. The entire code from the source files containing vulnerable code was imported,
and assigned identification numbers and comments were removed to prevent GPT from
gaining additional information while identifying the vulnerabilities.
We used the GPT-3.5-turbo-0125 API, GPT-4o-2024-05-13 API provided by OpenAI,
and Claude-3-5-Sonnet-240620 API provided by Anthropic, Visual Studio Code 1.91, and
Python 3.12.3, and saved the result list as a results.csv file after receiving the responses from
the APIs. The prompts we used were adapted from the work of Bsharat, Myrzakhan, and
Shen (2023) [14], who used the following prompts which are applicable to conversations
about vulnerability detection: cut to the chase, tip good answers, and give steps to consider.
â€œFind out if the given code has any vulnerabilities. Also, provide the prediction probability
for your assessment.â€ and then adding â€œIâ€™m going to tip $500k for a better solutionâ€ to
the first line and â€œLetâ€™s think step by stepâ€ to the second. The prompts are organized
as follows.
â€¢
First prompt (default, cut to the chase): Please evaluate if the above code has a CWE-***
vulnerability. Does this code have a CWE-*** vulnerability? (Yes/No). Please rate your
confidence in this answer on a scale from 0 to 100, where 100 means very confident
and 0 means not confident at all.
Electronics 2024, 13, 2657
7 of 16
This prompt will be referred to as the â€˜Concise Promptâ€™.
â€¢
Second prompt (How to set a tip for a good answer): Iâ€™m going to tip $500k for a
better solution. Please evaluate if the above code has a CWE-*** vulnerability. Does
this code have a CWE-*** vulnerability? (Yes/No). Please rate your confidence in this
answer on a scale from 0 to 100, where 100 means very confident and 0 means not
confident at all.
This prompt will be referred to as the â€˜Tip Setting Promptâ€™.
â€¢
Third prompt (a way to encourage you to think in steps): Please evaluate if the above
code has a CWE-*** vulnerability. Does this code have a CWE-*** vulnerability?
(Yes/No). Please rate your confidence in this answer on a scale from 0 to 100, where
100 means very confident and 0 means not confident at all. Letâ€™s think step by step.
This prompt will be referred to as the â€˜Step-by-Step Promptâ€™.

To evaluate the results returned by the API, we compared them using a confusion

In Table 6, a True Positive (TP) is when the code has a vulnerability and is detected
as vulnerable. A True Negative (TN) is when the code is not vulnerable and is correctly
detected as not vulnerable. A False Positive (FP) is when the code does not have a vulnera-
bility but is incorrectly detected as having a vulnerability, and a False Negative (FN) is when
code that does have a vulnerability is incorrectly detected as not having a vulnerability.
Accuracy is the ratio of correctly predicted instances to the total instances, measuring the
overall effectiveness of the model. Precision is the ratio of true positive instances to the sum
of true positive and false positive instances, indicating the accuracy of positive predictions.
Recall is the ratio of true positive instances to the sum of true positive and false negative
instances, measuring the modelâ€™s ability to identify all relevant instances. The F1 score is
the harmonic mean of Precision and Recall, providing a single metric that balances the
trade-off between precision and recall.

Our experiments found that GPT-3.5 Turbo with Think in Steps prompts produced
the least accurate results and the lowest prediction probability. The Set a Tip prompt was
not significantly different from the Straight to the Point prompt in terms of the accuracy of
results, but it had a higher predictive value. The accuracy of the answers decreased as the
number of characters in the entered code increased, with false positives (i.e., it determined
that the code was vulnerable when it was not) in all cases where the code was longer than
3000 characters. Overall, the potential for false positives is high, making it a poor tool for
vulnerability analysis.
