Table 9 indicates that the vulnerability category that receives the highest attendance is related
to Resource vulnerabilities, mentioned in 121 studies. This category primarily involves managing
a systemâ€™s resources, which are created, utilized, and disposed of according to a pre-defined set of
instructions. It is observable that CWE-119 [95, 107, 121] is the most frequent vulnerability type
addressed by the subject studies. This vulnerability occurs when a software system attempts to
access or write to a memory location outside the permitted boundary of the systemâ€™s buffer. The
second most frequent vulnerability type is Null Pointer Dereference (CWE-476), accounting for 13
subject studies. This vulnerability occurs when a program attempts to read or write to a memory
location through a pointer that has not been properly initialized and points to NULL (no valid
memory address).
Validation-related vulnerabilities is the second major family of vulnerability types, covered by 37
subject studies. In this type, the attackers exploit input and output data when they are malformed or
not validated properly. As can be seen, CWE-20 [20, 142] is the most frequent type of vulnerability,
accounting for 13 subject studies. CWE-20 refers to a situation where input validation is not done
properly in software systems, making them vulnerable to attacks by malicious individuals who
can exploit input data. This occurs when the input data is not verified to be safe or in line with the
pre-defined specifications. CWE-78 is the second major vulnerability type, covered by 9 subject
studies [11, 20, 38]. This category of security vulnerability pertains to OS command injection, in
which an external attacker can construct an OS command by using input data from components
that have not been adequately verified.
Vulnerabilities related to Numeric are the third most frequent type of vulnerabilities covered in
the subject studies, accounting for 36 studies in total. Within this class, Integer Overflow (CWE-
190) is the most frequently covered vulnerability type [20, 58, 142]. Integer overflow is a condition
that occurs when an arithmetic operation attempts to create a numeric value that is outside the
range that can be represented with a given number of bits. For example, an 8-bit unsigned in-
teger can represent values from 0 to 255, whereas a 32-bit signed integer typically ranges from
â€“2,147,483,648 to 2,147,483,647. When an arithmetic operation produces a value that exceeds these
limits, an overflow occurs.

RQ5: What Are the Most Frequently Used Tools for Software Vulnerability
Detection?
In this section, we summarize the most commonly used tools for software vulnerability detection.
Table 10 shows the distribution of the tools. We summarized the tools into three categories, includ-
ing Model Building Tools, Code Analysis/Compilation, and Data Tools.
As can be seen in the table, Keras with TensorFlow backend16 is the most commonly used library
for building ML-based software vulnerability detection techniques, accounting for 42 studies, and
PyTorch17 comes as the second most commonly used library, with 42 studies in total. Scikit-learn18
is the third most popular library for model building, accounting for 11 studies in total. Scikit-learn
provides a user-friendly and consistent API, making it easy to implement and experiment with var-
ious ML algorithms. Scikit-learn includes a diverse set of classification algorithms such as Logistic
Regression, SVM, Decision Trees, Random Forests, KN, and Naive Bayes. GenSim19 is the fourth
commonly used tool for building software vulnerability detection models. GenSimâ€™s ability to
efficiently handle large datasets, combined with its powerful topic modeling and word embedding
functionalities, makes it an indispensable tool for model building in natural language processing
and text mining. DGL20 is the fifth most commonly used model building tool, accounting for 6 stud-
ies. DGL is specifically designed for constructing and training GNNs, making it a go-to library for
researchers and practitioners working on graph-related problems. It abstracts the complexity of
implementing GNNs, providing easy-to-use APIs for building and applying various GNN models.
In the category of Code Analysis/Compilation, the most commonly used tool is Joern, accounting
for 24 studies in total. Joern was first proposed by Yamaguchi et al. [160], and it converts source
code into a graph representation, specifically AST, CFG, and PDG. The second most commonly
used tool for code processing is Soot,21 which provides various intermediate representations of
Java bytecode.
In the category of Data Tools, NetworkX is the most commonly used data tool, accounting for
five studies in total. NetworkX22 uses native Python data structures (like dictionaries and lists) to
represent graphs. This allows seamless integration with other Python libraries and makes it easy
to manipulate and explore graph data. NLTK23 provides robust tools for breaking down source
code and text into tokens, which is essential for analyzing software vulnerability data.

Answer to RQ5
4.6
RQ6: What Are Possible Challenges and Open Directions in Software
Vulnerability Detection?
4.6.1
Challenges.
Challenge 1: Heterogeneous Data Sources. The biggest challenge in vulnerability detec-
tion through learning is the inadequate modeling of the comprehensive semantics of complex
vulnerabilities by current models [26, 27, 126]. Existing ML models often fail to capture
the complex patterns of software vulnerabilities because they treat source code like natural
language. Unlike natural language, source code contains structural and logical information
requiring AST, dataflow, and control flow analysis. To address this, the detection pipeline
must use rich representation techniques like control flow and dataflow graphs and proper
embeddings to convert these representations into a numerical format for graph-based neural
networks.
ACM Comput. Surv., Vol. 57, No. 3, Article 55. Publication date: November 2024.
A Systematic Literature Review on Automated Software Vulnerability Detection Using ML 55:25
Challenge 2: Detection Granularity. The effectiveness of DL models in identifying vulnera-
bilities depends on input granularity. Current models use coarse inputs like methods and files.
To achieve finer granularity, program slicing can select crucial statements for detection, but it
must be done effectively to reduce noise. Existing tools focus on library/API calls and operations,
but these alone are insufficient. A promising approach is using code changes from GitHub,
focusing on added and deleted lines, which often have the highest impact on vulnerability
detection.
Challenge 3: Lack of Training Data. A significant weakness of DL models, particularly in soft-
ware vulnerability detection, is their insatiable need for data [24, 111]. In domains like image clas-
sification, abundant labeled data, and pre-trained models enable effective DL training. However,
in software vulnerability detection, data scarcity is a major issue due to the difficulty of label-
ing ground truth information. Platforms like Stack Overflow, GitHub, and issue-tracking systems
provide extensive records, but labeling is often manual and challenging. Automatic labeling is a
potential solution but tends to generate many false positives. Some researchers use unsupervised
classification, but this method also has limited precision.
(1) Most of the current models cannot capture the comprehensive semantics of complex vul-
nerabilities, as most of them fail to consider the structural and logical information present in
source code snippets.
(2) Most existing ML models process source code in a linear sequential manner, which limits
their ability to identify intricate vulnerability patterns.
(3) DL models require a significant amount of labeled data for effective training. However, in
software vulnerability detection, labeled data are scarce due to the challenging task of man-
ual labeling. Automatic labeling approaches often generate false positives, and unsupervised
classification suffers from limited precision.
Answer to RQ6: Challenges
4.6.2
Open Directions. Multi-Modal Learning. Performing a simple vulnerability detection
with source code snippets is not sufficient to have accurate and effective models. Various artifacts
are needed to feed into ML models to increase vulnerability detection performance. For example,
feeding code comments will increase classification performance remarkably. Some subject studies
that use commits [19] argue that feeding source code is not enough and commit characteristics as
metadata are required for software vulnerability detection.
Just-in-Time Vulnerability Detection. One possible direction for software vulnerability detec-
tion is using the just-in-time approaches. This approach focuses on detecting vulnerabilities as
they occur or are introduced, hence offering real-time protection [56, 114]. This method allows for
faster reaction and mitigation of vulnerabilities before they are exploited.
Leveraging Foundation Models (LLMs) for Vulnerability Detection. Recently, LLMs have been
used in a wide variety of software engineering tasks including automatic program repair [59], test
case generation, and root cause analysis of incidents in cloud environments. However, the appli-
cation of LLMs for software vulnerability detection has not been yet discovered comprehensively
as it should be. In our survey, we identified some subject studies that utilize LLMs for software
vulnerability detection [32, 98, 135, 169]. However, their frequency is still negligible compared to
the widespread usage of typical DL models.
ACM Comput. Surv., Vol. 57, No. 3, Article 55. Publication date: November 2024.
55:26
N. Shiri Harzevili et al.
(1) Leveraging LLMs for software vulnerability detection is a promising opportunity
due to their advanced understanding of both natural language and code. LLMs can
help with code analysis and recognize emerging vulnerability patterns.
(2) Multi-modal learning offers a significant opportunity to enhance software vulner-
ability detection by integrating diverse data sources, such as source code, natural lan-
guage comments, metadata, and runtime behaviors.
Answer to RQ6: Opportunities
5
Threats to Validity
In this section, we discuss threats to the validity of each RQ. We discuss various threats to the RQs
that we address in this study.
RQ1: Trend of Studies. The selection of studies might be biased if certain types of studies are
more likely to be indexed or retrieved by our web crawler. To address selection bias, we defined
diverse key terms to extract the most relevant research papers related to software vulnerability
detection. The target papers should use ML-based software vulnerability detection techniques. To
increase the accuracy of data selection, we refined the initial search results in three steps to ensure
that the most relevant studies were selected for taxonomy creation and refinement. These steps
have been performed by multiple authors simultaneously. The choice of digital libraries could im-
pact construct validity if they do not equally represent all relevant studies. To mitigate this threat,
we selected the most widely used digital libraries: ACM Digital Library, ScienceDirect, IEEE Xplore,
and Google Scholar. These libraries are representative of the software vulnerability detection field
because they contain a sufficient number of records that match our key terms for data extraction.
One of the major threats to the external validity of the first RQ is that the trends we observed from
January 2011 to June 2024 may not apply to future research beyond this period. As technologies
evolve rapidly, new techniques and tools for software vulnerability detection may emerge. How-
ever, we believe that our findings accurately represent the current state-of-the-art technology for
software vulnerability detection at the time of this study.
RQ2: Characteristics of Software Vulnerability Detection Datasets. Datasets might focus
on specific types of software or languages that threaten the generalizability of our findings. To
overcome this limitation, we focused on software vulnerability detection in three major language
domains, including software vulnerability in Java, C/C++, and smart contracts. Java is prevalent
in enterprise and web applications, C/C++ is fundamental in system and performance-critical pro-
gramming, and smart contracts are crucial in blockchain technology. This diverse selection re-
duces selection bias, provides a holistic view of vulnerabilities, and ensures that the findings are
more broadly applicable and relevant to real-world software development contexts. Although our
findings are based on datasets from studies published between January 2011 and June 2024, the
identified characteristics are expected to apply to future datasets due to ongoing advancements
in software vulnerability detection techniques. We provide detailed criteria and procedures for se-
lecting and analyzing datasets, enabling other researchers to replicate and validate our findings,
thus enhancing the generalizability and reliability of our conclusions.
RQ3: Distribution of ML and DL Models in Software Vulnerability Detection. There are
multiple threats to this RQ. First, ML models evolve quickly, and models that are effective today
might become obsolete or be replaced by more advanced ones soon. To overcome this threat, we
expanded our study selection bias to cover the last 2 yearsâ€”that is, 2023 and 2024 to cover the most
state-of-the-art ML technology for software vulnerability detection. This results in identifying
three promising studies that use foundation models for software vulnerability detection.
ACM Comput. Surv., Vol. 57, No. 3, Article 55. Publication date: November 2024.
A Systematic Literature Review on Automated Software Vulnerability Detection Using ML 55:27
RQ4: Frequent Software Vulnerability. To ensure construct validity in this RQ, it is crucial
to provide clear and precise definitions of each type of vulnerability. We first identify reputable
sources like OWASP and MITREâ€™s CWE. OWASP provides a widely recognized list of common
security vulnerabilities, particularly in web applications. CWE offers a comprehensive list of soft-
ware weaknesses, providing detailed descriptions and classifications. We then reviewed the subject
studies and identified the types of vulnerabilities that are mentioned frequently. Often these
vulnerabilities can be identified by CWE IDs that are explicitly mentioned in the research papers.
RQ5: Tools for Software Vulnerability Detection. The threat to this question is that there may
be biases in the selection of tools for study, influenced by an important factor such as popularity
(like TensorFlow and PyTorch). This can skew the findings toward more well-known tools, neglect-
ing equally effective but less publicized options. To overcome this threat, we classified the tools
into three broad categories. For each category, we extracted the most popular and the least popular
tools including a balanced mix of tools to avoid over-representation of any particular subset.
RQ6: Challenges and Open Directions. To ensure the construct validity of this RQ, we
thoroughly analyzed two key sections of each study. First, we examined the context section of the
abstract to gain a general understanding of the problem being addressed. Next, we analyzed the
introduction section to extract relevant text that further elaborates on the problem. By combining
this information, we generalized the problem and created a concise taxonomy for classification.
6
Conclusion
In this study, we conducted a systematic survey to investigate various characteristics of ML-based
software vulnerability detection studies using six RQs. We extracted initial studies from four
widely-used online digital librariesâ€”ACM Digital Library, IEEE Xplore, ScienceDirect, and Google
Scholarâ€”using a custom web scraper. After manually filtering out irrelevant studies unrelated to
software vulnerability detection, we created taxonomies and addressed the RQs.
Our findings indicated a notable increase in the use of ML techniques to detect software vulnera-
bilities in recent years. We found that prominent conference venues include ICSE, ISSRE, MSR, and
FSE, whereas the leading journal venues are IST, C&S, and JSS. Additionally, we found that 39.1%
of the subject studies use hybrid as the sources of data, whereas 37.6% of the subject studies use
benchmark data for software vulnerability detection. Among the data types analyzed, code-based
data is the most prevalent, with source code being the most common sub-type. Graph-based and
token-based input representations are the most popular techniques, utilized in 57.2% and 24.6% of
the studies, respectively. For input embedding, graph embeddings and token vector embeddings
are the most frequently employed methods, appearing in 32.6% and 29.7% of studies. Furthermore,
88.4% of the examined studies use DL models, with RNNs and GNNs being the most popular,
whereas only 7.2% use traditional ML models. The most frequently addressed vulnerability types
are CWE-119, CWE-20, and CWE-190. In terms of tools for software vulnerability detection, Keras
and PyTorch are the most widely used tools. Joern is the leading tool for code analysis and repre-
sentation. Finally, we summarized the challenges and future directions in the context of software
vulnerability detection, providing valuable insight for researchers and practitioners in the field.
This comprehensive survey aimed to bridge the existing gap and provide a clearer understanding
of the current landscape and future opportunities in the detection of software vulnerabilities using
ML techniques.

Predicting Vulnerable Code Changes Using
Technical Debt Indicators
RUSEN AKKUS HALEPMOLLASI
1,2 AND AYSE TOSUN

1Faculty of Computer and Informatics Engineering, Istanbul Technical University, 34467 Istanbul, TÃ¼rkiye

Corresponding author: Rusen Akkus Halepmollasi (halepmollasi@itu.edu.tr)
ABSTRACT
Technical debt refers to the cost of delayed technical work and poor design choices in
software systems. Software security focuses on protecting systems against vulnerabilities and exploits. In this
study, we explore the relationship between technical debt and software vulnerabilities to understand how
technical debt impacts software security. We collected real world data from six software projects, including
code changes and corresponding vulnerabilities. We investigate various technical debt indicators, such as
code smells, bugs, and software metrics, along with technical debt mitigation methods like refactoring
activities, to predict vulnerabilities. The findings reveal a significant association between technical debt
and vulnerabilities, highlighting the impact of technical debt on software security. We also identify specific
artifacts, such as code smells, that contribute to the emergence of vulnerabilities. By understanding this
relationship, software practitioners and project managers can gain insights into the risks associated with
accumulated technical debt and take appropriate measures to enhance software security and quality.
INDEX TERMS Code smells, software metrics, technical debt, vulnerability prediction.
I. INTRODUCTION
Software quality can be examined in two dimensions [1]:
The first is the absence/existence of bugs or vulnerabilities
in the software system, including missing or misinterpreted
requirements, design flaws, incomplete functional logic,
absent validity, and coding faults. The second is the extent to
which Technical Debt (TD) could be managed by complying
with various quality attributes. Ozkaya [1] states that assuring
quality is based on adhesion to product standards and
procedures and a systematic attitude to quality assessment.
TD is a concept that was coined by Cunningham to
elucidate the necessity of refactoring to nontechnical software
product stakeholders by inspiring from financial debt [2].
TD refers to the cost of delayed technical work related to poor
solutions in software systems developed by compromising
long-term quality to accomplish short-term objectives [3].
Similar to financial debt, TD can have interest payments
that are the extra effort for future development as a result of
hasty design decisions and code implementation. Kruchten
et al. [4] further categorize TD into visible components,
The associate editor coordinating the review of this manuscript and
approving it for publication was Claudia Raibulet
.
such as extra functionality and poor external quality, and
invisible components, such as documentation debt and code
complexity. When TD is left invisible and not repaid, that
is, cannot be managed, it can be accumulated and makes
maintainability and evolvability difficult. This can lead to
software security risks when it is not addressed and not
minimized [5]. To make matters worse, the ability to pay
â€˜â€˜interestâ€™â€™ on accumulated debts can be exceeded.
Software security is a quality characteristic among
many [6], and refers to the protection of systems and networks
against vulnerabilities and exploits by building secure soft-
ware [7]. To be able to develop secure software, security risks
must be identified and mitigated sufficiently early by integrat-
ing best security practices into the overall software develop-
ment life cycle [8], [9]. Harris and Maymi [10] state that pro-
viding functional and secure development together offers pro-
tection at all layers of software. Thus, in order to reduce the
possibility of vulnerabilities, incorporating security-oriented
thinking into the systems is a better strategy. Vulnerabilities,
less frequently observed but harder to fix compared to other
defects, are defects or weaknesses in systems and occur when
exploited by a threat actor attempting to perform malicious
and unauthorized actions within the system [11].

Software systems inevitably have vulnerabilities. How-
ever, identifying their causes and addressing them in
earlier stages of the life cycle can help developers avoid
spending a lot of time and effort on maintenance. Coding
and design flaws are reported to often be the causes of
vulnerabilities in software projects [12]. The quantification
and evaluation of TD becomes more significant in detecting
or predicting vulnerabilities. In recent years, many studies
have investigated the relationship of TD indicators such
as code smells [13], [14] and/or architectural smells [15],
[16], bugs [17], and TD mitigation methods [18] with
software vulnerabilities. Although some studies, e.g. [15]
and [16], argue that there is no significant relationship
between architectural smells and software vulnerabilities,
others mostly claim that software systems with code smells
and bugs have higher security risks, and refactoring bad
smells helps improve the security of software systems [14],
[17] [19], [20]. Studies have also widely used software
metrics, which are indirect TD indicators [17], to analyze the
relationship between them and vulnerabilities [21], [22] [23]
and to predict vulnerabilities [24], [25] [26], [27]. Therefore,
we can claim that TD and software security are related, and
in particular, TD in software development can be important
indicators of vulnerabilities.
In a recent study, authors examined the competence of
various TD indicators to predict security risks at the project
level and at class level in software systems [17]. They perform
static analysis via SonarQube to extract software metrics,
bugs, and code smells as TD indicators and vulnerability
density metrics as security indicators. According to their
results, TD indicators may be potentially used as software
vulnerability indicators as well. However, there is still a gap in
the comprehensive prediction of real software vulnerabilities
from the perspective of TD. TD indicators can be used
more extensively to explain software vulnerabilities in real
systems by building prediction models. To our knowledge,
very limited studies attempt to predict vulnerabilities using
more than one TD indicator.
In this study, our objective is to quantify TD in a
larger context and investigate their relationship with real
vulnerabilities at the code change level. To our knowledge,
this is the first paper that empirically analyzes the relationship
of software vulnerabilities with TD direct/indirect indicators,
i.e., code smells, bugs, and software metrics, and TD
mitigation approach, i.e., refactoring activities, at the code
change level using real vulnerability data. We define the
following RQs:
â€¢ RQ1: How can we predict vulnerable commits with
respect to coding artifacts leading to TD?
By addressing this RQ, the objective is to develop
predictive models for vulnerable commits by analyzing
certain TD artifacts(e.g., code complexity, code smells,
bugs, or refactoring activities) to understand the under-
lying causes and mechanisms by which TD indicators
emerge as vulnerabilities.
â€¢ RQ2: How does V-SZZ+ improve vulnerable commit
prediction compared to V-SZZ?
With RQ2, we aim to assess V-SZZ+, our new V-SZZ
based labeling approach, which tags vulnerability-
inducing commits and all subsequent commits contain-
ing vulnerabilities until they are fixed, its effectiveness
in terms of prediction performance compared to the
state-of-the-art approach, V-SZZ.
â€¢ RQ3: How does detecting code smells at every commit
perform in identifying vulnerable commits?
Lastly, we aim to evaluate the effectiveness of our fine-
grained, commit-level code smell detection in identi-
fying vulnerable commits against traditional snapshot-
based approaches. Our approach analyzes every file
modified in each commit, so that all commits are linked
to existing or newly introduced code smells of the
modified files.
In this context, the main contributions of our study are the
following:
â€¢ Experiments performed utilizing real-world data are
often better representative of industrial software prod-
ucts. Therefore, we collected code changes and corre-
sponding software vulnerabilities from six real-world
projects through their GitHub repositories and National
Vulnerability Database (NVD)1 records.
â€¢ We used the V-SZZ algorithm to extract the vulnerability
inducing commits, instead of SZZ variants, as vulnera-
bilities are usually introduced in the initial versions of
fixing commits, whereas bugs are usually introduced
in the recent versions of fixing commits [28]. We have
further proposed a new V-SZZ based labeling approach,
namely V-SZZ+, that identifies vulnerability-inducing
commits and tags all subsequent commits containing
vulnerabilities until they are fixed. Our approach
provides a more comprehensive labeling of vulnerable
commits and enables finer-grained analysis and predic-
tion in the context of TD. Using those, we automatically
identified vulnerable code commits, created the first
vulnerability data of six different real-world projects
from the SmartSHARK dataset, and shared it publicly.
â€¢ We have also contributed to SmartSHARK dataset by
preparing the first code smell dataset at file and commit
level. Unlike the common approach of capturing a few
snapshots of the source code, we extracted the code
smells from all versions of source files within the
projectsâ€™ version history. We run the PMD tool [29],
which is a well-known source code analyzer, on each
commit, and separately report all code smells in all
file changes. This is a relatively more detailed mapping
of commits and code smells, that takes into account
the temporal modifications on the files associated
to these commits. We believe it helps to eliminate
suspicions on consecutive code smells and relate them
to vulnerabilities.

â€¢ Although refactoring activities are among the most com-
mon TD repayment methods [30], refactoring activities
have never been used to predict vulnerabilities. In this
study, we empirically explore the ability of refactoring
activities that can mitigate TD to predict vulnerabilities
in software products.
â€¢ Exploratory studies are typically conducted in the early
stages of research when the researcher has limited
knowledge of the subject area, while explanatory studies
are designed to investigate cause-and-effect relation-
ships between different variables [31]. Previous studies
have widely explored mechanisms to detect TD and
identify its relationship with software security. In this
paper, we performed an explanatory study from a TD
perspective using indirect indicators (software metrics),
direct indicators (code smells and bugs), and the TD
mitigation method (refactoring activities) to predict real
software vulnerabilities.
â€¢ We also provide a replication package that includes
Python code for predictive models, real vulnerabilities,
code smells, and other collections extracted from the
SmartSHARK dataset and their MongoDB scripts.
The remainder of this paper is structured as follows:
Section II summarizes previous works on TD indicators,
TD mitigation methods, vulnerability prediction, and the
relationship between TD and vulnerabilities by providing a
state-of-the-art review. In Section III, we present the data
preparation steps. Section IV describes the methodology in
which we present used features, built models, and train/test
configuration phases to answer each RQ. The obtained results
of the study over the considered projects are reported and
discussed in Section V, while in Section VI, we analyzed and
discussed the threats that could affect the validity of our study.
Finally, Section VII concludes the paper.
II. RELATED WORK
We have organized this section into three sub-sections and
provide a detailed discussion on TD, vulnerability prediction,
and their relationships.
A. TECHNICAL DEBT INDICATORS AND MITIGATION
METHODS
There are many studies that report promising ways of
identifying, analyzing, and repaying TD. According to a
recent survey conducted by Alfayez et al. [32], which
analyzed 128,897 TD-related tweets to explore how the
popularity of TD has changed over time, as well as how TD
is discussed on Twitter, there is an overall rise of interest
in TD on Twitter. Also, TD causes and TD repayment
are among the most popular categories. Furthermore, in an
observational study [33], authors examined how TD term is
used on Stack Overflow, Software Engineering, and Project
Management Stack Exchange Q&A websites. They state that
the set of compiled and analyzed questions can be divided into
14 categories, including TD repayment, TD management,
TD identification, etc. [33].
Kruchten et al. [34] claim that in software intensive
systems, accumulated TD affects mainly the evolvability and
maintainability when it is not addressed and not minimized.
Moreover, several studies [35], [36] [37] reveal that TD
needs to be actively managed as it continues to accumulate
during the system development once occurring. Avgeriou
et al. [38] state that TD management, i.e., identification,
evaluation, and repayment, is a continuous process, hence,
it is important to integrate this process into the overall
software development process to ensure that the software
is maintainable and evolvable. TD provides a way to
measure the current sustainability of a system when managed
effectively, nevertheless, it can spiral out of control when not
managed properly [38].
Li et al. [30] carried out a systematic mapping study
for the comprehension of TD concept. They indicate that
TD identification and repayment are the most frequently
discussed and explored in TD management activities. Various
debt types due to intentional or unintentional technical
decisions in software systems can be detected by TD
identification activities. The detected TD can be resolved or
mitigated using TD repayment activities such as refactoring,
without changing the systemsâ€™ functionality [30].
Paudel et al. [39] conducted an industrial case study
to empirically investigate the relationship between TD
and software delivery lead time. They analyzed software
components using SonarQube and Jira issue data and found
that TD accounted for 5% to 41% of the variance in lead
time. Their findings highlight the multifactorial nature of
delivery performance and emphasize the need for broader
investigations beyond TD metrics alone. [39].
Previous studies uncovered various types of TD that can
be identified using several indicators. Some research efforts
focus mainly on the code-based analysis of the existing
debt due to lack of tools that can accurately identify TD.
To identify TD, those studies employ static analysis methods
(e.g., lines of code, code complexity, duplicate code, etc.) or
dynamic analysis methods (e.g., unit test, code coverage, etc.)
[40], [41] [42]. Also, some tools such as SonarQube [43],
SQUORE [44], and Kiuwan [45] used by development teams
are introduced to manage source code quality, including
TD. Besides, some studies suggest looking into the low
level design of the source code [46], [47], [48] to examine
their relationship with TD. Examples of such code analysis
include, but are not limited to code smells [49], design
smells [50] object oriented design such as coupling and
cohesion [51], and modularity violations [52].
Refactoring, which eliminates code smells and prevents the
faults occurring, is generally accepted as the most popular
TD repayment method [53], [54] [55], [56]. Therefore,
in the last two decades, the body of research on refactoring
and its relationship with code smells or faults has been
overgrowing [55], [57]. Benidris et al. [58] investigated
how Technical Debt Density (TDD) evolves across multiple
153898
VOLUME 13, 2025
R. A. Halepmollasi, A. Tosun: Predicting Vulnerable Code Changes Using Technical Debt Indicators
software releases and how it relates to refactoring activities
and highlighted the strategic importance of managing not just
the amount but also the intensity of TD throughout software
evolution. Observational papers examined the reasons and
methods behind developers carrying out refactoring [59], [60]
[61], which specific types of refactoring are associated with
performance indicators of the application [62], [63], and its
relation to developers behaviors [64], [65] [66] and the impact
of refactoring on TD indicators such as code smells and faults
[56], [67] [68].
PÃ©rez et al. [53] conducted an industrial survey research
study with 432 software practitioners to analyze the current
state of the practice of TD payment from the software
developersâ€™ point of view. They present the top five TD
repayment activities and their rates regarding the age and
size of the systems. Authors also compare the similarity
between TD repayment activities for the most cited TD
types, i.e., design debt, test debt, and code debt, and observe
a significant similarity in the code debt and design debt
repayment activities. They report that the most common TD
repayment practice used by developers is refactoring [53].
B. VULNERABILITY PREDICTION
Vulnerability prediction has received significant attention
from software researchers and practitioners as vulnerabilities
may have a greater impact than other defects in terms of
maintenance, costs, loss of organizationsâ€™ reputation, and
violation of user privacy. There exist many studies for vulner-
ability prediction in terms of the source code representations
(e.g., text mining techniques or static analysis approach), the
dataset(e.g., published vulnerability reports or static anal-
ysis), the granularity(e.g., class-file level, function/method
level, etc. ), or ML/DL algorithms. A recent systematic
mapping study provides a comprehensive overview of these
efforts, categorizing existing research based on techniques,
datasets, granularity levels, and prediction methods [69].
Wang et al. [70] investigated the impact of various
DL models on detecting vulnerabilities in Python code.
They compared the effectiveness of CNNs, RNNs, and
transformers in capturing code semantics for vulnerability
prediction. Their results demonstrated that transformer-based
models achieve higher accuracy in vulnerability detection
compared to traditional DL approaches [70].
Zhang et al. [71] proposed a GNN-based approach
for vulnerability detection and introduced counterfactual
explanations to improve model interpretability. They empha-
sized the importance of explainable AI in security-related
tasks. According to their results, proposed CFExplainer
outperforms state-of-the-art factual reasoning-based explain-
ers [71].
Zhou et al. [72] present Devign, a general GNN based
model to identify many types of vulnerabilities by combining
extensive code semantic representations. Their approach
contains a new Conv module that uses node features of a
graph extracted from gated graph recurrent units that are used
to learn the node embeddings. To train the model, they created
a manually labelled dataset from four large-scale open-source
C projects and used Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP). They
used accuracy and F1-measure to evaluate the performance,
and reported that Devign has significantly better performance
than the state-of-the-art, with an average of 10.51% higher
accuracy and 8.68% higher F1-measure.
Nguyen et al. [73] propose a code metric based on
two-level dependency graphs of software systems, i.e., com-
ponent dependency graphs and member dependency graphs,
in predicting vulnerable components. The dependencies were
based on the relationship among software granularities,
including components, classes, functions, and variables that
were extracted from static code analyzers and were stated
according to the nodesâ€™ and edgesâ€™ attributes. They built
ML models with Bayesian Network, Neural Networks, Naive
Bayes, SMO, and Random Forest using those attributes. The
precision is reported as 54% when they reach the highest
recall rate of 75% using Bayesian Network model, and the
recall was 39% when they reach the highest precision rate of
85% using SMO model.
Yamaguchi et al. [74] propose a graph based source code
representation, namely a code property graph combining
AST, program dependency graph, and control flow graph
into a joint data structure to model templates for common
vulnerabilities with graph traversals. They performed exper-
iments on the source code of the Linux kernel as a case study
and identified 18 unknown vulnerabilities. Moreover, they
analyzed the source code of Firefox, LibPNG, and Pidgin,
etc. in various studies [75], [76] [77].
Sahin et al. [78] also propose a vulnerability prediction
model that employed code representations through graph
node embeddings and token based embeddings to determine
the vulnerability of a function version. Their approach
involves representing function versions as node embeddings
derived from their Abstract Syntax Tree (AST). Next, they
developed models utilizing two Graph Neural Networks with
node embeddings, and compared these with Convolutional
Neural Network (CNN) and Support Vector Machine (SVM)
using token representations. The empirical analysis on real
vulnerability data reveals that node embeddings of function
versions can be used to detect vulnerability-inducing ones.
In [26], authors created developer profiles according to
vulnerabilities and examined the impact of those developer
profiles on vulnerability prediction models. They used Het-
erogeneous Information Network (HIN) analysis to profile
the developersâ€™ vulnerability inducing/fixing behaviors in
software products. Also, they compared developer profiles
against software code metrics and evaluated the performance
of constructed classifiers in terms of precision, recall, and
F1-score. According to their findings, developer profiles are
useful to predict vulnerabilities when combined with other
metrics.
Recent studies have explored the potential of Large Lan-
guage Models (LLMs) for software vulnerability detection
under various constraints. Le et al. [79] demonstrated that

C. TECHNICAL DEBT AND VULNERABILITIES
The relationships between vulnerabilities, TD, and defects
have become a topic of increasing interest in software
engineering as TD indicators and management get more
mature [5]. In this context, some studies argue the feasibility
of quantifying software security using TD concept. For
instance, Silva et al. [81] carried out research to identify the
different TD types that can result in the rejection of a pull
request and analyzed 1,722 pull requests. Authors classified
TD in seven categories, including design debt, performance
debt, and security debt, etc. They described security debt as a
specific solution that jeopardizes the systemâ€™s security.
Rindell et al. [22] offer guidelines for extending the TD
paradigm to include software security, and state the software
security risks in terms of TD. They examined the technical
and organizational impacts of implementing the concept of
managing security risks as TD in software systems. Authors
evaluated security-related TD in terms of identification,
measurability, management, and repayment. According to
study, addressing security risks and TD together can make
managing security risk and addressing underlying quality
issues more visible and enable more communication between
developers, security professionals, and managers [22]. Fur-
thermore, Rindell and Holvitie [23] offer a two-fold approach
to define security debt. They use the term: (i) to identify TD
using security validation or verification techniques, (ii) to
identify TD in a security-critical software component. They
provide a security debt management strategy to handle new
TD that can have security issues and to identify, evaluate, and
mitigate security debt.
Besides, Izurieta et al. [82] offer a five-step approach
for prioritising security related TD items by employing the
Quamoco and QATCH quality models, and catalog and
scoring systems, namely Common Weakness Enumeration
(CWE) and Common Weakness Scoring System (CWSS).
In [83], authors extended this approach by simulating attacks
and creating dependency graphs between external attacks and
the technological repercussions related to CWEs. In line with
the conclusions of both studies, they express that security is
a specific case as TD related to security can be quantified
both in terms of maintainability and in terms of damage to a
business, thus, TD needs to be dealt with as soon as possible
in relation to vulnerabilities.
There are also studies that report empirical evidence for
the relationships between TD, defects, and software security.
For example, Nord et al. [21] explored the relationship
between software vulnerabilities and TD indicators to
determine whether software components with accrued TD are
vulnerability-prone. They used TD based on problematical
design decisions to determine hard-to-find vulnerabilities.
Authors report their preliminary findings from an inves-
tigation of Chromium, including measurement based on
the classification of design consequences in issue tracking
systems, and the static analysis of the code anomalies such
as fault, vulnerability, and design flaw. They identified
79 software vulnerabilities related to 289 source code files
containing TD, that is, design flaws were detected. TD is
defined according to the methodology presented in [84],
in which a design model is constructed as a set of design rule
spaces.
Siavvas et al. [19] present an empirical study to explore
the relationship between TD and software security over
50 open source Java projects mined from GitHub. They
employed static analysis using SonarQube and FindBugs
to find out whether TD and software security have a
statistically meaningful relationship. When comparing TD
and vulnerability density, they calculated them based on
SQALE Density and Static Analysis Vulnerability Density
(SAVD), respectively. According to their preliminary results,
there exists a statistically significant, positive, and strong cor-
relation between TD and the vulnerability densities. Recently,
in [17], authors extended the preliminary analysis and mined,
both at the project and class level of granularity, 210 open
source Java projects to examine whether TD indicators
are also indicators of security risks. They calculated TD
indicators using SonarQube and quantified security risk in
terms of the SAVD metric by discretizing into Security Risk
Levels (SRLs). They state that TD indicators might also
function as security indicators [17].
III. DATA PREPARATION
One of the most essential and time-consuming phases of
building an ML pipeline is data preparation [85]. A recent
systematic literature review [86] highlights the challenges
and solutions about vulnerability related data preparation and
offers data-oriented steps in an ML based workflow. Authors
define four steps as data requirements, data collection, data
labeling, and data cleaning. In our analysis, we prepared
data according to those steps throughout our software
vulnerability prediction - data preparation pipeline (Figure 1).
A. DATA REQUIREMENTS
To achieve the desired model accomplishment, we have
determined the data requirements as follows:
â€¢ We chose to mine projects developed in Java, as it is
a widely used programming language, and there are
many tools that can extract TD indicators and mitigation
methods in code developed in Java language.
â€¢ We target detection capabilities for various vulnerability
types, rather than a certain vulnerability type. Thus,
we included entire vulnerability types in the mined
projects in our analysis.

â€¢ The commit granularity level is critical to evaluate
predictive models. There are different granularity levels,
such as component level, file-class level, function-

commit/change level to be able to analyse code changes
and enclose the vulnerable code snippets after each

â€¢ We applied mixed-project prediction approach, that is,

B. DATA COLLECTION
In this study, we used SmartSHARK dataset release
2.1 full version2 for extracting refactoring activities, bug
fixing/inducing commits, software metrics, and vulnerability-
fixing/inducing commits. SmartSHARK has recently been
created by Trautsch et al. [87], and contains 77 projects
from the well-known ecosystem, namely Apache Software
Foundation (ASF) repository.3 The size of the entire dataset
is 1.2 TB and is stored in a MongoDB. There are, in total,
47,303 pull requests, 366,322 commits, and 163,057 issues
across all projects developed in Java language. Each project
includes between 1,000 and 20,000 commits.
SmartSHARK is a very comprehensive dataset and
contains various important information about projects in
2SmartSHARK Dataset. https://SmartSHARK.github.io/dbreleases/
3Apache Software Foundation. http://apache.org
many MongoDB collections. Since we focus on analysing
the relationship between vulnerabilities and TD indicators
such as code smells and bugs, indirect indicators such as
software metrics, and mitigation methods such as refactoring
activities, we selected only the collections related to them.
We listed those collections in Table 1. Moreover, we extracted
code smells by executing the PMD tool on each commit,
as SmartSHARK does not contain the projectsâ€™ code smells.
PMD is an open source static analysis tool and reports the
issues detected in source code.
1) SOFTWARE METRICS
Software metrics can often be used as indirect TD indicators.
SmartSHARK dataset contains software metrics about the
source code for each commit in Java projects. We utilized
those metrics, i.e., complexity, coverage, and dependency,
when evaluating their impacts on vulnerability prediction.
To calculate the software metrics for each changed file in each
commit, SmartSHARK uses Open-Static-Analizer tool that
creates an abstract semantic graph from the source code and
applies static code analysis of projects. Open-Static-Analizer
is an open sourced version of the SourceMeter commercial
tool, and a plugin for the SmartSHARK infrastructure in
unification with an HPC-Cluster.
To obtain software metrics, we used code entity state
and commit collections. There are, in total, 237 code
metrics. The tool provides the code metrics at various levels,
such as method, file, and package. When predicting code
VOLUME 13, 2025
153901
R. A. Halepmollasi, A. Tosun: Predicting Vulnerable Code Changes Using Technical Debt Indicators
TABLE 1. MongoDB collections of SmartSHARK dataset used in this study.
changes that lead to vulnerabilities, we selected 91 file-
level metrics and aggregated them on commit-level to
represent the commit-level code quality. There are several
aggregation methods based on descriptive statistics (e.g.,
sum, mean, median, standard deviation, skewness), distribu-
tion parameter estimation (e.g., maximum likelihood), and
econometric methods (e.g., Hoover coefficient, Gini index)
[88]. Although we extracted the most common descriptive
statistics, we computed the sum of each metric over all
changed files in each commit.
2) REFACTORING ACTIVITIES
Refactoring activities are composed by code transformation
and aim to improve the structural quality. To find commits in
which refactoring activities are detected, we used commit, file
actions, and refactoring collections in SmartSHARK dataset.
The refactoring collection contains a list of refactoring activi-
ties that occurred in the repositories. There are 35 refactoring
types that were detected via an open source tool, namely
RMiner [89]. Through the use of a two-step methodology,
RMiner defines various refactoring types across the history
of Java projects. First, it extracts classes, methods, and fields
that are added/removed/replaced between two consequtive
commits based on a lightweight version of the UMLDiff
algorithm [90]. Next, it extends and uses a set of rules defined
by Biegel et al. [91] to discriminate the different types of
refactoring activities. RMiner can detect refactoring activities
with 98% and 87% of precision and recall, respectively.
We aggregated refactoring activities at commit level, and
there are 6,256 commits in which refactoring activities
occurred.
3) BUG-INDUCING & BUG-FIXING
Bugs are defects that cause incorrect and unexpected results
in software systems. To obtain bug-inducing and bug-
fixing commits, we used commit, issue, and issue systems
collections in SmartSHARK dataset. There is a label for
each commit indicating whether it is a bug-fixing, a bug-
inducing commit, or neither of the two. The issue collection
lists the results of the Open SZZ execution. The Open
SZZ algorithm is an implementation of the SZZ algorithm
that is widely used to identify bug-inducing changes from
the history of a software project. SZZ algorithm starts by
analyzing the bug-fixing commits, i.e., commits known to fix
a bug reported on an issue tracking system, to trace back to
their bug-introducing commits, i.e., commits containing the
code changes that induce a bug into the system. We matched
the commit hashes identified as bug-inducing and bug-fixing
according to the issue collection with the commit hashes.
There are 5,184 bug-inducing commits and 3,041 bug-fixing
commits.
4) CODE SMELLS
To detect code smells, we executed PMD source code
analyzer tool that has built-in rule sets and also supports the
creation of custom rules. We identified four types of code
smells, namely Excessive Class Length, Excessive Method
Length, Excessive Parameter List, and God Class, from
six projects. We matched each file with the corresponding
commits in which they are affected by the code smells.
In other words, code smells in every file changed in every
commit were individually reported by running the PMD tool
at commit level. Please note that ours is a very rigorous
process, and not typical to follow, as many studies run
PMD on the projectsâ€™ selected snapshots or versions or
patches only to find out code smells on the files due to
time and memory constraints [92], [93], [94]. We used the
PyDriller [95] framework to extract commit information
from Git repositories instead of directly connecting to the
GitHub API. PyDriller is a Python framework designed
for analyzing software development processes and can be
used to mine the commit history and changes in a Git
repository, to measure various metrics, and to analyze code
evolution. Thanks to PyDriller, we were able to save all
the information from the Git log, including details about
every file modified in each commit, without the need to
develop a custom script for connecting to the GitHub API or
parsing Git logs. Extracting code smells from every commit
took approximately 108 hours using four parallel threads
and resulted in a 17 MB log. We found, in total, 59,984
smelly commit-file pairs. The number of code smells ranges
from 1 to 225 among the commits. We aggregated smelly
commit-file pairs at commit level. Finally, we have the
following information: (i) number of code smells in each

commit, (ii) detected code smell type(s) in each commit, (iii)
dates when files are added or modified, and (iv) commit hash
values.
C. DATA LABELING
Datasets that are created from real-world vulnerability data
are generally considered to better represent industrial prac-
tice, as they reflect the complexity of real-world vulnerabili-
ties [96]. Therefore, when building a vulnerability prediction
model, we utilized real-world data for which the code and the
matching vulnerability reports were obtained from real-world
database and repositories. In other words, we mined projectsâ€™
GitHub repositories and extracted labels of vulnerabilities
that were reported by developers in NVD and ASF JIRA
systems, and other project-specific websites. To this end,
we performed the following three steps, summarized below.
1) EXTRACTING THE PUBLISHED VULNERABILITIES OF
PROJECTS
SmartSHARK dataset does not contain projectsâ€™ vulnera-
bility data. Thus, we had to extend the dataset by curating
the real-world vulnerability data analyzed from NVD for
SmartSHARK projects. Vulnerabilities published in NVD are
indexed according to Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures
Identifier (CVE ID). Thus, we found 118 vulnerability reports
as of December 2022.
2) EXTRACTING VULNERABILITY FIXING COMMITS
ASF projects, in general, do not have a specific template
for security advisories, and published vulnerability reports
may not contain references to CVE ID details. Hence, linking
vulnerabilities to certain commits of a software projectâ€™s
source code was a significant and laborious challenge.
We investigated the available information for each vulnera-
bility published in NVD and tried to find the associated fixing
commit(s) in the issue tracking system or project-specific
web sites. As a result of our manual search, we found
178 vulnerability fixing commits. Furthermore, we used
MSR2019 dataset [97] to set the ground-truth data and
validate the correctness of our mapping. MSR2019 dataset
contains 624 reported vulnerabilities from 205 distinct open
source Java projects and maps them onto the 1282 fixing
commits.
3) EXTRACTING VULNERABILITY INDUCING COMMITS
After vulnerabilities were linked to their fixing commits,
we had to find commits in which these vulnerabilities
were induced in order to build a vulnerability prediction
model. For this purpose, we utilized V-SZZ algorithm, which
is proposed to identify vulnerability inducing changes. V-
SZZ algorithm analyzes the vulnerability-fixing commits,
i.e., commits in which a vulnerability reported on an issue
tracking system is fixed, to trace back to their vulnerability-
inducing commits, i.e., commits that include code changes
inducing a vulnerability into the system. We have managed
TABLE 2. Number of extracted features based on direct/indirect TD
indicators and TD mitigation methods.
to match vulnerability fixing commits with 190 vulnerability
inducing commits.
D. DATA CLEANING
Software vulnerabilities are rarely observed compared to
other software defects, even in large projects, resulting in a
limited and imbalanced dataset. In our dataset, classes are
imbalanced, that is, the samples labeled as vulnerable are
very small compared to the entire dataset. The imbalanced
data may eventually cause low prediction performance of
ML models in terms of several evaluation metrics [98], [99].
To mitigate that, we applied some filtering strategies. Also,
we brought the collected data into the final dataset format
by applying the data cleaning steps for irrelevant code, noisy
code, and duplicated code.
â€¢ We filtered out projects with a small number of real
vulnerability data, as they may make the dataset more
imbalanced. We selected and analysed six projects with
the largest number of real vulnerability data out of
77 projects: Active-MQ, Cxf-fediz, Httpcomponents-
client, Nifi, Struts, and Tika.
â€¢ We removed duplicated commits, as duplicate entries
may introduce bias into a model. In other words, merged
commits have two parent commits, and those commits
could cause us to compute the same measure twice, thus,
we removed them in our analysis.
â€¢ Meanwhile, we filtered out commits according to the
number of their files when selecting. We removed
commits that have more than 20 changed files due to
the outlier and noise potential, which may affect the
features and model training. We chose 20 by observing
the number of commits and corresponding changed files,
and found out that less than 5% of commits constitute
more than 20 files, and an average of three files were
modified in a single commit.
E. FINAL SET OF EXTRACTED FEATURES
In this subsection, we report the final set of extracted features,
including software metrics, code smells, bugs, and refactoring
activities, which serve as indicators of TD. Table 2 reports the
number of extracted features from each set. The full list of
features are available in Table 9.
1) SOFTWARE METRICS
Object oriented software metrics such as complexity, cou-
pling, and cohesion, are closely related to TD [100],
VOLUME 13, 2025
153903
R. A. Halepmollasi, A. Tosun: Predicting Vulnerable Code Changes Using Technical Debt Indicators
[101] [102] and also critical in terms of several quality
characteristics such as maintainability, reliability, portability,
and security [30]. Thus, the software metrics can often be
used as indirect TD indicators [17], [103]. We used various
metrics including complexity, coverage, and dependency
metrics of the projects to predict real-word vulnerabilities.
These metrics are available in the SmartSHARK dataset, and
we have only applied aggregation operation to have commit-
level values. We refer to the websites and user manuals of
the tools for detailed explanations of the calculated metrics,
the documentation, libraries and API descriptions of the tools
published by the researchers.
2) CODE SMELLS
Fowler defined code smells as â€˜â€˜symptoms of poor design and
implementation choicesâ€™â€™ and contributed significantly to the
literature by categorizing 28 different types of smells [49],
[104]. Code smells can be considered as an indicator of TD
[17], [105], as they indicate areas of the codebase that may
be difficult to understand, test, or maintain [48]. As shown
in Table 2, we used four types of code smells that are all
extracted via PMD tool at file-level. These smells are later
aggregated at commit level. The features are in the form of a
row vector with four dimensions each of which includes the
number of specific code smell found over all files changed
in a commit. Excessive Class Length refers that a class file is
too long, containing a large number of lines of code or having
too many fields or methods. Excessive Method Length refers
that a method contains an excessive number of lines of code,
making it harder to read and maintain. Excessive Parameter
List refers that a method has too many parameters, making it
harder to understand, maintain, and modify. God Class is a
type of anti-pattern in software development that refers to a
class that has become overly complex and has taken on too
many responsibilities.
3) BUG-INDUCING & BUG-FIXING
Bugs are common TD indicators and can also indicate
security risk [17], [106]. There are two bug-related coding
activity that can be observed: (1) introduction of a bug,
which could be due to human errors [107], external software
dependencies [108], [109] or other factors, i.e., bug inducing,
and (2) bug fixing, which may also trigger TD in software
systems due to the trade-off between bug-fixing and new
release pressure [110], [111]. Thus, in this study, we utilized
bug-inducing and bug-fixing coding activities as two binary
features of a commit.
4) REFACTORING ACTIVITIES
TD repayment methods can solve the detected causes of
TD by applying various techniques such as refactoring,
rewriting, and re-engineering without changing the behavior
of the system, thus, mitigating or removing the principal or
interest of the identified debt [55]. Meanwhile, the internal
quality of the software system on which refactoring occurred
is expected to improve through mitigating or removing
the accumulated TD [30], [112]. In this paper, we used
35 different types of refactoring activities as features in
prediction models to analyze the impact of TD mitigation on
security vulnerabilities.
F. ADDITIONAL DATASET PACKAGE
All the query scripts, collected data, and extracted additional
dataset are available online [113]. Here, we also report
descriptive statistics for six projects in Table 3. The projects
have between 2,547 and 12,523 commits, though vulnerable
commits (VC) and vulnerability-inducing commits (VIC)
represent only a small portion of the total. While ActiveMQ
has the most vulnerability inducing commits (73), Tika and
Http Components Client have the least vulnerability inducing
commits (3).
IV. METHODOLOGY
In this section, we provide our methodology that involves
a comprehensive analysis of the relationship between TD
and software vulnerabilities. We considered various TD
indicators as features, and they were used to quantify the
presence of TD in the software systems. For the purpose
of predicting vulnerabilities, we employed three classifiers.
We trained those classifiers using the collected data with
the extracted features as input. We established a suitable
training configuration to ensure optimal performance of the
classifiers.
A. DIMENSIONALITY REDUCTION
The scale of the input data affects some of the models
we investigated using classification algorithms. To address
this issue, we applied standardization to the dataset before
experimenting with the algorithms.
Performance of the algorithms may be affected when
dealing with an enormous amount of features or when there
is a high correlation among the features [114]. To overcome
this challenge, dimensionality reduction techniques are
frequently used. In this study, we used Principal Component
Analysis (PCA) and Independent Component Analysis (ICA)
as dimensionality reduction techniques to evaluate their
impact on the performance of vulnerability classifiers.
PCA reduces the dimensionality of the original feature
set by calculating the eigenvectors of the covariance matrix
[115]. By linearly transforming the high-dimensional feature
vector into a low-dimensional vector with uncorrelated
components, the method is able to preserve most of the
important information of the original feature set. On the
other hand, ICA aims to obtain statistically independent
components instead of transforming unrelated components
[116]. In this way, ICA can potentially capture complex,
nonlinear relationships between the features that PCA may
not be able to capture.
In our study, we reduced the number of features to 15 when
applying both PCA and ICA. This may allow us to effectively
reduce the dimensionality of the feature set and simplify

the problem, while still preserving the essential information
required for accurate classification.
B. CLASSIFICATION ALGORITHMS
When predicting vulnerabilities based on code smells,
bug reports, refactoring activities, and software metrics,
we examined the feasibility of using three classifiers, namely
Support Vector Machine (SVM), eXtreme Gradient Boosting
(XGBoost), and Gradient Boosted Tree (GBT). To conduct
experiments, we employed Python programming language
and, in particular, scikit-learn ML package, which includes
the implementation of the utilized algorithms. We also
applied hyperparameter tuning to each classifier to optimize
their performance and presented the optimal parameters
for each classifier. The employed classifiers are, in short,
described below:
1) SUPPORT VECTOR MACHINE
The supervised learning model SVM aims to find the optimal
hyperplane that is equidistant from both classes [117]. When
the dataset can be linearly divided into classes in binary
classification problems, the distinction can be made with an
infinite number of hyperplanes. Therefore, SVM attempts to
learn a nonlinear function by linearly mapping the data points
to a high-dimensional feature space to find the linear function
with the largest margin to distinguish the classes from each
other. Thus, the misclassification error is reduced when new
data is encountered. We defined the optimal parameter set of
SVM by k-fold cross validation and performed the classifier
with poly kernel as it outperformed other kernels to predict
vulnerabilities [117].
2) GRADIENT BOOSTED TREE
GBT can be applied for classification or regression problems,
based on the principle that many weak learners can together
form a more accurate estimate. When predicting target
labels, it utilizes an ensemble of decision trees to optimize
the prediction result of a model with consecutive steps in
the learning phase. The algorithm incrementally adds new
models with iterations until no improvement is detected and
transforms weak learners into strong learners. Each iteration
of the trees covers tunning the values such as the coefficient,
weight, and bias applied to each input variable for minimizing
the difference between the predicted and actual, namely
loss function. Throughout the experiments, we performed
hyperparameter tuning on the GBT using grid search to
prevent overfitting, as lower variance would lead to more
accomplished results in samples outside of the training data.
3) EXTREME GRADIENT BOOSTING
XGBoost is a tree based ensemble ML method designed to
increase model performance and computational speed [118].
It uses multiple decision trees to predict an outcome based
on central boosting techniques through system optimization
such as parallel processing, tree punning, handling missing
values, and regularization overfitting/bias. XGBoost has
many hyperparameters, therefore, we implemented the grid
search with a limited combination of parameters to achieve
optimal performance [118].
C. TRAINING CONFIGURATION
1) SAMPLING METHODS
Many traditional ML classifiers are less powerful as a result
of the skewed distribution, when trying to predict minority
class samples in an imbalanced dataset [119]. As detailed in
Section III-D, we applied some filtering strategies. However,
the ratio of vulnerable samples to the entire dataset is still
0.01%. Thus, we applied additional steps when labeling the
data, that is, we selected commits that have files labelled as
vulnerable at least once in their entire change histories. For
instance, as seen in Figure2, we found that commit 28067a2
is the vulnerability-fixing commit, and the vulnerability was
induced at commit ee9bd94. So this vulnerability lives in the
system from the moment it is induced until it is fixed. Thatâ€™s
why we labeled all the commits after which the affected
files in the inducing commit were changed as vulnerable.
So, we labelled commits 44c9ea0, 710171f, and f60585a
as vulnerable in which splitJson, TestsplitJson, TestsplitXml,
and SplitXml files are modified. With this operation, class
distributions were more balanced.
As the final dataset is relatively balanced compared to a
real-life scenario, the prediction performance that we would
observe at the end of this study would not be generalizable to
our contexts. To evaluate the robustness and generalizability

2) TRAIN-TEST SPLIT
Our dataset, prepared for supervised learning, consists of
1,321 samples belonging to six real-world projects in total.
We randomly split 80% of the data for training and 20%
for testing. Random splitting of the dataset can result in
extremely different ratios in the target variable. In particular,
the distribution of target variables can potentially affect the
quality of model predictions as our dataset is imbalanced
and the number of samples in vulnerable class is quite
small. To overcome this challenge, we ensure that the data
is split with stratification. To achieve more robust results,
we repeated the experiments 10 times each using a different
random seed on the order of the samples, and we computed
the average of the overall performance scores.
3) HYPER-PARAMETER TUNING
To improve the prediction performance of models, a hyper-
parameter tuning procedure must be carried out before
learning. An external property of the model known as a model
hyper-parameter cannot be inferred from data during training.
We used GridSearchCV, a Python version of the Grid-search
method, to fine-tune our models as much as feasible [120].
Grid-search is frequently used to execute an exhaustive search
over predetermined parameter values for an estimator in
order to identify the model hyper-parameters that produce
the most accurate predictions. To assess a parameter setting,
we used the F1 score as the estimatorâ€™s objective function.

V. ANALYSIS OF THE RESULTS
In this study, when answering RQs, we evaluated the
performance of 9 ML models using direct/indirect TD
indicators as features to predict vulnerable code changes.
To this end, we used SVM, GBT, and XGB classifiers.
We also performed PCA and ICA separately for each model.
When measuring the performance of the models, we used the
recall, precision, false positive rate, and F1-Score. We report
our experimental results for all trained vulnerability models in
Table 5. Our research methodology involves a comprehensive
evaluation of the performance of the vulnerability prediction
model using both balanced and unbalanced test sets created
with various rates (70%,80%,90%). The results for each test
set created are shown in separate tables. This can provide
valuable insights into the robustness and generalizability of
the model for highly imbalanced datasets.
According to our results, direct/indirect TD indicators
within software development, such as software metrics,
code smells, bugs, or refactoring activities, contribute to the
occurrence of vulnerabilities in software projects. Moreover,
we observe that combining software metrics with code smells
achieves higher success rates in predicting vulnerabilities
than refactoring and bugs. In the subsections, we discuss the
answers to the research questions in detail and address the
impact and effectiveness of our proposed methods.
A. RQ1: HOW CAN WE PREDICT SOFTWARE
VULNERABILITIES WITH RESPECT TO CODING ARTIFACTS
LEADING TO TD?
Here, we compare the performance of different feature
set combinations, including Software Metrics (SM), Code
Smells (CS), Bugs (Bug), and Refactoring (Ref) features.
In addition, we evaluate the distinct contribution of code
smells to the prediction of vulnerable commits. As seen in
Table 5, using only SM provides good results in terms of
recall, precision, and F1-Score with rates of 98.9%, 74%,
and 76.9%, respectively. Those rates indicate that software
metrics alone can be a valuable indicator of vulnerabilities.
Combining software metrics with code smells (SM+CS)
significantly improves the results by achieving 99. 1% recall
rate, the 97. 1% F1 score rate, and the highest precision rate
with 96.9%. Nevertheless, SM+CS+Bug+Ref feature set
combination achieves slightly higher recall (99.3%) and F1-
Score (97.3%) rates compared to SM+CS. Combinations of
all features are effective in identifying a high proportion of
all software vulnerabilities.
We further analyze the feature sets with the Scott-Knott
ESD test by ranking their precision, recall, and F1-
Score rates, clustering them in non-overlapping groups,
and identifying significant differences. Figure 4 shows
the results of the Scott-Knott test among all feature set
combinations. Different colors (blue, green, purple, and
orange) of the plot indicate different Scott-Knott test ranks,
and the coloring of the violins represents distinct clusters
of the feature set combinations. When two feature sets
are not significantly different, they are illustrated with the
same color. In Figure 4b, SM+CS+Bug+Ref combination
(shown in blue) consistently achieves high precision scores,
while SM+CS (shown in orange) also exhibits promising
performance. Although we see different precision ratios in
Table 5 for SM, SM+Bug, and SM+Ref combinations, they
are grouped in the same cluster according to the Scott-
Knott results. Similarly, according to Scott-Knott results,
SM+CS+Bug+Ref feature combination and SM+CS again
have high recall rates, and are significantly different from
other models, while there is no significant difference between
the recall results of other models (SM, SM+Bug, and
SM+Ref). Furthermore, SM+CS+Bug+Ref combination
(shown in green) consistently achieves high F1 scores, indi-
cating its effectiveness in predicting software vulnerabilities.
In addition, SM+CS (shown in orange) falls into a different
ESD group with SM+CS+Bug+Ref.
More importantly, feature sets that do not contain code
smells (i.e., SM, SM+Bug, SM+Ref) provide good pre-
diction results in terms of recall, precision, and F1-Score.
However, it is clearly seen that when code smells are
added (i.e., SM+CS, SM+CS+Bug+Ref), they significantly
contribute to the performance of vulnerability prediction.
