1) EFFECT OF MACHINE LEARNING ALGORITHMS
Data-centric and model-centric AI represent two distinct
approaches in the development of AI systems [121].
153908
VOLUME 13, 2025
R. A. Halepmollasi, A. Tosun: Predicting Vulnerable Code Changes Using Technical Debt Indicators
Data-centric approaches focus primarily on the quality,
consistency, and pre-processing of data. In this approach,
the emphasis is on refining the dataset to improve model
performance, with the understanding that better data leads
to more accurate and reliable outcomes. This could involve
techniques like data augmentation, cleaning, and ensuring
diversity and representativeness in the dataset. On the other
hand, model-centric approaches prioritize the algorithmic
aspect, with a focus on selecting and tuning the right
machine learning algorithms to optimize performance. In this
paradigm, the effort is more on improving the model architec-
ture, tweaking hyperparameters, and employing sophisticated
algorithms to achieve the desired results. The choice between
a data-centric or model-centric approach often depends on the
specific problem, available resources, and desired outcomes.
We have adopted a data-centric approach, emphasizing
the meticulous analysis of our data set and the labeling of
the data, rather than focusing on finding the best model
architecture [96], [122]. Having said that, we picked three ML
classifiers, namely SVM, GBT and XGB, and evaluated our
analysis on these classifiersâ€™ performance. While comparing
the performances of ML models, we again applied the
Scott-Knott test to support our results. According to the
results in Table 5, SVM+PCA outperforms all other ML
models by achieving the highest score in terms of recall with
99.3% but its precision (64.4%) and F1-Score (78.2%) are
lower. On the other hand, we report the best results in terms of
precision and F1-Score with XGB and GBT classifiers across
all feature sets.
The results show that applying dimensionality reduction
techniques to some models improves overall performance.
However, the improvements are not consistently significant
across all models and all feature sets. In Table 5, we observe
that when PCA is applied with XGB and GBT classifiers,
the performance metrics often show a decrease in recall,
precision, and F1-score compared to the non-PCA models.
This reduction in performance may be due to the linear
nature of PCA, which may not effectively capture underlying
patterns in data when dealing with complex, nonlinear
relationships. On the other hand, while PCA is applied with
SVM, it improves the recall metric, while it cannot improve
the precision and F1-scores. Meanwhile, models with ICA
also show a decrease in performance compared to models
without ICA.
2) EFFECT OF USING MORE REALISTIC TEST SET
As stated in Section IV-C, the test set must align with
real-life scenarios for the results to have practical value.
Therefore, we have created an imbalanced test data and
evaluated the performance of the models with this version.
In this section, we will discuss the ratio of 90%-10% for
training-test set, while results for other ratios are provided
in Table 10 and Table 11 in Appendix, where similar
conclusions are obtained. When the ratio is 90%-10%,
as shown in Table 6, XGB model achieves the highest recall,
precision, accuracy, and F1-score when all the features (SM,
CS, Bug, Refactoring) are used.
In general, precision in all models decreases, as expected,
leading to a drop in the F1 score. This indicates that the false
positive rate (FPR) increases. In our previous studies [26],
[27], we did not apply additional steps when labeling the
training data, resulting in an imbalanced dataset. Although
we applied traditional under-sampling and over-sampling on
the imbalanced datasets, we could not reach a precision
rate of above 4%(in [26]) and 11.5%(in [27]). In this
study, we observe that our labeling approach, as detailed in
Section IV-C, is highly effective. As shown in Table 6, for the
90%-10% ratio, we have achieved precision rates of 45.2
On the other hand, when examining the results in terms
of feature sets, we have achieved the best precision rate
with the combined and SM+CS sets. This result emphasizes
that CS remains the most effective feature set for predicting
vulnerable commits in real-world scenarios. Regarding ML
algorithms, XGB stands out as the most successful model and
the most robust against imbalanced data.
B. RQ2: HOW DOES V-SZZ+ IMPROVE VULNERABLE
COMMIT PREDICTION COMPARED TO V-SZZ?
When answering RQ2, we evaluate the performance of
software vulnerability prediction models across three config-
urations:
â€¢ V-SZZ+/V-SZZ+: Both training and testing use V-
SZZ+ labeled data.
â€¢ V-SZZ+/V-SZZ: Training uses V-SZZ+ labeled data,
but testing uses V-SZZ labeled data.
â€¢ V-SZZ/V-SZZ: Both training and testing use V-SZZ
labeled data.
We assessed the performance in terms of recall, False
Positive Rate (FPR), and F1-score. The results are presented
using FPR instead of precision because V-SZZ considers
newly labeled instances as safe, which can lead to a high
number of false negatives (vulnerable instances misclassified
as safe). While FPR is moderately higher in the V-SZZ+
setting, this trade-off is acceptable since minimizing missed
vulnerabilities (high recall) is often prioritized over reducing
false alarms. In contrast, the traditional V-SZZ labeling
approach yields very low recall and F1 scores, despite a
low FPR, indicating that it fails to capture the majority
of vulnerable commits due to its snapshot-based and more
limited labeling scope.
V-SZZ+ approach, which labels vulnerability-inducing
commits and all subsequent commits containing vulnera-
bilities until they are fixed, significantly improves vulner-
able commit prediction compared to the standard V-SZZ
approach. The V-SZZ+/V-SZZ+ configuration achieves the
highest recall (up to 98.80%) and F1-scores (up to 76.90%).
It demonstrates its ability to effectively identify vulnerable
commits with a strong balance of precision and recall.
Moreover, V-SZZ+/V-SZZ configuration, despite bene-
fiting from V-SZZ+ during training, suffers from a high

In conclusion, V-SZZ+ significantly enhances vulnerable

the current results strongly favor V-SZZ+ as a robust and
effective method for vulnerability prediction.

C. RQ3: HOW DOES DETECTING CODE SMELLS AT EVERY
COMMIT PERFORM IN IDENTIFYING VULNERABLE
COMMITS?
To address RQ3, we analyze the results presented in
Table 8, which compares the performance of the proposed
commit-level code smell detection approach (referred to
as â€˜â€˜Our approachâ€™â€™) against the traditional snapshot-based
approach for software vulnerability prediction. The per-
formance metrics used to evaluate the models are recall,
precision, and F1-score across various ML models, including
XGB, GBT, SVM, and their variants with PCA and ICA.
The results demonstrate that our approach, which involves
fine-grained, commit-level code smell detection, consistently
outperforms the snapshot-based approach across all models
and metrics. For instance, the XGB model under our
approach achieves recall of 97.4%, precision of 96.9%,
and F1-score of 97.1%, compared to 84.36%, 79.49%,
and 81.80%, respectively, for the snapshot-based approach.
This represents an improvement of approximately 13.04%
in recall, 17.41% in precision, and 15.30% in F1-score.
Similarly, the GBT model shows substantial gains, with our
approach yielding a recall of 95.5%, precision of 91.7%,
and F1-score of 93.6%, compared to 86.93%, 82.01%, and
84.33% for the snapshot-based approach.
The performance of our approach can be attributed to
its ability to capture the temporal evolution of code smells
and their relationship with vulnerability-inducing changes at
a granular level. By analyzing every file modified in each
commit, our approach provides a detailed mapping of smelly
commit-file pairs, enabling a more precise identification
of vulnerable commits. This contrasts with snapshot-based
approaches, which typically analyze the codebase at specific
points in time, often missing intermediate states that may
introduce or exacerbate vulnerabilities.
The fine-grained nature of our approach provides a more
comprehensive perspective on the relationship between TD
and software vulnerabilities. By tracking code smells at
the commit level, we can better correlate specific changes
with the introduction of vulnerabilities, offering insights into
how TD accumulates over time. For example, the higher
recall and F1-scores in our approach suggest that it is
more adept at identifying commits where code smells (e.g.,
complex methods, god classes) align with vulnerability-
inducing changes. Also, this temporal alignment is critical for
understanding the causal links between TD and vulnerabili-
ties, which snapshot-based approaches may overlook due to
their static nature. The results have significant implications
for software development practices. Our approachâ€™s ability
to detect vulnerabilities with higher accuracy at the commit

VI. THREATS TO VALIDITY
In this section, we discuss possible threats to the validity of
our study, including threats to external, construct, internal,
and conclusion validity.
A. INTERNAL VALIDITY
Internal validity refers to the degree that a study provides
credible and accurate evidence for establishing a causal
relationship between variables. In this study, it concerns
the ability to establish a causal relationship between TD
and software vulnerabilities accurately. Possible threats to
internal validity that may have impacted our findings are
primarily associated with the measurement of constructs
at various levels of granularity or the comparison of
different items with one another. We conduct commit-
level analysis in terms of both TD and vulnerabilities to
avoid that problem. Furthermore, potential threats to internal
validity include confounding variables that may influence
the relationship, such as other factors impacting software
security or unobserved variables not accounted for in the
analysis. To mitigate this threat, we employed a rigorous
research design and performed a comprehensive analysis
using direct and indirect TD indicators. Moreover, in a
software project, we examined software metrics, code smells,
bugs, and refactoring activities that can affect the relationship
between TD and vulnerabilities. It is also possible that the
TD and its mitigation method in a file are affected by the
decisions and experience of the developers. But, it is beyond
the scope of this post to investigate the causality between
developers and TD.
B. EXTERNAL VALIDITY
External validity refers to the generalizability of the findings
beyond the specific context of the studied projects. Potential
threats to external validity relate to the extent to which
findings can be applied to different environments, such
as various software projects or programming languages.
However, this study solely focuses on open source Java
projects belonging to ASF. Therefore, we cannot establish the
generalizability of our study outcomes to industrial projects,
or to projects developed in different programming languages
or ecosystems. It is essential to consider the diversity of
projects, development practices, and organizational contexts
to enhance the external validity of the study. Please note
that the data set employed in our investigation provides
a comprehensive source of information, containing 47,303
pull requests, 163,057 issues, 2,987,591 emails, and 366,322
commits. We also chose six projects with the greatest
quantity of real vulnerability data. As a result, we can
confidently claim that our RQs have been addressed on the
most extensive and diverse data set available in this field.
Moreover, to mitigate threats related to reliability, we took
several measures. In Section III, we provide a comprehensive
description of the data preparation pipeline, ensuring trans-
parency and reproducibility and in Section IV, we thoroughly
outline the analysis steps and methods employed in the
study. Additionally, as we use a publicly available dataset,
provide all the query scripts, collected data and extracted
additional dataset in detail, other studies can also replicate
or refute our findings on the relationships between TD
and software vulnerabilities. To enhance the reliability and
balance of our dataset, we selected commits that have files
marked as vulnerable at least once throughout their change
histories as explained in detail in Section IV-C. Furthermore,
in order to assess the robustness and generalizability of our
models, we conducted supplementary experiments where we
153912
VOLUME 13, 2025

intentionally created an imbalanced ratio within the test set.
This involved varying the rates at 70%, 80%, and 90%.
By doing so, we aimed to simulate real-world scenarios where
the data distribution may significantly differ from the training
data.
C. CONSTRUCT VALIDITY
Threats in construct validity concerns the accurate measure-
ment and operationalization of TD indicators and software
vulnerabilities. It is crucial to ensure that the chosen
indicators effectively capture the concepts of interest and
provide reliable and valid measurements. There may be
alternative definitions or measures of TD and vulnerabilities
that were not considered in the study, potentially impacting
the construct validity. The dataset includes software metrics
collected by SourceMeter tool, and hence metrics that the tool
could not identify are excluded. Nevertheless, SourceMeter
is able to extract the majority of the most popular metrics.
Also, the dataset utilized in this study includes refactoring
actions captured by the RMiner tool. However, it is important
to note that the tool may not identify certain refactoring types,
as it primarily focuses on the most commonly employed ones
by developers. Additionally, we recognize the significance of
accurately calculating precision and recall to ensure precise
and comprehensive detection of refactorings. In this regard,
the RMiner tool exhibits a precision of approximately 98%
and a recall of 87%. Furthermore, RMiner is considered one
of the most advanced and widely adopted tools for detecting
refactoring activities in the field.
D. CONCLUSION VALIDITY
Conclusion validity relates to the reliability of the inferences
and conclusions drawn from the analysis. Threats to con-
clusion validity may arise from statistical issues, such as
small sample sizes or low statistical power, which can limit
the generalizability of the findings. Care should be taken to
appropriately analyze and interpret the results to minimize
the risk of drawing inaccurate or overly broad conclusions.
Our conclusions are limited to 6 projects implemented Java,
but the prediction results are statistically compared among
several representations and models, and validated through
non-parametric significance tests.
VII. CONCLUSION
TD and software security may have a strong relationship
in the sense that both can affect the quality attributes of
a software system including security maintainability, sus-
tainability and evolvability. TD refers to extra maintenance
cost and improvement of software projects due to past
decisions that can make it harder to add new features or
fix bugs. Software security, on the other hand, refers to the
measures for protecting against security risks by building
secure software. In this context, software systems with high
TD may be more vulnerable to attacks as it is more difficult
to understand, test, update, and maintain. In this study,

a b s t r a c t 
Usage of Deep Learning (DL) methods is ubiquitous. It is common in the DL/Artiï¬cial Intelligence domain 
to use 3rd party software. TensorFlow is one of the most popular Machine Learning (ML) platforms. Every 
software product is a subject to security failures which often result from software vulnerabilities. In this 
paper, we focus on threats related to 6 common types of threats in TensorFlow implementation. We iden- 
tify them using Common Weakness Enumeration. We analyze more than 100 vulnerability instances. We 
focus on vulnerabilitiesâ€™ severity, impact on conï¬dentiality, integrity and availability, as well as possible 
results of exploitation. We also use Orthogonal Defect Classiï¬cation (ODC). The results show that a ma- 
jority of vulnerabilities are caused by missing/incorrect checking statements, however some ï¬xes require 
more advanced algorithmic changes. Static Analysis Tools tested in our study show low effectiveness in 
detecting known vulnerabilities in TensorFlow, but we provide some recommendations based on the ob- 
tained alerts to improve overall code quality. Further analysis of vulnerabilities helped us to understand 
and characterize different vulnerability types and provide a set of observations. We believe that these 
observations can be useful for the creators of new static analysis tools as a source of inspiration and to 
build the test cases. We also aim to draw the programmersâ€™ attention to the prevalence of vulnerabilities 
in deep learning applications and a low effectiveness of automatic tools to ï¬nd software vulnerabilities 
in such products.

1. Introduction 
Artiï¬cial Intelligence (AI) and Deep Learning (DL) play a cru- 
cial role in digital transformation through automation of decision- 
making process. Although the beneï¬ts of these technologies are 
signiï¬cant, so are the concerns. In the domain of AI, new security 
threats appear. The AI threat landscape is very diï¬ƒcult to map, as 
it involves many advanced methods and complex pipelines. Also, 
AI products often use 3rd party platforms. TensorFlow is one of 
the most popular such platforms ( Abu Daoud et al., 2021 ), or even 
the most popular ( Pang et al., 2020 ). It used by the technology gi- 
ants such as PayPal or eBay ( TensorFlow, 2021 ). The same as for 
every other software product, it is a subject to security failures of- 
ten resulting from software vulnerabilities (a ï¬‚aw resulting from 
a mistake in software speciï¬cation, implementation or conï¬gura- 
tion ( Committee et al., 1990 )). Under some conditions faulty code 
execution can impact Conï¬dentiality, Availability, or Integrity (CIA 
triad) of a system ( Corallo et al., 2020 ). 
âˆ—Corresponding author. 
E-mail addresses: kï¬lus@iitis.pl (K. Filus), joanna@iitis.pl (J. Doma Â´nska) . 
To improve security, organizations such as MITRE and OWASP 
provide guidelines (e.g. OWASP Secure Coding Practices Guide 
( OWASP Secure Coding Practices Quick Reference Guide, 2021 )) and 
conduct standardization activities. The most common standards 
are MITREâ€™s Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVE) ( CVE - 
Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures, 2021 ) and Common Weak- 
ness Enumeration (CWE) ( CWE - Common Weakness Enumera- 
tion, 2021 ). Such standards facilitate weakness identiï¬cation, mit- 
igation, as well as prevention. Also, rankings are created to raise 
awareness regarding the most dangerous weaknesses, e.g. CWE 
TOP25 ( CWE Top 25 Most Dangerous Software Weaknesses, 2021 ). 
Moreover, it is recommended to use tools, e.g. Static Analysis Tools 
(SATs) to analyse software and ï¬nd potential vulnerabilities. 
Despite the fact that a lot of work is being done to improve se- 
curity, vulnerabilities are still extremely common. The most com- 
mon and dangerous vulnerabilities are those related to C/C++ lan- 
guages (According to Veracodeâ€™s report ( Veracode, 2020 ) and CWE 
TOP25 ranking ( CWE Top 25 Most Dangerous Software Weak- 
nesses, 2021 )). They offer high control and eï¬ƒciency, which come 
with a cost - high severity threats. Due to their eï¬ƒciency, C and 
C++ are used to build high-level numerical libraries (e.g. Tensor- 
https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cose.2022.102948 
0167-4048/Â© 2022 The Author(s). Published by Elsevier Ltd. This is an open access article under the CC BY license ( http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/ )

Flow or Caffe). Although there are many other (dedicated) threats 
in AI applications, it is essential to focus on these known vulner- 
abilities, as those are often forgotten in the battle against the AI- 
centred security threats. 
Our paper aims to characterize six different CWE types of soft- 
ware vulnerabilities in TensorFlow implementation (104 CVE in- 
stances): related to memory management issues, integer over- 
ï¬‚ow, improper input validation and NULL pointer dereference. To 
achieve this, our study consists of four complementary direc- 
tions: 
1. Analysis of metadata available on CVEDetails.com: statistics re- 
garding Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS) scores, 
impact on CIA triad and results of exploitation. 
2. Analysis of vulnerabilities and their ï¬xes in TensorFlow based 
on commits regarding these ï¬xes with Orthogonal Defect Clas- 
siï¬cation (ODC). 
3. Analysis of SAT alerts obtained with CppCheck, FlawFinder and 
Visual Code Grepper for vulnerable and neutral ï¬les (before and 
after ï¬x). 
4. Analysis of descriptions of vulnerabilities and their ï¬xes avail- 
able on CVE Details.com and TensorFlow github Advisory and 
code changes. 
Our contribution: The outcome of the study is an analytical 
study regarding the TensorFlow vulnerabilities along with the set 
of observations and the main ï¬ndings regarding these vulnerabili- 
ties. We describe vulnerabilities at the CWE type level along with 
examples from the TensorFlow implementation. We have compiled 
a comprehensive knowledge base regarding main causes of differ- 
ent CWE types, their results and exploitation ways. We also fo- 
cused on the ways to avoid/minimize the exploitation chance. We 
analyzed a larger number of CWE types than other works in the 
literature (they usually analyze one or two CWE types at once). 
Moreover, our work seems to be the ï¬rst one analyzing a DL li- 
brary itself and not its dependencies. We used our main ï¬ndings 
to create a checklist. The checklist includes the characteristic for 
the numerical libraries functionalities and cases, in which there is 
a high chance of introducing security vulnerabilities. We hope that 
our work will help the developers of numerical libraries to spot 
the parts of the code being developed that can become potential 
security hot-spots. When it comes to developers of static analysis 
tools - we believe that our insights can be used to create new rules 
in the rule-based systems, and also to build test cases for such so- 
lutions. Also, we could not ï¬nd any work testing the usefulness of 
SATs for detecting vulnerabilities in deep learning products, there- 
fore we decided to test 3 freely available SATs. Our concise eval- 
uation (mainly the qualitative one but with some quantitative re- 
sults) and discussion of different SATs can serve as a guide for se- 
lecting free tools to assess code quality. We hope that our paper 
will raise awareness regarding Tensorï¬‚ow and related security is- 
sues. Although the described vulnerabilities are well-known, they 
are still a major threat to C/C++ software products, therefore rais- 
ing awareness of these issues should be an ongoing effort - espe- 
cially in the domain of AI and Deep Learning, in which algorithms 
are often treated as miraculous black box machines for solving a 
plethora of problems. 
The rest of the paper is organized as follows: Section 2 ex- 
plains the term â€œsoftware vulnerabilitiesâ€ and describes methods 
that can be used to detect them. It also shortly outlines the AI vul- 
nerability landscape and introduces a clear division of â€œhigh-levelâ€
AI-dedicated and â€œlow-levelâ€ traditional threats - characteristic for 
C/C++ products (we focus on these vulnerabilities in our study). We 
also describe the related works in that section. In Section 3 , we de- 
scribe our approach to the analysis and the methods used in our 
study. In Section 4 , we analyze the metadata regarding different 
vulnerability types available at CVEDetails.com. In Section 5 , we 
perform the Orthogonal Defect Classiï¬cation and describe its re- 
sults. In Section 6 , we use three freely available SATs to analyze all 
of the code ï¬les taken into consideration in our study. Section 7 fo- 
cuses on the analysis of descriptions, advisories and source code 
ï¬les of known vulnerabilities. Section 8 concludes the paper. In 
Appendix A , we provide our checklist regarding the security threats 
and how to avoid them. 
2. Background and related work 
2.1. Software vulnerabilities 
Vulnerability 
is 
deï¬ned 
by 
ISO/IEC 
270 0 0:2018 
( ISO/IEC 270 0 0:2018, 2018 ) as a â€œweakness of an asset or con- 
trol that can be exploited by one or more threatsâ€. Undetected 
vulnerabilities ultimately entail signiï¬cant maintenance costs 
( Zhioua et al., 2014 ) and can cause potential violation of security 
policies ( Shin et al., 2010 ). CWE and CVE are two of the most 
important standards used to identify vulnerabilities. CWE deï¬nes 
vulnerability types (not speciï¬c instances) and CVE deï¬nes speciï¬c 
instances within a product or a system. 
A typical example of a CWE can be CWE-476 - NULL 
Pointer Dereference. Its instance in TensorFlow is CVE-2021-37638 
(in ï¬le tensorï¬‚ow/core/kernels/ragged_tensor_to_tensor_op.cc). A 
missing check results in a NULL pointer dereference when 
â€œrow_partition_types_â€ is empty and the code tries to access its 
ï¬rst element. Below, we present a ï¬x of this vulnerability (a yellow 
line was the one allowing vulnerability exploitation and the other 
ones had to be added to ï¬x it - a missing if statement and re- 
turn from the function with the corresponding error) ( Commit ï¬x- 
ing CVE-2021-37638 vulnerability, 2021 ): 
Listing. 1: Example of the CWE-476 vulnerability ï¬x in the Ten- 
sorFlow implementation 
2.2. Vulnerabilities regarding artiï¬cial intelligence 
Due to complexity, large scope and constant development of the 
AI domain, the AI threat landscape is still not completely deï¬ned 
and diï¬ƒcult to map. It is also impossible to predict all of the future 
scenarios, especially when DL algorithms are applied to solve prob- 
lems that are troublesome for humans. Some of the threats dedi- 
cated to AI include compromising AI inference, model poisoning 
and sabotage, data poisoning (malicious actors inject false train- 
ing data to corrupt the learned model ( Steinhardt et al., 2017 )) and 
tempering, as well as manipulation of data labelling. Models can 
also be tricked using adversarial examples ( Responsible AI prac- 
tices Google AI, 2021 ). 
Abstracting from these dedicated threats, which we cannot fully 
combat, there are other signiï¬cant threats that are often over- 
looked in the AI threat research papers - compromises of model 
frameworks and 3rd party provider failures. Many companies use 
external (often open-source) machine learning libraries to power 
their solutions. This 3rd party software itself can (and probably 
does) contain many software vulnerabilities, especially those using 
C/C++ for speed and high resource control. They are no less signif- 
icant than threats crafted speciï¬cally against AI. Moreover, these 
are the threats that we know and are able to handle and imple- 
ment some mitigation strategies. That is why, in this study we fo- 
cus on these particular vulnerabilities.

K. Filus and J. Doma Â´nska 
Computers & Security 124 (2023) 102948 
2.3. Vulnerability detection 
The approaches to software vulnerability detection can be di- 
vided into two main groups: Static Analysis and Dynamic Anal- 
ysis ( Ghaffarian and Shahriari, 2017 ). Dynamic analysis requires 
an executable version of a product and is usually very time- 
consuming, as it needs to test a suï¬ƒcient number of test cases 
( Zhioua et al., 2014 ). Static analysis can be applied directly to 
source code, thus we use it to examine the TensorFlow imple- 
mentation. Programs checking the source code ï¬les (based on a 
set of predeï¬ned rules ( Pereira et al., 2021b )) are called Static 
Analysis Tools (SATs). A compilation of static analysis products 
with a description of supported languages, availability and a brief 
characterization can be found on the OWASP organizationâ€™s web- 
site ( Source Code Analysis Tools - OWASP ). Alternatively, one can 
use a list provided by The National Institute of Standards and 
Technology (NIST) ( Source Code Security Analyzers - NIST ). The 
examples of such programs dedicated for C/C++ are CppCheck 
( CppCheck, 2021 ), FlawFinder ( FlawFinder, 2021 ) and Visual Code 
Grepper ( Visual Code Grepper, 2022 ). These tools are commonly 
used in the literature Croft et al. (2021) ; Kaur and Nayyar (2020) ; 
Khaled and Abdelbaki (2020) ; Li et al. (2018) ; Pereira et al. (2021a) ; 
Riom et al. (2021) ; Zhao et al. (2021) to examine general-purpose 
products. In this study, we use them to examine their ability to 
ï¬nd known and potentially unknown issues in TensorFlow. 
2.4. Related work 
ML-based Vulnerability Detection Some recent works use ML 
methods to ï¬nd vulnerabilities. In Medeiros et al. (2020) , differ- 
ent ML-based vulnerability detection methods have been tested. In 
Filus et al. (2021) , metrics generated via SonarQube and CCCC tool 
were used (with ML models) to detect resource management error 
vulnerabilities (CWE-399) and buffer error vulnerabilities (CWE- 
119). The study showed that the detection effectiveness depends 
on the CWE type. In Filus et al. (2020) , the system based on neu- 
ral networks and mixed features (text and from SonarQube) was 
tested to detect CWE-399 vulnerabilities ( Filus et al., 2020 ). In 
Li et al. (2018) , VulDeePecker was proposed - a vulnerability de- 
tection DL system - and tested on CWE-119 and CWE-399 vulner- 
abilities. 
Using SATs for vulnerability detection Although the ML mod- 
els are widely used in the area of vulnerability detection, 
the traditional rule-based Static Analysis Tools are still com- 
monly used. In Pereira et al. (2021b) , Buffer Overï¬‚ow Vulner- 
abilities (CWE-119) have been analyzed using ODC and two 
SATs. In Arusoaie et al. (2017) , eleven C/C++ SATs were bench- 
marked based on the Toyota test suite ( Shiraishi et al., 2015 ) (it 
was also used in Nong et al. (2021) , in which different tools 
were tested to ï¬nd memory-related vulnerabilities). Also works 
Croft et al. (2021) ; Kaur and Nayyar (2020) ; Khaled and Abdel- 
baki (2020) ; Riom et al. (2021) ; Zhao et al. (2021) aim to bench- 
mark different SATs. Their ï¬ndings showed us the potential of 
three SATs in the context of vulnerability detection: CppCheck, 
FlawFinder and Visual Code Grepper. We use these ï¬ndings as 
a guideline and test the effectiveness of these SATs in terms of 
ï¬nding known vulnerabilities in the TensorFlow implementation. 
Nevertheless, software developers can also reach for other alter- 
native products. A compilation of static analysis products with a 
description of supported languages, availability and a brief charac- 
terization can be found on the OWASP organizationâ€™s website along 
with the important selection criteria ( Source Code Analysis Tools - 
OWASP ). Alternatively, one can use a list provided by The National 
Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) ( Source Code Security 
Analyzers - NIST ). It is also worth mentioning a different kind of 
a static analysis tool, which can be used along with the described 
products - code clone detectors. Such tools aim to ï¬nd fragments 
of code copied and pasted within/between software products. The 
example of such a product is VUDDY ( Kim et al., 2017 ), which iden- 
tiï¬es code clones of known CVEs (exact and renamed clones in 
particular). Such tools can be effective in ï¬nding copied parts of 
vulnerable code, however, they show low effectiveness in ï¬nding 
restructured and semantic clones of such vulnerabilities ( Kim et al., 
2017 ). In fact, restructured and semantic clones are excluded from 
the VUDDY clone detection ( Kim et al., 2017 ). On contrary, the 
ï¬ndings presented in our work, do not focus on the code clones, 
but aim to summarize the semantic meaning of code, near which 
vulnerabilities are often introduced. As a result, our main ï¬nd- 
ings provide a more general description of potential security hot- 
spots. Nevertheless, tools such as VUDDY can be helpful, when 
programmers reuse some parts of code from the open-source 
libraries. 
Vulnerabilities in AI products Although numerous works regard 
software vulnerability detection based on Deep Learning models 
( Fang et al., 2019; Filus et al., 2020; Li et al., 2021; 2018; Pechenkin 
and Demidov, 2018 ), works on vulnerabilities in AI products them- 
selves are very limited. One work that we were able to ï¬nd, 
Xiao et al. (2018) , discusses security risks in DL frameworks (Ten- 
sorFlow, Caffe and Torch). However, they examine vulnerabilities 
mainly in their dependencies (i.e. NumPy for TensorFlow, opencv 
for Caffe/Torch) - and not directly in DL frameworks code. Given 
the ubiquity of DL models in a variety of applications, this is a 
large gap in the literature. 
Limitations of the related works Besides the lack of a thorough 
analysis of vulnerabilities in ML products, another limitation of 
the existing works is that they analyze vulnerabilities regardless 
of their CWE type or a very limited number of vulnerability types. 
Moreover, they do not focus on their signiï¬cance and severity. 
Our work in relation to the available literature With respect to 
the works present in the literature, our work can be embedded 
closest to that of Pereira et al. (2021b) in terms of methodology 
and Xiao et al. (2018) in terms of subject matter. Our work aims 
to ï¬ll the gap between them. First of all, we aim to focus on the 
implementation of a deep learning framework itself, and not on 
its dependencies, as in work ( Pereira et al., 2021b ). In terms of 
methodology, work ( Xiao et al., 2018 ) provides a systematic anal- 
ysis of CWE-119 issues (Improper Restriction of Operations within 
the Bounds of a Memory Buffer). Authors examined three C/C++ 
applications: Linux Kernel, Xen and Mozilla. In contrast to these 
old products, we examine a relatively new product in which at 
least some changed programming practices can be expected (al- 
though the development of Linux Kernel, Xen and Mozilla is con- 
tinuous, they have never been rewritten from scratch). Moreover, 
the numerical libraries, such as TensorFlow, mostly rely on math- 
ematical operations using arrays. Here, the root causes of vulnera- 
bilities can be different - e.g. they can result from an insuï¬ƒcient 
knowledge of the mathematical methods to be implemented (as- 
sumptions, boundary conditions, etc.). We aim to identify speciï¬c 
root causes of different CWE types. We take into consideration 
three types of memory issues: not only a generic memory-related 
type - CWE-119, but also its â€œchildrenâ€: Out-of-bounds Read and 
Write. We also analyze problems related to NULL Pointer Derefer- 
ence (CWE-476) and Integer Overï¬‚ow or Wraparound (CWE-190) 
- other common C/C+ issues that are critical for numerical opera- 
tions and dealing with dynamic data structures. We also analyze 
issues related to Improper Input Validation (CWE-20) - as one ex- 
ample of a language-independent CWE group. Work ( Pereira et al., 
2021b ) shows that SATs lack rules to detect most examined vul- 
nerabilities, however the can effectively ï¬nd some memory-related 
vulnerabilities in traditional products. Therefore, we aim to exam- 
ine whether free SATs can be used to improve the security of a 
different product kind - a modern numerical library.

Fig. 1. The overview of the approach used to analyze the TensorFlow vulnerabilities. 
3. Approach to analysis 
In our study, we aim to analyze different types of software vul- 
nerabilities in terms of their severity, impact on conï¬dentiality, in- 
tegrity and availability, as well as possible results of exploitation. 
We also analyze the characteristics of different vulnerability types 
and determine speciï¬c situations, in which these particular types 
can be introduced. We test three static code analysis tools to ex- 
amine their effectiveness in ï¬nding known software vulnerabilities. 
We use three sources of data: CVE Details, CWE TOP25 rank- 
ing and GitHub. We use CVE Details to ï¬nd known instances of 
vulnerabilities in TensorFlow. CVE instances are connected with a 
speciï¬c CWE type. We use this knowledge along with information 
from CWE TOP25 to ï¬nd the most prevalent and severe vulnera- 
bilities. This way we consider TensorFlow as an individual product 
(a numerical library) as well as an example of a modern C/C++ ap- 
plication. Then, we use CVE Details for the second time - to ï¬nd 
CVE instances under a speciï¬c CWE group and gather metadata re- 
garding those vulnerabilities. We take into consideration only those 
CVE pages that provide a single GitHub commit ï¬xing a speciï¬c 
vulnerability. We download vulnerable (before a ï¬x) and neutral 
(after a ï¬x) ï¬les. We inspect the ï¬les manually (with ODC) and 
via static code analyzers. As a results, we provide some numer- 
ical results regarding the effectiveness of SATs and statistics re- 
garding the examined vulnerabilitiesâ€™ metadata. We also provide 
a set of insights regarding different types of vulnerabilities and a 
list, in which we include speciï¬c situations, in which programmers 
can introduce security issues. We present this list in a form of a 
checklist for programmers of numerical libraries, programmers of 
applications using such libraries, as well as creators of SATs (they 
can use it to create new rules or to determine test cases for their 
solutions). In Fig. 1 we present the overview of the steps of our 
analysis. 
3.1. Selection of CWE types and CVE instances 
To choose the CWE types we considered the number of avail- 
able TensorFlow CVE instances per CWE type and its position in 
the 2021 CWE TOP25 ranking ( CWE Top 25 Most Dangerous Soft- 
ware Weaknesses, 2021 ). This way, we take into consideration 
three different aspects of different vulnerability types: their preva- 
lence and severity in software products in general, as well as their 
prevalence in Tensorï¬‚ow. CVE Details provides us with information 
regarding the occurrence of known vulnerability types in Tensor- 
Flow. CWE TOP25, on the other hand, takes into consideration not 
only the prevalence of different vulnerability types in diverse ap- 
plications, but also the severity of these vulnerabilities and their 
impact on the system in the case of exploitation. This allows us to 
treat TensorFlow individually and also as an example of a modern 
C/C++ application. 
Eventually, we included 6 CWE types ( CWE - Common Weak- 
ness Enumeration, 2021 ) (104 CVE instances in total). In Table 1 , 
we gathered all the examined CWE types along with the number 
of their instances in TensorFlow and their rank in the CWE TOP25 
ranking. The examined vulnerabilities seem to be adequate from 
a security point of view for a numerical library. Such libraries of- 
ten rely on mathematical operations using arrays. Although lan- 
guages such as C or C++ offer speed calculations, they do not 
provide built-in protection against memory access/overwriting or 
checks regarding buffer bounds. Our analysis includes a more 
generic memory-related CWE type - CWE-119, but also its â€œchil- 
drenâ€: CWE-125 and CWE-787 as more speciï¬c types of memory 
issues. We also analyze different problems characteristic for nu- 
merical operations and dealing with dynamic data structures: re- 
lated to NULL Pointer Dereference (CWE-476) and Integer Overï¬‚ow 
or Wraparound (CWE-190). We also analyze issues related to Im- 
proper Input Validation (CWE-20) - as one example of a language- 
independent CWE group affecting all kinds of applications.

source code ï¬les 
We used CVE Details page to ï¬nd the CVE metadata and links 
to github commits with the source code. On the particular CVE 
page, information on CVSS Score, impact on CIA triad (three levels 
are used: None, Partial and Complete) and potential exploitation

ï¬les include the ï¬x). 
3.3. Orthogonal Defect Classiï¬cation 
Orthogonal Defect Classiï¬cation ( Chillarege et al., 1992 ) is a sys- 
tematic approach developed by IBM, used to classify and analyze 
software defects by transforming semantic information into a mea- 
surement ( Pereira et al., 2021b ). The approach is frequently used in 
software root-cause analysis ( Pereira et al., 2021b ). Full analysis in- 
volves describing the defect before and after a ï¬x with a series of 
8 attributes (with predeï¬ned values). The following attributes can 
be used: activity, trigger, impact (attributes regarding an opened 
defect), target, defect type, qualiï¬er, source and age (attributes re- 
garding an opened defect). To examine vulnerabilities in our study, 
we use two attributes: defect type and qualiï¬er (the others do not 
include any additional relevant information regarding the charac- 
teristics of a particular vulnerability ( Pereira et al., 2021b )). 
Attribute defect type is used to represent the semantics of 
the ï¬x (it captures the meaning of the ï¬x, thus the nature 
of the particular issue)( Chillarege et al., 1992 ). Eight values can 
be assigned to this attribute. We exclude two of them from 
our analysis (build/package/merge and documentation, as we fo- 
cus only on the source code ï¬les). Based on deï¬nitions from 
Chillarege et al. (1992) and Bridge and Miller (1998) , we can de- 
ï¬ne the defect types in the following way: 
â€¢ Assignment/Initialization - problems related to no/incorrect 
assignment of the variable value. 
â€¢ Checking - problems related to conditional logic (incorrect, 
missing conditions). When multiple checking statements have 
to be added/corrected it can belong to type Algorithm/Method. 
â€¢ Timing - problems related to serialization of shared resources. 
â€¢ Algorithm/method - problems related to implementation (gen- 
erally no design ï¬x should be necessary). 
â€¢ Function - problems related to no or incorrect implementation 
of some signiï¬cant capability, end-user interfaces or global data 
structures (generally, it does require a design change). 
â€¢ Interface - problems related to communication issues between 
subsystems, components, device drivers etc. 
Types above have been described in more detail in work 
Bridge and Miller (1998) . 
Qualiï¬er is used to capture what had to be done to ï¬x a par- 
ticular vulnerability in terms of code changes: 
â€¢ Missing - to ï¬x the issue, new code had to be added. 
â€¢ Incorrect - to ï¬x the issue, some code had to be adjusted. 
â€¢ Extraneous - to ï¬x the issue, some code had to be removed. 
We can say, that it extends the semantic information provided 
via a defect type. It provides us with insights on whether a partic- 
ular defect resulted from an omission or rather from some kind of 
a programming mistake. 
Using these two attributes, allows us to associate a vulnera- 
bility with particular activities of different stages of software de- 
velopment and faults in this process ( Chillarege et al., 1992 ). They 
provide us with the causal information regarding an analyzed vul- 
nerability. The resulting insights describe the nature of different 
vulnerability types in a systematic and easy to interpret way. 
In our analysis, we select appropriate attribute values based on 
the changes occurring during the patch of a given vulnerability. 
The changes can be easily inspected via github - by displaying the 
corresponding commit. 
The ODC is a manual classiï¬cation, so similarly to work 
( Pereira et al., 2021b ), two researchers conducted the analysis for 
greater independence and fault tolerance. First, we performed the 
discussion, set the classiï¬cation criteria and analyzed the ï¬rst sev- 
eral examples together. We separately analyzed all of the remain- 
ing CVE instances, and at the end, discussed the non-overlapping 
results and found a common consensus - this is how the ï¬nal re- 
sults have been obtained. 
3.4. Running SATs and analysis of the alerts 
We used three commonly used static code analyzers: CppCheck 
(version 2.6), FlawFinder (version 2.0.19) and Visual Code Grepper 
(version 2.2.0.0). We decided to use only SATs that can be used for 
free - as those SATs can be used by everyone. We chose these par- 
ticular SATs as they showed superior performance over the other 
analyzers tested in the works ( Croft et al., 2021; Kaur and Nayyar, 
2020; Khaled and Abdelbaki, 2020; Riom et al., 2021; Zhao et al., 
2021 ). In work Riom et al. (2021) , 9 SATs were tested. Cppcheck 
was reported to produce very few false positive alerts and special- 
ize in ï¬nding undeï¬ned behaviours. Also in work Kaur and Nay- 
yar (2020) , it was shown that CppCheck was able to ï¬nd the max- 
imum number of the examined vulnerabilities out of the tested 
5
K. Filus and J. Doma Â´nska 
Computers & Security 124 (2023) 102948 
tools. In work Khaled and Abdelbaki (2020) , the results showed 
that although the Visual Code Grepper SAT gives a relatively large 
number of false positive alerts, it was able to report all the ex- 
amined vulnerabilities (false negative rate equaled zero). In work 
Zhao et al. (2021) , Flawï¬nder signiï¬cantly outperformed another 
tested traditional SAT in terms of ï¬nding CWE-119 memory-related 
issues and F1 Score. Also in work Croft et al. (2021) , Flawï¬nder was 
able to produce the highest recall values out of all tested SATs. 
We ï¬rst ran the analysis on vulnerable ï¬les corresponding to 
the chosen CWE group, and then we analyzed the respective neu- 
tral ï¬les. We did this for all the examined CWE groups. Dif- 
ferent levels of granularity can be used in the process of soft- 
ware vulnerability detection: among others package-level, ï¬le- 
level, function-level and line-level ( Kluban et al., 2022 ). Usually, 
at least a function-level is recommended, as it provides suï¬ƒcient 
information regarding a code functionality - unlike separate lines 
of code ( Kluban et al., 2022 ). While the Machine Learning models 
built to detect vulnerabilities usually operate on a function-level 
(e.g. works Russell et al. (2018) ; Wei et al. (2021) ), the ï¬le-level 
seems to be the most suitable in our case, as we aim to perform 
the overall assessment of adequacy of different warnings per ï¬le. 
We take into consideration not only a particular vulnerability, but 
also the warnings regarding the qualitative improvements, which 
can reduce the chance of introducing new vulnerabilities in the fu- 
ture. We believe that such an evaluation will be the most useful 
for those who would like to use these static code analyzers to ï¬nd 
security issues and to improve the overall quality of their code. 
When the ï¬les were analyzed for a speciï¬c CWE group, we an- 
alyzed the alerts in terms of their CWE ID (when given), accuracy 
of ï¬nding lines regarding the examined CVE instances (we used the 
information regarding the lines for which SATs found issues, found 
them in ï¬les regarding speciï¬c vulnerabilities on GitHub and com- 
pared with true lines that were responsible for some vulnerability). 
We also analyzed whether the given alerts should be considered 
(we chose alerts that can be used to improve the quality of Tensor- 
Flow code and described the potential issues and improvements). 
We also compared the results obtained for corresponding vulnera- 
ble and neutral versions of ï¬les. In the case of VCG, which offers 
an analysis of comments (to ï¬nd potentially unï¬nished fragments 
of code), we chose two example ï¬les and examined how many 
â€œTODOâ€ instances are found by VCG and how many instances of 
such comments truly are in a particular ï¬le (we used a Visual Stu- 
dio Code search engine for this purpose and simply typed â€œTODOâ€). 
We computed the number of false positives (false alarms - when 
a comment is just an explenation of the code) and false negatives 
(when a clear â€œTODOâ€ can be found and it was not reported by 
VCG). 
3.5. Analysis of text descriptions of vulnerabilities and source code 
elements 
After our primary analysis of information on CVE Details and 
ODC, we focused on the vulnerability descriptions regarding all of 
the examined CVE instances available on CVE Details and corre- 
sponding TensorFlow advisories, as well as code implementations 
(if necessary) to ï¬nd common causes and results of vulnerabili- 
ties occurrence and exploitation. We deï¬ned possible exploitation 
strategies of the users of application using TensorFlow background 
and possible ways to avoid their exploitation in a form of a check- 
list

ity, Integrity and Availability (CIA triad) of a system when a vul- 
nerability is exploited. Common Vulnerability Scoring System mea- 
sures the severity and characteristics of software vulnerabilities. A 
score ranges from 0 to 10. CVSS is considered to be a standard 
measurement system for organizations, governments and in indus- 
try, as it provides consistent and accurate vulnerability severity 
scores (according to National Institute of Standards and Technology 
- NIST ( National Vulnerability Database (NVD), 2021 )). CIA traid, on 
the other hand, refers to the fundamental elements of information 
systems: Conï¬dentiality, Integrity and Availability ( Samonas and 
Coss, 2014 ). Three categories are used to describe the impact on 
each CIA triad part: none, partial and complete ( Toloudis et al., 
2016 ). 
To gather our metadata, we used the CVE details searching en- 
gine (â€œVulnerability Searchâ€) and typed Tensorï¬‚ow in the â€œProd- 
uctâ€ box. We exported all available data to a csv ï¬le and processed 
it. We calculated average, standard deviation, minimum and max- 
imum values of the CVSS scores for different types of examined 
vulnerabilities. We also counted the CVE instances from each CWE 
group belonging to different categories of the CIA triad impact (for 
all parts of CIA triad separately). We used these values to compute 
the percentage of these impact categories per each CWE type. The 
results can be observed in Fig. 2 and Tables 2 and 3 . CWE groups 
in Fig. 2 have been sorted in the descending order of the average 
CVSS score. 
It can be observed that the highest values of CVSS score have 
been obtained for memory-related issues (CWE-787, CWE-119 and 
CWE-125) - 7.5 (they usually impact all of the CIA triad elements). 
These vulnerabilities are also the most diversiï¬ed in terms of pos- 
sible exploit results (overï¬‚ows, bypasses, code executions, memory 
corruptions and DoS - see Table 2 ). CWE-190 group (Integer Over- 
ï¬‚ow or Wraparound) obtained the lowest CVSS values on aver- 
age (they usually impact only Availability - see Table 3 ). CWE-190 
vulnerabilities result in overï¬‚ows and DoS. The examined CWE- 
20 examples (Improper Input Validation) obtained higher average 
and maximum values than CWE-190 vulnerabilities (also, the high- 
est standard deviation - suggesting the most varying CVSS scores). 
These vulnerabilities have an impact mainly on Availability of sys- 
tems (via Denial of Service - see Table 2 ). The results obtained for 
CWE-476 vulnerabilities are similar to those obtained for CWE-20 
in terms of statistics of CVSS scores (almost the same mean, std 
and the same minimum and maximum values). Also these vul- 
nerabilities impact mainly Availability, but in contrast to CWE-20 
vulnerabilities, almost 50 percent of them can also impact Conï¬- 
dentiality or Integrity. For the majority of the examined CVE in- 
stances, the exploitation results were not classiï¬ed to any of the 
given groups, but some of the vulnerability instances can result in 
bypasses, denials of service and code execution.

For the memory-related vulnerability types (CWE-787, CWE-

â€œCheckingâ€ and â€œAlgorithm/Methodâ€, indicating the need for more 
extensive improvements. This type of CWE is the parent type of 
the other memory-related CWE-types, so it can deal with more di- 
verse cases. The prevalence of â€œMissingâ€ values for the attribute 
â€œQualiï¬erâ€ means that probably in the implementation phase of 
some functionalities, the need for simpler or more complex valida-

problem can be observed for CWE-20. For CWE-125 also values 
â€œFunctionâ€ and â€œInterfaceâ€ of attribute â€œDefect Typeâ€ were ob-

change.

to be ï¬xed (â€œDefect Typeâ€: â€œAlgorithmâ€). For CWE-476, the ODC 
showed that the problem was mainly missing checks (which is log- 
ical, since in many cases to ï¬x a vulnerability, a check is needed 
whether the pointer to be accessed is not a nullpointer).

We can summarize our ï¬ndings as follow: CppCheck performs 
a more in-depth analysis in addition to simple checks for â€unsafeâ€
functions. Visual Code Grepper besides code, also analyses com-

for â€unsafeâ€ functions - its practical application to improve security

6.1. Flawï¬nder 
For the majority of CWE groups, the number of issues was ex-

787 : 7 issues found, CWE-20 : 9 with 1 CWE-20/CWE-807, CWE-

in a particular context the warning is not appropriate. E.g. CWE-

are false alarms, since random was not used for security purposes 
in the analyzed context. Problems related to CWE-120, consid-

memcpy issue was reported by the SAT (â€œmemcpy: Does not check

6.2. CppCheck 
For all of the CWE groups, the results were exactly the same 
for vulnerable and neutral versions of ï¬les (see Table 5 ). In no 
case the instance of a true CWE type was found by CppCheck. 
Issues with the following CWE IDs were found: CWE-398 (Code 
Quality), CWE-563 (Assignment to Variable without Use), CWE-571 
(Expression is Always True), CWE-197 (Numeric Truncation Error). 
Generally, the great majority of warnings were of type CWE-398 
(Quality) and considered e.g. raw loops, local variable shadowing 
outer argument, reducing the scopes of some variables and the 
presence of the same if conditions - some of them were reasonable 
and changes could be applied. This prompted us to include one of 
the suggestions that can be used to improve the code quality. For 
ï¬les ( Commit ï¬xing CVE-2021-29566 vulnerability (2021) ) related 
to CVE-2021-29566 (CWE-787), CppCheck returned the following 
warning: â€œLocal variable â€™dâ€™ shadows outer argument (CWE-398)â€: 
It is not a good practise to redeï¬ne a function argument and 
use it as a counter in a loop - it should be ï¬xed. A different vari- 
able should be used here to obtain better code quality. A comment 
shows that it is planned to write a multi-thread implementation of 
this function and potentially const CPUDevice& d will be used there 
(which is now shadowed). Similar issues were found, e.g. variable 
â€œiâ€ in ï¬le tensorï¬‚ow/core/kernels/save_restore_v2_ops.cc. It can of- 
ten be tempting to use variables such as â€iâ€, â€dâ€ or other single 
letters as loop counters, but it should always be checked whether 
this variable is not already taken - this, even if it does not cause 
problems at the moment, may introduce problems in the future 
(e.g. when the code is rebuilt by another programmer). 
6.3. Visual Code Grepper 
Unfortunately, Visual Code Grepper does not provide Com-

warnings with different tags (e.g. â€œpotentially unsafeâ€, â€œsuspicious 
commentâ€, â€œcriticalâ€). The highest severity of a warning was â€œhighâ€
- no cases with â€œcriticalâ€ warnings were observed. Besides analyz- 
ing code, VCG also processes comments and analyzes its contents 
via text analysis (e.g. it searches for terms such as â€œTODOâ€). In 
some cases it can be useful - e.g. see Section 6.2 for an example of 
a planned functionality. It also ï¬nds StrCat and memcpy instances 
and suggests replacing them with different functions, as those 
functions appear in Microsoftâ€™s banned function list. VCG returns 
warnings when it ï¬nds multiple deletes for a particular variable 
or when it cannot ï¬nd a delete for a new (in the cases examined 
by us manually, these were false positives - they regarded the

7. Analysis of descriptions, advisories and source code 
Our manual analysis resulted in the identiï¬cation of common 
effects of exploitation of different CWE types: 
â€¢ CWE-787 : heap buffer overï¬‚ows (writes and reads), segfaults, 
corruptions of the memory. Chained with other types can result 
in more advanced exploits and can trigger undeï¬ned behavior 
by null pointer dereference. 
â€¢ CWE-20 : access to data outside the bounds of heap allocated 
data, segmentation faults, assertion failures, DoS (by query-of- 
death vulnerability, â€˜SIGABRTâ€˜ signal raised by the operating 
system or â€˜CHECKâ€˜-failure), data corruption and undeï¬ned be- 
haviors. 
â€¢ CWE-190 : dereferencing invalid pointers - which can cause 
memory allocation problems and denials of service (via 
â€˜CHECKâ€˜-fail). 
â€¢ CWE-119 : read from outside the bounds of the heap buffer al- 
located buffers, segmentation faults, data corruption (by access- 
ing data out of bounds), a heap buffer overï¬‚ow (by accessing 
data out of bounds), undeï¬ned behaviors and DoS (via out of 
memory allocation). 
â€¢ CWE-125 : reads/writes outside of bounds of heap allocated 
data (and disclosure of the contents of process memory), seg- 
mentation faults, undeï¬ned behaviors due to binding to nullptr, 
uninitialized memory accesses and DoS. 
â€¢ CWE-476 : segmentation faults, read from/write to memory out- 
side the bounds of heap allocated data, undeï¬ned behavior, 
crashes and DoS. 
7.1. CWE-787 - Out-of-bounds Write 
CWE-787 vulnerabilities can be caused by no/incomplete/invalid 
validation of input parameters and include wrong types (e.g. CVE- 
2021-37650 - implementation assumes that all records in the ex- 
amined dataset are strings), wrong values (e.g. CVE-2021-29571 - 
implementation assumes using correct values whereas an incor- 
rect value can be passed) and empty variables as arguments (e.g. 
CVE-2021-29535 - it is assumed that input arguments are valid 
scalars and their numeric values are accessed directly. In the case 
of empty tensors, accessing the index 0 results in overï¬‚ow). An- 
other source is no/incomplete/invalid validation of the values calcu- 
lated inside the function , e.g. CVE-2021-29540 - the computed size 
of the ï¬lter is not validated and used instead of the number of 
ï¬lter elements during convolutional ï¬lter backpropagation, which 
can result in an overï¬‚ow when the computed size is too large. 
Another source can be no validation for empty data structures or 
no validation whether the examined data structure has enough ele- 
ments for some operation (e.g. backpropagation) - e.g. CVE-2021- 
29578 - it is not checked whether the pooling sequence arguments 
have enough elements for the required shape. Also, when more 
than one tensor is used in the operation, the source can be lack 
of shape compatibility validation of the tensors (e.g. CVE-2021-29609 
- it is not validated whether the second dimensions of sparse ten- 
sors used in the operation match). Last but not least, the issue can 
be connected to no/improper validation of ML models and specially 
crafted models can cause the vulnerability exploitation (e.g. CVE- 
2021-29603 - for TFLite).

How to exploit? - specially crafted inputs, models, - using func- 
tion arguments with wrong values, wrong types and empty 
variables, - using empty structures or the incompatible ones for 
the operation (both one- and multi-tensor ones) 
7.2. CWE-20 - Improper Input Validation 
Main sources of CWE-20 vulnerabilities are no/improper/ 
insuï¬ƒcient checks whether examined data structures are not empty or 
have a proper dimension (shape) and lack of handling of these oc- 
curences (e.g. CVE-2020-15190 based on the boolean value, one of 
the tensors is the input tensor and the other one should be empty. 
The eager runtime traverses all output tensors, hence when the 
second tensor is examined, a reference to â€˜nullptrâ€˜ is bind. Vulnera- 
bilities can occur, because sometimes the implementation depends 
on the default values of axes, some quantities of the examined data 
structures are used to create different structures (it should be val- 
idated whether the original data structures shapes are proper for 
the new ones - e.g. CVE-2020-15199 - no validation whether the 
examined tensor has the minimum number of elements - required 
for the operation. This quantity is used to initialize a different data 
structure. which needs at least one element to not be â€˜nullptrâ€˜.). 
The improper shape of one structure can entail the risk of another 
structure becoming a null pointer. Another issue can be that all 
assumptions of a method are not satisï¬ed (e.g. CVE-2021-37674 - 
input tensors in this particular method have to be 4-dimensional, 
but it is not checked). Also, some external methods can be not pre- 
pared to operate with empty data structures - e.g. CVE-2020-26270 
- running an LSTM/GRU model where the LSTM/GRU layer receives 
an input with results with 0 elements. The result is a CHECK fail- 
ure when CUDA backend is used. 
How to exploit? - wrong values of parameters and shapes of 
data structures, - empty structures, - using null pointers 
7.3. CWE-190 - Integer Overï¬‚ow or Wraparound 
One source of CWE-190 vulnerabilities can be using implementa- 
tions and unsafe functions , e.g. â€œInitDimsâ€ instead of â€œAddDimWith- 
Statusâ€ (or â€œBuildTensorShapeBaseâ€ in a tensor constructor), which 
can result in â€˜CHECKâ€˜-failures in the presence of overï¬‚ows. This 
function is still used by some APIs, e.g. in ï¬le mkl_util.h (tensor- 
ï¬‚ow/tensorï¬‚ow/core/util/) - it is a potential vulnerability. Other 
source can be no/improper validation of tensorsâ€™ and modelsâ€™ sizes - 
simple operations (e.g. concatenation - CVE-2021-29601) used with 
large models in TFLite can cause overï¬‚ows (even more frequently 
than in traditional TensorFlow, as in this implementation int32 in- 
stead of int64 is often used). The example can be CVE-2021-29605 
(TFLite code used for array allocation is vulnerable to an integer 
overï¬‚ow - a special large model can be crafted such that the â€˜sizeâ€˜ 
multiplier returns the value that overï¬‚ows the â€œintâ€ datatype and 
becomes negative. This negative value is given to â€œmallocâ€ and as 
a result an invalid pointer is dereferenced. The other example can 
be CVE-2021-41198 - the number of elements in the output ten- 
sor is too large for â€œint64_tâ€, overï¬‚ow occurs and is detected via a 
â€œCHECKâ€ statement (and process is aborted). 
How to exploit? - using large inputs and demanding large out- 
puts, - using speciï¬c APIs that still use â€˜AddDimâ€˜ instead of â€˜Ad- 
dDimWithStatusâ€˜, - using specially crafted (also large) models, - 
building tensors without dimension bounds 
7.4. CWE-119 - Improper Restriction of Operations within the Bounds 
of a Memory Buffer 
Main sources of CWE-119 vulnerabilities are no/incomplete/ 
improper validation of input parameters of a function used to ac- 
cess and process the data structures (CVE-2020-15205 - one of 
the arguments lacks validation, thus values can be passed that 
can cause heap overï¬‚ow error/leak of contents of memory, which 
can contain return addresses and can be used to defeat the Ad- 
dress Space Layout Randomization - ASLR). Other issue can be 
no/incomplete/improper validation of values calculated to use for ac- 
cessing and processing the data (also when validation is imple- 
mented for the debug mode, but not for the release mode). Here, 
problems related to mimicking Pythonâ€™s indexing with negative val- 
ues can be considered - e.g. CVE-2020-15207 - to mimic Pythonâ€™s 
indexing with negative values, TFLite converts negative values to 
positive ones. The only check of the converted index is present 
in the debug builds. In the release mode, code execution contin- 
ues with a negative index. Also, no/incomplete/improper validation 
of indexes obtained using double indexing pattern can be problem- 
atic (e.g. accessing the values of gradients in the reversed order - 
CVE-2020-15195). The next issue is no/incomplete/improper valida- 
tion of shapes of examined tensors . Issues often occur when data 
structures are processed in parallel - (e.g. when more than one 
tensor is used in the operation and their shapes have to be equal 
and fully speciï¬ed - e.g. CVE-2020-15198 - no validation whether 
the tensor with weights has the same shape as the data. Weights 
are accessed in parallel with the data, and since there is no val- 
idation, passing fewer weights than the data values can cause an 
out-of-bound read). Another problem is no validation whether val- 
ues given as parameters are not too large for the types used in the 
function and for memory allocation - e.g. CVE-2020-15266 - when 
one of the arguments is very large, the CPU kernel implementa- 
tion reads it as a C++ â€˜nanâ€˜ ï¬‚oating point value. Operation on this 
variable can cause an undeï¬ned behavior and a segfault. The last 
issue found in the analysis regards no/incomplete/improper checks 
whether the initialized values are created properly . 
How to exploit? - using large values of parameters, - using val- 
ues (as indexes) not in the proper range of data, both positive 
and negative ones (also using operations based on reverse in- 
dexing), - using data structures with mismatched shapes when 
these structures are processed in parallel 
7.5. CWE-125 - Out-of-bounds read 
CWE-125 vulnerabilities can be caused by no/incomplete/ 
improper validation of user given parameters . These issues can re- 
gard to axis values (e.g. CVE-2020-15265 - invalid axis value can be 
passed, resulting in accessing a dimension outside the tensor rank), 
no checks of validity of strings (e.g. representing format - see CVE- 
2020-26267), no tensor bounds checks for tensor operations (nega- 
tive numbers, numbers exceeding the size), no checks whether pa- 
rameters used for a speciï¬c data structure speciï¬cation are correct for 
its type (e.g. CVE-2021-29559 - implementation assumes that the 
given parameters specify a valid sparse tensor.). Other issues re- 
gard no/incomplete/improper validation of user given data structures 
(usually arrays): empty checks (e.g. CVE-2021-41219 - sparse matrix 
multiplication was vulnerable to binding a reference to â€œnullptrâ€
when tensors with dimensions 0 or less were used). The ï¬x has 
been introduced in the newest version of TensorFlow - 2.7.0. Also, 
no/incomplete/improper validation of compatibility of data structures 
can introduce vulnerabilities when they are all used together in 
the operation (also in parallel). Incompatibility can often result 
in binding a reference to a null pointer (e.g. CVE-2021-37655). 
Also, very large values of parameters and tensors can cause integer 
overï¬‚ows resulting in an out-of-bounds read and disclosure of the 
process memory contents - CVE-2018-21233. The problem can be 
caused by a missing check of correctness of array ranks . Issues can 
be caused by no control regarding incrementation of pointers and 
trying to access data (e.g. CVE-2021-29532) or using one variable

K. Filus and J. Doma Â´nska 
Computers & Security 124 (2023) 102948 
for indexing two separate arrays in parallel and also using the debug 
checks (e.g. CVE-2020-15208 - when determining the common di- 
mension size of two examined tensors, â€œDCHECKâ€ is used - no-op 
outside of the debug mode. Attackers can use a larger tensor as the 
ï¬rst argument to trigger the attack.) Also, no/incomplete/improper 
validation of models used in the operations can cause vulnerabilities 
(e.g. CVE-2021-29606 - a specially crafted TFLite model can cause 
OOB read). The last issue speciï¬ed in the analysis is improper con- 
trol of the program ï¬‚ow (e.g. CVE-2021-29551 - the implementation 
fails to terminate kernel execution if one validation condition fails 
and only returns from a function). 
How to exploit? - specially crafted input parameters (e.g. 
shapes out of correct bounds), - using large data structures and 
values of parameters (also negative ones), - using empty struc- 
tures as input parameters, - using tensors with different dimen- 
sions when the same dimension is a condition of a mathemat- 
ical operation, - using incompatible values of parameters and 
input data structures in operations 
7.6. CWE-476 - NULL pointer dereference 
CWE-476 vulnerabilities are often caused by problems with ses- 
sion (no validation of availability of a session state, old TF ver- 
sions do not set this state - e.g. CVE-2020-15204), no/incorrect val- 
idation of tensor type (conversion from a Python array to a C++ 
array is vulnerable to a type confusion - CVE-2021-29513) and 
no/improper validation of tensor shape (e.g. CVE-2021-41215 - the 
shape inference function assumes that the tensor has a positive 
rank and that the last dimension is correct). The problems can be 
introduced by no/improper/incomplete validation whether input ten- 
sors are not empty or exist (e.g. CVE-2021-41217 - the control ï¬‚ow 
graph building can cause null pointer exception when nodes can- 
not be paired). Problems can occur when no/improper validation 
of input arguments in terms of their availability and correctness is 
provided (e.g. CVE-2021-37639 - restoring tensors using raw APIs, 
TF can be tricked into dereferencing a null pointer if the tensor 
name is not provided). The next cause can be no/improper valida- 
tion of corner cases and all of the constraints of the operator (e.g. 
CVE-2021-29616 - an undeï¬ned behavior can be triggered due to 
a dereference in corner cases that result in optimizing a no-input 
node). Yet another cause can be improper control of the programme 
ï¬‚ow (e.g. CVE-2021-37648 after unsuccessful validation kernel ex- 
ecution was not terminated, because it only exits a current func- 
tion). Also, using unmaintained APIs can introduce vulnerabilities 
(e.g. CVE-2021-41208 - unmaintained boosted trees). The problem 
can be planned and not implemented validation (e.g. CVE-2021- 
29565 - missing validation under a â€œTODOâ€). 
How to exploit? - using tensors of non-numeric types, using 
empty tensors, - using parameters of the operation not satis- 
fying the constraints of the operation (also corner cases), - us- 
ing specially crafted models, - using one empty tensor and the 
other one/ones valid in multi-tensor operations, - using tensors 
with incorrect shape for the operation 
8. Conclusions 
While dedicated AI threats are undoubtedly extremely impor- 
tant and need to be addressed, we donâ€™t yet know to effectively 
combat them. That is why, in our study we focus on threats caused 
by standard C/C++ vulnerabilities in TensorFlow implementation. 
We analyze 6 common vulnerability types by summarizing meta- 
data regarding various vulnerabilities. We use Orthogonal Defect 
Classiï¬cation, manual code analysis, and descriptions of speciï¬c 
CVEs to characterize their causes and results. 
Though Tensorï¬‚ow is a relatively new product, numerous se- 
curity vulnerabilities regarding this framework have been found 
and potentially many more are still undetected. Some vulnerabil- 
ities considered in this study are very recent and they were only 
patched in the latest version of the product. The results show that 
the majority of TensorFlow vulnerabilities are not entirely different 
from issues regarding general-purpose products written in C/C++. 
However, they can be more diï¬ƒcult to ï¬nd as it often requires 
deep semantic interpretation and good understanding of mathe- 
matical methods used. This seems to be the most likely cause of 
virtually zero effectiveness of examined SATs in detecting known 
vulnerabilities. Only one reported warning was included in one of 
the examined vulnerability ï¬xes. Nevertheless, we ï¬nd that some 
of the warnings can be used to improve the code quality and re- 
duce the chance of introducing new issues. Potentially, some com- 
mercial SATs can be more effective (e.g. they can include more 
rules), however in our study we decided to use only freely avail- 
able SATs that can be used by every researcher/programmer. 
Since automated analysis is failing, it is up to developers to fo- 
cus more on preventing the introduction and ï¬xing existing vul- 
nerabilities. Based on the results of our analysis in Appendix A , we 
provide a checklist for developers/users of TensorFlow (and other 
numerical and DL libraries) that can be used to check their source 
code and potentially eliminate some common programming mis- 
takes (we do not claim that these remarks are groundbreaking, 
however, the issues they relate to are still common and promi- 
nent). This list can also be used by programmers of non-AI plat- 
forms along with other secure programming guidelines, as the ma- 
jority of the described issues also applies to general-purpose appli- 
cations written in C/C++. We also believe that our checklist can be 
useful for the creators of new SATs (especially those that aim to be 
effective for the numerical libraries) - as a source of inspiration for 
new rules and to build the test cases. Here, we would like to en- 
courage other researchers to use these insights to create tools that 
would aim to improve the security of numerical libraries - since 
this type of software is widely used and its security is becoming 
critical. It is vital to provide automatic tools that would be able to 
ï¬nd at least some of the vulnerabilities in such products. We also 
aim to build such a tool in our future work based on the ï¬ndings 
presented in the current paper. We would also like to encourage 
other researchers to examine different vulnerability types in Ten- 
sorFlow (and possibly other numerical libraries) to describe even 
more thoroughly the threat landscape in these types of libraries.

Appendix A. Vulnerability Checklist 
Based on the results of our analysis presented in the article, we 
provide a checklist for developers and users of TensorFlow library 
(and other numerical and DL libraries written especially in C/C++) 
that can be used to check their source code and potentially ï¬nd 
and eliminate some common programming mistakes. This list can 
also be used by programmers of non-AI platforms along with other

guidelines - the majority of the issues also applies to general- 
purpose C/C++ applications. We also encourage creators of new 
static analysis tools to use this checklist as a source of inspiration 
for creating new rules and for building their test cases. 
What can developers of DL libraries and TensorFlow do? 
â–¡use SATs to improve the quality of source code (be sure alerts 
are only false positives - e.g. memcpy usages) and use good 
programming practises to facilitate work of future program- 
mers. 
â–¡cover important parts (e.g. validation) with code and not 
â€™TODOâ€™s. 
â–¡when dealing with C/C++ arrays (1) : 
â–¡empty checks. 
â–¡proper shape checks (dimensionality, number of necessary 
elements, they should be clearly described in the speciï¬ca- 
tion). 
â–¡type checks. 
â–¡checks for overï¬‚ows regarding large data structures. 
â–¡compatibility check when more than one array is used in an 
operation 
â–¡check all the arrays - do not assume correctness by 
checking only some of them. 
â–¡be careful when accessing arrays in paralell with one in- 
dex - be sure that it is safe. 
â–¡be careful when you use reverse indexing 
â–¡when dealing with pointers: 
â–¡nullpointer checks. 
â–¡when pointer is used to access array elements, check 
whether it is possible (e.g. pointer incrementation). 
â–¡when dealing with variables in general (2) : 
â–¡check whether they are assigned. 
â–¡use type checks. 
â–¡use format checks (e.g. when strings are given as an input). 
â–¡use value checks 
â–¡check limits for the type (to prevent overï¬‚ows). 
â–¡check assumptions of the method (they should be clearly 
described in the speciï¬cation). 
â–¡check compatibility with other arguments (e.g. when 
variable is used as an index). 
â–¡do not use obsolete functions and replace them with safer 
alternatives (e.g. use â€˜AddDimWithStatusâ€˜ instead of â€˜Ad- 
dDimâ€˜) (3) . 
â–¡do not shadow the variables used in the functions - this can 
make future developersâ€™ work more diï¬ƒcult and potentially 
lead to vulnerabilities. 
What can developers of DL applications using TensorFlow do 
(or other similar libraries)? 
For developers of external applications, the same advice as in 
(1) and (2) applies. They should validate the parameters and data 
structures passed to tensorï¬‚ow. They do not have control over the 
implementation of tensorï¬‚ow, e.g. over pointer incrementation or 
the use of obsolete functions - see (3), but in the second case they 
do have control over what APIs they use and here a risk assess- 
ment should be performed whether it is worthwhile to use an API 
that uses a particular function that may cause vulnerabilities. 
Additionally, an extension of the above list can be introduced 
for developers of external applications using DL libraries: 
â–¡when it does not require to create very advanced method, bet- 
ter create your own solutions - this way you know what EX- 
ACTLY is implemented and even when the failure happens, you 
can easily correct them (no waiting for a 3rd party library ï¬x 
required). 
â–¡use only maintained APIs, check for alternatives, when the de- 
sired API is unmaintained or create your own one.

A Comparative Study of Commit Representations for JIT
Vulnerability Prediction
TamÃ¡s Aladics 1,2,*
, PÃ©ter HegedËus 1,*
and Rudolf Ferenc 1
1
Department of Sofware Engineering, University of Szeged, 6720 Szeged, Hungary; ferenc@inf.u-szeged.hu
