On the Impact of Refactorings on Software 
Attack Surface  
Estomii Edward1 (Student), Ally S. Nyamawe1, Member, IEEE, and Noe Elisa1 
1Department of Computer Science and Engineering, The University of Dodoma, Dodoma, Tanzania  
Corresponding author: Estomii Edward (e-mail: eestomii@gmail.com). 
 
This work was carried out with the aid of a grant in the UNESCO-TWAS programme, "Seed Grant 
for African Principal Investigators" financed by the German Federal Ministry of Education and 
Research (BMBF). The views expressed herein do not necessarily represent those of UNESCO-TWAS 
or BMBF. 
ABSTRACT Refactoring is one of the techniques mostly employed by software developers to improve the 
quality attributes of their systems. However, little has been done to investigate how refactoring operations 
specifically aimed at improving the internal structure of software can impact its security. Refactoring usually 
entails different code change operations including the decomposition of classes, methods, and the reallocation 
of code elements. While this refinement aims to improve the internal design of a system, it might inadvertently 
disperse security-critical code elements throughout the codebase. Consequently, such dispersion could affect 
the software attack surface. To this end, this paper presents an empirical study of 30 open-source software 
systems developed in Python, C, and Javascript. The study scrutinized two subsequent versions of each 
subject application to uncover the refactoring operations applied and the trend of the software attack surface. 
Specifically, the study focused on the injection or removal of bugs, code smells and other vulnerabilities 
aiming to discern the impact of refactorings on the software attack surface. Data was collected using well-
known tools, namely SonarQube, RefDiff, and PyReff. The findings suggest that refactorings can have 
multiple impacts (i.e., positive, negative, or neutral) on bugs, code smells, and vulnerabilities. The findings 
further confirm that developers must be aware of the combination or sequence of refactoring operations that 
can improve software quality without compromising its security. 
INDEX TERMS Attack Surface, Bugs, Code Smells, Refactoring, Vulnerabilities 
 
I. INTRODUCTION 
Refactoring is defined as â€œthe process of changing the 
internal working or structure of a software system without 
causing any change to the external behaviour of the systemâ€ 
[1]. According to Fowler and Beck [2], software refactoring 
has been widely used by software developers to improve 
software quality by changing the internal structure while 
leaving the external structure unchanged. Rochimah et al. [3] 
supported this observation by listing the benefits of software 
refactoring which include: eliminating code smells, helping 
to find bugs, making developers program faster, improving 
the quality of software design, improving code readability, 
improving software maintenance and extensibility, and 
reducing software evolution time. Refactoring techniques are 
commonly used in software maintenance as they are highly 
recommended strategies employed by developers to improve 
software security by addressing vulnerabilities that attackers 
can exploit [4],[5]. Because an attacker could exploit an 
attack surface to prevent the system from working properly. 
However, the impacts of refactoring on the software attack 
surface are not well-documented and are still uncertain, 
despite the popularity of refactoring in software maintenance 
[6]. Previous scholars such as [7] and [8] found that there is 
a positive and significant relationship between refactoring 
and software security while [9] found that despite security 
improvement refactoring also increases the attack surface 
due to the created abstractions.  
Most of the research in software refactoring has 
mainly focused on improving the design of existing code [2], 
securing information flows [10], fixing bugs [11], improving 
software quality [12],[13],[14], and code smells removal 
[15].  However, these studies did not specifically investigate 
the effects of refactorings on software attack surface. 
Therefore, conducting an in-depth empirical evaluation of 
E. Edward et al.: On the Impact of Refactorings on Software Attack Surface 
                                                                                        
 
the impacts of refactorings on software attack surface is 
crucial. 
Abid et al. [16] proposed a security-aware 
refactoring approach that utilizes the Apriori algorithm to 
establish the associations between implemented refactorings 
and the fitness function employed to improve software 
security. The methodology was evaluated by conducting 
empirical studies and experiments on open-source projects. 
The findings show that certain refactorings when performed 
with security awareness, can have a positive impact by 
reducing security vulnerabilities and improving overall 
system security. Abid et al. [9] proposed a security-aware 
refactoring approach that considers the impact of refactoring 
on software security. The author proposed a systematic 
process for identifying potential security vulnerabilities 
during the refactoring process and developing security-
aware 
refactoring 
patterns 
to 
address 
identified 
vulnerabilities. 
The 
findings 
indicate 
that 
security 
vulnerabilities can effectively be addressed in software 
systems by identifying and considering trade-offs between 
security and other qualities during refactoring. Siavvas et al. 
[17] proposed a static analysis technique to enhance software 
security by applying refactoring. The study explored several 
methodologies, including data flow analysis, control flow 
analysis, and symbolic execution, highlighting how these 
techniques can be utilized to identify security vulnerabilities 
and guide code refactoring efforts to improve the security of 
the software. The study findings were evaluated using case 
studies and was revealed that the static analysis approach 
enhances security by promoting effective refactoring 
practices. However, limited information is available 
regarding the impacts of refactorings on the software attack 
surface.  
To this end, this paper presents an empirical study that 
involved 30 open-source software systems, developed in 
Python, C, and Javascript to discern the impact of 
refactorings on software attack surface. We analyzed the 
effect of frequently applied refactorings on bugs, code 
smells, and vulnerabilities. Our investigation focuses on two 
main aspects: firstly, we aim to determine the most common 
applied refactorings and the most prevalent elements of the 
software attack surface. Secondly, we seek to evaluate the 
effectiveness of refactoring in addressing bugs, code smells, 
and vulnerabilities in open-source software projects. Using 
the state-of-the-art tools namely SonarQube, RefDiff, and 
PyReff, we extracted a total of 3,523 applied refactorings, 
18,303 instances of code smells, 2,975 instances of bugs, and 
43 instances of vulnerabilities that formulated the basis of 
our analysis in this study.  
The contributions of this paper are as follows:  
1) This paper presents an empirical study that assesses 
the impact of refactorings on software attack 
surface. 
2) This paper provides a methodological contribution 
to how experiments can be used to uncover the 
common software attack surface and evaluate how 
they are impacted by refactoring. In addition, this 
study serves as a foundation for ongoing research 
on security-focused refactoring to improve software 
quality. 
3) The findings and recommendations presented in 
this paper can be a reference for other researchers 
interested in undertaking additional research in this 
field. 
 
The subsequent sections of this paper are structured in 
the following manner: Section II summarizes previous 
studies in refactorings and attack surface to set an 
understanding of these key aspects and what has been done 
so far. Section III describes the methodology used in this 
study, whereas Section IV presents our experimental results. 
Section V presents a discussion of the findings. Finally, 
Section VI concludes the paper and highlights areas for 
further research. 
 
II.  RELATED WORK 
This section presents previous studies and concepts relevant to 
this study. 
A. REFACTORING 
Refactoring is a systematic technique for modifying the 
internal structure of an existing codebase without affecting 
its external behavior. Originally [2] defined refactoring as 
â€œA change made to the internal structure of software to make 
it easier to understand and cheaper to modify without 
changing its observable behavior. It is a disciplined way to 
clean up code that minimizes the chances of introducing 
bugs.â€ Opdyke [18] defined refactoring as the process of 
making program modifications that enable design, evolution, 
and reuse while maintaining the functionality of the software 
application. Despite being an old definition, it is still valid to 
date. Refactoring is the process of altering a software system 
to make it simpler to understand and less expensive to 
modify, without changing the external behavior [19]. Alves 
et al. [1] have further defined refactoring as â€œthe process of 
changing the internal working or structure of a software 
system, without causing any change to the external behavior 
of the systemâ€. The goal is to improve its comprehensibility, 
adaptability, and maintainability while minimizing the 
likelihood of introducing bugs and code smells. 
Refactoring entails source code modifications that take 
place at various points throughout the development, evolution, 
and maintenance of a program [20]. Murphy-hill [21] 
uncovered two tactics for implementing refactorings such as 
floss and root canal refactoring. The use of floss refactoring is 
for implementing new features or resolving bugs. However, in 
root canal refactoring the developer's primary objective is to 
apply refactorings to enhance the code's quality. Murphy-Hill 
et al. [22] have demonstrated that floss refactoring is a widely 
adopted practice. Refactorings are detectable through the 
utilization of both automated and manual tools. In software 
maintenance projects, automated refactoring detection tools 
outperform their manual counterparts [23],[24],[25],[26].

2 
VOLUME XX, 2024 
B. ATTACK SURFACE OF SOFTWARE SYSTEMS 
The attack surface of the software system encompasses the 
entry, and exit points of a system, the data that is transmitted 
through these points, and the code that safeguards both the 
paths and the data [27]. The attack surface of software refers 
to the total number of potential entry points through which 
unauthorized users can attempt to input or extract data from 
a system or environment to compromise a system, 
application, device, or network [28],[29]. For example, 
Kurmus et al. [30] highlighted that the presence of 
vulnerabilities in the Kernel can lead to security weaknesses 
and defects in various operating systems. By addressing 
these vulnerabilities, the software attack surface can be 
minimized, thereby enhancing the software's resistance to 
attacks. Theisen et al. [31] confirmed that software bugs and 
vulnerabilities can be regarded as the attack surface of any 
software because they provide potential entry points and 
opportunities for attackers to gain unauthorized access to the 
software and hence compromise its security. Similar findings 
were confirmed by Szefer et al. [32] that software 
vulnerabilities and bugs serve as prominent examples of the 
software attack surface. Furthermore, Alraddadi et al. [33] 
has observed a correlation between code smells and software 
vulnerabilities and established that code smells can give rise 
to security vulnerabilities. 
C. EFFECTS OF REFACTORINGS ON BUGS 
Bug refers to an error, defect, or flaw in a computer program 
or system that leads to the generation of an inaccurate or 
unforeseen outcome, or causes the program to behave in 
unintended manners [34]. Software bugs also refer to 
imperfections, flaws, errors, faults, inconsistencies, or 
deviations in computer programs or systems [35]. The study 
conducted in [36] highlighted that there are sets of bugs that 
manifest in the codebase as a result of certain refactorings, 
and on the other hand, there are also sets of bugs that trigger 
developers to apply refactoring. The study conducted by 
Almogahed et al. [37] provided a comprehensive analysis of 
the impact of refactorings on software quality. A total of 30 
empirical studies were analyzed to investigate the effects of 
refactorings on bug reduction in software. The findings of 
these studies revealed that refactorings can have both 
positive and negative impacts on bug reduction. Da Costa et 
al. [38] proposed a framework for assessing the effectiveness 
of the Sliwerski, Zimmermann, and Zeller (SZZ) algorithm 
in detecting software bugs. The findings of the study indicate 
that the process of refactoring in software maintenance can 
potentially result in adverse effects, specifically the 
introduction of bugs in the software. 
 
Gigante et al. [39] conducted an empirical 
investigation on software projects to evaluate the efficacy of 
refactorings in removing software bugs. The results 
indicated that certain refactorings have the potential to 
introduce additional bugs into the software. These findings 
are consistent with the study conducted by Shafiq et al. [36], 
which suggests that the application of refactorings can 
potentially introduce bugs in software even after successful 
implementation. Moreover, [40] conducted a longitudinal 
study that analysed 20,689 refactorings and 1,033 bug 
reports from 5 Java open-source projects. The findings 
indicated that bugs are introduced into the refactored code 
when refactorings are applied to the code. In addition, code 
elements that are affected by refactorings performed 
alongside other changes are more likely to have bugs 
compared to those affected by pure refactorings. 
D. IMPACT OF REFACTORINGS ON CODE SMELLS 
Code smells refer to implementation issues that arise due to 
inadequate design and/or coding choices [41]. These are 
perceived as problematic issues that can complicate the 
maintenance and evolution of software [2],[42]. Code smells 
can be introduced by software developers either during the 
system's early stages of development or as the system 
progresses over time [41] and have been associated with the 
increase in risk of vulnerabilities and bugs according to 
Palomba et al.[43]. Numerous studies have been conducted 
to examine the effects of refactorings on code smells. 
Bibiano et al. [44] investigated the use of composite 
refactoring to eliminate code smells. The results showed that 
combining the Extract Method, and Move Method removes 
both Long Method and Feature Envy code smells. However, 
in the same study, composites formed by Extract Methods 
not only remove Long Method code smells but also introduce 
Feature Envy and Intensive Couplings code smells into the 
software.  Hamdi et al. [41] revealed that Extract Method, 
Move Method, Extract and Move Method, Rename Method, 
and Push Down Method refactorings were applied to remove 
complex class and long method code smells. This finding 
aligns with the catalogue proposed in [2] stating that the 
mentioned refactorings could be applied to fix complex class 
and long method code smells. The Extract Method 
refactoring is frequently applied to address the following 
code smell types: Lazy Class, Complex Class, Long Method, 
and Feature Envy. However, this finding also implies that 
refactorings are context-dependent and that there is no single 
refactoring that can be used to address a specific code smell 
[41].  
Further, Cedrim et al. [45] analyzed various types of 
refactoring and found that the application of these 
refactorings did not reduce code smells. Instead, the 
introduction of new code smells was observed. The study 
examined 23 software projects and conducted analyses on 13 
different types of code smells. The findings revealed that 
57% of the refactorings performed did not effectively 
remove code smells. Additionally, 9.7% of the refactorings 
successfully eliminated code smells, while 33.3% of the 
refactorings introduced new code smells into the software. 
Moreover,  the study conducted by Yoshida et al. [46], 
investigated the correlation between code smells and 
refactorings in desktop applications. The analysis indicated 
that the refactorings successfully eliminated code smells by 
a mere 2.24%, while simultaneously introducing new code 
smells at a rate of 2.66%. 
E. Edward et al.: On the Impact of Refactorings on Software Attack Surface 
                                                                                        
 
 
Halepmollas and Tosun [47] performed research to 
determine how refactoring affects code smells. The study 
explored 33 Java projects and detected 57,528 refactorings, 
37,553 smells, 27,340 faults, and 134,812 commits. The 
findings indicate that certain types of refactoring are utilized 
more frequently by programmers. The study also showed 
that code smells are typically eliminated or remain 
unaffected by refactorings. Counsell et al. [48] conducted an 
empirical study on the removal of code smells by analyzing 
a set of five open-source Java projects followed by 
proprietary software developed in C# and finally a 
theoretical study on why smell-related refactorings were not 
addressed. The study's key findings indicate no evidence of 
a widespread elimination of smells. However, it was 
observed that smells that could be resolved through simple 
refactoring operations were eliminated in favor of smells that 
required more complex refactoring. 
 
E. EFFECTS OF REFACTORINGS ON 
VULNERABILITIES 
Vulnerabilities are defined as unintended characteristics of a 
computer component or system configurations that increase 
the risk of an adverse event or loss occurring through 
inadvertent exposure, malicious attack, or accidental 
exposure [7]. Vulnerability in computer software refers to a 
specific weakness present in the code that allows an attacker 
to bypass the implemented security measures [49]. 
Therefore, vulnerabilities that are associated with bypassing 
a restriction refer to situations where an unauthenticated 
party can gain access to services or read and manipulate files 
[50]. The study conducted by Ikegami et al. [28] examined 
the application of refactoring techniques in addressing 
security vulnerabilities. The results revealed that the 
identified vulnerabilities within the 143 analyzed Maven 
libraries 
were 
successfully 
addressed 
through 
the 
implementation of refactoring techniques. According to the 
white paper by New Relic [51], the goal of refactoring is to 
reduce the occurrence of security vulnerabilities in the 
software system. 
 
III. METHODOLOGY 
This section presents a summary of the stages required to 
address our research questions. The proposed approach 
consists of three steps as represented in Figure 1. The steps 
are:  selecting subject systems, detecting refactorings, and 
identifying attack surfaces. These steps were adopted from 
the study by Hamdi et al. [41] and modified accordingly to 
fit the current study.

source software projects from the GitHub repository to serve 
as subject systems for the study. The reason for selecting 
open-source software systems is simply because they are 
publicly available on software repositories and their source 
code and change histories can be easily accessed [52]. 
However, they are constantly exposed to unavoidable 
security 
threats such as bugs, code smells, and 
vulnerabilities.

B. PREVIOUS REFACTORINGS DETECTION 
We collected all the refactorings applied to the selected 
open-source software projects. We used PyReff [23] and 
RefDiff [53] to facilitate the identification of applied 
refactorings. PyReff is a tool that was developed specifically 
for mining refactoring operations in Python projects. It has 
been reported that PyReff attains a recall of 95% and 
precision of 79% [23]. PyReff provides the capability to 
identify a range of prevalent refactoring types, as proposed 
by Fowler and Beck [2]. 
Similarly, RefDiff is a tool that was developed for 
mining refactoring operations in C and JavaScript projects. 
It has been documented that RefDiff attains a recall of 88% 
and a precision of 100% [53].  RefDiff provides the 
capability to detect thirteen (13) different types of 
refactoring operations. The detection of refactorings between 
two revisions of a system is accomplished through the 
utilization of a combination of heuristics based on static 
analysis and code similarity [25]. We extracted eight (8) 
common refactoring types from the supported refactorings, 
as presented in Table 2.
Table 2: The List of Considered Refactorings 
SN 
Refactoring Type 
Description 
1.  Move Method 
Moves a method from a class to another class 
2.  Extract Method 
Creating a new method from an existing code block. 
3.  Rename Method 
Renames Method 
4.  Rename Class 
Renames a class 
5.  Inline Method 
Reduce the number of unneeded methods while simplifying the code 
6.  Add Parameter 
Add a default parameter to the method in all implementors 
7.  Remove Parameter 
Removes an unused parameter from all implementors of the method 
8.  Pull Up Method 
Move the method to the superclass.

C. DETECTION OF SOFTWARE ATTACK SURFACE  
In this step we identified bugs, code smells and 
vulnerabilities instances in the source code of the selected 
subject applications. For each project, we conducted a 
comprehensive source code analysis to determine any 
occurrences of bugs, code smells, and vulnerabilities. 
SonarQube was used to detect such elements of the attack 
surface. SonarQube is a tool for ensuring the quality of code 
by gathering and analyzing source code and generating 
reports on the code quality of the project [54]. It brings 
together static and dynamic analysis and allows for the 
constant measurement of quality over time. The tool offers 
various code analyses, such as static code analysis, code 
coverage, and code duplication analysis. Notably, the 
SonarQube tool utilizes rule-based static code analysis, 
complexity metrics, and security rule sets to identify bugs, 
code smells, and vulnerabilities in the code base. 
 
D. ANALYZING THE IMPACT OF REFACTORINGS

impact on the presence of bugs, code smells, and 
vulnerabilities [45][55][14]. This section outlines how each 
instance of refactoring type is categorized by quantifying the 
number of bugs, code smells, and vulnerabilities that are 
either not affected, introduced, or eliminated because of the 
refactorings applied.

IV. EXPERIMENT AND RESULTS 
In this section, we present the research questions that this 
study intends to address and highlight the findings of our 
empirical study followed by the results discussion in 
response to each of the research questions. 
A. RESEARCH QUESTIONS 
Our study aims to answer the following research questions. 
â€¢ 
RQ1: How about the software attack surface of open-
source software systems? This initial research question 
seeks to empirically identify the software attack 
surface of open-source software systems. 
â€¢ 
RQ2: What are the commonly applied refactorings 
on the studied subject systems? This research 
question intends to identify refactorings applied to 
open-source 
software 
systems 
through 
a 
comprehensive code analysis and understand which 
refactorings were commonly applied to the same. 
â€¢ 
RQ3: What is the impact of refactorings on the 
software attack surface of the analyzed open-source 
software systems? The goal of this research question 
is to investigate the impact of refactorings on the 
software attack surface. This question enables a deeper 
understanding of the connection between refactorings 
and the attack surface, specifically in terms of bugs, 
code smells, and vulnerabilities 
 
To address RQ1, we utilized the bugs, code smells, and 
vulnerabilities information that have been gathered for each 
subject application as outlined in section III (C). The 
experiment was carried out by performing the static code 
analysis of the selected 30 open-source projects to scan for 
vulnerabilities, bugs, and code smells. The selection of these 
three elements of the attack surface is in line with [39] who 
performed a comparative study of the two source code 
analysis tools namely SonarQube and Fortify Static Code 
Analyzer. As mentioned earlier, we used SonarQube 
Community Edition version 9.6.1, a software application that 
executes rules given by Gigante et al. [39] to identify the 
instances of bugs, code smells, and vulnerabilities. 
On the other hand, RQ2 is answered using the 
refactoring instances data collected by PyReff and RefDiff 
from the 30 subject systems. This process enabled us to 
identify the common refactorings applied in open-source 
software projects. As for the refactorings, the study selected 
purposely eight (8) types that belong to the catalogue defined 
by Fowler and Beck [2] and are also reported to be the 
commonly performed refactorings from other studies [15]. 
 
E. Edward et al.: On the Impact of Refactorings on Software Attack Surface 
2 
VOLUME XX, 2024 
Furthermore, the choice of these eight refactorings is also 
inspired by Murphy-Hill et al. [22]. 
To address RQ3, we examine the relationship between 
refactoring operations and the occurrence of bugs, code 
smells, and vulnerabilities. First, we identified the code 
elements containing bugs, code smells, or vulnerabilities in 
a given version of the system. Next, we tracked the 
refactorings applied to these code elements in the subsequent 
version. Finally, we analyzed to determine the extent to 
which the previously identified bugs, code smells, and 
vulnerabilities were impacted by these refactorings. This 
approach enables us to determine whether these elements of 
the attack surface have been reduced or remain unchanged. 
Additionally, further analysis was conducted on the 
refactored code elements to identify any newly introduced 
bugs, code smells, and vulnerabilities. The RQ3 is therefore 
aiming at discerning whether a particular applied refactoring 
operation had a positive, neutral, or negative impact. 
 
B. HOW ABOUT THE SOFTWARE ATTACK SURFACE 
OF OPEN-SOURCE SOFTWARE SYSTEMS? (RQ1) 
 The information revealed by SonarQube helped to 
establish the common attack surface elements available in 
software projects that have an impact on software security, 
on the one hand, and help the developer to understand the 
most occurring elements of attack surface on the other hand. 
The distribution of bugs, code smells and vulnerabilities are 
presented in Table 4.

As presented in Table 4, code smells contribute significantly 
to the total number of attack surface elements. Code smells 
have a total of 18,303 (85.8%) instances. This implies that 
code smells are the most common type of attack surface on 
the analyzed project. The second most common attack 
surface of the studied open-source software projects was 
bugs which contributed to a total of 2,975 (14%) instances of 
attack surfaces. Vulnerabilities are the least common type of 
attack surface elements which contributed to 0.2% (43 out of 
21,321) of all instances of the attacks in the analysed 
projects. This implies that vulnerabilities in the analyzed 
software accounted for a smaller fraction of the attack 
surface than others. However, it is important to note that the 
vulnerabilities studied here are not exhaustive. Other several 
vulnerabilities were not considered in this initial attempt of 
our study. The following subsections highlight each of the 
attack surface elements in detail.

As shown in the table, the two most common code smell 
types were Duplicated code and Speculative generality. 
These code smell types accounted for 34.5% and 17.5% 
respectively of all instances. In general, these code smell 
types, which occur with a high frequency, make up a 
significant 50% of the total code smell count. These findings 
were in line with the  study by Menshawy et al. [56] which 
indicated that Duplicated code and Speculative generality 
are the most popular code smells among all. We also 
observed that code smells such as Long Parameter List, 
Temporary Field, and Comments are moderately prevalent in 
the analyzed projects. These code smell types accounted for 
14.1%, 13.2%, and 12.6% of all instances, respectively. In 
general, these three code smell types, which occur with a 
moderate frequency, make up a significant 39.9% of the total 
code smell count. These  findings are supported by  Sotto-
Mayor et al. [57] who found out that code smells such as  
Long Parameter List, Temporary field, and Comments are 
commonly found in software projects. 
Furthermore, we observed that code smells such as 
Long Method, Switch Statement, Data Clumps, Large class, 
and Feature Envy were slightly prevalent in the analyzed 
projects. These code smell types accounted for 6.1%, 1.2%, 
0.4%, 0.1% and 0.1% of all instances, respectively. In 
general, these five code smell types accounted for only 7.9% 
of the total code smell instances. Overall, it has been noticed 
that the highly, moderately, and slightly prevalent code 
smells in the analysis are consistent with the previously 
reported results [56],[43]. In their study, Alraddadi et al. [33] 
observed a correlation between code smells and software 
vulnerabilities. It has been established that code smells can 
give rise to security vulnerabilities, thereby compromising 
the security of the software and making it susceptible to 
attacks.

As shown in the table, the three most recurring bug types

often manifest in either high, moderate, or slight frequency.

We observed that the neutral impact of refactorings on bugs 
was the most common outcome. Out of all refactoring types 
analyzed, the total number of 2,643 refactoring instances 
(i.e., 75.8% of all instances) did not result in any changes to 
the existing bugs in the projects. We noted that Move 
Method, Extract Method, Rename Method, Inline Method, 
Add Parameter, Remove Parameter, and Pull Up Method are 
the most frequently implemented refactorings and at least 
50% of their instances had no impact on bugs. In contrast to 
Rename Class refactoring only 39% of its instances had a 
neutral impact on bugs. Moreover, as shown in Table 9, 
overall, 12.6% (438 out of 3,488 instances) of the refactoring 
instances were found to add bugs to the refactored code 
elements.  
Furthermore, we observed that only Move Method, 
Extract Method, Rename Method, Rename Class, and Inline 
Method refactorings demonstrated a negative impact. In 
contrast to Inline Method refactoring which had a significant 
percentage of instances (47.4%) with a negative impact, the 
rest of the refactorings had a slight negative impact on bugs. 
However, the other three refactorings (i.e., Add Parameter, 
Remove Parameter, and Pull Up Method) had no negative 
impact on bugs.  In the case of positive impact, surprisingly, 
Rename Class refactoring had a significant number of 
instances (50.8%) that recorded positive impact, followed by 
Add Parameter refactoring with only 21.2%. Other 
refactorings had very few instances with positive impact on 
bugs, whereas, the Pull Up Method had no positive impact at 
all.     
In summary, most of the instances of applied 
refactorings had neutral impacts on the bugs (i.e., 75.8%) and 
almost comparable negative (12.6%) and positive (11.7%) 
impacts. These results further indicate that the effectiveness 
of refactoring strategies is contingent upon the specific 
context in which they are implemented. It would be 
interesting in the future to make further analyses to establish 
how these refactorings lead to positive and negative impacts 
on bugs. 
The results presented in Table 9 were produced based 
on bug-detection strategies similar to the one used by Bavota 
et al. [55]. Figure 2 displays the distribution of the impact of 
refactorings on bugs, categorized as neutral, positive, and 
negative. This analysis was conducted using two 
classification methods: Tight and Bavota thresholds. The 
thresholds for bug detection were defined in [55]. Macia et 
al. [61] validated the first set of bug detection rules, called 
tight. This strategy is tight because it uses high thresholds to 
detect only critical bug types across projects. The second 
approach, referred to as Bavota, employs relaxed thresholds 
intending to identify as many bugs as possible as proposed 
by Bavota et al. [55]. An analysis in Figure 2 demonstrates 
that the proportion of neutral, positive, and negative 
refactorings is the same irrespective of the threshold used for 
bug detection.

both neutral and negative effects on vulnerabilities.

effects on vulnerabilities based on the analyzed projects. 
This observation suggests that the specific refactorings 
employed in the analyzed projects were not related to the 
reduction of the identified vulnerabilities. For instance, the 
study by Nafees et al. [66] revealed that Extract Method 
refactoring can address Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) 
vulnerabilities, however, this vulnerability was not among 
the identified vulnerabilities in the current study.

V. DISCUSSION 
This section contains a discussion of the implications our 
findings have on (1) the identification of the software attack 
surface, (2) the identification of refactorings applied, and (3) 
the impact of refactorings on the software attack surface of 
open-source software systems. 
A. IMPLICATIONS FOR ATTACK SURFACE 
IDENTIFICATION (RQ1)  
It has been revealed that the most occurring attack surface 
element in the analyzed open-source software projects was 
code smells with a total of 18,303 (85.8%) instances 
followed by bugs which contributed to a total of 2,975 (14%) 
instances and last was vulnerabilities which contributed to 43 
(0.2%) of all instances. Moreover, the prevalence and 
severity of attack surface elements in the selected projects 
vary, and it is important to recognize this distinction. For 
example, code smells and bugs are both prevalent software 
attack surface elements in the studied projects accounting for 
99.8% of all the attack surface elements. Notably, bugs, code 
smells and vulnerabilities contribute to software attack 
surface by providing potential entry points and opportunities 
for attackers to exploit flaws and cause harm to the software 
[67]. 
B. THE COMMON APPLIED REFACTORINGS (RQ2)  
The results for RQ2 showed that Extract Method, Inline 
Method, Move Method, Pull Up Method, Add Parameter, 
Remove Parameter, Rename Class, and Rename Method are 
the most applied refactorings on the studied software 
projects. These refactoring types are the most common and 
frequently studied by other researchers as well [68][15][37]. 
As presented in Section IV (C), the Move Method has been 
identified as the most frequently performed refactoring 
operation with an occurrence of 1,174 (33.3%) instances.  In 
line with these findings is the study proposed by Kurbatova 
et al. [69] which emphasized that Move Method refactoring

is frequently employed due to its perceived effectiveness in 
addressing Feature Envy code smell. The Extract Method 
was the second most common refactoring operation 
performed with 693 (19.7%) instances. This finding is 
similarly reported in  [55]. It is important to acknowledge 
that the relatively large number of Extract Method 
refactorings may lead to a correspondingly high number of 
Rename Method refactorings. This observation was justified 
in the sense that Rename Method and Rename Class are the 
third and fourth most common refactoring activities 
performed with occurrences of 551(15.6%) and 521 (14.8%) 
respectively. These results were also reported by previous 
studies [22][47]. These refactorings were applied to make 
method and class names more meaningful to reflect their 
latest functions. 
C. THE IMPACT OF REFACTORINGS ON SOFTWARE 
ATTACK SURFACE (RQ3) 
1) IMPACT OF REFACTORINGS ON BUGS 
The findings of this study suggest that refactorings can have 
multiple effects on bugs as they can be positive, negative, or 
neutral. It is worth noting that, bugs had two scenarios 
including the growing trend and the unchanging trend. The 
growing trend was observed for Code complexity, incorrect 
data validation, and unused code bugs. Whereas, the 
unchanging pattern included Memory leak and Unhandled 
exception bugs. This signifies that these types of bugs are 
difficult to fix by simple refactorings that were performed on 
the analyzed projects. Yin et al. [70] support these findings 
by stressing that among the most difficult bugs to fix are 
Memory leak and Unhandled exception. Xuan et al. [71] 
noted that Memory leak and Unhandled exception are the 
problematic bugs to be addressed by developers using 
refactorings. 
2) IMPACT OF REFACTORINGS ON CODE SMELLS 
The findings revealed that refactorings demonstrated 
positive, negative, and neutral effects on code smells.  These 
findings are consistent with the studies conducted in [55] and 
[72] which suggests that some refactorings decrease the 
number of code smell instances, on the other hand, some 
refactorings may have no effects on code smells and some 
are likely to introduce code smells. The findings of this study 
further confirm that in the course of the evolution of a 
software system, particular code smells may increase, 
decrease, or remain unchanged between subsequent 
versions. The first scenario that showcased the growing trend 
of code smell types includes Comments, Duplicated Code, 
and Temporary Field. These findings were in line with the 
study by Counsell et al. [48] which explored the eradication 
of code smells and the results revealed that Duplicated Code, 
Comments, and Temporary Field code smells were not 
eradicated by any refactoring. According to the study, these 
smell types were categorized as complex code smells and 
they are difficult to remove through simple refactorings like 
the ones detected by the tools in this study. Wangberg [73] 
also supported these findings, documenting that Duplicated 
Code, Comments, and Temporary Field smells are difficult 
to eliminate through simple refactorings and the same 
require complex refactorings, or in other words, composite 
refactorings. 
Other categories of code smells that showed the 
unchanging trend include Long Method, Large class, and 
Feature Envy. This finding suggests that the refactorings that 
were applied likely aimed to address other issues rather than 
just code smells. Noting that refactorings may be applied for 
different purposes including preparing the codebase when 
implementing new requirements [12]. Counsell et al. [48] 
documented that Long Method, Large class, and Feature 
Envy code smells require more instances of refactorings to 
be removed. The unchanging instances of this code smell 
type imply that some refactorings should be applied in a 
certain sequence to be effective, for instance, according to 
Cedrim et al.  [45], Extract Method should be followed by 
Move Method to eliminate the Long Method, and Feature 
Envy code smells. 
3) IMPACT OF REFACTORINGS ON VULNERABILITIES 
The findings revealed that refactorings demonstrated only 
negative and neutral effects on the identified vulnerabilities. 
In line with these findings was the study by [64] which found 
that refactorings can have negative and neutral effects on 
vulnerabilities. According to the analysis in this study, there 
were no refactorings that positively impacted vulnerabilities.  
The premise could be the performed refactorings did not 
suffice to remove the identified vulnerabilities. However, we 
note that refactoring may have a positive impact on 
vulnerabilities as the study by Nafees et al. [66] revealed that 
Extract Method refactorings can address Cross-Site 
Scripting (XSS) vulnerabilities. Another similar observation 
by Shaw et al. [74] documented that Extract Method and 
Move 
Method 
refactorings 
can 
address 
overflow 
vulnerabilities. These vulnerabilities were not included in 
this study. 
In conclusion, it is important to note that the analysis in 
this study focused on the quantity of attack surface elements 
rather than examining how specific elements (e.g., a 
particular code smell) were affected by specific refactoring 
operations. Future research could provide deeper insights by 
analyzing, for example, how a specific refactoring type, such 
as Move Method, impacts its corresponding smell, like 
Feature Envy, and other types of smells. This detailed 
analysis would offer a better understanding beyond just the 
quantity of instances. Notably, each refactoring operation 
typically addresses certain types of code smells and may 
have a neutral impact on others. This analysis could also be 
applied to bugs and vulnerabilities.  
VI. THREATS TO VALIDITY 
One of the major limitations of the study is the identification 
of software attack surface elements. Detecting attack surface 
elements with only one tool limits the generalizability of our 
findings. To reduce the threat the software attack surface was 
identified using a widely recognized state-of-the-art tool 
namely SonarQube Community Edition. As a result, the 
scope of the study is restricted to the analysis of attack 
 
E. Edward et al.: On the Impact of Refactorings on Software Attack Surface 
8 
VOLUME XX, 2024 
surfaces identified by only one tool which may pose a threat 
to the validity of the study, as any attack surface elements 
not identified by the tool were not part of the analysis.  
Moreover, the dataset utilized in this study comprises 
refactorings identified by PyRef and RefDiff. Consequently, 
any types of refactorings that were missed by these tools 
were not considered in the analysis. The second threat could 
stem from the fact that we quantitatively presented our 
findings by using the data produced by our classification 
strategies. It is worth noting that, different thresholds can 
produce entirely different outcomes. Hence, the selection of 
thresholds may present a challenge to the validity of this 
research. Hence, three different sets of thresholds were used 
to minimize this threat: tight, relaxed, and Bavota thresholds 
[55]. These three strategies for attack surface detection 
enable us to establish classifications for refactoring based on 
three distinct sets of bugs, code smell, and vulnerability 
instances. 
VII. CONCLUSION AND FUTURE WORK 
This paper presents an empirical study conducted on a 
dataset that includes 3,523 instances of refactorings, 18,303 
occurrences of code smells, 2,975 instances of bugs, and 43 
vulnerabilities found in 30 open-source projects written in 
Python, C, and JavaScript. These projects are part of a widely 
recognized ecosystem, the GitHub repository. We initiated 
our research by conducting a preliminary analysis on the 
identification of the software attack surface and the 
previously applied refactorings in open-source software 
systems. Finally, we investigated the impact of refactorings 
on the software attack surface of the studied systems. Several 
important conclusions are drawn from our study. Firstly, 
results indicated that the most common attack surfaces on the 
studied open-source software projects are bugs, code smells, 
and vulnerabilities. The study also found that the common 
bugs 
were 
Code 
Complexity, 
Inconsistent 
Naming 
Convention, Insecure Code, Unused Code, Memory Leak 
and Unhandled Exception. Secondly, Extract Method, Inline 
Method, Move Method, Pull Up Method, Add Parameter, 
Remove Parameter, Rename Class, and Rename Method are 
the most refactorings applied to the analyzed open-source 
software projects. Thirdly, we observed that refactorings can 
have multiple effects (i.e., positive, negative, or neutral) on 
bugs, vulnerabilities, and code smells.  
Potential avenues for further research include 
extending our study to a large sample of open-source 
software projects written in other programming languages 
such as Java, Ruby, Rust, and C#, and including other 
elements of software attack surface to better generalize our 
results. In addition, this study focused on the quantity of 
attack surface elements rather than how specific elements, 
like particular code smells, were impacted by specific 
refactoring operations. Future research could provide deeper 
insights by analyzing how specific refactorings affect their 
corresponding smells and other types of smells. This detailed 
approach could also be applied to studying the impact of 
refactorings on bugs and vulnerabilities.

A reinforcement learning based fuzzing technique for binary programs 
vulnerabilities detection
Guoyan Cao a
,âˆ—, Yanhui Ma b, Mengjiao Geng a
a School of Cybersecurity in Northwestern Polytechnical University, Shaanxi, China
b China Aviation Industry Corporation Jinan Special Structure Research Institute, Shandong, China
A R T I C L E  I N F O
Keywords:
Binary program
Fuzzing
Reinforcement learning
Vulnerability probability
 
A B S T R A C T
Binary programs are susceptible to vulnerabilities that can lead to unauthorized access, data breaches, and 
system damage. Fuzzing is a promising technique for identifying vulnerabilities in binary programs. However, 
fuzzing is time-consuming and inefficient as many seeds are random and recurrently executed. This paper 
proposes a novel approach called Vulnerable State Guided Fuzzing (VSGFuzz) employs a heuristic mechanism 
for generating seeds to optimize vulnerability detection. This mechanism assesses the vulnerable probability 
of each function within the target binary program and employs reinforcement learning to mutate seeds based 
on a comprehensive reward calculation algorithm considering vulnerable probability and coverage assessment. 
Experiments evaluating VSGFuzz compared with other typical methods on several datasets demonstrated the 
superiority of the proposed method over other methods.
1. Introduction
Binary programs have become the cornerstone of modern com-
puting by providing efficient computing power and possessing cross-
platform characteristics. Security considerations regarding binary pro-
grams are crucial for the reliability of modern computing platforms, 
guarding against unauthorized access, leakage of sensitive information, 
and system damage. However, binary programs may suffer from nu-
merous unknown vulnerabilities that can compromise the security and 
reliability of systems. These vulnerabilities may arise from insecure 
usage of binary programs or dangerous operations involving them, such 
as data fabrications, service interruptions, and system attacks. Binary 
vulnerability playing as a form of malwares poses a significant security 
treat to computer environments and network surroundings [1], shown 
as in Fig. 1.
Fuzzing is one of the influential and powerful techniques for de-
tecting and discovering vulnerabilities in binary programs [2]. Fuzzing 
involves executing unexpected inputs, carefully observing program 
feedback and crash statuses, capturing coverage paths associated with 
the inputs, and repeatedly testing mutated inputs to uncover vulnera-
bilities in the target program. While this process is effective, it is also 
time-consuming and inefficient. Recently, significant research efforts 
have been focused on enhancing the efficiency of fuzzing by refin-
ing coverage-based methodologies under the assumption that greater 
path coverage increases the likelihood of discovering vulnerabilities. 
However, research methodologies that solely rely on path coverage 
âˆ—Corresponding author.
E-mail addresses: guoyan.cao@nwpu.edu.cn (G. Cao), vivian2855@163.com (Y. Ma), gmj_2000@163.com (M. Geng).
Fig. 1. Examples of binary program vulnerabilities.
often fail to produce optimal outcomes of high quality [3]. This is 
because a significant number of covered paths, resulting from code 
logic, conditional constraints, or error handling conditions, do not con-
tribute to finding potential vulnerabilities. Furthermore, the proportion 
of hidden vulnerabilities within the program code itself is relatively 
small. For example, an investigation by Shin and Williams [4] revealed 
that vulnerabilities were present in less than 5% of the source code files 
in Mozilla Firefox.
In light of the above considerations, this paper proposes a vul-
nerable state-guided fuzzing methodology (VSGFuzz) to enhance the 
https://doi.org/10.1016/j.array.2025.100458

efficiency of vulnerability detection. VSGFuzz is modeled as a Markov 
decision process, employing a reinforcement learning algorithm to 
direct superior mutation operations for generating higher-quality seed 
inputs. This approach optimizes the fuzzing process, making it more 
effective in identifying vulnerabilities in binary programs. VSGFuzz 
also leverages the RL algorithm to guide the mutation of input seeds 
with a higher likelihood of reaching vulnerable code segments. Unlike 
the equal seed mutation strategy commonly used by existing coverage-
based fuzzers, VSGFuzz emphasizes triggering crashes or attaining 
higher seed values. This approach capitalizes on the strengths of vul-
nerability prediction and coverage while mitigating their respective 
limitations. The contributions of this paper are summarized as follows:
(1) A novel fuzzing method is proposed to enhance coverage effi-
ciency and reduce runtime overhead. The fuzzing process is modeled 
as a Markov decision-making process, with a Reinforcement Learning 
mechanism designed to guide seed mutation, thus improving fuzzing 
efficiency and reducing overhead.
(2) Design a new metric for assessing the quality of seed files 
that not only evaluates vulnerability probability but also considers 
path weight and HugeScore to characterize the probability of program 
crashes.
(3) VSGFuzz has been demonstrated to detect more vulnerabilities 
in both general datasets and real-world programs compared to other 
methods. We implemented VSGFuzz on the LAVA-M dataset as well 
as several real-world programs to evaluate its fuzzing performance on 
binary programs. The results illustrated that VSGFuzz identified more 
vulnerabilities than state-of-the-art methods.
2. Related work
Fuzzing techniques have become integral for software testing and 
vulnerability discovery [5]. In this section, we have compiled some 
research in fuzzing to build upon existing work.
2.1. Fuzzing
Fuzzing techniques originated in the 1980s when Barton Miller and 
his colleagues first introduced the concept of fuzz testing, applying it 
to UNIX systems [6]. In the early 2000s, the mutation-based fuzzing 
approach emerged, involving a random or semi-random mutation of 
input data to generate test cases [7]. In 2005, the book â€˜â€˜Fuzzing for 
Software Security Testing and Quality Assuranceâ€™â€™ by Takanen, DeMott, 
and Miller provided a comprehensive overview of fuzzing techniques 
in software security testing [8]. The year 2006 saw the introduction of 
the SAGE (Scalable Automated Guided Execution) fuzzing framework, 
enabling automated fuzz testing in large-scale programs [9]. In 2010, 
TaintScope [10] employed dynamic taint analysis and symbolic execu-
tion to test x86 binary programs. The next year, SimFuzz [11] utilized 
test case similarity metrics to explore program semantics deeply.
A significant advancement occurred in 2013 with the release of 
American Fuzzy Lop (AFL) [12], which employed coverage-based
strategies and intelligent input mutation to discover program vul-
nerabilities. Dowser [13], a guided fuzzier, integrates taint tracking, 
program analysis, and symbolic execution to detect buffer overflow 
and underflow vulnerabilities. By 2016, the integration of symbolic 
execution and fuzzing gained popularity, enhancing the accuracy and 
efficiency of fuzz testing [14]. QuickFuzz [15] leveraged existing 
Haskell libraries to test various file formats without manual specifica-
tions in 2017 efficiently. Another fuzzier, VUzzer [16], on the other 
hand, utilizes control-flow and data-flow analysis to pinpoint bugs 
in deeper program paths, assigning increased significance to these 
intricate code components. Another strategy entails employing program 
analysis to support fuzzing efforts [17]. V-Fuzz [18] is designed to 
identify a wider array of vulnerabilities than Dowser.
2.2. Learning-based fuzzing
In recent years, researchers have combined machine learning with 
traditional fuzzing techniques, integrating machine learning methods 
into the stages of seed file generation and mutation strategy selection in 
the fuzzing process. Those integrations with different machine learning 
approaches, such as supervised (Regress and Classification), unsuper-
vised (Clustering and Desity estimation), semi-supervised and reinforce-
ment learning, bring in varies features, perspecitves and evolutions on 
fuzzing techniques [19].
In the seed file generation process, SmartSeed [20] utilizes Gen-
erative Adversarial Networks (GANs) to generate new binary samples 
from valid sample data identified by AFL. This approach triggers more 
crashes and execution paths than AFL and other selection strategies. 
REINAM [21] employs a reinforcement learning algorithm to generate 
program input grammar, thereby improving the quality of generated 
variation samples. In addition to traditional seed input in file format, 
software testing engineering encompasses other forms of seed input. For 
instance, Luong et al. [22] employed the Q-Learning algorithm to test 
Android applications. This involved selecting and arranging operations 
to trigger GUI event sequences, resulting in higher code coverage and 
more application errors being triggered. Deng et al. [23] use LLMs 
for black-box fuzzing testing Mutation, proving the effectiveness of 
pre-trained LLMs not only for seed generation but also for mutation. 
Cheng et al. [24] introduces a generative model built on a recurrent 
neural network (RNN) framework to provide high-quality sequences for 
PDF-based program targets. She et al. [25] proposed using a gradient-
guided input generation scheme and procedural smoothing techniques, 
in which the neural network learns smooth approximations. Scott 
et al. [26] leverages multi-agent RL guidance to improve SMT solver 
performance. The core idea revolves around training a single or a 
group of agent explorers to maximize reward signals that indicate the 
effectiveness of the generated inputs, particularly in achieving high 
code coverage or identifying bugs.
In selecting mutation strategies, researchers have been exploring 
integrating reinforcement learning techniques to enhance fuzz-ing ef-
ficiency. Bottinger [27] and colleagues utilized the Deep Q Network 
(DQN) of reinforcement learning to fuzz the Japanese standard program 
pdftotext. This approach employs strings as the state and six self-
defined mutation methods as actions. Compared to the traditional 
random mutation action selection strategy, this design significantly 
improves the code coverage rate and reduces the running time.FUZZ-
BOOST [28] shares a similar concept. FuzzerGym [29] integrates lib-
Fuzzer [30] and Double Deep Q Network (DDQN) via the Remote 
Procedure Call (RPC) method for target programs libjpeg, libpng, bor-
ingssl, re2, and sqllite. In fuzz testing, libFuzzer is guided to select the 
mutation function through the reinforcement learning algorithm. This 
approach leads to a significant improvement in code coverage com-
pared to the original random selection strategy. Kuznetsov et al. [31] 
also employed the DQN algorithm to select mutation actions, resulting 
in a reduction of approximately 30% in the number of sample muta-
tions required to detect vulnerabilities. Zhang et al. [32] introduced 
two key enhancements to traditional grey-box fuzzing: a multi-player, 
multi-armed bandit model and a non-dominated sorting genetic algo-
rithm for fuzzing. Wang et al. [33] use Deep Neural Network (DNN) 
to optimize the selection strategy of samples and improve the coverage 
of vulnerable paths. Suzzer [34] predicts the vulnerable probability of 
functions based on a deep learning-based model and gives each basic 
block in the vulnerable function a static score. Then, for each input, the 
sum of the static score of all the basic blocks on its execution path is 
calculated, and the inputs are prioritized with higher scores.

3. Overview
This section details the proposed vulnerable state-guided fuzzing 
methodology (VSGFuzz). As depicted in Fig. 2, VSGFuzz architecture 
consists of six steps and is grouped into two main processes: (1) static 
analysis and dynamic analysis.
In the static analysis process, the first step is to formulate binary 
functions into an ACFG data structure, which can used in a graph 
embedding network [35,36] to estimate the vulnerability probability of 
functions within binary programs in the second step. Based on function-
level vulnerability probability analysis, a basic block value calculation 
mechanism is designed to seed evaluation during the fuzzing phase.
An RL-based and vulnerable state-guided fuzzy logic is proposed in 
the dynamic analysis process. The core part of the fuzzer is finding 
effective seeds to point to highly vulnerable areas and cover function 
paths as many as possible. The details of the techniques are introduced 
in Step 4 - Step 6. Using the RL algorithm, the fuzzing process is trained 
to select more effective mutations progressively.
4. Methodology of VSGFuzz
4.1. Step 1: Data preprocessing
Vulnerability prediction at the program level cannot capture the 
nuanced relationship between the program and vulnerable code seg-
ments. This limitation hampers the effective mining of vulnerabilities 
and impedes subsequent mutation processes of the fuzzer. To address 
this, we adopt function-level analysis to assess program vulnerabilities, 
and therefore, we need to characterize the specific features of binary 
functions.
Conventional approaches to binary programs are grouped into three 
methods: (1) converting function contents into byte arrays, (2) col-
lecting information on the type and quantity of identifiers within a 
function, and (3) utilizing program abstract syntax trees, among others. 
However, the former two methods disregard the structural information 
of the function, while the latter sacrifices its statistical information. To 
comprehensively account for both the structure and semantic informa-
tion of functions, based on the third method, we build the Attributes 
Control Flow Graph (ACFG) [35,37â€“39] representation to characterize 
the binary function.
ACFG [35] is a directed graph denoted as

the nodes in the graph. The construction of ACFG relies on a control 
flow graph (CFG), which employs diagrams to illustrate all possible 
execution paths within a computer program.
The process of obtaining the ACFG of a binary function is illustrated 
in Fig. 3. Firstly, the binary program is disassembled to derive the 
Fig. 3. Procedure for binary programs to extract the ACFG.
CFG of each function within the program. Subsequently, attribute 
information is extracted from each basic block, and each basic block is 
transformed into a numerical vector. By following these steps, the ACFG 
representation of the function is obtained. These attributes encompass 
essential components such as string and numerical constants, transfer 
and call instructions, arithmetic instructions, and child nodes, all of 
which provide insights into the functionâ€™s behavior. Furthermore, the 
betweenness centrality measure captures the significance of a node 
within the overall graph structure, aiding in the identification of po-
tential vulnerabilities within the function. Both the functionâ€™s statistical 
and structural information are stored as vectors in the nodes, serving 
as attribute vectors for the basic block nodes. Each node in the ACFG 
possesses an attribute vector with eight dimensions, representing the 
function as a collection of eight-dimensional vectors. Subsequently, the 
extracted ACFG of the binary function is utilized as input for the model.

4.4. Step4: Seed score
Upon completion of program execution, VSGFuzz records the in-
put execution path. The seed score of the input is calculated as the 
cumulative sum of the ðµð‘‰ values associated with the basic blocks 
along the execution path. Suppose the execution path is defined as 
ð‘ð‘Žð‘¡â„Žâˆ¶ð‘1 â†’ð‘3 â†’ð‘6 â†’ð‘8. Consequently, the corresponding reward 
value for this input can be expressed as 
ð‘†ð‘’ð‘’ð‘‘ð‘†ð‘ð‘œð‘Ÿð‘’= ðµð‘‰(ð‘1) + ðµð‘‰(ð‘3) + ðµð‘‰(ð‘6) + ðµð‘‰(ð‘8) + ð¶Ã— ð»ð‘¢ð‘”ð‘’ð‘†ð‘ð‘œð‘Ÿð‘’(6)
where ð¶ is a binary parameter to control the seed score, if a crash 
occurred, ð¶ is set to 1; otherwise, ð¶ is set to 0. ð»ð‘¢ð‘”ð‘’ð‘†ð‘ð‘œð‘Ÿð‘’ is set to 
be a large numerical value that significantly contributes to the reward

4.5. Step5: Dynamic execution
VSGFuzz is a repetitive process. It maintains a seed pool to store 
high-quality inputs as seeds. Initially, VSGFuzz executes the binary 
program using an initial input provided by the user. Concurrently, 
it utilizes Dynamic Binary Instrumentation (DBI) to track program 
execution information, including basic block coverage. Leveraging ðµð‘‰
and execution information, VSGFuzz calculates a seed score for each 
executed test case (i.e., input). Test cases with higher seed scores are 
considered high-quality inputs and added to the seed bank. Test cases 
that trigger crashes are also included in the seed pool and assigned 
higher seed scores. Next, VSGFuzz generates next-generation test cases 
by mutating the seeds present in the seed pool. The new seeds are also 
stored in the seed pool. Then, we repeat the process to select a seed 
from the pool to run a fuzzing test.
In general, control flow is used to specify path priority and identify 
error-handling blocks, and data flow is utilized to determine the loca-
tion of variation and specific operations. Specifically, AFL is improved 
to give greater weight to paths of interest. Based on analyzing the basic 
block weight calculation in line with Markov properties, we conclude 
that the transfer probabilities between blo-cks are independent, and 
their probabilities are only related to connected blocks, so the inverse of 
the probability is set as the weight. In the paper, error-handling blocks 
are designed with weights set to negative numbers, and the sum of 
the weights of the blocks on the path is defined as the path weights. 
The higher the score, the higher the weight and the higher priority the 
input corresponding to the path is considered to have, and it will be 
preferred for seed mutation and being selected again as the seed file. 
Vuzzer recognizes magic bytes by Pin insertion, and through continuous 
iteration, it matches the information in ð‘ð‘šð‘ and address fetching class 
operation ð‘™ð‘’ð‘Ž with the seed file input and the newly generated inputs 
and finds the magic bytes in the input to find the possible locations of 
magic bytes and mutate them more accurately.
4.6. Step6: RL for fuzzing
4.6.1. Modeling based on RL
This section introduces a methodology for constructing the state, 
action, reward and environment components in reinforcement learn-
ing (RL) problems, which takes inspiration from the operations and 
environment of fuzzing. The Markov property is satisfied by ensuring 
that the systemâ€™s state in the subsequent moment is solely dependent 
on its current state and is not influenced by other states. Within 
the context of fuzzing, the mutation strategy is utilized to select an 
appropriate mutating operation for the current seed. Subsequently, the 
target program processes the mutant seed, and the specific reward is 
computed based on the runtime feedback received.

state, action, and reward elements in the fuzzing problem modeling 
based on RL.

4.6.2. Strategy selection of reinforcement learning algorithm
To effectively select mutation operations for fuzzing, choosing RL 
algorithms that can handle large state and action spaces is essential. 
In 2014, David Silver et al. proposed the deterministic policy gradient 
(DPG) algorithm, which demonstrated the existence of a deterministic 
policy gradient through mathematical analysis. Subsequently, the deep 
deterministic policy gradient (DDPG) algorithm [41] emerged by com-
bining the DPG algorithm with deep neural networks, enhancing its 
practicality. Given the relatively large mutation operation space and 
input seed state space in the fuzzing process model, we opt for the 
DDPG algorithm to construct the RL model [42].
The DDPG algorithm comprises four neural networks, which are

5. Implementation and settings
5.1. Graph embedding-based vulnerability prediction model
As shown in the previous design, we need to accomplish two parts 
to implement a graph embedding-based vulnerability prediction model. 
Those two parts are (1) an ACFG extractor and (2) a vulnerability 
prediction model. The ACFG extractor was implemented by a plugin 
provided by the widely used disassembly tool IDA Pro [43]. The 
vulnerability prediction model was developed using the popular deep 
learning framework TensorFlow.
Based on the Genius project [35], the ACFG extractor for binary 
program functions was developed. By modifying and enhancing the 
feature extraction method of Genius, we can customize and incorporate 
the specific feature data required for our purposes. The vulnerability 
prediction model takes the ACFG of the function along with its corre-
sponding label as input. Therefore, during model training, we require a 
dataset consisting of functions with known vulnerabilities. This exper-
iment uses the Juliet Test Suite as the training dataset, widely used in 
various vulnerability-related studies. The Juliet Test Suite, published by 
the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST), comprises 
C/C++ language programs, where each function is labeled as â€˜â€˜goodâ€™â€™ 
(indicating â€˜â€˜secureâ€™â€™) or â€˜â€˜badâ€™â€™ (indicating â€˜â€˜vulnerableâ€™â€™).
Our parameter settings are shown in Table 2 based on the training 
data analysis and the modelâ€™s tuning.
In terms of the system platform, we utilized the hardware environ-
ment detailed in Table 3.
5.2. RL based and vulnerable states guided fuzzing
In the paper, we developed a fuzzier VSGFuzz based on VUzzer [16], 
an advanced evolutionary fuzzer designed for binary targets. Each 
fuzzing experiment was performed on a virtual machine running
Ubuntu 20.04 LTS. The virtual machine had a 64-bit single-core Intel 
CPU running at 4.2 GHz and 4 GB of RAM.
RL model training and fuzzing efficiency are closely related to its 
hardware and software environment. For the training model, we set 
the hardware environment in Table 3, and the software environment 
is shown in Table 4. We also use library files such as Tensorflow, 
Keras-RL2, and Gym to build a RL model based on the DDPG algorithm.
6. Evaluation
In this section, we evaluate VSGFuzz through the following two 
aspects: (1) the evaluation results of the vulnerability prediction model 
and (2) the evaluation results of the RL-based fuzzer.
6.1. Graph embedding based vulnerability prediction model evaluation
Evaluation metrics:. Accuracy, loss, ACFG extraction time, and training 
time were used to measure the performance of the vulnerability predic-
tion model. Table 5 summarizes our evaluation results. We use the cross 
entropy loss function to calculate the loss of the model. The VPModel-
evaluation table records the loss rate and accuracy of the model. We 
use the cross-entropy loss function to calculate the loss of the model, 
which quickly drops to a low value, then stabilizes, and the surface 
model rapidly converges. The accuracy curve of the model is more than 
0.995, which means that the model can correctly distinguish between 
positive and negative cases to a large extent.
The figure (Fig. 7) depicts the reward graph generated during 
the training of a fuzzy test model using the Deep Q Network (DQN) 
and DDPG. The orange line represents the reward values obtained by 
DDPG, while the brown line represents the reward values obtained 
by DQN. The graph illustrates that DDPG outperforms the DQN algo-
rithm regarding model training performance. The higher reward values
achieved by DDPG indicate its superior performance in optimizing 
fuzzy test models. The red dashed line at the top of the chart represents 
the maximum reward value attained under the DDPG model, while the 
blue dashed line represents the maximum reward value achieved under 
the DQN model. The reward values are designed to be the seed score 
after the seed is executed.
The abscissa in the figure (Fig. 7) represents the number of execu-
tion steps during the fuzz testing process, and the ordinate represents 
the reward feedback value obtained. The image analysis shows that in 
the early stage of fuzz testing, a higher reward value feedback is not 
obtained each time a new seed file is executed. However, about 700 
steps after triggering, the feedback value suddenly increased signifi-
cantly. It is speculated that it may be because the seed file generated 
by the mutation triggered a certain critical path at this stage, which 
may have been marked as possible in previous predictions. Loopholes. 
Subsequently, it remains stable for some time, possibly because the 
mutations performed during this period were local-scale changes that 
failed to induce substantial or larger-scale path changes. It should be 
emphasized that the changes in the two lines shown in the figure all 
come from changes in path coverage, and there is no program crash 
event. In the later experiments, we also used DDPG to train the model.

6.2. RL based and vulnerable states guided fuzzing evaluation
In this section, we demonstrate VSGFuzzâ€™s ability of discovering vul-
nerabilities on three different datasets: A. LAVA-M Dataset, B. DARPA 
CGC binaries and C. Real-Word Dataset. The results demonstrated that 
VSGFuzz was able to not only precisely evaluate vulnerability proba-
bility to detect more vulnerabilities, but also consume less computation 
time with a promising efficiency.
A. LAVA-M Dataset
Table 6 shows the number of bugs found by VSGFuzz, Vuzzer,

bers triggered by the LAVA-M program during the fuzz testing process 
are as shown in the following Table 7. Furthermore, VSGFuzz can 
trigger several unlisted bugs and exhibits better performance than V-
Fuzz in this case. VSGFuzz excels in terms of coverage as shown in 
Table 8. Compared to other methods, it can explore a wider range of 
execution paths within the program.
B. DARPA CGC Dataset
We obtained a total of 149 CGC binaries. However, we were unable 
to run VSGFuzz on all of these devices due to the following reasons:
(1) All binaries are interactive by accepting input from STDIN. 
Once launched, many display a menu to select actions, including an 
exit option. Additionally, there are many menus (in different states of 
the program) with varying options for exit. Since VSGFuzz requires 
one step to complete with completely random input, performing such 
input would put the application in a loop looking for valid possibilities, 
including an option to exit, which would cause the application to run 
forever. This is an interface issue, not a fundamental limitation of our 
fuzzing approach.
(2) Some binaries involve interactions with others, which CSGFuzz 
cannot handle.
(3) Since VSGFuzz is based on Pin, we cannot run some binaries 
with Pin.

7. Conclusion
This paper presents an innovative fuzzing method named VSGFuzz, 
designed for vulnerability analysis in binary programs. Our approach 
comprises several key steps. Firstly, we develop a vulnerability pre-
diction model to estimate the vulnerability probability of individual 
functions within a binary program. Next, we leverage these vulnera-
bility probabilities and basic block values to compute seed file scores. 
Subsequently, a reinforcement learning model is trained to guide the 
mutation operations applied to the seed file, enhancing both the quality 
and efficiency of the fuzz testing process. Finally, our test results on 
the LAVA-M dataset, DARPA CGC dataset and Real-Word Dataset high-
light the effectiveness of VSGFuzz. Moreover, the training results on 
real programs demonstrate the toolâ€™s usability, especially in enhancing 
program coverage. These findings underscore the effectiveness of our 
approach to identifying vulnerabilities and fortifying the security of 
binary programs.
