TableÂ  9 reports the three complementary static repair metrics, SRSR, OIRR, and SSR, 
across all evaluated models. Because SRSR is the most restrictive metric, requiring successÂ­
ful AST-based parsability, complete resolution of all originally reported SonarQube issues, 
and the absence of newly introduced violations, it serves as the primary basis for ranking. 
In contrast, OIRR and SSR capture partial aspects of repair quality by focusing separately 
on issue resolution and non-regression. Accordingly, the comparative ranking derived from 
SRSR is illustrated in Fig.Â 6, which provides a clearer visual representation of the perforÂ­
mance differences between models.
Based on SRSR, the models separate into three clear performance tiers. The top tier consists 
of Grok (62.08%) and GPT-4o (59.13%), which achieve the highest rates of complete repairs. 
Grok leads across all three metrics, recording the strongest OIRR (66.70%) and the highest 
SSR (90.80%), indicating both effective elimination of original issues and strong resistance 
to introducing new violations. GPT-4o follows with consistently high scores in completeness 
(59.13%), resolution (62.89%), and non-regression (90.62%). Together, these two models 
demonstrate the most reliable ability to satisfy all static repair constraints simultaneously.
The second tier includes DeepSeek (58.40%), Claude (58.15%), and Mistral (56.68%). 
Their SRSR values fall within a narrow interval of less than two percentage points, indiÂ­
cating closely comparable levels of complete repair capability. Within this group, Claude 
records a slightly higher OIRR (62.48%) than DeepSeek (61.66%) and Mistral (60.60%), 
suggesting marginally stronger effectiveness at resolving original issues. In terms of SSR, 
Mistral reaches 90.11%, slightly above Claude (89.51%) and DeepSeek (89.15%). Overall, 
these three models show balanced and competitive performance, though they remain just 
below the top tier under the strict SRSR criterion.
The third tier is represented solely by Gemini (50.89%), notably lower than the other modÂ­
els. Although its OIRR (59.01%) remains within the general range of the second tier, its SSR 
(81.11%) is substantially lower than all other models. This lower non-regression rate indiÂ­
cates a higher tendency to introduce new static violations, which limits its ability to achieve 
complete, rule-compliant repairs. Consequently, Gemini ranks last under the most restrictive 
evaluation criterion, despite demonstrating a moderate capacity to resolve original issues.
In summary, this subsection evaluated model performance at the function level using 
three complementary static metrics that capture completeness, issue resolution, and safety. 
By analyzing SRSR, OIRR, and SSR jointly, we distinguished between fully correct repairs, 
partial resolutions of original issues, and non-regressive transformations. The results show 
clear performance tiers under the strict SRSR criterion, while also revealing differences 
in how consistently models eliminate original violations and avoid introducing new ones. 
However, this analysis remains confined to static properties and does not yet examine the 
specific rule categories affected or the semantic implications of the generated changes. 
These aspects are explored in the subsequent subsection.

5.3â€‚ Issue-Level Repair Effectiveness
We continue the analysis by examining the same set of 22,259 functions considered in the 
previous subsection in order to provide an answer to RQ3. For each of these functions, we 
inspected the SonarQube issues originally reported before repair, then compared them with 
the issues remaining and any new issues introduced after applying each LLMâ€™s suggested 
fix. This detailed inspection aims to confirm that the reductions observed at the project and 
function levels correspond to meaningful improvements in code quality rather than superfiÂ­
cial changes or offsetting errors. The post-repair SonarQube analysis was conducted under 
identical conditions for each model to ensure consistency and fairness in the evaluation. 
This finer-grained perspective also allows us to detect rule-specific patterns that may influÂ­
ence the interpretation of higher-level repair metrics.
This issue-level analysis focuses specifically on the SonarQube rule identifiers associÂ­
ated with the fixed and added issues, enabling us to assess not just how many issues were 
addressed but also which types of issues each model handled most effectively and where 
new problems might arise. As we mentioned in Section 2.1, SonarQube issues can be classiÂ­
fied by the rule that triggers them, which provides a structured way to analyze the nature of 
the repairs. At this stage, we set the groundwork for understanding how the repairs interact 
with the specific rule categories and whether the observed patterns align with the modelsâ€™ 
strengths suggested by the earlier function-level results. Overall, the 22,259 functions in 
this subset were originally marked by one or multiple rules drawn from a set of 104 distinct 
SonarQube rule identifiers. Further details on the observed distributions and trends will folÂ­
low as the analysis progresses.
To illustrate the issue-level behavior of the models in more detail, we selected the 10 
most frequently occurring Python-specific SonarQube rules observed in the original, pre-
repair version of the 22,259 functions. This selection highlights the most common and 
impactful types of issues present before any model intervention, providing a representative 
Fig. 6â€‚ Static Repair Success Rate (SRSR) by model
 
1â€¯3

â€ƒ

Empirical Software Engineering          (2026) 31:118 
overview of the recurring code-quality problems addressed by the models. As shown in preÂ­
vious studies, a relatively small subset of SonarQube rules is responsible for the majority of 
detected issues, and focusing on the ten most frequent rules is a well-established approach 
for summarizing such distributions (Baldassarre etÂ al. 2020; Molnar and Motogna 2020).
Table 10 lists these 10 rules along with their descriptions. These rules account for a 
substantial proportion of the total violations in the function-level dataset considered in this 
issue-level analysis, rather than in the global SonarQube totals reported earlier in the paper. 
Table 11 presents, for each of these rules and each model, the number of remaining vioÂ­
lations, including those not fixed and any new ones introduced by the model, alongside 
the percentage reduction compared to the original violations. All counts reported in this 
table are computed on the validated set of 22,259 function-level issue groups described in 
SectionÂ 5.2, and therefore differ from the global SonarQube totals presented earlier. This 
provides a detailed view of how effectively each model addressed the most frequent issues 
within the evaluated function-level scope and to what extent they reduced the original 
violations.
As presented in Table 11, our dataset is imbalanced, with certain SonarQube rule violaÂ­
tions occurring far more frequently than others. The most frequent rules are S117, S1192, 
and S3776, which account for 9,158 (28.45%), 6,595 (20.49%), and 2,436 (7.57%) of the 
total 32,186 recorded issues, respectively. Together, these three rules comprise 56.51% of 
all violations, clearly illustrating the significant skew in the distribution of rule violations. 
Imbalance in software quality datasets is a well known phenomenon observed in many 
contexts, and several studies have proposed methods to mitigate its effects. As shown in 
Rathore etÂ al. (2022), generative oversampling techniques have been applied to address 
imbalance in software fault prediction tasks, emphasizing that uneven distributions of issues 
are a common characteristic of software engineering data.
Although the models evaluated in this study are not trained on the dataset, such an imbalÂ­
ance still influences the interpretation of results. Aggregate metrics such as the overall issue 
reduction rate or function-level static repair metrics (e.g., SRSR, OIRR, and SSR) are domiÂ­
nated by the most frequent rule categories, meaning that high performance on common and 
often simpler rule types (e.g., naming conventions or string duplication) can disproporÂ­
tionately increase the overall effectiveness. Consequently, this skews the evaluation toward 
these prevalent issue types and may underrepresent model behavior on less frequent but 
more semantically complex rules, limiting the generality of the conclusions.
The issue-level analysis presented above is based on the validated subset of functions 
described in SectionÂ 5.2 and therefore differs from the global SonarQube totals reported 
earlier in SectionÂ 4.1, which refer to all detected issues across the analyzed repositories. 
TableÂ 12 also relies on this validated subset and reports repair outcomes only for functions 
where extraction, repair generation, and validation were successfully completed. Using this 
subset, we aggregate repair outcomes by SonarQube issue type to examine how model perÂ­
formance varies across broader categories of issues.
As expected, code smells exhibit the highest reduction rates across all models, ranging 
from 42.9% (Gemini) to 60.6% (Grok). These results align with the predominantly strucÂ­
tural and stylistic nature of code smells, which can often be addressed through localized 
refactorings. Bug-level issues, which are less frequent and typically require deeper semanÂ­
tic reasoning, show consistently lower but still substantial reduction rates, between 31.8% 
(Gemini) and 49.4% (Grok). This suggests that LLMs are not limited to correcting frequent 
1â€¯3
Page 29 of 45â€ƒ
  118 
Empirical Software Engineering          (2026) 31:118 
stylistic patterns, but are also capable of repairing a meaningful portion of semantically 
grounded defects.
Vulnerability-related results should be interpreted with caution. Although relatively high 
reduction percentages are observed, ranging from 45.8% (Gemini) to 70.8% (DeepSeek), 
the total number of vulnerabilities in the dataset is very small (24 issues), which precludes 
statistically robust conclusions. Consequently, the vulnerability figures are reported for 
completeness but are not used to draw comparative claims between models. Overall, this 
issue-type-based analysis complements the rule-level evaluation by providing a broader 
view of LLM repair capabilities beyond the dominant class of code smells.

Both TablesÂ 10 and 11 highlight a clear imbalance in the distribution of rule violations. 
In particular, the top three rules, S117, S1192, and S3776, account for more than half of all 
detected issues, which explains their strong influence on aggregate repair metrics. These 
rules correspond to enforcing naming conventions, avoiding duplicated string literals, and 
limiting cognitive complexity, respectively, and are considered important for achieving 
maintainable and understandable code. As shown in Feitelson etÂ al. (2020), naming is a cogÂ­
nitively demanding activity for developers, which makes violations of naming conventions 
a common occurrence detected by static analysis tools. Similarly, Gergel etÂ al. (2011) shows 
that adherence to conventions and avoidance of duplication are associated with improved 
maintainability. Cognitive complexity has been empirically validated in MuÃ±oz BarÃ³n etÂ al. 
(2020) as a factor that increases the effort required to comprehend and modify code.
Table 11 shows that none of the evaluated models achieves superior performance across 
all rules, indicating that each model has distinct strengths and trade-offs. Grok attains the 
highest overall rank and delivers substantial reductions on key rules, standing out particuÂ­
larly on S117 naming conventions, where its reduction achieves 73.6%. However, it perÂ­
forms less strongly on S112, raising Exception or BaseException, where Claude achieves 
the highest reduction. GPT-4o and Claude also perform strongly overall, with Claude showÂ­
ing particular strength on rules like S112 and S1172, achieving 91.3% and 83.0% reducÂ­
tions respectively. These findings suggest that while all models are capable of addressing 
frequent and impactful issues to a significant degree, their effectiveness varies considerably 
depending on the rule category, which highlights the importance of tailoring LLM use to the 
specific quality concerns of a project.
A similar pattern emerges when examining the performance of the lower-ranked models. 
Although Gemini generally lags behind the others in overall performance, it does not come 
in last in every scenario. For example, on S3776, which measures cognitive complexity, 
Gemini achieves a reduction of 57.9%, better than GPT-4o (50.5%), Mistral (41.6%) and 
DeepSeek (55.3%), but still lower than the top performer, Grok, which achieves 76.4%. 
These observations underscore that no single model can yet fully address the breadth of 
SonarQube rule violations optimally, and that combining models or selecting the most 
appropriate one based on the predominant issue types could lead to more effective autoÂ­
mated repairs.
While most frequent rules are effectively handled through localized refactorings, certain 
rule types expose structural limitations of a function-scoped repair strategy. Among the top 
ten most frequent SonarQube rules analyzed, S1192 (String literals should not be dupliÂ­
cated) stands out as the only one for which all models achieved relatively low reduction 
rates, consistently below 50%. This outcome likely stems from the nature of the violation 
and its misalignment with our function-level repair approach. Duplicated string literals can

be distributed across multiple functions or outside function bodies within the same file, so 
eliminating them within a single function does not necessarily resolve the overall issue. 
Even if an LLM refactors a function to remove repeated strings locally, SonarQube may 
continue to flag the file if the same literal appears in other functions, global variables, or 
class definitions. This highlights a limitation of function-scoped refactoring when addressÂ­
ing problems that inherently depend on file-level or module-level context.
The low reduction rates observed for rule S1192 (String literals should not be duplicated) 
prompted us to examine whether other SonarQube rules are similarly unsuitable for funcÂ­
tion-level refactoring. We reviewed the rules by initially querying the GPT-4o API with: 
â€œWhich SonarQube rules cannot be fixed by editing a single function because the issue 
involves multiple functions, or the fix requires changes across more than one function?â€ 
GPT-4o recommended several rules as potentially requiring broader, cross-function, or file-
level context, among which S1192 and S930 were included.
To assess these recommendations, we subsequently performed a comprehensive manual 
review of the Python rules observed in the dataset. Each rule was examined with respect 
to whether its resolution inherently depends on file-level or cross-function context, which 
would make it unsuitable for isolated function-level refactoring. This manual analysis indeÂ­
pendently confirmed that S1192 and S930 fundamentally and consistently require broader 
contextual information. While other rules suggested by GPT-4o, such as S2638 (Method 
overrides should not change contracts, 235 original issues) and S4144 (Functions should 
not have identical implementations, 135 original issues), may benefit from wider context, 
they either represented a small fraction of the total issue volume or could still be partially 
addressed at the function level and were therefore retained in the evaluation.
Across all analyzed rules, S1192 and S930 were the only ones for which both the GPT-4o 
recommendations and our independent manual review converged in concluding that funcÂ­
tion-scoped repair is structurally insufficient. S1192 accounted for 6,595 original issues, 
representing the second largest rule category in the dataset, and its resolution inherently 
requires cross-file knowledge of duplicate occurrences. Because duplicated string literals 
may appear in multiple functions or outside function bodies, isolated function-level refactorÂ­
ing cannot reliably eliminate the violation at the file level. This structural mismatch explains 
the consistently low reduction rates observed for S1192 across models and confirms that the 
limitation lies in the repair granularity rather than in model capability.
Rule S930, although comprising only 24 original issues, exhibited severe negative reducÂ­
tions across all six models after repair, further confirming the same structural limitation. 
Following LLM-generated refactorings, the number of S930 violations increased to 334 
for Claude, 242 for DeepSeek, 199 for Gemini, 373 for GPT-4o, 379 for Grok, and 283 
for Mistral. Manual inspection showed that these new violations were typically introduced 
when unused parameters were removed to satisfy S1172, while corresponding function calls 
elsewhere in the codebase were not updated. This created inconsistencies between funcÂ­
tion definitions and their callers, producing cross-functional mismatches. Consequently, we 
excluded S1192 and S930 from the evaluation dataset to ensure that the function-level repair 
assessment reflects rule categories compatible with the chosen repair scope.
These observations regarding rules S1192 and S930 reveal inherent limitations of our 
function-level refactoring approach, suggesting that the low reduction rates and increased 
violations were not solely due to the LLMsâ€™ capabilities but to a mismatch between the 
rulesâ€™ nature and a function-scoped strategy. Because these limitations directly affect the 
1â€¯3
  118 
â€ƒ
Page 32 of 45
Empirical Software Engineering          (2026) 31:118 
assessment of function-level static correctness, they also impact the interpretation of the 
static repair metrics introduced in the previous subsection, particularly the Static Repair 
Success Rate (SRSR). Including rules that fundamentally require cross-function or file-level 
context biases SRSR, OIRR, and SSR downward by penalizing models for cases that cannot 
be resolved under a function-scoped repair strategy.
To mitigate this effect, we repeated the function-level static evaluation after excluding 
functions affected by rules S1192 or S930. Specifically, functions were excluded if either 
rule appeared in the original code or in any of the LLM-generated refactorings. From the 
subset of 22,259 function groups discussed above, we identified 5,147 functions that met 
this criterion and excluded them from the evaluation. This resulted in a final set of 17,112 
function-level repairs per model used for the revised static repair analysis.
Among the excluded cases, most of the removed functions were affected only by rule 
S1192. These cases provided limited analytical value, as violations of this rule cannot be 
effectively resolved through function-scoped refactoring and therefore do not meaningfully 
reflect the LLMsâ€™ repair capabilities. As a result, the refactored versions remained effecÂ­
tively identical to the originals from a code quality perspective, with no real opportunity for 
improvement under a function-level strategy. Rule S930 appeared in only 295 functions 
overall, making its impact on the overall evaluation comparatively small. Consequently, 
this filtering step was methodologically justified, as it removed cases that could not be effecÂ­
tively addressed within our function-based refactoring approach, while retaining those for 
which this strategy was appropriate and informative.
After applying the filtering that excludes functions affected by rules S1192 and S930, 
all evaluated models exhibit substantial and consistent improvements across Static Repair 
Success Rate (SRSR), Original Issue Resolution Rate (OIRR), and Static Safety Rate (SSR). 
In particular, SRSR increases by approximately 10â€“13 percentage points for every model, 
indicating that a significant portion of previously unsuccessful repairs was attributable to 
rule categories that are structurally incompatible with function-scoped refactoring rather 
than to deficiencies in the modelsâ€™ repair capabilities.
As shown in TableÂ 13, Grok remains the top-performing model after filtering, achieving 
an SRSR of 74.21%, followed by GPT-4o at 70.79%. DeepSeek and Claude reach comÂ­
parable levels of complete static repair at 69.79% and 69.47%, respectively. Mistral and 
Gemini also show improvements, although they remain comparatively less effective under 
the strict SRSR criterion, with 67.61% and 60.92%, respectively. Importantly, the relative 
ranking of models remains unchanged after filtering, demonstrating that the original orderÂ­
ing was not driven by these rule categories. The magnitude of the SRSR increase before and 
after filtering is illustrated in Fig.Â 7.
The observed improvements across all three metrics confirm that rules S1192 and S930 
systematically penalized models under strict static correctness criteria despite being unsuitÂ­
able for resolution at the function level. By excluding these cases, the revised metrics proÂ­
vide a more accurate, unbiased, and methodologically sound assessment of each modelâ€™s 
ability to generate syntactically valid, rule-compliant, and non-regressive repairs within the 
intended scope of the repair strategy. This filtering step therefore strengthens the internal 
validity of the function-level evaluation and clarifies that the remaining performance differÂ­
ences reflect genuine variation in repair effectiveness rather than artifacts of rule granularity 
mismatch.

Empirical Software Engineering          (2026) 31:118 
The issue-level analysis shows that model performance depends strongly on the nature of 
the underlying SonarQube rules. Localized rules, such as naming or unused variable detecÂ­
tion, were handled effectively, whereas broader rules like duplication or structural depenÂ­
dencies remained difficult to address. This alignment between issue-level limitations and 
function-level correctness metrics reinforces the validity of the adjusted evaluation.
5.4â€‚ Test-Suite-Based Validation Results
Following the test-suite-based validation protocol described in SectionÂ 4.4, this subsection 
addresses RQ4 by introducing an execution-based evaluation applied to the filtered set of 
17,112 function-level repairs identified in SectionÂ 5.3, after excluding cases associated with 
rules S1192 and S930. From this set, a random sample of 139 original functions per 
project was selected for evaluation, and the same sampled set was used across all six LLMs 
to assess whether LLM-generated repairs preserve the observable runtime behavior of the 
original code, as captured by the projectsâ€™ test suites. The only exception is the Requests 
project, which contains fewer eligible modified functions; therefore, all 56 available funcÂ­
tions were included. This sampling strategy produced a total of 1,863 candidate functions 
for execution-based validation.

function-level repair is considered plausibly correct if the summary of test outcomes after 
applying the modification is identical to the baseline execution on the original, unmodiÂ­

based results.
In this execution-based setup, AST validation was not applied before test execution, since 
AST parsing does not capture runtime-breaking issues such as missing imports. Instead, we 
performed a lightweight string-based sanity check to detect incomplete outputs, including 
unbalanced code fences, unmatched parentheses, or truncated function bodies. Such cases 
were treated as execution errors and counted as implausible repairs in the PCR calculation.
All test outcomes are evaluated relative to project-specific baseline executions, and each 
function-level modification is tested in isolation following the sampling strategy described 
in SectionÂ  4.4. This design ensures that observed differences can be causally attributed 
to individual repairs rather than interactions between multiple changes. In the following 
analysis, we report and interpret execution-based results across projects and models. Due 
to hardware constraints, environment incompatibilities, and long execution times (approxiÂ­
mately two days per project on average), some projects (keras, pandas, openpilot, zulip, 
and jumpserver) execute test suites that exclude specific categories of tests, such as those 
marked as slow, network, or other resource-intensive markers. In the case of ansible, due to 
execution constraints, only unit tests were executed.
TableÂ 14 reports the plausible correctness rate for function-level repairs across the subset 
of projects with stable test-suite behavior. Only 14 out of 20 analyzed projects satisfied the 
stability requirements described in SectionÂ 4.4, namely reproducible baseline executions 
with consistent test outcome summaries. Consequently, the PCR results reported in TableÂ 14 
are computed only on the sampled functions belonging to these stable projects.
The remaining six projects could not be used in the execution-based validation because 
repeated baseline runs on the original, unmodified code produced inconsistent numbers of 
passed and failed tests. In other words, even the original version without any refactoring 
triggered fluctuating outcomes. This instability was caused by factors such as reliance on 
random number generation without fixed seeds, hardware-dependent behavior, partial or 
state-dependent database initialization requirements, and dependencies on external services 
or cloud resources. For example, yt-dlp depends on online platforms such as YouTube, 
where rate limiting and network variability affect test determinism.
For the 14 stable projects, the reported values indicate the proportion of sampled repairs 
for which the execution summary of the test suite remained identical to the baseline, proÂ­
viding an execution-based view of behavioral preservation. The observed variation across 
projects reflects differences in test coverage, architecture, and sensitivity to localized code 
changes. Across most included projects, all evaluated models achieve non-trivial plausible 
correctness rates, suggesting that a considerable fraction of function-level repairs do not 
introduce observable behavioral regressions under stable test conditions.
Although the 14 retained projects satisfied the stability requirements in terms of reproÂ­
ducible baseline executions, their test suites are not uniform in size or execution completeÂ­
ness. As shown in TableÂ 15, several projects exhibit skipped tests according to the last 
observed execution logs, with skip rates ranging from negligible values (e.g., 0.05% in 
Zulip) to more substantial proportions (e.g., 12.88% in Fairseq). While skipped tests do 
not invalidate the execution-based validation, they reduce the effective runtime coverage 
and may limit the detection of certain behavioral regressions. As mentioned before, some 
1â€¯3
Page 35 of 45â€ƒ
  118 
Empirical Software Engineering          (2026) 31:118 
Docker configurations may exclude tests before collection, so they may not be reflected in 
the skipped counts.
In addition, for one project, Jumpserver, we identified only a single executable test in its 
default test suite during our analysis. Although this test appeared stable and reproducible, 
its extremely limited scope significantly constrains the strength of behavioral conclusions 
that can be drawn for this project. Consequently, the execution-based results for Jumpserver 
should be interpreted cautiously. More generally, the results across projects should be conÂ­
sidered in light of differences in test-suite size, skipped-test rates, and coverage, rather than 
as uniformly strong behavioral guarantees.
To compare the models from a ranking perspective, we apply the Friedman test across 
the same 14 projects with stable test-suite behavior. In this setting, each project is treated 
as a block, and the models are ranked within each project according to their Plausible CorÂ­
rectness Rate (PCR). The average ranks across projects are then computed and reported in 
TableÂ 16. The ranking shows that Grok achieves the best overall position, followed closely 
by DeepSeek, while Mistral and GPT-4o occupy intermediate positions, and Claude and 
Gemini appear in the lower ranks.
Complementing this rank-based comparison, descriptive statistics of PCR values across 
the projects are summarized in TableÂ 17. Across models, mean PCR values range between 
71.65% and 79.43%, indicating that a substantial fraction of function-level repairs do not 
introduce observable behavioral regressions when evaluated under stable test-suite condiÂ­
tions. Grok and DeepSeek achieve the highest mean PCR, both at 79.43%, followed by 
Mistral at 78.68% and GPT-4o at 78.30%. Claude reaches 77.94%, while Gemini records 
the lowest mean PCR at 71.65%.
Standard deviations reported in TableÂ 17 are comparable across models, ranging from 
12.24 to 15.43, reflecting moderate variability driven by project-specific factors such as 
test coverage and sensitivity to localized changes. DeepSeek shows the lowest variabilÂ­
ity (12.24), indicating the most consistent execution-based behavior across projects, while 
Gemini exhibits the highest variability (15.43). Overall, these statistics reinforce the conÂ­
clusion that while all models can generate behavior-preserving repairs in many cases,

5.5â€‚ Estimated Semantic Equivalence via LLMs
This subsection further addresses RQ4 by introducing a complementary, estimation based 
assessment of semantic equivalence applied to the complete filtered set of 17,112 function-
level repairs identified in SectionÂ 5.3. While the execution-based validation presented in 
SectionÂ 5.4 relies on concrete program execution and test outcomes, its applicability is limÂ­
ited to projects with stable and reproducible test suites, and test coverage may not exercise 
all repaired functions.
To complement this limitation, we introduce a semantic consistency evaluation that proÂ­
vides a scalable approximation of functional equivalence at the function level. The goal of 
this evaluation is not to replace execution-based validation, but to estimate whether refacÂ­
tored functions preserve the intended behavior of the original code in scenarios where runÂ­
time evidence is unavailable or incomplete.

In this evaluation, we employed a large language model, GPT-4o, as an automated 
semantic equivalence estimator. The choice of GPT-4o is motivated by prior work that 
proved its applicability to software engineering classification and code analysis tasks, as 
proved in Ghammam etÂ al. (2025), as well as studies that showed the suitability of large lanÂ­
guage models for automated GitHub issue classification in software engineering contexts, 
as shown in Heo and Lee (2025).
For each repaired function, the model was provided with the original and the modified 
version and prompted to assess, as a heuristic judgment, whether the change preserves the 
intended behavior of the original code. Each comparison was framed as a binary decision 
task, where the model responded with â€œYESâ€ if the two versions were estimated to be funcÂ­
tionally equivalent and â€œNOâ€ otherwise.
This process yields an estimated semantic equivalence rate, defined as the proportion 
of repairs judged to preserve functionality. Importantly, this evaluation should be interpreted 
as an approximation of semantic equivalence rather than a definitive oracle, as it relies on 
probabilistic model judgment rather than on program execution.
TableÂ 18 reports the estimated semantic equivalence rate for each evaluated LLM on the 
filtered set of functions, after excluding cases associated with rules S1192 and S930. The 
results range from 66.01% to 74.25%, indicating that for a majority of repairs the generated 
changes are estimated to preserve the original behavior. Grok achieves the highest semantic 
equivalence rate, followed by DeepSeek and GPT-4o, while Gemini exhibits the lowest 
estimated preservation rate among the evaluated models.
Although semantic equivalence estimation and test-suite validation rely on different sigÂ­
nals, their model rankings are largely consistent. The Friedman ranking based on the PlauÂ­
sible Correctness Rate (PCR) places Grok first, followed by DeepSeek, Mistral, GPT-4o, 
Claude, and Gemini (TableÂ 16). A very similar ordering appears in the LLM-based semantic 
equivalence results (TableÂ 18), where Grok and DeepSeek again lead, while Gemini ranks 
last. The main difference is the relative position of GPT-4o and Mistral, which swap places 
depending on the evaluation metric.
To further investigate the relationship between these two evaluation approaches, we 
measured their agreement on the subset of 1,863 functions that were evaluated using test-
suite execution. For each function, six repairs were generated, one by each evaluated LLM, 
resulting in six repair evaluations per function. For every repair, we compared the binary 
decision produced by the LLM-based semantic estimator (whether the refactoring preserves 
functionality) with the outcome observed through the test-suite validation protocol. An 
agreement occurs when both methods reach the same conclusion regarding whether the 
refactoring preserves or changes the behavior of the original function.

Across the resulting 11,178 repair evaluations (1,863 functions Ã— 6 model-generated 
repairs), the two approaches produced identical outcomes in 7,962 cases, corresponding 
to an overall agreement rate of 71.23%. Among these agreements, 7,128 cases represent 
situations where both methods concluded that the repair preserves the original behavior, 
while the remaining agreements correspond to cases where both methods detected behavÂ­
ioral changes.
To further quantify the level of agreement between the two evaluation methods, we comÂ­
puted Cohenâ€™s kappa, a statistical measure commonly used to assess inter-rater agreement 
while accounting for agreement that may occur by chance. The resulting value of 0.158 indiÂ­
cates only slight agreement between the semantic estimation and the test-suite-based validaÂ­
tion. This relatively low value suggests that the two approaches capture different aspects of 
behavioral correctness: test suites provide execution-based evidence limited by test coverÂ­
age, whereas LLM-based semantic estimation evaluates functional intent at the code level. 
Nevertheless, the substantial number of cases in which both methods agree on preserved 
behavior provides additional evidence that many LLM-generated refactorings maintain the 
intended functionality of the original code.
The semantic equivalence estimation complements execution-based validation by 
extending the behavioral analysis to a larger set of repairs. Although the two approaches 
rely on different signals, their results consistently suggest that many LLM-generated refacÂ­
torings preserve the intended behavior of the original code. Similar to the execution-based 
validation, minor differences in model rankings can be observed, particularly in the relative 
positions of GPT-4o and Mistral, which switch places depending on the evaluation metric. 
Together, these perspectives provide a broader view of behavioral correctness in LLM-
assisted code repair.
6â€‚ Discussion
The results of this study, viewed through a multi-layer evaluation framework combining 
static, issue-level, execution-based, and semantic analyses, provide a nuanced understandÂ­
ing of the strengths and limitations of large language models in repairing SonarQube-
reported issues. At the project level, LLMs consistently reduced static analysis findings 
across diverse, complex Python projects, demonstrating their potential as practical tools for 
automated code remediation. These reductions show that LLMs can scale improvements 
even in large, heterogeneous codebases. However, the magnitude of improvement varied by 
project, likely influenced by differences in structure, modularity, and adherence to best pracÂ­
tices. While project-level metrics highlight the promise of LLMs in large-scale scenarios, 
they also obscure the quality and nature of individual fixes. Thus, these reductions should be

seen as encouraging signals of potential rather than definitive evidence of uniformly high-
quality repairs throughout the codebase.
At the function level, the analysis further evaluated the correctness of LLM-generated 
repairs by their ability to produce syntactically valid, rule-compliant function-level fixes 
that eliminate all originally reported SonarQube issues without introducing new violations, 
as measured by the Static Repair Success Rate (SRSR). Grok and GPT-4o achieved the 
highest SRSR values, indicating they were most effective at producing repairs that were 
parsable and statically complete with respect to the reported quality problems. Their sucÂ­
cess suggests a stronger understanding of issues within the functionâ€™s context. In contrast, 
Mistral and Gemini exhibited the lowest SRSR scores, though still above 50%, showing 
that all models contributed meaningfully but with varying reliability under strict static corÂ­
rectness constraints. Overall, this analysis highlights the modelsâ€™ capacity to make precise, 
meaningful corrections to localized issues, with clear differences in their ability to deliver 
fully resolved and non-regressive static repairs.
At the issue level, the analysis examined how effectively each model addressed the speÂ­
cific SonarQube rules behind the reported issues. No single model was best across all rules, 
and each had strengths in different areas. Grok excelled in naming and code complexity, 
while Claude handled improper exception usage well. Rules tied to localized concerns, such 
as naming standards, removing unused variables or parameters, avoiding empty functions, 
and simplifying complex code, were handled most successfully. These results show the 
modelsâ€™ ability to improve stylistic and maintainability aspects of functions while revealing 
limitations on rules requiring broader file-level or cross-function context. This suggests that 
choosing the right model depends on the specific quality issues in the project rather than 
expecting one model to excel universally.
In addition, behavioral validation adds an execution-aware dimension to the analysis, 
assessing whether LLM-generated repairs preserve observable runtime behavior, while the 
semantic layer complements this view by estimating whether the generated functions preÂ­
serve the intended functionality of the original code. By extending the evaluation beyond 
static parsability validation and issue resolution, these layers clarify how often repairs 
remain faithful to the original behavior.
Across all models, roughly two-thirds of the analyzed fixes were estimated to preserve 
the original functionality based on both test-suite execution results and LLM-based semantic 
evaluation, with Grok achieving the highest overall results across both execution-based validaÂ­
tion (based on mean PCR across projects) and semantic estimation, while Gemini consistently 
obtained the lowest scores under both evaluation strategies. This additional perspective reinÂ­
forces that structural validity does not always imply semantic correctness and that both static 
and dynamic behavioral dimensions are essential for assessing real code quality improvements.
Taken together, the multi-layer evaluation framework demonstrates that large language 
models hold strong potential for improving software quality through automated repairs. 
At the project level, they achieve measurable reductions in static analysis findings across 
diverse Python codebases. At the function and issue levels, static correctness metrics show 
that LLMs can produce syntactically valid and rule-compliant repairs, with effectiveness 
varying across rule categories. Execution-based validation and semantic estimation further 
indicate that many repairs preserve observable behavior and intended functionality. Overall, 
these findings point to a promising direction where LLMs can enhance code quality when 
applied with careful model selection and context-aware evaluation.

7â€‚ Threats to Validity
We adopt the recommendations from SjÃ¸berg and Bergersen (2023) and Verdecchia etÂ al. 
(2023) to discuss construct, internal, and external validity. Regarding construct validity, our 
study assumes that reducing SonarQube-reported issues improves code quality. However, 
as noted by Lenarduzzi etÂ al. (2020), blindly fixing all warnings may introduce unnecessary 
or harmful changes.
Some of the analyzed projects, such as scikit-learn, pandas, and Zulip, already integrate 
static analysis tools or linters, including Ruff and SonarCloud, the cloud version of SonarÂ­
Qube that relies on the same analysis rules. This does not eliminate reported issues, as 
addressing all findings requires developer time and prioritization, and some warnings may 
remain unresolved or correspond to false-positive cases. Consequently, SonarQube still 
identified a substantial number of issues in these projects, and the results should be interÂ­
preted as a conservative estimate of LLM effectiveness.
Another construct validity concern relates to the evaluation of functional preservation. In 
this study, behavioral correctness is supported by execution-based validation through projÂ­
ect-specific test suites, which provide runtime evidence of whether LLM-generated repairs 
preserve observable behavior. However, this validation depends on test coverage and deterÂ­
minism; if certain behaviors are not exercised, semantic regressions may remain undetected. 
As mentioned earlier, some project configurations may also exclude specific categories of 
tests, further reducing the effective behavioral coverage.
In addition to execution-based validation, we employed GPT-4o as an automated semanÂ­
tic equivalence estimator to scale the analysis across all filtered function-level repairs. 
While this approach complements test-suite evaluation and extends coverage to scenarios 
where execution-based validation is limited, LLM-based judgments remain probabilistic 
and approximate rather than definitive. Moreover, recent work highlights broader construct 
validity risks in LLM-based software engineering studies, including closed-source model 
opacity, potential implicit data leakage, and limited traceability of model reasoning proÂ­
cesses (Sallou etÂ al. 2024). These factors should be considered when interpreting both the 
semantic evaluation and the overall conclusions.
Internal validity is influenced by the experimental setup. Even with a unified prompt 
template, different models may react differently to the same formatting or contextual cues, 
which can affect their outputs. Using public API endpoints also exposed our results to facÂ­
tors like server load or throttling, which may have caused some of the incomplete or malÂ­
formed responses we classified as parsability failures during AST-based validation.
External validity is limited by our focus on popular, open-source, actively maintained Python 
projects. Other languages, such as Java, Ruby, or C++, and less mature or proprietary codeÂ­
bases may produce different outcomes. Performance observed via public APIs under shared 
conditions might also differ from that in controlled private deployments or offline settings.
8â€‚ Conclusions and Future Work
This study shows that large language models can assist in repairing SonarQube-identified 
code issues in diverse Python projects. By systematically comparing several state-of-the-
art models, the study revealed that LLMs can substantially reduce the number of reported 
1â€¯3
Page 41 of 45â€ƒ
  118 
Empirical Software Engineering          (2026) 31:118 
issues, improve maintainability, and enhance code quality. At the same time, the results 
highlight that effectiveness varies across models and issue types, and that generated fixes 
sometimes introduce new problems or fail to integrate cleanly. These findings highlight the 
potential of LLMs in software maintenance, while also emphasizing the need for careful 
validation and human oversight.
Looking ahead, several promising directions emerge. Integrating LLM-dri-ven repairs 
into tools like VS Code or Cursor could deliver automated suggestions during development. 
Hybrid systems combining LLMs with rule-based tools may produce more reliable, context-
aware fixes. Beyond benchmarking accuracy, future research can investigate why and under 
what contextual conditions LLMs succeed or fail to resolve code issues. A systematic ablaÂ­
tion of prompt components, such as including or omitting file-level imports, neighboring 
functions, or project-specific coding conventions, can help identify which contextual eleÂ­
ments are necessary and sufficient for effective remediation.
Future work can also include a qualitative review of a representative sample of repaired 
functions, supported by direct human analysis of selected patches. Such an examination 
would clarify how the generated changes affect readability, structure, and clarity, and would 
complement the quantitative results. This line of inquiry could deepen understanding of 
LLM behavior and guide more principled prompt designs for automated code repair.
Additional research may explore advanced prompt engineering strategies, including 
multi-step or iterative prompting approaches that address one issue at a time or continuously 
refine generated patches until convergence. Such methods may reveal deeper insights into 
model reasoning and improve the precision and consistency of automated repairs. Adaptive 
prompting aligned with project conventions and developer feedback can improve repair qualÂ­
ity and acceptance. Using more real-world static analysis data could further enhance model 
performance. Finally, evaluating LLMs on additional languages, larger codebases, and more 
complex issues would help generalize these findings and broaden their applicability.
By building on these insights and addressing the current limitations, future research and 
practice can move closer to seamlessly embedding LLMs into everyday software developÂ­
ment, supporting developers with intelligent, reliable, and context-sensitive maintenance 
assistance. Further investigation into dynamic prompting and interactive repair workflows 
could provide a more nuanced understanding of how LLMs adapt to feedback and increÂ­
mental corrections, contributing to more stable and context-aware repair strategies.

Research Article
A systematic literature review on security testing of Ethereum smart 
contracts
Marwa Mnasri âˆ—, Afef Jmal MaÃ¢lej
,âˆ—, Mohamed Jmaiel
ReDCAD Laboratory, National School of Engineers of Sfax, University of Sfax, BP 1173, Sfax 3038, Tunisia
A R T I C L E 
I N F O 
A B S T R A C T 
Keywords:
Security testing
Smart contract vulnerabilities
Blockchain security
Ethereum smart contracts
The security testing of Ethereum smart contracts has become increasingly important with the rise of decentralized 
applications and blockchain technology. This systematic literature review (SLR) aims to provide a comprehensive 
overview of the state-of-the-art techniques, methodologies, tools, and challenges in the security testing of 
Ethereum smart contracts. By synthesizing and analyzing existing research articles, conference papers, and 
other relevant sources, this SLR identifies common trends, gaps, and areas for future research in this domain. 
The review covers various aspects of security testing, including vulnerability detection, testing frameworks, 
automated analysis tools, and best practices. In addition, it explores the impact of security vulnerabilities on 
smart contract ecosystems and proposes recommendations to improve the eï¬€ectiveness and eï¬ƒciency of security 
testing processes. This SLR serves as a valuable resource for researchers, practitioners, and developers interested 
in improving the security and reliability of Ethereum smart contracts.
1. Introduction
Smart contracts are revolutionizing the way agreements and transÂ­
actions are executed in the digital world. Imagine a real estate transÂ­
action between Alice and Bob using smart contracts on the Ethereum 
blockchain. Traditionally, this process would involve multiple intermeÂ­
diaries, paperwork, and verification steps, leading to delays and inÂ­
creased costs. With smart contracts, Alice and Bob can automate the 
entire process [1].
1.1. Background and motivation
The emergence of smart contracts on blockchain platforms like 
Ethereum has ushered in a new era of trustless and eï¬ƒcient transactions. 
These contracts, powered by immutable code and distributed consenÂ­
sus mechanisms, oï¬€er unparalleled security and transparency compared 
to traditional agreements. However, these advantages come with chalÂ­
lenges, particularly concerning ensuring the robustness and security 
of smart contract code. Addressing these challenges through rigorous 
testing, auditing, and continuous research is essential to fully exploit 
the potential of smart contracts and foster the widespread adoption of 
blockchain technology across various sectors [2].

1.1.1. Smart contracts and Ethereum
Smart contracts are computer programs stored on the Ethereum 
blockchain. They are executed automatically and transparently, withÂ­
out the need for an intermediary. This revolutionary technology oï¬€ers 
several advantages:
â€¢ Enhanced security: smart contracts are immutable and transparent, 
making them more resistant to fraud and manipulation.
â€¢ Increased eï¬ƒciency: smart contracts automate manual processes, 
saving time and reducing costs.
â€¢ Improved accessibility: smart contracts are accessible to everyone, 
regardless of their location or background.
In the context of Ethereum, smart contracts play a crucial role in 
creating decentralized applications (dApps). dApps are applications that 
run on the Ethereum blockchain and are not controlled by a single entity. 
They oï¬€er a wide range of services, such as decentralized finance (DeFi), 
gaming, and marketplaces [3].
1.1.2. Challenges and risks of smart contract security
Despite its advantages, smart contract technology also presents sigÂ­
niï¬cant risks. Smart contracts are complex software that can be suscepÂ­
tible to vulnerabilities. Hackers can exploit these vulnerabilities to steal 
funds, manipulate data, or disrupt the functioning of smart contracts 
[4]. The stakes involved in smart contract security are high. Financial

1.1.3. Need for a systematic literature review (SLR)
Given the challenges and risks associated with smart contract secuÂ­
rity, it is crucial to comprehensively understand the techniques and tools 
available for testing and securing smart contracts. An SLR is a valuable 
tool for addressing this need. An SLR is a rigorous and scientific method 
for identifying, analyzing, and synthesizing existing research on a given 
topic. In the context of smart contract security, an SLR is necessary to 
provide a comprehensive and up-to-date understanding of this critical 
research area. This SLR will contribute to improving smart contract seÂ­
curity and promoting the adoption of blockchain technology.
Software testing is an essential practice to ensure the quality, reliaÂ­
bility, and security of computer applications. In the context of smart 
contracts, where trust and security are paramount, testing takes on 
particular importance. Security testing aims to identify potential vulÂ­
nerabilities in the code of smart contracts and ensure that they function 
as expected, without risks of flaws or compromises.
Several aspects of security testing are relevant to smart contracts, 
including:
â€¢ Static analysis: this method examines the source code of smart conÂ­
tracts without executing them, identifying potential errors such as 
logic vulnerabilities or security flaws.
â€¢ Dynamic analysis: in contrast to static analysis, dynamic analysis 
involves executing smart contracts in a controlled environment to 
detect vulnerabilities in real time, such as stack overflow attacks or 
denial-of-service attacks.
â€¢ Security audits: security audits are in-depth examinations of smart 
contract code conducted by cybersecurity experts. These audits aim 
to identify and correct vulnerabilities before deploying smart conÂ­
tracts on the blockchain.
By integrating rigorous security testing practices into the development 
and deployment of smart contracts, developers can reduce the risks of 
exploitation by malicious actors and enhance user confidence in the 
smart contract ecosystem [8].
1.2. Objectives and research questions
The security of smart contracts on the Ethereum platform represents 
a major challenge in the blockchain domain. This SLR aims to contribute 
to a comprehensive understanding of this critical area. Furthermore, by 
identifying future research needs, this analysis aims to guide eï¬€orts to 
enhance the security of smart contracts on the Ethereum blockchain.
1.2.1. Main objectives
The primary objective of this SLR is to provide a comprehensive and 
in-depth understanding of security testing for Ethereum smart contracts. 
This SLR aims to:
1. Map existing approaches and techniques for security testing of 
Ethereum smart contracts.
2. Evaluate the eï¬€ectiveness and limitations of each approach and 
technique.
3. Identify best practices for secure development and testing of smart 
contracts.
4. Determine future research needs in the field of security testing for 
smart contracts.
1.2.2. Research questions
To achieve the main objective, our SLR will address the following 
research questions:
â€¢ RQ1: What are the main security testing techniques for smart conÂ­
tracts used in the literature?
â€¢ RQ2: What are the primary tools and frameworks available for seÂ­
curity testing of smart contracts?
â€¢ RQ3: What are the most common vulnerabilities identified in 
Ethereum smart contracts?
â€¢ RQ4: What metrics are used to evaluate the quality and eï¬€ectiveness 
of security testing for Ethereum smart contracts?
â€¢ RQ5: What are the current challenges and limitations in the field of 
security testing for Ethereum smart contracts?
Research questions in an SLR play a crucial role in guiding the research 
process, identifying gaps in the literature, and addressing the needs of 
the scientific community.
1.3. Research methodology
SLRs are a cornerstone of research in many fields, including softÂ­
ware engineering. They oï¬€er a comprehensive and objective way to 
evaluate existing research on a specific topic. This section explores a 
well-established approach for conducting SLRs: the Kitchenham method.
1.3.1. The Kitchenham method
The Kitchenham method [9] is a rigorous and well-established apÂ­
proach for conducting SLRs in the field of software engineering. It oï¬€ers 
several advantages:
â€¢ Rigor and reproducibility: the Kitchenham method is based on 
scientific principles and provides a clear and documented process 
to ensure the rigor and reproducibility of the SLR.
â€¢ Comprehensiveness and accuracy: the methodology aims to idenÂ­
tify and analyze all relevant primary studies for the SLR topic, minÂ­
imizing the risk of bias and omissions.
â€¢ Transparency and evaluation: the Kitchenham method encourÂ­
ages detailed documentation of each step of the SLR, allowing for 
transparent assessment of the quality and validity of the research.
1.3.2. Stages of the Kitchenham methodology
The Kitchenham methodology consists of the following stages:
1. Planning the review
â€¢ Defining the objectives and research questions of the SLR.
â€¢ Developing a review protocol that describes the methodology 
and inclusion/exclusion criteria.
â€¢ Identifying potential sources of research (databases, libraries, 
etc.).
2. Conducting the review
â€¢ Identifying and selecting relevant primary studies.
â€¢ Extracting data from the selected studies.
â€¢ Analyzing and synthesizing the extracted data.
3. Reporting the review
â€¢ Presenting the results of the SLR in a clear and concise manÂ­
ner.
â€¢ Discussing the implications of the results and the limitations 
of the research.
â€¢ Formulating conclusions and recommendations for future reÂ­
search.
1.3.3. Details of key stages
â€¢ Defining research questions and inclusion/exclusion criteria
â€“ The research questions should be clear, precise, and relevant 
to the topic of the SLR.
â€“ Inclusion/exclusion criteria should be defined to identify relÂ­
evant primary studies and exclude those that are not.
â€¢ Identifying and selecting primary studies
â€“ The search for primary studies should be conducted in multiÂ­
ple sources of research.
â€“ Primary studies should be selected based on the defined inÂ­
clusion/exclusion criteria.
â€¢ Data extraction and analysis

â€“ Relevant data should be extracted from the selected primary

â€“ The extracted data should be analyzed methodically to answer

â€¢ Synthesis and interpretation of results
â€“ The results of the data analysis should be synthesized and inÂ­
terpreted in a coherent manner.
â€“ The conclusions of the SLR should be drawn from the syntheÂ­
sized results.
1.3.4. Conclusion
The Kitchenham methodology provides a robust framework for conÂ­
ducting a rigorous and high-quality SLR. By following its steps and 
documenting each stage in detail, researchers can ensure the production 
of a reliable and useful SLR that will contribute to the advancement of 
knowledge in the field of software engineering.
2. Literature review
In this section, we will discuss the inclusion and exclusion criteria 
used to select relevant studies for understanding Ethereum smart conÂ­
tract security testing. These criteria encompass a wide range of study 
types, methodologies, and topics to ensure a comprehensive analysis. 
The rigorous search process, following the Kitchenham methodology, 
was employed to identify potential sources and define relevant keyÂ­
words. The application of inclusion and exclusion criteria resulted in 
the selection of 26 high-quality articles for the literature review, conÂ­
tributing to a better understanding of Ethereum smart contract security 
testing.
2.1. Inclusion and exclusion criteria
â€¢ Relevant study types
To gain a comprehensive understanding of Ethereum smart conÂ­
tract security testing, a wide range of studies is necessary, covering 
theoretical, practical, and empirical aspects:
â€“ Empirical research evaluating security testing methods.
â€“ Theoretical analyses exploring best testing practices.
â€“ Case studies detailing specific smart contract vulnerabilities

2.4.1.1. Fuzzing testing
Fuzzing, also known as fuzz testing, is an auÂ­
tomated software testing technique that involves providing invalid, unÂ­
expected, or random inputs to a computer program [11,13]. The goal is 
to detect bugs and vulnerabilities that traditional testing methods might 
not identify.
â€¢ How it works
A fuzzing tool generates random or semi-random data that 
matches the format expected by the input of the program to be 
tested. It then injects these data into the program and monitors its 
behavior. If the program crashes, hangs, or exhibits unexpected beÂ­
havior, it may indicate the presence of a bug or vulnerability.
â€¢ Advantages
â€“ Automation: fuzzing allows for the automated testing of a 
large number of input cases, which is especially useful for 
complex programs with many possible inputs.
â€“ Eï¬€ectiveness: fuzzing can identify bugs and vulnerabilities 
that traditional testing methods, such as unit testing or inteÂ­
gration testing, might not detect.
â€“ Code coverage: fuzzing can explore code execution paths that 
are not always reached by traditional testing methods, which 
can help improve code coverage.
â€¢ Disadvantages
â€“ False positives: fuzzing can generate input cases that do not 
cause real bugs, which can lead to false positive alerts.
â€“ Execution time: fuzzing can be time-consuming, especially 
for complex programs with many possible inputs.
â€“ Required skills: setting up and using fuzzing tools can require 
specific skills.
â€¢ Types of fuzzing
â€“ Black-box fuzzing: this approach does not require any knowlÂ­
edge of the source code of the program to be tested. The 
fuzzing tool generates random or semi-random data based on 
the format expected by the programâ€™s input.
â€“ White-box fuzzing: this approach uses information from the 
programâ€™s source code to generate more precise input cases.
â€“ Mutation-based fuzzing: this approach generates input cases 
by modifying existing valid input cases.
â€¢ Fuzzing tools
â€“ Generic fuzzers: these tools can be used to test diï¬€erent types 
of programs.
â€“ Specific fuzzers: these tools are designed to test specific types 
of programs, such as web browsers or web applications.
2.4.1.2. Symbolic execution
Symbolic execution [28] is a static softÂ­
ware analysis technique that explores the diï¬€erent execution paths of 
a program by using symbolic values instead of concrete values. Unlike 
concrete execution, which only follows one possible path, symbolic exÂ­

ecution explores all possible paths, considering the diï¬€erent values that

â€¢ How it works
Symbolic execution works by instrumenting the programâ€™s

Symbolic execution has several advantages over other static analÂ­

â€“ It can test all execution paths of the program, including those

2.4.1.3. Mutation testing
Mutation testing [34] is a software testing 
technique that involves the intentional injection of modifications, called 
â€œmutations'', into the source code of a program. The goal is to determine 
whether existing tests are capable of detecting these mutations and enÂ­
suring the robustness of the code.
â€¢ How it works
1. Mutant generation: specific tools generate mutants by modÂ­
ifying the source code in diï¬€erent ways. Mutations can be 
simple, such as changing a constant value or a logical operaÂ­
tor, or more complex, such as deleting a condition or a loop.
2. Test execution: existing tests are then executed on the origiÂ­
nal program and on each mutant.
3. Result analysis: mutation testing is considered successful if 
all mutants are detected by at least one test. If a mutant is not 
detected, it means that there is a missing test case and that 
the code is vulnerable to an error.
â€¢ Advantages
â€“ Improved test coverage: mutation testing helps identify 
parts of the code that is not suï¬ƒciently tested and fills coverÂ­
age gaps.
â€“ Detection of hard-tofind bugs: mutation testing can idenÂ­
tify bugs that are not detected by other testing techniques, 
such as unit tests or integration tests.
â€“ Improved code quality: mutation testing encourages develÂ­
opers to write more robust and error-resistant code.
â€¢ Limitations
â€“ High cost: mutation testing can be expensive in terms of time 
and resources, as it requires the generation and execution of 
a large number of mutants.
â€“ Diï¬ƒcult to interpret results: it can be diï¬ƒcult to deterÂ­
mine whether an undetected mutant represents a real bug or 
a harmless mutation.
â€“ Not applicable to all types of programs: mutation testing is 
more eï¬€ective for programs whose source code is accessible 
and easy to modify.
Example
Suppose we have the following Python code:
function(x):
if x > 0:
return x
else:
return -x
A mutation testing tool could generate the following mutants:
â€“ Mutation 1: Change the > operator to >=.
â€“ Mutation 2: Change the == operator to !=.
â€“ Mutation 3: Delete the else condition.
If the existing tests do not detect all of these mutants, it reveals a 
gap in test coverage, indicating that the test suite may be incomplete 
or insuï¬ƒciently robust. This exposes the code to potential errors 
similar to the undetected mutants.
2.4.1.4. Metamorphic testing
MT [33] is a property-based software testÂ­

â€¢ Principle
MT is based on the idea that certain properties (called metamorÂ­

3. Execute test cases and compare results: compare the obÂ­

2.4.2. Static security testing
2.4.2.1. Formal verification
Formal verification [35] is a rigorous 
method used in software and hardware development to prove or disÂ­
prove a systemâ€™s compliance with formal specifications, which are mathÂ­
ematically defined properties. Unlike traditional testing methods, which 
check the proper functioning of a system through specific scenarios, forÂ­
mal verification examines all possible states of the system to ensure it 
Blockchain: Research and Applications 7 (2026) 100314 
5 
M. Mnasri, A.J. MaÃ¢lej and M. Jmaiel 
meets the given properties. Two of the most commonly used techniques 
in formal verification are model checking and theorem proving.
a. Model checking:
Model checking is an automated method of formal verification 
that involves exhaustively exploring the state space of a system 
model to check whether it satisfies certain specified logical properÂ­
ties, often expressed in terms of temporal logic, such as computation 
tree logic or linear temporal logic.
â€¢ Process: the model checking process involves three main elÂ­
ements:
â€“ Modeling: the system to be verified is represented as 
a formal model, such as a finite automaton, Petri net, 
or state transition system.
â€“ Specification: the properties to be verified are specÂ­
ified as logical formulas.
â€“ Verification: a model checking algorithm systematiÂ­
cally explores the modelâ€™s state space to determine if 
the specified properties are satisfied. If a violation is 
found, a counterexample is provided, indicating the 
sequence of states leading to the violation.
â€¢ Advantages:
â€“ Exhaustiveness: it verifies all possible states, ensurÂ­
ing complete coverage.
â€“ Counterexamples: in case of a violation, it provides 
a precise counterexample, facilitating the localization 
and correction of the issue.
â€¢ Limitations:
â€“ State space explosion: the number of states can 
grow exponentially with the systemâ€™s size, making 
verification challenging for complex systems.
b. Theorem proving:
Theorem proving is another formal verification technique, based 
on using mathematical logic to prove that specified properties of a 
system are satisfied. Unlike model checking, which is automated and 
verifies a model through exhaustive exploration, theorem proving 
may require human intervention and is often applied to the verifiÂ­
cation of infinite systems or properties too complex to be handled 
by model checking.
â€¢ Process:
â€“ Modeling: the system is described by mathematical 
formulas in a formal logical language, often predicate 
calculus or constructive logic.
â€“ Specification: system properties are expressed as 
theorems to be proven.
â€“ Proof: the theorem proving tool, sometimes assisted 
by a human, attempts to prove the theorems as true 
using logical rules. This may involve automatic or 
semi-automatic deduction of new formulas until the 
theorem is proven or refuted.
â€¢ Advantages:
â€“ Expressive power: capable of handling systems 
with infinite states or complex properties that model 
checking cannot address.
â€“ Precision: allows for very detailed verification of sysÂ­
tems, down to the level of mathematical logic.
â€¢ Limitations:
â€“ Complexity: may require signiï¬cant expertise to corÂ­
rectly formulate theorems and to guide the proving 
tool.
â€“ Less automation: the process is often less automated 
than model checking, making it longer and more 
complex.
Formal verification is a powerful tool for ensuring that critical sysÂ­
tems adhere to essential properties for their proper functioning. 
Model checking and theorem proving are two complementary techÂ­
niques that, despite each having advantages and limitations, conÂ­
tribute signiï¬cantly to the reliability of complex systems across 
many domains.
2.4.2.2. Static code analysis
a. Abstract interpretation
Abstract interpretation is a static analysis technique that transÂ­

â€¢ Process:
â€“ Define abstractions: identify and abstract key conÂ­

â€“ Construct abstract model: develop an abstract verÂ­

c. Taint analysis
Taint analysis [36] is a dynamic security analysis technique used

â€¢ Process
â€“ Mark sensitive data: the process starts by labeling

â€“ Track data propagation: as the contract executes,

â€“ Identify dangerous interactions: when tainted data

â€“ Report findings: finally, the analysis produces a reÂ­

â€¢ Advantages:

security.
â€“ Eï¬€ective detection of data propagation issues:

â€“ Dynamic analysis: unlike static analysis, taint analÂ­

â€“ Detection of complex vulnerabilities: it helps idenÂ­

â€¢ Disadvantages:
â€“ Overhead and performance cost: taint analysis can

â€“ False positives: it may flag benign interactions as

â€“ Limited scope: while useful for detecting dataÂ­

Taint analysis is a valuable technique for identifying security vulnerÂ­
abilities in smart contracts, particularly when examining data flows 
and potential sources of malicious input. However, it is not a testÂ­

4.1. Exploitable vulnerabilities
Exploitable vulnerabilities [37] in smart contracts are weaknesses 
that allow attackers to manipulate or compromise the functioning of 
these contracts for malicious purposes. These flaws, often subtle and 
complex, enable critical attacks that jeopardize funds and compromise 
the reliability of dApps. Although numerous audit and security tools 
have been developed to detect these vulnerabilities, many of them evade 
existing detection mechanisms, making identification challenging and 
prevention essential.
These vulnerabilities are termed ``exploitable'' because they provide 
attackers with tangible attack vectors that can be leveraged to gain 
unauthorized privileges or benefits. Unlike minor errors or inconsequenÂ­
tial bugs, an exploitable vulnerability presents a real and immediate 
breach in contract security, which can be used to cause financial damÂ­
age, distort transactions, or alter contract behavior.
4.1.1. Methodology for classifying exploitable bugs in smart contracts
The article ``Demystifying Exploitable Bugs in Smart Contracts'' is 
based on a systematic empirical analysis of 516 unique vulnerabiliÂ­
ties found in deployed smart contracts between 2021 and 2022. This 
methodology comprises several key steps, each contributing to an inÂ­
depth understanding of exploitable bugs.
â€¢ Data collection: the authors gathered information on real-world 
vulnerabilities, focusing on incidents that led to signiï¬cant financial 
losses. This comprehensive dataset, drawn from multiple sources, 
oï¬€ers a broad perspective on exploitable vulnerabilities in practical 
scenarios and their financial impacts.
â€¢ Exploitability analysis: each vulnerability was assessed to deterÂ­
mine its potential to be exploited by attackers. The authors speciï¬Â­
cally focused on weaknesses that escape conventional analysis tools, 
highlighting gaps in current auditing practices. This step was crucial 
in identifying the most dangerous vulnerabilities for smart contracts.
â€¢ Categorization by type: the identified vulnerabilities were grouped 
into seven distinct types based on their characteristics and exÂ­
ploitability. This classification involves analyzing the root causes of 
each vulnerability, their distribution across various contracts, and 
the challenges associated with their auditing. The goal of this clasÂ­
sification is to facilitate understanding and management of these 
vulnerabilities.
â€¢ Impact assessment and mitigation strategies: for each type of 
vulnerability, the authors examined the potential consequences of 
exploitation and proposed remediation strategies. This analysis inÂ­
cludes possible financial impacts and provides developers with best 
practices to mitigate risks in future smart contract deployments.
â€¢ Abstraction of bug patterns: whenever possible, the authors genÂ­
eralized each type of vulnerability into bug patterns. These abÂ­
stractions enable the identification of similar weaknesses in other 
contracts and support the automation of future detection processes, 
allowing developers and security auditors to proactively identify and 
ï¬x these vulnerabilities.
This empirical analysis and structured classification framework 
provide a valuable tool for understanding and managing exploitable 
vulnerabilities in smart contracts, contributing to improved security 
in the blockchain ecosystem.
4.1.2. Types of exploitable vulnerabilities identified
4.1.2.1. Price oracle manipulation
Description: this vulnerability occurs 
when an attacker manages to influence the price values provided by 
oracles for personal gain by manipulating the information transmitted 
to smart contracts. This can lead to economic imbalances and signiï¬cant 
losses for users. Attack mechanism: the attacker manipulates the price 
of assets by exploiting the dependency of contracts on external oracles. 
This manipulation allows altering financial transactions in the attackerâ€™s 
favor, often at the expense of other participants.
4.1.2.2. Privilege escalation
Description: this type of vulnerability hapÂ­
pens when an unauthorized user gains access to normally restricted 
functions or privileges, enabling unintended actions such as accessing 
funds or modifying sensitive data. Attack Mechanism: The attacker exÂ­
ploits flaws in permission management or gains indirect access to certain 
functions, achieving a higher level of control than what should be perÂ­
mitted. This flaw can be used to divert funds or take control of sensitive 
contract functions.
4.1.2.3. Atomicity violations
â€¢ Description: this atomicity issue occurs when sequences of transacÂ­
tions, which are supposed to be executed as an indivisible unit, are 
interrupted, leading to inconsistencies in the contractâ€™s state.
â€¢ Attack mechanism: by inserting transactions during critical operaÂ­
tions, an attacker can disrupt the logical sequence of operations and 
compromise the integrity of data or funds, resulting in inconsistenÂ­
cies or losses.
4.1.2.4. ID uniqueness violations
â€¢ Description: these violations involve errors in generating or managÂ­
ing unique identifiers, which can lead to traceability issues or data 
collisions.
â€¢ Attack mechanism: by exploiting weaknesses in the generation or 
verification of identifier uniqueness, an attacker can create conflicts 
in identification, potentially allowing unauthorized access or modiÂ­
ï¬cation of resources tied to those identifiers.
4.1.2.5. Inconsistent state updates
â€¢ Description: this type of vulnerability arises when state updates are 
not properly synchronized, creating contradictions in the informaÂ­
tion stored by the contract.
â€¢ Attack mechanism: by disrupting the logical flow of state update 
operations, an attacker can introduce inconsistencies into the data. 
This can lead to unexpected behaviors, such as incorrect fund transÂ­
fers or execution errors.
4.1.2.6. Contract implementation specific bugs
â€¢ Description: these vulnerabilities result from errors or flaws speÂ­
cific to the internal logic of a contract, inherent to the individual 
implementation of a contract.
â€¢ Attack mechanism: attackers exploit logical weaknesses or codÂ­
ing errors specific to a contractâ€™s implementation. These errors may 
include flaws in calculating critical values, handling certain transÂ­
action types, or missing security checks.

4.1.2.7. Erroneous accounting
â€¢ Description: accounting errors occur when the contract fails to

â€¢ Attack mechanism: by manipulating or exploiting errors in the conÂ­

4.2.1. Analysis methodology
Smart contracts form the cornerstone of blockchain systems, facilÂ­
itating transactions among entities. Despite their pivotal role, smart 
contracts, like conventional software, are susceptible to defects, includÂ­
ing critical security vulnerabilities.
A) Addressing vulnerabilities: research initiatives and classificaÂ­
tion frameworks
Various research endeavors aim to detect and mitigate vulneraÂ­
bilities in smart contracts, leading to the development of specialized 
vulnerability detection tools. While classification frameworks like 
DASP and SWC have emerged to categorize these vulnerabilities, 
their relevance has diminished over time due to evolving threats 
and advancements in smart contract technology.
B) Introducing OpenSCV: a novel taxonomic approach
To address the shortcomings of existing classification schemes, 
OpenSCV [38], a novel hierarchical taxonomy of smart contract 
vulnerabilities, has been devised. Unlike its predecessors, OpenSCV 
remains open to community contributions and is designed to evolve 
alongside emerging threats and technological advancements.
C) Constructing OpenSCV: methodology and rigor
The development of OpenSCV involved a meticulous analysis 
of existing vulnerability classifications and an extensive examinaÂ­
tion of 49 research works on vulnerability detection. The taxonomy 
comprises 76 vulnerabilities meticulously organized into a coherent 
hierarchical structure, ensuring comprehensive coverage of potenÂ­
tial risks.
D) Flexibility and practical utility
OpenSCV stands out for its adaptability and practical utility. 
With a dedicated support infrastructure on GitHub, it welcomes conÂ­
tinuous feedback and updates from the community. Moreover, each 
vulnerability entry is accompanied by a concrete code example, enÂ­
hancing clarity and facilitating understanding.
E) Advancements and signiï¬cance
OpenSCV represents a signiï¬cant leap forward in smart conÂ­
tract vulnerability research, oï¬€ering a dynamic and comprehensive 
classification framework. By addressing the limitations of outdated 
schemes and embracing the ever-evolving nature of smart contract 
technology, OpenSCV serves as an indispensable resource for reÂ­
searchers, developers, and security professionals alike, empowering 
them to better understand, prevent, and mitigate smart contract vulÂ­
nerabilities.
After detailing the analysis methodology used to assess the smart 
contract vulnerabilities and presenting the OpenSCV taxonomy along 
with its benefits, we showcase these concepts through Table 2. This table 
lists various security vulnerabilities of smart contracts, providing details 
on each vulnerability category, as well as relevant research works that 
have studied or addressed these specific issues. 
Fig. 3. Number of research works addressing each open smart contract vulnerÂ­
abilities (OpenSCV) taxonomy.
