III. FRAMEWORK: TEDVIL
TEDVIL, standing for Transformer-based Embeddings for
Discovering Vulnerabilities in Lifted Code, introduces a
systematic approach to detect vulnerabilities in lifted code
using embeddings from transformer-based models. This
section describes the key components of TEDVIL, illustrated
in Figure 3. Furthermore, Section IV presents details of an
implementation of this framework, focusing on the evaluation
of transformer-based unidirectional (GPT-1 and GPT-2) and
bidirectional (BERT and RoBERTa) embeddings.
A. SOURCE CODE DATASET SELECTION
1) EMBEDDING MODEL DATASET
This dataset should consist of valid source code that can
be successfully compiled. The code will be compiled and
lifted into IR to train a custom transformer-based embedding
model (e.g., BERT, GPT) to capture the codeâ€™s semantics.
Therefore, the code must be sufficiently complex to effec-
tively convey its semantic richness. Although transformer-
based embedding models are typically trained on millions of
samples, as highlighted in Section II-C, the implementation
described in Section IV achieved strong performance with a
dataset of only approximately 48,000 samples. Furthermore,
the training samples for these embedding models only need
valid representations of the code used to teach the model
code-level semantics. These samples can be generated by
compiling and lifting legitimate software projects, such as
open-source projects.
2) NEURAL NETWORK MODEL DATASET
Although this framework focuses on discovering vulnera-
bilities in lifted code, it achieves this by selecting a source
code dataset, compiling the samples, and applying techniques
to lift the compiled code. The first step in this process
involves selecting a high-quality source-code-based dataset
that includes the classification of the vulnerabilities to be
identified. For example, the National Institute of Standards
and Technologyâ€™s (NIST) Software Assurance Reference
Dataset (SARD) [53] project provides several test suites of
source code samples, encompassing various classifications
of vulnerabilities such as insecure direct object references,
local file inclusion, and command injection. Although the
implementation of TEDVIL in this paper utilizes the Juliet
1.3 dataset, other datasets could be substituted as alternatives.
Here are a few considerations when selecting a source-code
dataset:
â€¢ Does the dataset include the classification of the
vulnerability that the model aims to identify?
â€¢ Does the dataset provide sufficient samples of this
vulnerability classification to train a model to detect the
vulnerability?
â€¢ Are the source-code samples provided in a format that
can be easily compiled into machine code?
â€¢ Are the functions named in a way that helps identify
where the vulnerability occurs within the code?
B. COMPILATION AND LIFTING
Once each source code-based dataset is selected, the source
code samples must be converted into compiled code, either
as object files or fully executable binaries. It is also essential
to understand the compilation flags used by the selected
76898
VOLUME 13, 2025
G. A. McCully et al.: TEDVIL: Leveraging Transformer-Based Embeddings for Vulnerability Detection
FIGURE 3. TEDVIL framework.
compiler and the potential impact these flags may have on
the compiled code.
Once the source code samples have been compiled,
the binaries will be lifted to an IR. Some IR languages
include VEX [54], Binary Analysis Platform (BAP) [55], P-
Code [56], and LLVM [42]. Various tools can be used to
lift the binaries to these IR representations, including angr
(VEX IR) [57], BAP (BAP IR) [57], Ghidra (P-Code) [56],
and RetDec (LLVM IR) [58]. One of the advantages of
using an IR over assembly instructions is that an IR is a
cross-architecture language. This means it can take assembly
code from different architectures (e.g., ARM, x86-64, etc.)
and lift it into a uniform representation consistent across all
architectures.1
C. PREPROCESSING
The purpose of preprocessing is to eliminate patterns specific
to a single code sample without affecting its functionality.
The goal of an effective machine learning model is to
generalize from specific examples to broader patterns. Rather
than training the model to classify whether a specific sample,
such as sample XYZ, is vulnerable or not, it is preferable
for the model to learn the patterns in sample XYZ that result
in a vulnerability. Thus, data specific to a particular sample
that does not affect its functionality should be flattened into
a more generalized token sequence. A good example of this
kind of unique function-specific pattern would be a function
1It is important to note that this compilation and lifting process will be
applied to both source-code datasets.
name. A function name is unique to a program and specifies
a set of instructions executed when the function is called.
However, the actual name of the function does not affect its
behavior. For example, a function named A that prints Hello
World to the console will perform the same operation
even if renamed to B. Therefore, a common preprocessing
step is to standardize function names, such as renaming
Uniquely_Named_Function to Function_One.
D. PREPROCESSED DATASET CREATION
1) EMBEDDING MODEL DATASET
Once these code samples have been preprocessed, they are
ready to train the embedding models. The remaining step in
this process is to ensure they are in the correct format (e.g.,
CSV, TXT) for training the embedding model.
2) NEURAL NETWORK MODEL DATASET
The second dataset will be used to train neural networks to
discover vulnerabilities in the lifted code. Thus, these code
samples must track which samples contain the vulnerability
and which do not. In many cases, such as the Juliet dataset,
the function names can be used to determine which functions
contain the vulnerability. The implementation described later
in this study achieved strong results using a dataset of
approximately 4,000 samples.
E. EMBEDDING MODEL TRAINING
There are several choices of transformer-based embed-
ding models that can be selected, including BERT [48],
VOLUME 13, 2025
76899
G. A. McCully et al.: TEDVIL: Leveraging Transformer-Based Embeddings for Vulnerability Detection
RoBERTa
[49],
DistilBERT,
GPT
[50],
GPT-2
[51],
XLNet [59], ALBERT [60], ELECTRA [61], DeBERTa [62],
Longformer [63], and BigBird [64]. Each of these models
possesses architectural features that may produce interesting
or unique characteristics when generating embeddings to
capture the semantics of the IR. This list is not exhaustive, and
it remains to be seen which transformer-based models would
generate the most effective embeddings for representing the
semantics of a specific IR suitable for training a neural
network.
F. NEURAL NETWORK TRAINING
The last step in TEDVIL is to train neural networks to
identify vulnerable and non-vulnerable IR code segments.
This process involves dividing the dataset used to train and
test neural networks into distinct subsets for training, testing,
and, optionally, hyperparameter tuning. The training process
involves providing IR code samples to the embedding models
that generate embeddings. These embeddings are passed
to the neural network to teach it to differentiate between
vulnerable and non-vulnerable code. After each epoch, the
network is evaluated using embeddings from the testing
subset to assess its performance at that stage.
Research projects can use several types of neural networks
for this task. For example, various Recurrent Neural Net-
works (RNNs) have been used to discover vulnerabilities
in compiled code, including LSTM, Bidirectional LSTM
(BLSTM), Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU), and Bidirectional
GRU (BGRU), as mentioned in Section VIII. Furthermore,
several other types of neural networks may be used in
the vulnerability discovery process, including Feedforward
Neural Networks (FNN), Message Passing Neural Networks
(MPNN), Graph Neural Networks (GNN), and Convolutional
Neural Networks (CNN).
G. NEURAL NETWORK EVALUATION
Several metrics can be used to evaluate the performance of
the model. Four of the most common scores used to evaluate
neural networks are accuracy [align 1], precision [align 2],
recall [align 3], and F1-score [align 4]. In the following
equations, TP stands for true positive, TN stands for true
negative, FP stands for false positive, and FN stands for false
negative.
â€¢ Accuracy: This metric measures the ability of a model
to correctly classify whether a given sample contains a
vulnerability [65, p. 289]. The formula for accuracy is
as follows:
Accuracy =
TP + TN
TP + TN + FP + FN.
(1)
â€¢ Precision: This metric measures the proportion of
samples accurately classified as vulnerable out of all
samples that were predicted to be vulnerable; it is
particularly important for assessing how well the model
minimizes false positives [65, p. 289]. The following
equation provides the formal definition of this metric:
Precision =
TP
TP + FP.
(2)
â€¢ Recall: This metric measures the proportion of correctly
classified vulnerable samples relative to the total number
of actual vulnerable samples; this metric is especially
significant when determining a modelâ€™s ability to limit
false negatives [65, p. 289]. The recall formula is defined
as follows:
Recall =
TP
TP + FN.
(3)
â€¢ F1: This fourth metric combines precision and recall
into a single formula and is defined as follows [66,
p. 93]:
F1 = 2 Â· Precision Â· Recall
Precision + Recall.
(4)
IV. IMPLEMENTATION
This section demonstrates how the framework can be
implemented in practice. While TEDVIL focuses primarily
on generating embeddings with transformer-based mod-
els, the implementation in this section also incorporates
word2vec: Skip-Gram and CBOW models for comparative
reasons. These simpler models serve as effective baselines
for comparison with the more complex transformer-based
approaches. As illustrated in Fig. 4, the steps followed to
implement TEDVIL included:
1) Samples from the Juliet dataset were compiled into
object files (Section IV-A).
2) The RetDec tool was used to lift the object files to LLVM
IR (Section IV-B).
3) A series of preprocessing steps was applied to each
LLVM IR file (Section IV-C).
4) Datasets were created for training embedding models
and neural networks (Sections IV-D and IV-E).
5) The dataset used to train the embedding model was
utilized to train the following models (Section IV-F):
â€¢ word2vec: CBOW embedding
â€¢ word2vec: Skip-Gram embedding
â€¢ BERT
â€¢ RoBERTa
â€¢ GPT-1
â€¢ GPT-2
6) Several LSTMs were created using the embeddings from
these models (Section IV-G).
7) LSTM
model
performance
was
compared
using
accuracy,
precision,
recall,
and
F1-score
metrics
(Section IV-H).
The following subsections describe these steps in more detail.
A. DATASET SELECTION
1) EMBEDDING MODEL DATASET
The source code dataset used to train the embedding models
consisted of C/C++ samples from the Juliet 1.3 dataset. This
76900
VOLUME 13, 2025
G. A. McCully et al.: TEDVIL: Leveraging Transformer-Based Embeddings for Vulnerability Detection
FIGURE 4. Building embedding models using lifted code.
dataset includes code samples that demonstrate vulnerabil-
ities across several vulnerability classifications, along with
variants where these vulnerabilities have been remediated.
Examples of these classifications include categories such
as use-after-free, null pointer dereference, and command
injection vulnerabilities. In most cases, the dataset contains
multiple samples with different variants of the same vulner-
ability classification. This makes it well-suited for training
models to detect such vulnerabilities and has been extensively
used for this purpose (Section VIII).
The dataset used to build the embedding models consisted
of samples from the Juliet dataset, excluding those with
CWE-121 vulnerabilities. These samples were chosen for
their structural complexity, making them well-suited for
capturing patterns in the LLVM IR language. Additionally,
the datasetâ€™s manageable size made it ideal for testing
TEDVIL in resource-constrained environments.
2) NEURAL NETWORK MODEL DATASET
The source code samples used to train the neural networks
were the C/C++ samples from the Juliet dataset that contained
CWE-121 vulnerabilities.
B. COMPILE AND LIFT CODE SAMPLES
Code samples from the Juliet dataset were compiled into
object files on a Kali Linux 2023.3 system using gcc/g++ and
lifted to LLVM IR with the RetDec tool [58]. The samples
were also compiled on a Windows 10 system; however, these
samples were excluded from the dataset after analysis showed
that calls to the standard C library were stripped during the
lifting process.
C. LLVM PREPROCESSING
This study applied the preprocessing steps outlined in Table 4
to all lifted LLVM functions in both LLVM IR datasets.
One of the initial steps in this process was renaming unique
function names within LLVM to a more generalized form that
focused on function order. For example, functions containing
vulnerabilities included the word bad in their names. This
naming convention could unintentionally leak information
about vulnerable samples to the model. As a result, rather
than detecting code patterns that lead to vulnerabilities,
the model could instead learn to differentiate based on the
presence of the word bad. To mitigate this issue, functions
were renamed from their unique identifiers to generic
names such as func_one, thereby minimizing the risk of
leaking information about function capabilities through their
names.
A second preprocessing step involved replacing special
characters and numbers with their corresponding word
representations. This ensured that any tokenizer used would
treat these tokens similarly to words. The rationale behind
this approach was that special characters function differently
in natural language compared to code. In natural languages,
words serve as the primary medium of communication,
whereas in most programming languages, meaning is con-
veyed mainly through a combination of a limited set of
keywords and frequent use of special characters.
VOLUME 13, 2025
76901
G. A. McCully et al.: TEDVIL: Leveraging Transformer-Based Embeddings for Vulnerability Detection
Another preprocessing step involved breaking down
numerical sequences into their individual digits. For example,
the number 1068 would be represented as one zero six
eight. The rationale behind this approach is that while
specific numerical sequences like 1068 may be rare in
code, individual digits and their relative positions are more
common. By representing numbers in this way, embedding
models can learn general numerical relationships within the
code rather than memorizing exact numeric sequences.
TABLE 4. Preprocessing steps.
D. EMBEDDING DATASET CREATION
The embedding dataset was composed of the functions from
the LLVM IR samples that did not contain stack-based buffer
overflows. Although the samples in this dataset contained
samples from several classes of vulnerabilities as well as the
fixed varlets, the vulnerable status of these samples was not
tracked since these samples were only used by the embedding
models to learn the semantics of the LLVM IR language.
All samples were stored in a text file, with one function
per line. While there were 457,529 functions in total, only
48,157 remained after duplicate removal. Table 5 breaks these
numbers down.
E. NEURAL NETWORK DATASET CREATION
The remaining preprocessed LLVM IR samples from the
Juliet dataset (i.e. those containing CWE-121 vulnerabilities)
were placed in a dataset used to train neural networks to
detect code samples containing stack-based buffer overflows.
Although the dataset initially contained 12,069 samples,
it was reduced to 3,901 samples after removing duplicates
from the preprocessed functions. Manual analysis of the
duplicate code revealed that several functions provided
minimal functionality, such as calling secondary functions
containing vulnerabilities. Additionally, samples with more
than 2,048 tokens were excluded due to resource limitations
on the systems used to train the neural networks. This further
reduced the dataset to 3,802 samples. The loss of 99 samples
was considered acceptable, as retaining them would have
introduced unnecessary complexity into the implementation.
A breakdown of this dataset is in Table 5.
TABLE 5. Embedding and LSTM training datasets.
F. EMBEDDING MODEL TRAINING
The decision to focus on BERT, RoBERTa, GPT-1, and
GPT-2 was based on their significance as some of the
first transformer-based embedding models and their second-
generation variants. Evaluating these foundational models
provides a solid starting point for conducting a com-
parative analysis of transformer-based embedding models.
Furthermore, the CBOW and Skip-Gram models are useful
baselines for comparison with the more complex transformer-
based embedding models, as they have been extensively
used in prior studies to identify vulnerabilities in compiled
binaries (Section VIII). This section details the specific
implementation choices for each of these models.
There are some aspects of the transformer-based modes
that remained constant among all models:
â€¢ HuggingFaceâ€™s transformers library (v4.43.3) was used
to build all embedding models (BERT, RoBERTa, GPT-
1, and GPT-2).
â€¢ HuggingFaceâ€™s tokenizers library (v0.19.1) was used for
all tokenization processes used to train these models.
â€¢ The maximum size of the LLVM IR functions was
limited to a token length of 2048.
â€¢ All embedding models consist of 12 hidden layers, each
with 100 nodes and ten attention heads.
â€¢ The dataset used to train the embedding models was
split into two subsets: 90% for training and 10% for
validation.
â€¢ The loss from the training and validation steps reported
every 1,000 steps, and training occurred over the course
of 20 epochs.
â€¢ All training occurred on an Ubuntu system running dual
NVIDIA TI 4090 GPUs.
1) WORD2VEC: CBOW AND SKIP-GRAM MODEL CREATION
The Gensim (4.3.0) library was used to train the CBOW and
Skip-Gram embedding models, and the nltk (3.8.1) libraryâ€™s
word tokenizer was used to tokenize LLVM IR tokens. The
models were built using a dataset of preprocessed LLVM IR

the loss scores for the last five thousand steps. The embedding
model generated at step 108,000 was used for generating
embeddings, since it had the lowest validation loss score.
This choice was made because it aligns with the criteria
used to select the best-performing embedding model during
the training of other transformer-based embedding models.
However, step 108,000 did not yield the best score on the
training dataset. Thus, although the model at this step was
used for generating embeddings to train neural networks,
it is reasonable to suggest that the model generated at
step 107,000 may have been a better choice, as both the
training and validation scores were lower at that step.
The GPT2LMHeadModel class was used to build the
GPT-2 model and the ByteLevelBPETokenizer class
was used to tokenize the LLVM IR code. Unlike the GPT-1
model, no issues arose during training with both GPUs. The
model showed steady improvements in accuracy every 1,000
steps, as shown in Table 8, with the validation set achieving
its lowest loss score at step 54,000.

G. LSTM NEURAL NETWORK CONFIGURATION
Several LSTM neural networks were created during this
implementation of TEDVIL. The neural network architecture
included an input layer that received embeddings generated
by the respective embedding models. These embeddings
were passed through two LSTM layers, each containing
128 neurons. The Leaky Rectified Linear Unit (Leaky ReLU)
activation function was applied to these layers, with a dropout
rate of 20% used between them to mitigate overfitting. This
falls within the recommended range of 20â€“30% for recurrent
neural networks, as suggested by [66, p. 365]. The second
LSTM layer passed its output to a single dense neuron with
a sigmoid activation function, which determined whether the
sample contained a buffer overflow. The dataset described in
Section IV-E was split into training (80%) and testing (20%)
subsets to train and evaluate the modelâ€™s performance. Each
LSTM was trained over 50 epochs.
Several LSTM models were trained using embeddings
generated by each embedding model. These models were
optimized using both Adam and SGD optimizers, with
variations in the hyperparameters. The Adam optimizer was
selected due to its proven success in [18] and [23]. However,
as discussed in Section V, when using this optimizer, neural
networks trained with embeddings from transformer-based
models struggled to achieve better accuracy than simply
assigning all samples to a single category. Thus, the simpler
SGD optimizer was used as a secondary optimizer to
train neural networks, leading to significant performance
improvements in models trained with transformer-based
embeddings.
Additionally, each model was trained twice, once with
frozen embedding layers and once with unfrozen layers. The
hyperparameters used for the LSTMs in this study are as
follows:
â€¢ Adam optimizer: learning rates of 0.01, 0.001, and
0.0001
â€¢ SGD optimizer: a learning rate and momentum of 0.01
â€¢ SGD optimizer: a learning rate of 0.0001 and momen-
tums of 0.01, 0.001, and 0.0001.
The learning rates for the Adam optimizer were based
on Kerasâ€™ default value (0.001). The models were trained
to explore variations using the default learning rate and
VOLUME 13, 2025
76903
G. A. McCully et al.: TEDVIL: Leveraging Transformer-Based Embeddings for Vulnerability Detection
values of an order of magnitude higher (0.01) and lower
(0.0001). The primary learning rate for the SGD optimizer
was intentionally set at 0.0001, one order of magnitude below
the default Keras value. This decision was made due to the
instability and lack of convergence observed with the Adam
optimizer. Consequently, momentum [66, p. 352] was the
primary hyperparameter explored with the SGD optimizer,
focusing on low values to ensure stable updates and reduce
noise sensitivity. Finally, a model was trained using the
SGD optimizer with a higher learning rate (0.01) and a
low momentum of 0.01. This final model serves as a point
of comparison with models trained using more controlled
gradients.
H. MODEL EVALUATION CRITERIA
LSTM neural networks were evaluated using accuracy,
precision, recall, and F1-score, as detailed in Section III-G.
Accuracy alone is not a strong indicator of model perfor-
mance. For example, if a model had high accuracy but poor
precision, someone responsible for locating and remediating
vulnerabilities would struggle to make progress due to the
many false positives they would need to sift through [65,
p. 289]. Likewise, poor recall would be problematic because
the model would fail to achieve its objective of identifying
vulnerable code samples [65, p. 289]. However, the F1-score
is a strong indicator of model performance, as it balances
precision and recall, providing a more comprehensive
measure of the modelâ€™s ability to minimize false positives
while effectively identifying vulnerabilities [65, p. 290].

VI. DISCUSSION
A. GPT-2 VS. BERT & ROBERTA EMBEDDINGS
The neural networks trained with GPT-2 embeddings signifi-
cantly outperformed their bidirectional counterparts (BERT
and RoBERTa). These findings suggest that embeddings
produced by unidirectional models, which simulate the
sequential manner in which humans typically read text, were
more effective at capturing semantics in lifted code compared
to bidirectional models. Interestingly, [48] highlights that
BERT excels at classification tasks, suggesting it might have
performed well in the code classification tasks in this study.
However, it is important to note that BERT was not directly
used for classification in this implementation. Instead,
BERT provided token-level embeddings to an LSTM neural
network, which was ultimately responsible for classifying
vulnerable code samples. In contrast, as demonstrated in [50],
GPT models excel at generative tasks. This suggests that the
generative capabilities of GPT models may better capture
the code-level semantics required by neural networks for
76908
VOLUME 13, 2025
G. A. McCully et al.: TEDVIL: Leveraging Transformer-Based Embeddings for Vulnerability Detection
classification tasks than bidirectional models. Nevertheless,
additional testing is necessary to validate this potential
conclusion.
B. GPT-2 VS. SKIP-GRAM EMBEDDINGS
The best-performing LSTM model built with GPT-2 embed-
dings slightly outperformed the best model built with Skip-
Gram embeddings. The GPT-2 model surpassed the Skip-
Gram model by 0.5% in accuracy and 0.1% in F1-score.
However, the Skip-Gram model achieved a recall that
was 5.4% higher than the best model trained with GPT-2
embeddings. At first glance, these results suggest that both
models produce comparable performance. Nevertheless, it is
noteworthy that models built using the SGD optimizer and
a learning rate of 0.0001 consistently achieved accuracy
scores above 92%. In contrast, models built with Skip-
Gram embeddings, aside from the best-performing neural
network, consistently produced top scores in the mid-
80% range. Thus, not only did the best model built
with GPT-2 embeddings achieve higher accuracy, precision,
and F1-scores than its Skip-Gram counterpart, but it also
maintained this high accuracy even when the momentum
hyperparameter was adjusted. These findings indicate that
GPT-2 embeddings are better suited for the task outlined in
this study.
C. BERT, ROBERTA, & GPT-1 VS. SKIP-GRAM
EMBEDDINGS
The best-performing neural networks trained using Skip-
Gram embeddings outperformed those utilizing BERT,
RoBERTa, or GPT-1 embeddings. This suggests that, with
smaller datasets, the simpler techniques employed by Skip-
Gram models may be more effective at capturing code-
level semantics than the more complex transformer-based
models. Transformer models, however, are typically trained
on much larger datasets than the modest dataset used in this
project. For example, the original BERT model was trained
on BooksCorpus (800 million words) and English Wikipedia
(2.5 billion words) [48], while RoBERTa was trained on
datasets ten times larger [49]. Despite using a modest dataset
of approximately 48,000 samples, the LSTMs trained with
embeddings from the BERT and RoBERTa models achieved
an impressive 88.8% accuracy.
D. SKIP-GRAM VS. CBOW EMBEDDINGS
The neural networks built using Skip-Gram embeddings
outperformed those using CBOW embeddings. Skip-Gram
models are particularly effective at learning token-level
embeddings when the sample size is limited [47]. In contrast,
CBOW models excel at generating embeddings for high-
frequency tokens, which aligns with this dataset, as the
word2vec model reported only 332 unique tokens at the
end of training [47]. Despite the high-token frequency,
which typically favors CBOW, the Skip-Gram embeddings
likely held an advantage due to the smaller training
dataset.
VII. FUTURE WORK
A. DATASET SIZES
The datasets used to train the transformer-based models
in this study were relatively modest compared to the
massive datasets typically used for such models. Despite
the limited number of training samples, the LSTMs built
with these embeddings performed reasonably well. The
models built with GPT-2 embeddings consistently achieved
over 92% accuracy when trained with the SGD optimizer
and a learning rate of 0.0001. However, performance could
potentially improve further with larger datasets for training
the embedding models.
B. EVALUATE OTHER EMBEDDING MODELS
As mentioned in Section III-E, there are several transformer-
based embedding models beyond those evaluated in this
implementation of TEDVIL. Many of these models incorpo-
rate architectural choices that could substantially impact how
embeddings are generated. Future research should explore
and compare these models in the context of TEDVIL to
determine their effects on the generated embeddings.
C. NEURAL NETWORKS AND HYPERPARAMETERS
LSTM neural networks were chosen for their particular
implementation of TEDVIL. However, there are several other
neural networks such as SRNN, BLSTM, GRU, BGRU,
CNNs, etc. It may be possible to achieve higher accuracy with
a different neural network. Furthermore, neural networks
such as GNNs can be used to model program flow, potentially
improving model performance.
D. LLVM FUNCTION SIZE
In this study, samples containing more than 2,048 tokens
were excluded from the dataset used to train neural networks
for vulnerability detection due to memory limitations. As a
result, nearly 100 samples were removed from this dataset.
Future research should explore methods for handling samples
with long token lengths without overextending system
resources.
E. DATA SNOOPING
Reference [68] highlights that one of the most prevalent
design flaws in applying machine learning to cybersecurity
problems is data snooping. A specific type of data snooping,
known as test snooping, occurs when there is insufficient
separation between datasets used to train and validate
machine learning models; this flaw can manifest when
data used to train embedding models is reused to validate
performance, leading to potentially inflating evaluation
metrics [68]. Although the research described in this paper
avoids this issue, [69] explored the effects of data snooping
on the Skip-Gram, CBOW, RoBERTa, and GPT-2 models.
Their findings indicate that even when a test snooping design
flaw was introduced, the ranking of the best-performing
models remained consistent (GPT-2, Skip-Gram, RoBERTa,
VOLUME 13, 2025
76909
G. A. McCully et al.: TEDVIL: Leveraging Transformer-Based Embeddings for Vulnerability Detection
and CBOW). Moreover, the accuracy differences between the
best-performing models in each study were minimal: GPT-
2 differed by only 0.4%, Skip-Gram by 1.5%, RoBERTa by
0.3%, and CBOW by 0.4%.
F. EMBEDDING LAYER TUNING ENHANCEMENTS
This study employed a binary approach to freezing or
unfreezing embedding model layers. However, [70] empha-
sizes the advantages of methods such as discriminative
fine-tuning and gradual unfreezing. If implemented, these
approaches could lead to potential improvements in model
performance.
G. VULNERABILITY COVERAGE
This studyâ€™s implementation of TEDVIL focused on identify-
ing CWE-121 vulnerabilities. However, other classifications
of vulnerabilities exist, including use-after-free, null pointer
dereference, and heap corruption vulnerabilities. Future
research should explore the application of TEDVIL to these
and other vulnerability types.
VIII. RELATED WORK
Several studies have utilized transformer-based embedding
models to detect vulnerabilities in source code. Examples
include BERT [71], [72], [73], [74], [75], [76], [77],
RoBERTa [74], [77], [78], GPT-based models [79], [80],
[81], [82], [83], [84], [85], [86], [87], [88], [89], and Distil-
BERT [74], [77], [90], [91]. Furthermore, these models have
been utilized for code similarity tasks, encompassing both
bidirectional [33], [34], [35], [36] and unidirectional [37]
approaches.
The implementation of TEDVIL in this study utilized
C/C++ samples from the NIST SARD [53] Juliet 1.3 source
code dataset. Datasets from this project have been extensively
used in research focused on identifying vulnerabilities in
compiled code. References [17], [18], [19], and [26] mentions
using the SARD dataset for their research but do not specify
the exact dataset employed. In contrast, [20], [23], [27],
[28], [30], [31], [92], [93] explicitly state that they used
the Juliet dataset. Additionally, [94] reports using MIT
Lincoln Laboratoryâ€™s MLL05b dataset, and [30] utilized
the STONESOUP datasets (IARPA12 and IARPA14), all of
which are available in the SARD project.
Several projects have focused on identifying vulnerabil-
ities in compiled code and have employed the word2vec
model to generate token-level embeddings [15], [18], [19],
[22], [23], [25], [29]. However, there are known limitations
associated with using word2vec in this capacity. To address
these weaknesses, several projects have proposed their
own solutions, which are either inspired by word2vec or
incorporate it as part of their approach. These models include
Instruction2vec [30], Bin2vec [20], VDGraph2Vec [31],
BinVulDet [28], and VulANalyzeR [27].
There have been relatively few projects that utilized
transformer-based models to detect vulnerabilities in com-
piled code. For example, [31] trained a RoBERTa model
on assembly instructions and leveraged these embeddings to
train an MPNN, enabling it to distinguish between vulnerable
and non-vulnerable code. Similarly, [38] trained a RoBERTa
model using LLVM IR and employed these embeddings to
train a neural network to identify vulnerabilities in IR code.
Finally, [39] trained a BERT model with P-Code and used
these embeddings to detect vulnerabilities in P-Code samples.
Several studies have employed recurrent neural networks
(RNNs) to detect vulnerabilities in compiled code. For
example, [15], [16], [17], [18], [19], [20], [21], [22], [23]
utilized long short-term memory networks (LSTMs) for
this purpose, while [17], [18], [19], [21], [23], [25], [26],
[27] adopted the bidirectional variant of LSTMs (BLSTMs).
Furthermore, [18], [19], [23], [24] employed gated recurrent
units (GRUs), and [17], [18], [19], [21], [23], [26], [27], [28]
used the bidirectional variant of GRUs (BGRUs) for a similar
purpose.
The aspects of TEDVIL, as well as the specific implemen-
tation adopted by the research for dataset selection, lifting
assembly code to LLVM, and preprocessing the lifted code
in this study, are strongly influenced by the approaches
described in [18] and [23]. These studies leveraged the
SARD source code dataset, compiling the samples, and
converting the resulting compiled code to LLVM IR using
the RetDec tool. The lifted LLVM code was then employed
to train a word2vec model, which generated embeddings
subsequently used to train a neural network for vulnerability
detection. Building on these foundations, the current research
extended this approach by utilizing LLVM IR to train
custom transformer-based embedding models (i.e., BERT,
RoBERTa, GPT-1, and GPT-2). These embeddings were
further used to train multiple LSTM neural networks with
varying hyperparameters, enabling a comparative analysis of
LSTMs trained using multiple embedding models.
IX. CONCLUSION
This study introduced TEDVIL, a novel framework that lever-
ages transformer-based embeddings to detect vulnerabilities
in lifted code. Using this approach, LSTMs trained with
GPT-2 embeddings achieved strong performance, attaining
an accuracy of 92.5% and an F1-score of 89.7%. These
models outperformed LSTMs trained with embeddings from
bidirectional transformers (e.g., BERT and RoBERTa) and
simpler word2Vec models (e.g., Skip-Gram and CBOW).
These findings underscore the potential of transformer-based
models for vulnerability detection in compiled code, even in
resource-constrained settings.
This study highlights the influence of optimizers on the
performance of neural networks trained with transformer-
based embeddings and the simpler word2vec models. In all
cases, neural networks trained with embedding models
that had trainable layers outperformed those with frozen
layers. However, networks using word2Vec embeddings
achieved optimal performance with the Adam optimizer,
whereas LSTMs trained with transformer-based embeddings
performed better with the SGD optimizer. LSTMs built with
76910
VOLUME 13, 2025
G. A. McCully et al.: TEDVIL: Leveraging Transformer-Based Embeddings for Vulnerability Detection
GPT-2 embeddings consistently outperformed those built
with other embeddings, underscoring their suitability for
vulnerability detection tasks.
The promising results of this study open multiple
avenues for future exploration. Future implementations of
TEDVIL could evaluate additional transformer architectures
(e.g., XLNet, Longformer) or neural network models (e.g.,
BLSTM, GRU). Furthermore, the frameworkâ€™s performance
with larger datasets or alternative lifted code representations,
such as VEX, warrants further investigation.

Causal reasoning in Software Quality Assurance: A systematic review
Luca Giamattei âˆ—, Antonio Guerriero, Roberto Pietrantuono, Stefano Russo
DIETI, UniversitÃ  degli Studi di Napoli Federico II, Via Claudio 21, 80125, Napoli, Italy
A R T I C L E
I N F O
Keywords:
Causal reasoning
Causal discovery
Causal inference
Software quality
A B S T R A C T
Context: Software Quality Assurance (SQA) is a fundamental part of software engineering to ensure stakehold-
ers that software products work as expected after release in operation. Machine Learning (ML) has proven to
be able to boost SQA activities and contribute to the development of quality software systems. In this context,
Causal Reasoning is gaining increasing interest as a methodology to go beyond a purely data-driven approach
by exploiting the use of causality for more effective SQA strategies.
Objective: Provide a broad and detailed overview of the use of causal reasoning for SQA activities, in order to
support researchers to access this research field, identifying room for application, main challenges and research
opportunities.
Methods: A systematic review of the scientific literature on causal reasoning for SQA. The study has found,
classified, and analyzed 86 articles, according to established guidelines for software engineering secondary
studies.
Results: Results highlight the primary areas within SQA where causal reasoning has been applied, the
predominant methodologies used, and the level of maturity of the proposed solutions. Fault localization is
the activity where causal reasoning is more exploited, especially in the web services/microservices domain,
but other tasks like testing are rapidly gaining popularity. Both causal inference and causal discovery are
exploited, with the Pearlâ€™s graphical formulation of causality being preferred, likely due to its intuitiveness.
Tools to favor their application are appearing at a fast pace â€” most of them after 2021.
Conclusions: The findings show that causal reasoning is a valuable means for SQA tasks with respect to
multiple quality attributes, especially during V&V, evolution and maintenance to ensure reliability, while it is
not yet fully exploited for phases like requirements engineering and design. We give a picture of the current
landscape, pointing out exciting possibilities for future research.
1. Introduction
Software engineering is an intellectually demanding and creative
activity involving complex interdependent tasks aimed at building
software products and ensuring their quality. The advancement of
Machine Learning (ML) fostered a human-machine co-design view to
develop dependable systems [1]: ML algorithms are able to search for
significant patterns in large historical datasets gathered throughout
the system life cycle, thus supporting several software engineering
tasks, aimed for instance at fault avoidance (e.g., testing), fault removal
(e.g., debugging) and prediction.
While recognizing patterns in data is a fundamental tool for
decision-making, well supported by ML, engineers do much more
when building and validating a system. They tend to infer causeâ€“effect
relationships among the involved variables, and, based on that, infer
hypotheses, simulate possible actions, and derive explanations to then
support decisions â€” in other words, they reason on what have learned.
âˆ—Corresponding author.
E-mail address: luca.giamattei@unina.it (L. Giamattei).
Researchers have been trying to explain causality using statistical and
ML methods for years. However, these methods are able to identify
connections between variables like correlation and regression but fall
short in detecting causality. Techniques that merely recognize patterns
in data only get us to what Pearl and Mackenzie [2] call the first rung
of the causation ladder (i.e., â€˜â€˜associationâ€™â€™). At this level, we are limited
to reason about what has been observed.
Currently, software engineering researchers are exploring the usage
of Causal Reasoning (CR) methodologies to go beyond a purely data-
driven approach and to exploit the use of causality for finer-tuned
strategies. Through the years, researchers have designed a number of
techniques able to capture the essence of CR and provide mathematical
frameworks for it. This enables the replication of human reasoning
on modern machines, greatly enhancing it with computational power.
While CR finds consolidated ground in many domains (e.g., epidemi-
ology, economics, social sciences, etc.), it has recently raised interest
https://doi.org/10.1016/j.infsof.2024.107599

Fig. 1. Number of papers on Causal Reasoning in SQA per year..
in software engineering, particularly in the context of software quality
assurance (SQA), mainly due to the seminal work of the Turing award-
winner Pearl [3]. Fig. 1 shows the number of papers on the topic of
CR in SQA between 2003 and (June) 2024 (we explain the search and
collection process of these papers in Section 3). Notably, almost 70%
of the papers have been published in the last three years (i.e., starting
from 2021), highlighting the emergence of CR as a methodology for
SQA practices.
Given its inherent multi-disciplinary history, the study of causality
is very fragmented and this has been reversed also in the software
engineering literature. For this reason, systematic reviews can greatly
contribute to a better understanding of the current landscape and guide
future research directions. A recent study by Siebert [4] reviews the use
of CR in software engineering, covering 25 papers published between
2010 and 2022. They focus on the use of graphical causal models
(introduced by Wright [5] and more recently by Pearl [3]) and notice
an increasing trend, with works mostly pertaining to root cause analysis
and fault localization.
We present a systematic review aiming to comprehensively in-
vestigate diverse causal models and their applications across various
dimensions of SQA within the software engineering process. Starting
from an initial set of 770 papers, we ended up with a final list of 86
papers that depict the current landscape of ideas, trends, and challenges
in using CR for a variety of quality-related tasks (e.g., fault prevention,
prediction, tolerance, removal) and attributes (e.g., reliability, security,
performance), along the whole lifecycle.
The study investigates three research questions concerning: the
activities CR is used for along the software life cycle (RQ1), how CR is
used (RQ2), and if the CR-based solutions are experimentally validated,
and in which domain (RQ3). The work provides a comprehensive
overview of the state of the art in the use of CR in quality-related
activities in software engineering.
Besides corroborating and updating the trends identified by
Siebert [4], results show the main areas of SQA in which CR has been
employed, identifying the main methodologies for causal discovery and
inference, and the maturity of the proposals. Additionally, we provide
an extensive discussion highlighting the main findings, open challenges
and research opportunities. The findings provide evidence that the
software engineering community today considers CR as a valuable
means for several SQA tasks, including testing, fault localization, fault
and quality attributes prediction.
The paper is structured as follows. Section 2 provides background
on CR and SQA. Section 3 presents the three research questions and the
methodology followed from the search to the analysis of the literature.
Sections 4 and 6 show the results for the research questions. Section 7
discusses the main findings of the analysis, as well as open challenges
and research opportunities. Section 8 analyzes threats to validity. Sec-
tion 9 reviews the related secondary studies. Section 10 provides the
conclusions. We release data and scripts to replicate this study in the
online repository.1

2. Background
This Section sets out the background concepts and the terminology
used throughout the paper, with respect to the two drivers of this work:
causal reasoning and software quality assurance.
2.1. Causal reasoning
CR has its roots in the 20th century. It had its first applications
in a variety of domains, like epidemiology [6], economics [7], social
and medical sciences [8,9], education [10,11], with significant impact
on better understanding and explaining complex phenomena, making
predictions, and managing decision processes. CR mimic something
natural in human logic, namely the identification of causes and effects
and the answering of â€˜â€˜what if â€™â€™ (causal) questions. Pearl and Macken-
zie [2] have conceptualized a framework describing three levels of
understanding and reasoning about causation, called the â€˜â€˜ladder of
causationâ€™â€™. The first level is association (correlation), based only on
what we observe. It is a basic understanding that two variables tend to
co-occur, making no claims about causation. CR allows to stair up to
the second and third rung of the ladder, by performing, respectively,
â€˜â€˜interventionsâ€™â€™ (evaluating the impact of actively manipulating one
variable to observe the effect on another) and â€˜â€˜counterfactualsâ€™â€™ (ex-
ploring hypothetical scenarios, that did not occur but help understand
what might have happened under different conditions).
Through the years a number of frameworks have been proposed
to allow machines to reason with causality, by modeling causeâ€“effect
relations and quantifying the effects of causes through what is called
â€˜â€˜causal inferenceâ€™â€™.
2.1.1. Causal frameworks
Causal frameworks are mathematical and/or graphical representa-
tions of causal relationships within an individual system or popula-
tion [12,13]. They embed some form of external knowledge, like prior
knowledge of the data generation mechanism and assumptions about
plausible causal mechanisms, that distinguishes them from associa-
tional methods [14]. They are used to learn and estimate causal effects
between involved variables of a certain system, facilitating causal infer-
ence. One of the first conceptual frameworks is the â€˜â€˜potential outcomeâ€™â€™
by Neyman [15,16] and Rubin [17] (also called Neymanâ€“Rubin Causal
Model). It allows estimating counterfactuals, i.e., estimating the causal
effect of a treatment on an individual by comparing what happened
(observed outcome) to what would have happened in the absence of that
treatment (potential outcome). The formal definitions follow [3,12,18].
Definition 1. Potential Outcome (PO)
A potential outcome ð‘Œð‘‡=ð‘¡(ð‘¢) of a variable Y is the value that Y would
have taken for individual ð‘¢, had ð‘‡(treatment variable) assumed the
value t.

A potential outcome is fundamentally distinct from an actual out-
come. The first is a hypothetical outcome that, differently from the
second, has not been observed. For instance, in case of a binary treat-
ment ð‘‡= {0, 1}, if we observe an outcome ð‘Œð‘‡=1(ð‘¢), we cannot observe
ð‘Œð‘‡=0(ð‘¢) at the same time â€“ e.g., if an individual took a medicine (ð‘‡= 1),
we cannot observe the case in which (s)he did not take it (ð‘‡= 0)).
This is a potential outcome (also called counterfactual outcome), and one
retrospectively reasons about â€˜â€˜what would have happened ifâ€™â€™, as opposed
to the observed outcome (or factual outcome).
The PO framework, defined at the level of an individual, aims to
estimate a potential outcome and then compute the treatment effect.
An example metric is the Individual Treatment Effect (ITE):
ð¼ ð‘‡ ð¸(ð‘¢) = ð‘Œð‘‡=1(ð‘¢) âˆ’ð‘Œð‘‡=0(ð‘¢)
(1)
The impossibility of simultaneously observing both potential out-
comes, and consequently observing the effect of a treatment t on
an individual u, is the fundamental problem of causal inference [19].
However, statistical solutions allow to replace this impossible problem
of observing the causal effect of t on a specific individual with the
feasible estimation of the average causal effect of t over a population
of individuals. At the population level, we define the treated group,
including all the treated individuals (ð‘‡= 1), and the control group
(ð‘‡= 0). For simplicity, we use a binary treatment; otherwise multiple
treated groups are formed. The ITE computed at population level is
called Average Treatment Effect (ATE):
ð´ð‘‡ ð¸= ð¸[ð‘Œð‘‡=1 âˆ’ð‘Œð‘‡=0]
(2)
ATE is also often called Average Causal Effect (ACE) in the coun-
terfactual literature [8]. In general, ACE refers to the estimation of
the effect of the change of value of a certain cause to a variable of
interest [3]. More broadly average causal effects include a variety of
metrics, such as Average Treatment effect on the Treated group (ATT),
and Conditional Average Treatment Effect (CATE) [12].
To compute (when feasible) an unbiased estimation of these metrics,
randomized controlled trials (i.e., random assignment of control and
treatment groups) are performed. Otherwise, in presence of observa-
tional data, a number of causal inference methods can be employed
(introduced in the next section). To ease the estimation of treatment
effects, some assumptions are usually made, such as the Stable Unit
Treatment Value Assumption (SUTVA) [20,21]. SUTVA specifies that
the value of Y for unit u when exposed to treatment t will be the same
no matter what mechanism is used to assign treatment t to unit u and
no matter what treatments the other units receive.
Another powerful way of dealing with causality is to use graphi-
cal models - usually in the form of Direct Acyclic Graphs (DAG). In
a CausalDAG, nodes are the variables of the system and edges are
interpreted as causal relationships between them [18].
Definition 2. Causal Direct Acyclic Graph (CausalDAG)

A number of other models and frameworks to deal with causality
have been conceptualized through the years. Difference-in-Differences
(DiD) [25], a common framework in econometrics and health care
for estimating the ATE, compares the changes in outcomes over time
between a treatment group and a control group [12]. DiD is based on
typical assumptions made also for the PO framework, like SUTVA, but
requires additional key assumptions. For instance, it assumes that in the
absence of treatment, the average treatment and control groups would
have followed parallel trends, and that in the pre-treatment period the
treatment had no effect on the pre-treatment population [25]. Fuzzy

Cognitive Maps [26] are graph structures for representing causal rela-
tionships, with their strength encoded as fuzzy values. It is especially
applicable to soft knowledge domains, in presence of uncertain system
concepts and relationships. It implements a fuzzy causal algebra aiming
at estimating, through backward and forward chaining, direct and indi-

frameworks, its purpose is not to provide rigorous and precise causal
methods, but â€˜â€˜semi-quantitativeâ€™â€™ (i.e. using and producing indicative
rather than predictive numerical values) [27]. Finally, Causal trees [28]
are types of decision tree structure that incorporates causal modeling
principles. They are based on the PO framework and estimate treatment
effects (usually Heterogeneous Treatment Effect [29]) with the use of
tree-based methods, like classification and regression trees [28,30].
2.1.2. Causal inference (CI)
CI aims to estimate the causal effect of a specific variable (referred
to as the treatment) on an outcome of interest [12]. There are two
primary strategies for quantifying causal effects: performing random-
ized experiments, where treatment is randomly assigned, or using
CI methods to estimate the treatment effect from observational data.
Randomized experiments are the gold standard, they enable causal
identification by design but can be too costly, unethical or otherwise
not feasible for certain situations [31]. In contrast, methods that rely
on observational data have gained popularity due to the abundance
of available data. This study focuses on CI methods that leverage
observational data.
Given a causal framework, the fundamental objective of CI is to
estimate how the outcome variable Y changes when we intervene to
assign a specific value t to the treatment variable T (i.e., ð‘ƒ(ð‘Œ|ð‘‘ ð‘œ(ð‘‡=
ð‘¡))).
Reaching this objective involves several steps. The first step is
the identification, which consists in distinguishing spurious correlations
from true causal effects and determining whether and how a causal
effect can be estimated from available data. It consists in finding the
mathematical formula that generates the answer to a causal query
or, in other words, a â€˜â€˜statistical quantity to be estimated from the
data that, once estimated, can legitimately represent the answer to
the queryâ€™â€™ [2]. However, it may not always be possible to identify
this quantity: for example, imagine an unmeasured variable Z that
affects both X and Y, with X also having a direct effect on Y. In this
case, identifying the causal effect ð‘ƒ(ð‘Œ|ð‘‘ ð‘œ(ð‘‹)) is challenging due to the
confounding introduced by Z. To address this, model refinement or
additional assumptions (e.g., assuming Zâ€™s effect is negligible) may be
necessary. In graphical causal models, the do-calculus provides a set
of rules that leverage the structure of the causal graph to transform
an interventional/counterfactual query into an observational query.
In general, a number of methods can be exploited to control for
confounding bias (e.g., the back-door, front-door, mediators, instrumental
variables [2,3,32]). The second step is the estimation of a causal effect
from observational data. Once identification is established, a variety
of statistical methods can be used to this purpose [12], including
propensity-based stratification [33], propensity score matching [34],
inverse propensity weighting [35], regression discontinuity [36], two-
stage least square [37], and generalized linear models [12]. For our
investigation, we consider the classification given by Guo et al. [18]
on methods to estimate causal effects starting from observational data2,
shown in Fig. 2. Depending on the assumptions of data, CI methods are
separated into two categories: observational data with unconfoundness
and with confounding (i.e, without and with unobserved confounders).
Methods without unobserved confounders include three categories
of adjustment: regression adjustment, propensity score-based methods, and
covariate balancing. Adjustments eliminate the confounding bias based
on a set of observed features. In essence, these methods isolate the true
causal effect of the treatment by statistically controlling the influence
of confounding variables, assuming that all confounder variables are
among the observed ones.
Methods with unobserved confounders relax the assumption of un-
confoundness, making them more related to real-world scenarios where
unobserved confounders may play a role. In terms of SCM, the as-
sumption on unconfoundness implies that conditioning on a subset of
observed variables blocks all back-door paths. These are indirect paths
between the treatment and outcome through confounders, which, if not
blocked, introduce bias into the causal effect estimation. Without the
unconfoundness assumption, conditioning is insufficient, and alterna-
tive information must be utilized. These methods include instrumental
variables, front-door criterion, and regression discontinuity design.
With the increasing availability of Big Data, machine learning-based
methods have been designed for learning causal effects, mainly through
the use of neural networks and ensembles. To go beyond the uncon-
foundeness assumption, most of these methods learn representations
of confounders, under the assumption that they can be learnt from
observational data [18]. For instance, Louizos et al. [38] propose a
Causal Effect Variational Autoencoder (CEVAE), aiming at estimating
a latent-variable model where they simultaneously discover the hidden
confounders and infer how they affect treatment and outcome.
Finally, following the Pearlian inference methodology, recently
BlÃ¶baum et al. [39] have proposed a simulation-based method called
Do-Sampler, based on sampling from post-intervention distribution of
variables. Given a set of interventional variables, Do-Sampler: (i) cuts
all their incoming edges (they are intervened, hence no longer causally
affected by any other), (ii) sets the values of these variables to their
interventional quantities, and (iii) propagates those values through the
causal graph to compute interventional outcomes with a sampling pro-
cedure. Comprehensive discussions on CI methods have been published
by Guo et al. [18], Yao et al. [31], and Nogueira et al. [12].

2.1.3. Causal discovery (CD)
CD aims at learning causal relationships between variables [12] to
build a causal framework explicitly embedding causeâ€“effect relation-
ships, i.e., graphical models.3 These can be built in three main ways: by
randomized controlled experiments, manually with domain knowledge,
or by employing CD algorithms on observational data [40]. As for CI
methods, the focus of this section is on the latter, that aims at extracting
a graphical causal structure from observational data, avoiding con-
trolled experiments, which may be too expensive or even technically
infeasible [41]. To achieve this, CD algorithms assume that causality
can be derived from statistical dependencies. These algorithms rely
(to a different extent) on various subsets of assumptions, the main
ones being the Causal Markov, Faithfulness, and Sufficiency assumptions
[12,40,42,43], to derive correspondences between the (conditional)
independence in the probability distribution and the causal connectiv-
ity relationships in the generated DAG [42]. The first two conditions
are the most important ones and respectively state that: (i) every
vertex X in the graph G is probabilistically independent of its non-
descendants given its parents; (ii) if a variable X is independent of Y
given a conditioning set Z in the probability distribution,4 then X is
d-separated5 from Y given Z in the DAG (in other words, the statis-
tical dependence between variables estimated from the data does not
violate the independence defined by any causal graph that generates
the data [18]). Markov and faithfulness conditions are sufficient to
define an equivalence structure over directed acyclic graphs, where
graphs that are in the same Markov equivalence class have the same
(conditional) independence structure. Sufficiency requires that, for a
pair of observed variables, all their common causes must also be
observed in the data.
Wang et al. [43] provide a classification of CD methods, shown in
Fig. 3. In particular, they are divided in contstraint-based, score-based,
FCM-based
(Functional Causal Models), Continuous Optimization-
based, and Hybrid or Prior Knowledge-based methods.
Constraint-based algorithms use conditional independence tests on
observed data to identify a set of edge constraints [44]. These algo-
rithms have the advantage of being generally applicable, despite being
based on the strong assumption of causal faithfulness, therefore often
requiring large sample sizes to perform well [40]. Typical (conditional
independence) constraint-based algorithms are PC, FCI [44] and its
improvement RFCI [45].
Score-based algorithms optimize a score assigned to candidate
graphs, exploiting adjustment techniques such as the Bayesian Infor-
mation Criterion, that approximates the posterior probability of the
3 Non-graphical causal frameworks, such as PO, do not require CD.
4 Roughly, X and Y are independent conditional on a set of variables Z
if knowledge about X gives no extra information about Y once you have
knowledge of Z.
5 Let ð‘‹, ð‘Œ, and ð‘be disjoint subsets of all the vertex in the DAG. ð‘d-
separates ð‘‹and ð‘Œjust in case every path from a variable in ð‘‹to a variable
in ð‘Œcontains at least one vertex ð‘‹ð‘–such that either: i) ð‘‹ð‘–is a collider (i.e. the
arrows converge on ð‘‹ð‘–in the path), and no descendant of ð‘‹ð‘–(including ð‘‹ð‘–)
is in ð‘; or ii) ð‘‹ð‘–is not a collider, and ð‘‹ð‘–is in ð‘[13].
model given the data (assuming a uniform prior probability distribution
over the DAG space) [46]. They relax the faithfulness assumption
by replacing conditional independence tests with the goodness-of-fit
tests. They are computationally expensive, as they enumerate (and
score) every possible graph for the given variables. Well known score-
based algorithms are GES [47] and its successor FGES [48], that use
parallelization to optimize performance, and GFCI, that combines FCI
and FGES [49].
FCM-based algorithms determine the causal direction of edges, iden-
tifying the true causal structure out of all the graphs within a Markov
equivalence class. The most noticeable example, working for contin-
uous variables, is LiNGAM, proposed by Shimizu et al. [50], where
the model is assumed to be linear and non-Gaussian. Under the causal
Markov assumption, acyclicity and a linear non-Gaussian parameteriza-
tion (i.e., each variable is determined by a linear function of the values
of its parents and an additive non-Gaussian noise term), it has been
proved that the causal structure can be uniquely determined [51]. FCM-
based algorithms have the advantage of not relying on the faithfulness
assumption and of learning substantially more about the causal struc-
ture, sometimes even determining a unique model. However, to relax
faithfulness, they introduce other assumptions that can be controversial
or difficult to test [46] and generally require a larger sample size to be
accurate.
Continuous optimization-based algorithms combine the benefits of
score-based methods with gradient optimization by converting the
discrete DAG search space into a continuous and optimizable constraint
space [43]. Usually these methods are machine learning-based and the
most representative ones are NOTEARS [52] and DAG-GNN [53].
Many CD algorithms allow to specify some constraints (e.g., required
or forbidden causal relationships), based on prior human knowledge.
The category of Hybrid or Prior Knowledge-based methods like Joint
Causal Inference (JCI) [54] and Max-Min Hill-Climbing (MMHC) [55]
aim to build on top of these algorithms and incorporate specific domain
knowledge in addition to observational data in an effective way.
CD for time series. The conditional-based algorithms like PC, FCI,
LiNGAM, although applicable to extract causal relationships between
time series, are not specifically designed to this aim. Many extensions
and specialized algorithms have been developed to address this specific
task [56]. Among these, a strategy relying on Granger causality [57]
and its generalization based on (Multivariate) Transfer Entropy [58]
are common choices. Given two time series X and Y, the idea behind
Granger causality is to investigate whether the prediction of the current
value of time series X improves by incorporating Yâ€™s past into its own
past [56]. In this case, we say that Y Granger causes X.
Extensive discussions on CD algorithms have been published by
Glymour et al. [40], Nogueira et al. [12], Guo et al. [18], Wang
et al. [43], and Moraffah et al. [56].
2.2. Software Quality Assurance
Software quality is the â€˜â€˜capability of a software product to conform
to requirementsâ€™â€™ [59,60]. Software Quality Assurance (SQA) activities
Information and Software Technology 178 (2025) 107599 
5

Fig. 4. Taxonomy of quality attributes [1].
aim to support a justified confidence that the software product con-
forms to its established requirements [61]. The SQA process refers to
â€˜â€˜a set of activities that assess adherence to, and the adequacy of the
software processes used to develop and modify software products. SQA
also determines the degree to which the desired results from software
quality control are being obtainedâ€™â€™ [60].
A failure of a system is a deviation from its intended service. It is
due to the presence of faults or defects which, once activated, corrupt
the system state and may provoke a failure if they reach the interface.
Since in the wide literature about software quality some terms have
different meanings in different contexts, we hereafter report the mean-
ing of the basic terms as used throughout this paper. We refer to the
terminology adopted by the IFIP WG 10.4 on Dependable Computing
and Fault Tolerance6 â€“ due to the foundational work on dependability
by Avizienis, Laprie, et al. [1] - as it better reflects the one adopted in
the surveyed papers.
A Failure is a deviation of the delivered service from correct service.
An Error is that part of the system state that may cause a subse-
quent failure: a failure occurs when an error reaches the service
interface, making the service deviate from correct service.7
A Fault is the adjudged or hypothesized cause of an error. An active
fault produces an error; a fault not activated is said to be
dormant. Throughout this paper, with fault we implicitly refer
to software faults if not differently specified. In addition, a fault
in the code, i.e., a fault introduced by a human mistake at some
point in the life cycle and that slipped through the code, is also
called a software defect [63] or a bug.8
The SQA process entails activities spanning the whole life cycle, con-
cerning both functional and non-functional requirements. We categorize
activities and quality attributes by borrowing again the taxonomy of
dependability and security by Avizienis, Laprie, et al. [1], extending it
with tasks and attributes not related to dependability and security as
reported in Fig. 4.
As for the means for assuring quality related to software faults, we
refer to the following categories:
Fault avoidance/prevention, to limit the introduction of faults. This
is typically achieved by good engineering practices, such as
requirements engineering, design modularity, encapsulation and
information hiding, reuse.

Fault removal, to reduce the number and severity of faults. This
refers to activities aiming at detecting the presence of faults
(e.g., testing), localizing them (fault localization) and subse-
quently correcting the code (debugging).
Fault tolerance, to tolerate failures, through techniques such as error
detection and recovery.
(Fault) forecasting, to (i) estimate the present number, the future
incidence, and the likely consequences of faults, as well as (ii)
to predict key performance indicators (KPIs) not necessarily
related to faults, but whose monitoring and prediction sup-
ports future quality improvement actions (hence the parentheses
around â€˜â€˜Faultâ€™â€™). Strictly, the category departs from the task
of forecasting a fault [1]; it is included in our analysis since
we target quality attributes beyond dependability and security
(e.g., performance, usability).
As for the quality attributes addressed, we include:
Dependability attributes. Dependability is the trustworthiness of a
computing system which allows reliance to be justifiably placed
on the service it delivers.4 It is an umbrella term encompassing
concepts such as reliability, safety, availability and security.
We borrow from Avizienis, Laprie, et al. [1] the following
definitions for dependability quality attributes:
â€¢ Availability refers to the readiness for correct service, defined
as â€˜â€˜the ability of a system to be in a state to perform a required
function at a given instant of timeâ€™â€™ (recovery after failure is al-
lowed). It is expressed by the probability of failure-free operation
at a given point in time.
â€¢ Reliability refers to the continuity of a service, that is, for how
long it is provided without failures; precisely, it is â€˜â€˜the ability of a
system to perform a required function under given conditions for
a given time intervalâ€™â€™. Once the system fails, no recovery takes
place (while there can be recovery upon component failures). It
is expressed by the probability of failure-free operation in a time
interval. Note that in the ISO/IEC 25010 [64] standard reliability
has a broader meaning, encompassing concepts like availability
and maturity.
â€¢ Safety refers to the absence of catastrophic consequences on the
user(s) and the environment; it is the probability of catastrophic-
failure-free operation during mission time interval.
â€¢ Maintainability is the ability to undergo modifications and re-
pairs.
â€¢ Integrity is the absence of improper system alterations.
Security is a macroattribute encompassing Availability, Integrity and
Confidentiality.
â€¢ Confidentiality is the absence of unauthorized disclosure of in-
formation.

Performance is the degree to which (i) the response and process-

of resources used, and (iii) the maximum limits of a prod-

requirements.

3. Methodology
3.1. Research questions
This study aims to answer the following research questions (RQ)
about CR in the context of SQA.
RQ1: Which SQA activities is CR used for and for what quality
objective?
This RQ characterizes what CR is used for, namely what are
the quality-related tasks and quality objectives addressed by
researchers by means of CR (CI and/or CD) methods.
RQ2: How is CR used?
This RQ aims to characterize how researchers adopted CR for
quality improvement and assessment. We investigate what
causal task is performed (i.e., CD and/or CI), the causal frame-
work, the CD and CI methodologies, and the tools used.
RQ3: Are the solutions using CR experimentally validated?
We finally aim to check the maturity of the proposal; being it a
relatively new field of application, we aim to check how many
solutions are experimentally validated and, if any, how many
solutions are being experimented in industrial environments,
and in what domain.
3.2. Search and selection
To address the above questions, we conducted the research accord-
ing to the protocol shown in Fig. 5.
The search and selection process started from the formulation of
the query shown in Listing 1. We executed the query in June 2024
on four of the most popular digital libraries - Scopus, IEEEXplore,
ACM Digital Library, ISI Web of Science (step 1). Then, we
merged the results and removed duplicates (step 2), obtaining an initial
list of 770 papers.
To the list of unique 770 papers we applied the following inclusion
and exclusion criteria.
â€¢ Inclusion criteria
â€“ IC1: the paperâ€™s primary goal is software quality assur-
ance/assessment (namely, activities to assure/assess quality
related to software faults according to the categories defined
in Section 2.2) with the use of CR.
â€“ IC2: the target of the software quality assurance/assessment
activity is a software application, or a software-enabled
component (e.g., a machine learning model like a Deep
Neural Network) or system where software quality has a
non-negligible impact on system quality.
â€¢ Exclusion criteria
â€“ EC1: the paper is a thesis, book, or review.
â€“ EC2: the paper is not subject to peer review, e.g., it is a tech-
nical report, a white paper, a project report, government
document (i.e., grey literature) or it is a preprint.
â€“ EC3: the paper presents a CI or CD method, algorithm,
library or tool not used for an SQA task.
â€“ EC4: the paper is a secondary or tertiary study.
â€“ EC5: the paper is not written in English.
Two researchers were involved in applying the criteria to the entire
set of papers, with the support of a senior author as arbiter. Since we
only have two raters evaluating identical items, a good fit is to use
the Cohenâ€™s kappa to assess the level of agreement. According to the
common interpretation in literature [65], the results (k = 0.778) in-
dicate substantial agreement. This inclusion/exclusion process allowed
us to exclude 693 papers while including 76, listed in Table 1. Most of
the papers were excluded due to violation of IC1 (a few IC2), as they
focus on CR techniques applied in healthcare and economics, not SQA.
A subset of papers were excluded due to EC3 and EC4. Additionally,
we compiled a list of papers we knew and believed should be part of
the list, creating a reference test set. We then compared the selected
papers with this reference set, following established guidelines for
secondary studies, as recommended by Petersen et al. [66], Kitchenham
and Brereton [67]. The reference test set was composed by 21 papers.
17/21 papers are selected from a set of 25 papers reviewed in a similar
previous survey by Siebert [4], specifically, by taking those that match
also our inclusion/exclusion criteria (P1, P8, P11, P15-17, P20-21, P24,
P26-28, P30, P32, P44, P48, P86 - Table 1). To this, we added 4
further papers that we expected to be in the search (P31, P33, P34,
and P42 - Table 1). 19/21 papers were included in the list of papers
selected by our query, ensuring representativeness of the selection â€“ the
remaining two papers (i.e., P17 and P86) did not appear in the query
results since they do not contain the words included in the last two
â€˜â€˜ANDâ€™â€™ of the query (i.e.,â€˜â€˜softwareâ€™â€™ and â€˜â€˜caus*â€™â€™) in their title, abstract,
or keywords. We considered these terms pivotal for the scope of the
search, and decided to not further refine the query to avoid side effects,
e.g., explosion of false positives. Thus, considering the list of 76 papers
resulting from the query and the list of 21 papers from the test set (19
of which are in both lists), we got to 78 included papers at this stage.
Starting from the list of 78 included papers we included additional 8
papers (i.e., P35, P38-41, P49, P77-78) by snowballing, for a final list
of 86 papers.

L. Giamattei et al.
Fig. 5. Literature search protocol.
3.3. Data extraction, classification, and analysis
The data extraction step 3 provides key information about each
paper, useful for classification. Starting from the RQs, we defined an
initial RQs scheme (Fig. 5). Then, to refine and agree on the scheme,
we proceeded iteratively, beginning with a horizontal classification.
We divided the list of papers into equal subsets and assigned them
to three authors, who independently classified them according to all
dimensions of the scheme. With the classified papers (i.e., the filled
scheme), we validated the classification in plenary meetings. The val-
idation phase was useful to decide whether refining the scheme was
necessary (e.g., adding, removing, or modifying dimensions). In such
cases, a refined scheme was agreed upon in phase 5. This iterative
process concluded with the agreement on the final scheme with 17
dimensions, as reported in Table 2. Finally, to ensure homogeneous
classification, the papers were re-classified vertically: each author was
assigned a subset of sub-dimensions and classified all 86 papers for
only the assigned dimensions. This favored the detection of inconsistent
classifications performed during the horizontal classification phase.
Dedicated meetings solved such disagreements.
On the classified papers, we present in Sections 4 and 6 the analysis
(step 6) we performed to answer the RQs. We highlight the main
findings, implications, and open challenges derived by the analysis in
Section 7.

total of 86 papers for classification. Fig. 6 shows the distribution of the
