The persistence of this vulnerability over an extended period can be 
attributed to the patchâ€™s seemingly straightforward and rational nature. 
Moreover, code reviewers probably overlooked essential contextual 
details regarding the interaction between the patch and the pre-existing 
code, indicating a notable deficiency in standard review procedures.
2.2. Patch
In this paper, we define a â€˜patchâ€™ as a code modification that is still 
undergoing review and has not yet been merged into the repository. 
We specifically focus on minor patchesâ€”those containing fewer than 
30 lines of code (LOC). This emphasis is well-justified, as previous 
research has demonstrated that over 70% of bug-fixing patches involve 
modifications of less than 30 LOC (Li and Paxson, 2017; Wu et al., 
2020).
Bug-fixing patches can unintentionally activate underlying problems 
within the current codebase. This paper focuses on analyzing these 
interactions during the code review process, prior to the permanent 
integration of changes into the main codebase.
Minor patches present a unique security challenge despite their lim-
ited scope. These small code modifications, precisely because of their 
targeted bug-fixing purpose and apparent simplicity, often receive less 
rigorous scrutiny during review. This reduced attention leads reviewers 
to miss potential interactions between changes and surrounding code.
2.3. Code property graph
We analyze source code for security vulnerabilities using the code 
property graphâ€”a comprehensive representation of program structure 
and behavior. The CPG integrates three fundamental program analysis 
structures (Yamaguchi et al., 2014): the abstract syntax tree (AST) for 
syntactic structure, the control-flow graph (CFG) for execution paths, 
and the program dependence graph (PDG) for data and control depen-
dencies. Vulnerability analysis using the CPG has become a leading 
methodology in static analysis because most vulnerability types cannot 
be adequately modeled using a single code representation.
3. Approach overview
This section provides a comprehensive overview of our detection 
architecture and explains the fundamental concepts that underlying our 
proposed approach.
3.1. System architecture
CAPRA is based on the observation that open-source projects con-
tain numerous potential code defects that may develop into actual 
vulnerabilities under specific conditions. Fig. 2 shows the detection 
architecture of CAPRA and its integration method with the standard 
CI/CD pipeline.

3.2. Detection scripts
The detection scripts represent another crucial design component, 
with each script focusing on a distinct category of software vulnerabil-
ity. All detection scripts consist of two core modules: a decision module 
and detection rules. The decision module invokes appropriate detection 
rules based on the patch modification type (addition or deletion) and 
the modification content. The detection module conducts targeted risk 
assessments, allowing for the coexistence of multiple detection rules 
within a single script to tackle diverse risk scenarios.
Both the decision-making module and detection rules are designed 
based on fundamental principles of vulnerability formation. To more 
clearly illustrate CAPRAâ€™s detection process, Fig. 3 shows a detection 
example for UAF vulnerability. In this example, when dynamically 
allocated memory is freed but its corresponding pointer is not nullified 
and continues to be used later in the code, a UAF vulnerability occurs.
Upon identification by CAPRA that a patch involves the removal 
of statements assigning NULL, the Decision Module forwards the re-
moved line alongside the source fileâ€™s CPG to the Detection Module. 
The Detection Module then assesses whether this removal satisfies the 
conditions necessary to activate a UAF vulnerability, considering both 
the contextual details of the line and the predefined Detection Rules.

4. Methodology
This section details CAPRAâ€™s methodology for identifying security 
vulnerabilities introduced during code modifications, focusing specifi-
cally on our detection mechanisms for memory leak and UAF vulnera-
bilities.
4.1. Memory leak detection
Memory leak constitute a significant vulnerability class in C/C++ 
applications. Analysis of the CVE database reveals that such vulnerabil-
ities represented over 23% of all memory-related security issues among 
the top 1000 C/C++ GitHub projects between 2020 and 2023.
Effective code review practices combined with static analysis tools 
can reduce memory leak incidents by approximately 55%. Given this 
significant prevention potential, along with the economic impact de-
scribed previously, CAPRA prioritizes memory leak as a primary detec-
tion target.
4.1.1. Vulnerability mechanism
Memory leak fundamentally occurs when programs fail to deal-
locate dynamically allocated memory, leading to progressive system 
resource depletion. There are three primary scenarios that precipitate 
memory leak:
I. Forgotten Deallocation: This most common memory leak sce-
nario occurs when code dynamically allocates memory but fails to 
include corresponding deallocation statements. Recent OpenSSH fix 
commit (Larrosa, 2024) exemplify this vulnerability pattern.
II. Pointer Reassignment Leaks: This scenario occurs when a pointer 
that already references allocated memory is reassigned before the 
original allocation is freed.
III. Incorrect Memory Management: This category encompasses sub-
tle logical errors in complex data structures. For example, a common 
mistake in linked list implementation where only the head node is 
deallocated, while memory allocated for subsequent nodes remains 
unreleased.
4.1.2. Script detection logic
Memory leaks triggered by patches manifest in two primary man-
ners. Initially, such leaks may occur upon the removal of essential 
deallocation statements from pre-existing code. Additionally, they may 
arise when new memory allocation operations are introduced without 
the necessary deallocation statements. CAPRA is designed to specifi-
cally focus on these modifications at the patch level to detect potential 
memory leaks before they are deployed in production code.
Based on these patterns, CAPRA implements a targeted analysis 
approach: when examining patch modifications, the system analyzes source 
files when detecting deleted memory deallocation operations, and ana-
lyzes target files when identifying newly added memory allocation oper-
ations. This dual-focused strategy ensures comprehensive detection of 
potential memory leak vulnerabilities introduced during code changes.
CAPRAâ€™s detection rules center on contextual memory management 
analysis. When the system identifies memory allocation or deallocation 
operations in a patch, it evaluates whether proper memory manage-
ment practices are maintained within the relevant scope. Algorithm 2 
details this analytical process, which systematically identifies potential 
memory leak introduced by code modifications.

4.2. Use-After-Free detection
C/C++ and other memory-unsafe programming languages remain 
fundamental to critical systems development, including kernels and 
browsers, despite generating thousands of memory safety vulnerabili-
ties annually. UAF vulnerabilities â€“ a temporal memory error occurring 
when programs access previously deallocated memory â€“ represent one 
of the most prevalent memory safety flaws. Researches of the CVE 
database reveals that UAF vulnerabilities constitute an increasing pro-
portion of severe security issues, highlighting the need for enhanced 
detection methods (Wickman et al., 2021).
Computers & Security 157 (2025) 104540 
7 
B. Tang et al.
4.2.1. Vulnerability mechanism
Vulnerabilities associated with UAF are fundamentally linked to the 
mechanisms of dynamic memory allocation. Dynamic memory, or the 
heap, allows programmers to allocate blocks of arbitrary sizes, which 
can subsequently be altered or deallocated.
Programs access data in dynamic memory through pointers. A dan-
gling pointer occurs when memory is deallocated or relocated with-
out updating the corresponding pointer references. When these dan-
gling pointers are subsequently dereferenced, they access either invalid 
memory locations or, more critically, memory regions that have been 
reallocated to new objects.
There are two typical cases of UAF vulnerabilities. The most com-
mon UAF vulnerability case is that a buffer is deallocated but without 
nullifying the buffer pointer. Consequently, the buffer in the global 
variable becomes a dangling pointer, and the UAF vulnerability is trig-
gered when the pointer is subsequently called. A more implicit trigger-
ing mechanism is reference counting in a multi-threaded environment, 
such as CVE-2019-12819.
4.2.2. Script detection logic
To trigger a UAF vulnerability during patch integration, one of 
two conditions must be met: either introducing code that manipulates 
dangling pointers referencing deallocated memory, or removing pointer 
nullification operations where the affected memory is subsequently 
accessed. Our detection algorithm therefore implements the following 
decision logic: If an added line contains memory deallocation or memory 
access operation, analyze the target file; if a removed line contains pointer 
nullification operation, analyze the source file.
Our detection rules focus primarily on analyzing pointer opera-
tions and memory access patterns following deallocation events. This 
approach enables identification of potential UAF vulnerabilities by 
tracking the relationship between memory management operations and 
subsequent pointer usage. The detailed algorithmic implementation is 
presented in Algorithm 4.

It should be noted that we must examine the control dependencies

design is intended to address hypocrite commit attacks where nullifi-

Adding processing logic for conditional nodes undoubtedly increases

reachability analysis comparable to symbolic execution methods.

We mask â€˜SOURCE_FILEâ€™ edges during path computation because 
in the CPG, these edges connect nodes to their respective source 
files (Fabian et al., 2023). If these edges were not excluded dur-
ing variable reachability analysis, the algorithm would erroneously 
establish data flow or control flow relationships between different 
variables solely based on their presence within the same source file. 
This masking operation is implemented by specifically excluding edges 
of â€˜SOURCE_FILEâ€™ type when constructing traversal paths, ensuring 
our analysis considers only genuine data dependencies and control 
dependencies. This approach significantly reduces false positive detec-
tions, particularly when analyzing complex codebases where numer-
ous variables may share the same source file without having actual 
dependencies between them.
A UAF vulnerability is considered triggered if no nullification op-
erations exist between the memory deallocation operation and ð‘›, oth-

The path computation process also takes into account the impact of

Since vulnerabilities associated with memory frequently extend be-
yond individual function boundaries, it is crucial to monitor vari-
able usage through the course of function calls. As elaborated in 
Section 4.1.2, memory operations initiated through indirect function 
calls can establish vulnerability chains involving multiple functions. 
Consequently, our analysis of successive usage paths incorporates ex-

5. Experimental evaluation
We present the experimental data and test environment for validat-
ing CAPRA, including our key evaluation metrics. We then demonstrate 
CAPRAâ€™s detection logic and analytical workflow through representa-
tive case studies.
5.1. Experimental setup
5.1.1. Experimental dataset
CAPRA identifies potential triggers of immature vulnerabilities
rather than focusing on detection accuracy, which complicated the 
selection of suitable sample repositories from mainstream datasets. 
Therefore, we constructed a dedicated dataset for the purpose of 
validating CAPRA. We selected 100 memory leak and UAF vulnerability 
samples from SARD as baseline data and constructed 400 test cases. 
To analyze CAPRAâ€™s false positive rate in real-world scenarios, we con-
structed a dataset RealWorld comprising approximately 120 samples of 
legitimate commits from multiple open-source projects including Linux, 
OpenSSH, ffmpeg, and others. Additionally, the dataset incorporates 
hypocrite commit samples and documented vulnerabilities triggered by 
legitimate commits, including CVE-2019-12819.
For each SARD base case, we created four test categories:
vulnerability-triggering code additions, vulnerability-triggering code 
deletions, safe code additions, and safe code deletions. These test cases 
simulate realistic scenarios where developers inadvertently introduce 
vulnerabilities through both simple and complex code changes.
Our experimental dataset2 and source code have been uploaded to 
the CAPRAâ€™s git repository, where researchers can access the dataset 
and reproduce our experimental results.
5.1.2. Tool implementation and experimental environment
CAPRA operates on Python 3.10 in an Ubuntu 22.04.4 LTS environ-
ment with 8 CPU cores and 8 GB memory. Dependencies include Joern 
2.0.441 for code property graph generation and NetworkX 3.3 for graph 
analysis.
5.2. Case study
We analyze three representative cases, including real-world vulner-
ability and hypocrite commit attack. Each analysis presents the case 
origin and defect type, followed by CAPRAâ€™s detection logic and results.

5.3. Additional findings
According to CAPRAâ€™s detection results, some positive memory 
leak cases in SARD exhibit potential immature UAF vulnerabilities. 
For instance, the ð‘”ð‘œð‘œð‘‘ðµ2ðº2ð‘†ð‘–ð‘›ð‘˜() function in sample 99220-v1.0.0 
does not nullify the input parameter data after memory deallocation. 
This scenario mirrors the hypocrite commit cases analyzed in Sec-
tion 5.2.2, and using such a function as a secure coding example would 
undoubtedly increase the risk of immature vulnerabilities. Moreover, 
these issues affect machine learning solutions based on this database: 
in multi-classification scenarios, these potential UAF vulnerabilities 
hidden within positive memory leak samples could interfere with the 
modelâ€™s learning of UAF patterns.
These risks are not merely theoretical concerns. Research (Wu and 
Lu, 2021) has successfully demonstrated hypocrite commit attacks 
against the Linux kernel using analogous code patterns. Additionally, 
certain samples in SARD explicitly warn developers about potential 
vulnerabilities, as evidenced in the CWE416_UAF_char_03 test case. 
This test case for UAF vulnerabilities includes comments indicating 
potential memory leak risks.
This finding substantiates the hypothesis that developersâ€™ focus on 
specific vulnerabilities may inadvertently generate ancillary security 
risks. The observation has significant methodological implications, par-
ticularly for machine learning research, emphasizing the necessity of 
critical dataset evaluation in vulnerability detection studies.
5.4. Experimental results analysis and tool limitations
5.4.1. CAPRAâ€™s detection modes
Before analyzing the experimental results, we need to explain 
CAPRAâ€™s detection modes. CAPRA not only provides alerts for com-
mits that explicitly trigger known immature vulnerabilities but also 
identifies code submissions that may cause null pointer exceptions or 
introduce new immature vulnerabilities. In the statistical analysis of 
experimental results, we differentiated these two alerting strategies: the 
former was defined as strict mode, while the latter was defined as non-
strict mode. Strict mode focuses exclusively on commits that explicitly 
trigger identified vulnerabilities, offering higher precision; Non-strict 
mode provides broader coverage, including potential security concerns.
This distinction is based on practical security engineering require-
ments. We observed that many non-targeted risk notifications (such as 
newly introduced immature vulnerabilities) are often viewed as false 
positives by developers and reviewers, as their actual harm level is 
relatively low, or they do not currently produce substantial impacts. Im-
portantly, should future commits trigger these vulnerabilities, CAPRA 
would be able to detect them. However, from a security governance 
perspective, completely ignoring these risks could lead to cumulative 
security issues.
To balance alert precision with comprehensiveness while reduc-
ing false positive rates, CAPRA employs a dual-mode design. Strict 
mode ensures high-confidence alerts, suitable for security-critical sce-
narios requiring immediate response; Non-strict mode provides more 
comprehensive security monitoring, appropriate for security audits or 
quality assurance phases. This flexibility allows security teams to adjust 
CAPRAâ€™s sensitivity according to project phases and security require-
ments, optimizing development resource allocation without compro-
mising security.

improving tool performance by expanding the scope of risk detection. 
In non-strict mode, since the tool flags more potential risks beyond the

analysis of the samples revealed that the vast majority of these risks 
do indeed exist.

Among these metrics, accuracy (ACC) represents the overall propor-
tion of correct results (both defective and secure commits) detected by 
CAPRA; Precision indicates the percentage of commits flagged as defec-
tive that actually contain defects; Recall (TPR) denotes the proportion 
of detected defects relative to the total defective samples; False positive 
rate (FPR) represents the percentage of secure commits incorrectly 
identified as containing defects; False negative rate (FNR) indicates the 
proportion of defective commits misclassified as secure relative to all 
defective samples. The performance metrics of CAPRA on the current 
dataset are presented in Table 2.
In strict mode, CAPRA maintained high TPR for defect detection 
in both code additions and deletions that trigger immature UAF vul-
nerabilities, with FPR of only 2% and 0%, respectively, resulting in 
an overall ACC of 99.5%. CAPRAâ€™s performance declined somewhat 
when detecting defects that trigger potential memory leaks, particularly 
for defective deletion modifications, where the TPR decreased to 94%. 
Since CAPRA cannot calculate the reachability of conditional branches 
like symbolic execution, to prevent defects from evading detection 
through conditional statements, CAPRA defaults to considering all con-
ditional branches as reachable and therefore does not deeply analyze 
changes to conditional statements, leading to the aforementioned TPR 
decrease. The FPR for identifying secure commits as containing memory 
leak defects was approximately 10%, significantly higher than for UAF 
defect detection. This phenomenon is attributed to constraints in the 
CAPRA detection framework: when a patch simultaneously deletes both 
memory allocation and release code, the tool, analyzing the base file 
line by line before patch integration, incorrectly assumes that memory 
allocation behavior still exists, thereby generating false positives. How-
ever, these types of false positives are relatively easy to review, and we 
consider them acceptable. CAPRA ultimately maintained overall detec-
tion accuracy and precision rates of approximately 95% for memory 
leak defects.
In non-strict mode, due to the expanded types of risk detection, 
while more security risks were identified, the toolâ€™s false positive rate 
also increased, with comprehensive FPRs for UAF and memory leak 
samples rising to 30% and 34%, respectively. It should be explained 
that the false positive rate in non-strict mode cannot objectively indi-
cate CAPRAâ€™s performance (only 6.7% for RealWorld dataset), because 
we understand CARPAâ€™s limitations and therefore designed the legiti-
mate commits with certain biases. Additionally, non-strict mode also 
generates alerts for risks of introducing immature vulnerabilities, and 
these risk notifications also contribute to the increased false positive 
rate.
CAPRA still maintained an overall ACC of around 83% in non-strict 
mode. Since the tool exhibited high TPR in strict mode, expanding the 
types of risk detection did not significantly increase the detection pre-
cision for defective samples, with results remaining largely consistent 
with those from strict mode. These experimental results indicate that 
expanding the types of risk detection not only does not actually increase 
false positives, but rather enables the discovery of more potential 
security risks introduced by patches.
Overall, within the current dataset, CAPRAâ€™s strict mode achieves 
good results in both defect trigger detection precision and false positive 
rate for legitimate commits, but loses the ability to identify a wider 
range of potential risks; Non-strict mode compensates for strict modeâ€™s 
limitations in potential risk detection, but significantly increases the 
false positive rate. Users can make trade-offs according to the actual 
project requirements.
5.4.3. Practical considerations for false positives
While CAPRA achieves relatively low false positive rates in strict 
mode across multiple datasets (3.5% for SARD-based dataset; 4.2% 
for RealWorld dataset), it is essential to address how remaining false 
positives, particularly in non-strict mode (32% for SARD-based dataset; 
6.7% for RealWorld dataset), affect developer workload.
As shown in Fig. 2, CAPRA functions both as a standalone patch 
analysis tool and as a plugin within CI/CD pipelinesâ€™ static code anal-
ysis phase. Unlike traditional detection tools, CAPRA analyzes only 
modified code segments containing potential risk operations, signifi-
cantly limiting the number of generated alerts and avoiding redundant 
warnings for pre-existing defects in the baseline code.

CAPRAâ€™s line-by-line analysis approach produces alerts that are 
inherently more comprehensible and verifiable. When detecting vul-
nerabilities, CAPRA provides precise code line information and concise 
explanations of its reasoning. For example, if a patch adds â€˜ð‘“ð‘Ÿð‘’ð‘’(ð‘‘ð‘Žð‘¡ð‘Ž);â€™, 
CAPRA identifies this as a risk operation and begins analysis. Upon 
finding subsequent usage of data, it generates a specific alert: â€˜â€˜Adding 
â€˜ð‘“ð‘Ÿð‘’ð‘’(ð‘‘ð‘Žð‘¡ð‘Ž);â€™ may trigger a UAF vulnerability as variable â€˜dataâ€™ is accessed 
later in the code.â€™â€™ This precision enables reviewers to quickly locate 
risk points and determine actual vulnerability existence, substantially 
reducing verification effort.
Our analysis of CAPRAâ€™s false positives reveals four primary cate-
gories:
I. Simultaneous deletion of vulnerability triggers and critical con-
text. For instance, removing memory deallocation code for variable 
ð‘‘ð‘Žð‘¡ð‘Ž might trigger a memory leak alert, but if the patch also removes 
memory allocation for ð‘‘ð‘Žð‘¡ð‘Ž, a false positive occurs. Despite this ar-
chitectural limitation, reviewers can quickly dismiss such alerts by 
examining the target file using the precise information provided.
II. Conditional logic in control flow. CAPRA cannot definitively 
determine code reachability in conditional branches, potentially flag-
ging unreachable paths as security risks. While experienced developers 
can easily evaluate conditional logic, retaining this design helps iden-
tify hypocrite commits concealed within conditional constructs. Future 
work will explore LLMs-assisted approaches to mitigate this issue.
III. Extended context spans or missing files leading to absent critical 
nodes. For example, if developers implement a memory allocation func-
tion in a utility library without including external calls in the current 
patch, CAPRA cannot determine whether the memory will be manually 
released and thus flags a potential memory leak. However, such alerts 
serve a valuable purpose in highlighting external call relationships 
requiring review.
IV. Inaccuracy in code property graphs generated by third-party 
tools. Joern uses a fuzzy parsing approach (island grammars) to parse 
code as completely as possible, but this method may lead to incomplete 
parsing, especially for complex code structures (Joern, 2024). These 
rare occurrences will diminish as third-party tools continue to improve.
The last two categories present greater verification challenges and 
moderately increase manual review workload.

In addition to our comparative experiment, there are also studies

In summary, CAPRAâ€™s impact on development workflows is man-

provision of precise and easily verifiable warning information, and the 
predictable pattern of false positives. Apart from several categories, 
which moderately increase manual review effort, most false positives 
can be efficiently addressed without significant workflow disruption. 
Furthermore, this elevated false positive rate is offset by the favor-
able cost-benefit ratio in critical systems, where early-stage vulnerabil-
ity detection substantially reduces resource expenditure compared to 
post-deployment remediation.
5.4.4. Limitation analysis
Due to constraints in application scenarios and technical approaches, 
CAPRA has certain limitations. This section provides an objective analy-
sis from two aspects: detection capabilities and detection effectiveness.
Detection Capabilities
CAPRAâ€™s novel patch behavior analysis approach, while innovative, 
remains constrained by its static analysis architecture. This fundamen-
tal limitation impedes detection of resource competition-based and con-
ditional judgment-based vulnerabilities, which often require dynamic 
execution context to identify reliably.
This static analysis constraint further manifests when CAPRA ana-
lyzes distributed codebases. Using a file-level analysis approach, CAPRA 
may lack sufficient cross-module contextual information when examin-
ing patches that span multiple modules or repositories. This can lead 
to incomplete analysis or false positives when dependencies extend 
beyond the analyzed files, particularly in large-scale systems with 
complex inter-module relationships.
We propose two complementary strategies to navigate these ar-
chitectural constraints in large-scale implementations. Organizations 
might retain comprehensive scanning tools for periodic full-codebase 
audits while positioning CAPRA for focused protection of critical mod-
ules. Alternatively, they could augment CAPRAâ€™s configuration frame-
work with detailed interface specifications that define cross-module 
memory management protocols. Such approaches reconcile the practi-
cal realities of complex systems with the imperative for comprehensive 
security coverage.
Detection Effectiveness
Beyond architectural limitations, detection script quality directly 
impacts CAPRAâ€™s performance. Currently, our implementation only 
supports UAF and memory leak vulnerability detection. Extending 
CAPRA to cover additional vulnerability types requires developers 
with strong security expertise, creating a potential adoption barrier in 
resource-constrained environments.
Additionally, the system faces a fundamental trade-off between 
detection sensitivity and false positive ratesâ€”a common challenge 
in vulnerability detection tools (Goseva-Popstojanova and Perhinschi, 
2015). To mitigate late-stage remediation costs, CAPRA prioritizes com-
prehensive risk identification during development and review phases, 
particularly when defending against sophisticated threats like hypocrite 
commit attacks executed through conditional constructs. This security-
first approach necessarily yields higher false positive rates compared to 
conventional static analysis tools.
Nevertheless, based on the analysis in Section 5.4.3, the current 
relatively high false positive rate still imposes a manageable additional 
workload on developers and reviewers. We will continue to optimize 
CAPRA in our future work (Section 7), for example, by incorporating 
LLMs technology to simultaneously improve detection accuracy and 
enhance extensibility.
6. Related works
6.1. Bottlenecks in static analysis methods
During software development, delays in code review and static 
scanning hinder the detection of malicious code at the source level. 
Traditional static analysis tools like Sorald (Etemadi et al., 2023) and 
CheckCPP (MarjamÃ¤ki, 2025) employ full-code scanning with time 
complexity proportional to code size and program complexity, failing to 
meet efficiency requirements in large projects with frequent commits. 
Research by Huang et al. (2024) developed DONAPI for NPM packages, 
combining static analysis with dynamic API call sequence extraction. 
Pan et al. (2021) proposed grammar-agnostic symbolic execution for 
testing complex parsing programs efficiently.
Recent advances in deep learning have enhanced software security 
analysis. Li et al. (2022a) introduced VulDeeLocator using code at-
tention to identify vulnerability types. Research by Li et al. (2022b) 
proposed SySeVR for C/C++ vulnerability detection, while Han et al. 
(2024) developed bjCnet using contrastive learning for defect pre-
diction. Large language models have also shown promise, with Dun-
lap et al. (2024) improving the pairing of security advisories with 
vulnerable functions.
Some commercial static security testing tools, such as Coverity (Black 
Duck Software, 2024), Fortify (OpenText, 2024), etc., have been proven 
to have good comprehensive detection capabilities and support multi-
ple vulnerabilities and languages. However, full-scale scanning is not 
suitable for frequent execution and has higher requirements for system 
resources and environment configuration, the limitations of full-scale 
analysis persist.
6.2. Limitations of dynamic detection methods
Dynamic vulnerability detection offers superior accuracy but faces 
temporal challenges in large-scale development. Zhao et al. (2017) 
found that configuring runtime environments and executing test cases 
introduces significant delays, disrupting rapid iteration cycles. Research 
by Egele et al. (2008) confirms substantial time overhead in environ-
ment preparation, complicating integration into CI/CD pipelines and 
exacerbating defect detection delays.
Based on the analysis of limitations in existing detection methods, a 
comprehensive comparison is needed to understand how CAPRA relates 
to and complements these approaches. Table 4 presents a qualitative 
comparison between CAPRA and established vulnerability detection 
techniques including symbolic execution, taint analysis, fuzzing, and 
AI-based methods. This comparison highlights CAPRAâ€™s distinctive con-
tributions in addressing challenges specific to high-frequency code 
submission environments, where traditional approaches face significant 
practical constraints.
As illustrated in Table 4, conventional methods such as symbolic 
execution, taint analysis, and fuzzing offer robust assurance in vul-
nerability detection. However, their computational demands and re-
quirement to analyze the entire codebase restrict their effectiveness 
in fast-paced development environments. Conversely, AI-driven tech-
niques have enhanced efficiency, though they remain largely concen-
trated on analyzing code after development is complete. CAPRA stands 
out by concentrating specifically on code patches during the review

6.3. Research on patch-level security analysis
Attacks carried out around malicious patches have been proven 
capable of bypassing most traditional static security detection tools. Re-
search by Gonzalez et al. (2021) demonstrates malicious patch attacks 
targeting GitHub, and Wu and Lu (2021) revealed â€˜hypocrite commitâ€™ 
attacks where defects introduced through multiple patch submissions 
bypass static scanning.
Recent patch security research has focused on deployment sta-
tus, recurring vulnerability patterns, and post-patch analysis. Yang 
et al. (2023) proposed Robin to identify recurring vulnerabilities, while 
Wang et al. (2023) developed GraphSPD using graph neural networks. 
He et al. (2023) utilized developer logs to identify vulnerable code 
versions, and Xiao et al. (2024) created FirmRec for IoT firmware.
We analyze the differences between CAPRA and existing works, as 
well as its additional contributions, from the following perspectives:
I. Analysis timing. Previous methods like Wang et al.â€™s PatchRNN
(Wang et al., 2021) and Zhou et al.â€™s SPI (Zhou et al., 2021) excel 
at identifying security-relevant patches after integration, while CAPRA 
operates during review before patches are merged. This timing dif-
ference allows CAPRA to serve as a preventive measure during code 
review while other tools provide valuable post-integration security 
verification.
II. Patch-vulnerability relationship analysis. Existing approaches an-
alyze relationships between patches and vulnerabilities through differ-
ent lenses: Zhang et al. (2023) and VULDEFF (Zhao et al., 2023) focus 
on identifying vulnerabilities by examining patch similarities and code 
differences in known vulnerable functions. Sun et al.â€™s VDSimilar (Sun 
et al., 2021) advances this concept by analyzing both similarities be-
tween vulnerability pairs and differences between vulnerability-patch 
pairs using Siamese networks. CAPRA takes a complementary perspec-
tive by examining how pending patches might complete vulnerability 
trigger chains in existing code. These diverse analytical approaches 
demonstrate the strong connection between patches and vulnerabilities 
while offering complementary insights at different stages of the security 
lifecycle.
III. Types of vulnerabilities of concern. PatchScope (Zhao et al., 
2020), Vul-LMGNNs (Liu et al., 2025) and other traditional tools pro-
vide strong detection capabilities for mature vulnerability patterns, 
while CAPRA addresses immature vulnerabilities that exist in a transi-
tional state. These complementary focuses enhance the security ecosys-
temâ€™s overall effectiveness.
IV. CI/CD integration efficiency. Wadhams et al. (2024) focus on 
integrating traditional SAST tools into development pipelines, while 
CAPRAâ€™s line-by-line analysis targets modified code. Each approach 
offers benefits depending on security requirements and development 
velocity.
A significant research gap exists in high-frequency iteration envi-
ronments of open-source projects. While code review processes exist, 
research has focused on functionality (Beller et al., 2014) and automa-
tion (Tufano et al., 2021) rather than security. The CAPRA architecture 
addresses this critical gap in patch security analysis, complementing 
existing approaches by providing targeted vulnerability risk assessment 
during the code review phase. CAPRA offers substantial practical value 
for open-source projects through its ability to perform efficient, focused 
analysis on patch modificationsâ€”a capability not adequately addressed 
by existing patch security tools.
7. Discussion and future works
7.1. Challenges
Based on the analysis in Section 5.4.4, CAPRA currently faces 
several technical challenges. First, static analysis struggles to establish 
complete associations when vulnerability trigger points are distant from 
their occurrence locations. Second, there are no simple and efficient 
algorithms to accurately calculate path connectivity in conditional 
statements and resource competition scenarios. To reduce false neg-
atives, CAPRA must increase detection sensitivity, which results in 
higher false positive rates.
For the first challenge, the industry typically relies on periodic full-
scale static scanning and dynamic testing methods (such as fuzzing) 
to compensate for the limitations of localized analysis. For the second 
challenge, more complex path analysis algorithms would be necessary, 
but this could increase computational overhead, contradicting CAPRAâ€™s 
Computers & Security 157 (2025) 104540 
16 
B. Tang et al.
lightweight design principles. Additionally, the specialized knowledge 
required for script development limits CAPRAâ€™s extensibility to different 
vulnerability types.
7.2. Future research direction
To address these challenges, we plan to explore integrating large 
language models (LLMs) with the CAPRA architecture. CAPRAâ€™s core 
concept is analyzing whether pending patches complete vulnerability 
trigger chains. While vulnerability mechanisms are well-understood, 
the key challenge lies in identifying and analyzing vulnerability trigger 
chains. We propose creating a chain-of-thought analysis framework 
(similar to finite state machines) for each vulnerability type, designed 
based on vulnerability triggering principles. Like CAPRAâ€™s existing de-
tection process, this chain-of-thought would determine the next analy-
sis direction based on currently available information, while delegating 
code property graph static flow analysis and reachability analysis to 
LLMs.
Preliminary experiments suggest this approach could optimize path 
reachability analysis and search precision, reduce false positives, and 
ease script development difficulties when expanding vulnerability types. 
However, this direction faces several challenges, including how to 
fine-tune or distill knowledge into smaller parameter models (as large 
models would compromise CAPRAâ€™s lightweight advantage), and how 
to design universal chain-of-thought templates that effectively map 
vulnerability principles to model-recognizable rules.
Through further research and improvements, CAPRA shows promise 
in playing a more significant role in software supply chain security, con-
tributing to building safer and more reliable open-source ecosystems.
8. Conclusion
This paper introduces CAPRA, a security detection methodology 
that analyzes pending patches to address quality risks in open-source 
software development. As open-source ecosystems expand, security 
vulnerabilities emerge from diverse coding practices and limited review 
processes. CAPRA employs static analysis to examine line-level patch 
modifications, identifying potential memory leak and UAF vulnerabili-
ties.
CAPRAâ€™s primary contribution is its incremental approach to defect 
detection, focusing on patches that might activate immature vulnerabil-
ities rather than analyzing entire codebases. This methodology detects 
both unintentional defects and deliberate attacks like hypocrite com-
mit, strengthening supply chain security. The code property graph ap-
proach enables effective detection without complete compilation envi-
ronments or full codebases. Additionally, its modular design accommo-
dates project-specific requirements through independently configurable 
detection scripts.
Our validation using a custom dataset from SARD, historical vulner-
abilities, open-source projects, and hypocrite commit research demon-
strates CAPRAâ€™s effectiveness. In SARD-derived tests, CAPRA achieves 
97.3% accuracy with a 3.5% false positive rate in strict mode.
Despite its effectiveness, CAPRA has limitations: detection script 
creation requires security expertise; static analysis struggles with dy-
namic execution logic; and the lenient decision approach generates 
higher false positives.
Future works will expand vulnerability detection types, improve 
algorithms to reduce false positives, explore hybrid analysis, investigate 
and integrate machine learning for improving performance.
In conclusion, CAPRAâ€™s distinctive design offers a new research 
perspective for open-source software security detection systems. Its 
incremental detection approach, lightweight implementation, and ex-
tensible architecture make it particularly suitable for large-scale, high-
frequency iterative modern open-source projects. CAPRA effectively 
complements traditional solutions, working synergistically to ensure 
open-source software security and quality.

Understanding warnings generated by PMD and SonarQube, their 
rules and compliance to established coding standards
Lakmal Deshapriya *
, Sherlock A. Licorish
, Brendon J. Woodford
School of Computing, University of Otago, Dunedin Campus, Dunedin, New Zealand
A R T I C L E  I N F O
Keywords:
Code violation dataset
PMD rules
SonarQube rules
False positives
Vulnerability detection
Static code analyser
Software code quality
A B S T R A C T
Context: Static Code Analysis (SCA) tools play a vital role in software development, reducing the 
cost and time required for code reviews. However, high false-positive and false-negative rates are 
reported for the best tools in the community. Accordingly, studies often aim to develop datasets 
for learning SCA warning patterns to reduce false positive results. These datasets are meant to 
possess high-quality and high-volume in covering the full range of faults/rules that typically 
result in false warnings and be compliant with established coding standards. However, existing 
studies have not utilised such datasets or identified the breadth of rules that are prone to false- 
positives and their compliance to coding standards.
Objectives: We analysed code from Stack Overflow and Apache Tomcat to capture variations in 
code length and style in detecting false-positive warnings from best-performing tools PMD and 
SonarQube, addressing this gap.
Method: In deriving false-positive warnings, outcomes from the tools were labelled using estabÂ­
lished coding standards. Deeper analyses were then conducted to identify the rules that are prone 
to false-positives, reasons for these, and agreement/gaps between SCA rules and established 
standards.
Results: Among our main outcomes, we observe that only a few SCA rules generate false-positives, 
ranging from 4.64 to 18.45% across four datasets. Additionally, eliminating rules that contradict 
established standards significantly reduce the false-positive rate. Additionally, our findings reveal 
discrepancies between tools and established standards.
Conclusion: Given the evidence established in this study, we recommend further investigations 
into gaps between tools and established standards, including the use of machine learning apÂ­
proaches to annotate larger datasets.
1. Introduction
Detecting and fixing bugs have become an essential day-to-day task of the software engineering process, and researchers have 
found that software engineers use more than half of their time on improving software (e.g., fixing bugs and refactoring source code) 
[1]. Static Code Analysis (SCA) tools were introduced to identify common quality issues in source code [2], in supporting developersâ€™ 
effort aimed at delivering high quality code. However, due to the massive amount of warnings generated by SCA tools, similar to the 
* Corresponding author.
E-mail addresses: lakmal.deshapriya@postgrad.otago.ac.nz (L. Deshapriya), sherlock.licorish@otago.ac.nz (S.A. Licorish), brendon.woodford@ 
otago.ac.nz (B.J. Woodford).

examples shown in Fig. 1, the number of false-positive warnings1 is also considerable, making it difficult to identify actual warnings2
creating a challenging task [3â€“5]. The SCA tools aim to identify as many code quality violations as possible, in trying to minimise 
false-negatives [6â€“8]. Consequently, SCA tools generate many false alarms (false-positives), wasting developers' time figuring out the 
actionable code quality violations among the large volume of warnings generated [3â€“5]. Therefore, identifying actual code quality 
violations suggested by SCA tools is essential to the software engineering Practitioner Community.
Efforts are being made to identify actual warnings among the warnings generated by SCA tools [9,10]. However, these studies have 
been based on unreliable datasets [11]. Automatically annotated datasets, artificially generated datasets, and datasets with limited 
rules or warning types are regarded as unreliable or incomplete [11]. In this regard, Hegedus and Ferenc [10] annotated a set of 
warnings generated using SonarQube. They annotated these warnings, analysing â€œ//NOSONARâ€ comments in the source code, which 
developers use to disregard a SonarQube warning suggested for the same line. However, this approach can be unreliable, as developers 
may apply the â€œ//NOSONARâ€ comments based on personal judgements rather than following any accepted standards or guidelines. 
Furthermore, the authors have not validated the dataset, and as a result, there can be incorrect labels in the dataset. Therefore, the 
dataset is not trustworthy for further analysis.
On the other hand, the Juliet vulnerability dataset is an artificially generated dataset [12]. This synthetic dataset was created using 
predefined patterns, which caused a lack of diversity in the data, even though the dataset size was large [11]. Consequently, models 
generated using this dataset might produce promising results. However, their generalizability will be low, as there are only a few 
unique patterns in the dataset [13]. In another work, Li et al. [14] used a Use Before Initialization (UBI) bug dataset to experiment with 
ChatGPT3. The dataset had 20 items, and these authors evaluated whether the bug was real or false-positive using ChatGPT. As they 
used only UBI bugs for their study, the results produced by this study cannot be generalised.
Correspondingly, according to Meldrum et al. [2], SCA rules/warning types should be classified based on a range of source code 
quality aspects: 1. Reliability and conformance to programming rules, 2. Readability, 3. Performance, and 4. Security. However, 
existing studies focus only on a few aspects of source code quality to train Machine Learning (ML) models to identify actionable 
warnings among the large set of warnings typically generated by SCA tools [14â€“16]. In fact, relying on a few aspects of source code 
quality does not fully encompass the overall quality of source codes, and the results generated by such studies cannot be generalised to 
the wide breadth of source code quality indicators [2].
The limitations of automatically generated datasets, synthetic datasets, and datasets with limited rules or warning types undermine 
the results produced by those studies, making outcomes unreliable. In addition, the poor quality of the existing annotated datasets 
makes it significantly challenging to build good-performing ML models to identify actionable warnings as models trained with 
inaccurate datasets tend to generate inadequate outcomes [11â€“13]. Among the poor quality of existing annotated datasets, incorrect 
labels, duplicate data points, and a lack of diversity of data points in synthetic datasets are significant [11].
Therefore, to address these limitations, we created four manually annotated sample datasets with true-positive and false-positive 
warnings covering a wide range of source code quality indicators that facilitate analyses to understand false-positive patterns better. 
These datasets were used to explore the SCA rules that are prone to false-positives, reasons for the reported false-positives and 
agreement/gaps between SCA rules and established coding standards. Our study makes the following contributions for academia and 
the software engineering Practitioner Community. 
1. We analysed current software standards and identified their application to rules that generated warnings for PMD and SonarÂ­
Qube. This mapping provides developers clearer insight into the connection between these tools and industry standards, also 
outlining gaps between SCA rules and defined standards.
2. Unlike in existing studies, defined standards were used to annotate warnings. Four datasets were labelled manually, providing a 
testbed for future studies.
3. We identified SCA rules that are prone to false-positives and examined the reasons for false-positives.
The remainder of this study is organised as follows. Section 2 describes the background and related studies. In Section 3, the 
methodology is introduced and discussed, and Section 4 provides the results. Section 5 discusses the findings of our work, while threats 
to the outcomes are evaluated in Section 6. Finally, the conclusion and suggested future works are discussed in Section 7. We provide a 
replication package, which consists of the datasets generated from this study, justifications for decisions, coding rules and standards, 
and appendices. This will be useful for those interested in further examining our research methodology and performing replication 
studies (refer to Section 8) [17].
2. Background and Related Studies
In existing studies, several approaches were taken to create datasets, including real-world program vulnerability datasets and 
artificially synthesised vulnerability datasets [13]. In this section, the approaches to creating real-world program vulnerability datasets 
are reviewed, setting the tone for a review into the strategies for creating artificially synthesised vulnerability datasets. Then, the

2.1. Vulnerability datasets
Real-world source codes from GitHub repositories were used to create warning datasets, which generate large amounts of datasets 
mostly using automatic labelling methodologies, which are reviewed in this sub-section. Zheng et al. [18] introduced a methodology to 
label SCA warnings using differential analysis of bug fixes commits. They created a dataset called D2A with more than 1.3 million 
examples using the Infer SCA tool to analyse source codes from multiple C/C++ open-source projects. To annotate the warnings in the 
dataset, they analysed the commit histories (both the previous and subsequent versions of bug fixes) to determine whether the reported 
warning in the previous version had been resolved in the subsequent version. If the warning was resolved, it was assumed to be an 
actual (true-positive) warning, otherwise, it was deemed a false-positive warning. However, according to Croft et al. [11], the quality 
of the D2A dataset is poor due to its high volume of duplicate data points; consequently, models developed with this dataset may 
exhibit strong validation results, as there is an increased likelihood of overlapping data points in both the training and validation sets 
[11]. As a result, the model can exhibit signs of overfitting to the training data, leading it to predict identical labels for the validation 
dataset. This behaviour, where the model essentially remembers the training examples rather than learning generalisable patterns, 
artificially inflates its apparent accuracy on the validation dataset.
Cabral et al. [19] introduced the RVprio to rank runtime verification violations based on the likelihood of a code violation being a 
true bug. They claimed that RVprio was the first and most comparable tool for ranking runtime verification violations. However, the 
study did not label the dataset but instead predicted the likelihood value. In another study, Aladics et al. [20] introduced a method 
based on the SZZ [21] to create a dataset of vulnerability-introducing commits as oppose to existing datasets focussed on 
vulnerability-fixing commits. The dataset consisted of the vulnerability introducing commits with the details of the vulnerability as 
well. This dataset was created using an automated procedure, and only a sample of the created dataset was validated manually. 
Consequently, the reliability of the dataset is questionable. Pereira et al. [22] created a dataset of vulnerabilities for C/C++ using five 
open-source projects by analysing the commit history. The dataset contained 5,214 data points. As the study did not specify whether 
the generated dataset was manually verified, the dataset is deemed to be unreliable. Chen et al. [23] also created a similar dataset of 
vulnerabilities called DIVERSEVUL, which consisted of 18,945 vulnerable functions. The dataset was used to identify vulnerabilities in 
Fig. 1. True-positive and false-positive warning examples for PMD and SonarQube.
L. Deshapriya et al.                                                                                                                                                                                                    
Science of Computer Programming 252 (2026) 103470 
3 
software source code employing 11 ML models.
Furthermore, Wang et al. [24] created a similar dataset of vulnerabilities called ReposVul using 1,491 projects. However, these 
datasets were not labelled in terms of whether the vulnerabilities were true-positives or false-positives. Instead, these datasets were 
labelled automatically, primarily by analysing commit histories. According to Croft et al. [11], such datasets are of low quality and 
contain incorrect label information. Consequently, artificially synthesised datasets were introduced to address this issue. For instance, 
the SAMATE project has developed the Juliet vulnerability dataset [12]. The Juliet dataset is used in multiple studies to evaluate ML 
models; however, the advantages of using artificially synthesised vulnerability datasets come with a cost [11]. Despite the large dataset 
size, the synthetic dataset was created using predefined patterns, resulting in a lack of diversity in the data [11]. Consequently, ML 
models generated from this dataset may yield promising results. However, their generalisability is likely to be low, as there are only a 
limited number of unique patterns in the dataset [13].
2.2. Datasets used in ML model building
This sub-section discusses warning datasets used in ML model-building tasks from recent studies. Tan and Tian [15] trained various 
ML models, including Bidirectional Gated Recurrent Unit Neural Network (BGRU), Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN), and 
Multilayer Perceptron (MLP), to classify bugs using a real bug database called Defects4J [25]. Furthermore, Yang et al. [26] used three 
datasets: a bug dataset created by Yang et al. [26], Defects4J [25], and a dataset created by Liu et al. [27], which is an annotated 
warning dataset derived from commit history analysis. Furthermore, Yerramreddy et al. [28] used four datasets (three Java and one C), 
created from the analysis results of the JBMC and CBMC SCA tools. The four datasets comprised one real-world dataset for Java and 
three synthetic datasets. The real-world dataset is manually labelled. However, all the datasets utilised by Yerramreddy et al. [28] 
merely addressed certain aspects of source code quality, such as vulnerabilities and bugs.
Similarly, Li et al. [14] used a UBI bug dataset, which consists of 20 data items, to experiment with ChatGPT in order to assess 
whether the bugs were real or false-positives. Nguyen et al. [16] used the Juliet test suite (for C/C++) to train ML models. The dataset 
is a collection of test cases organised under 118 different CWEs4. Nagaraj et al. [29] created a security bug dataset by analysing 2,740 
Java files using the FindSecBugs SCA tool. However, the dataset did not provide details on whether the bug was real or synthesised. 
Kharkar et al. [30] created a data set of 539 null dereference warnings. The dataset was generated by analysing seven Java repositories 
using the Infer SCA tool and was labelled by experienced software developers.
Furthermore, Hegedus and Ferenc [10] created a dataset analysing 9,958 different open-source Java projects hosted on GitHub. 
The dataset consisted of 224,484 sample data points, which include true-positive (actionable) and false-positive (explicitly discarded) 
warnings. To compile the dataset, these authors employed SonarQube to analyse the projects and pinpoint the code violations 
warnings. However, the study depends on â€œ//NOSONARâ€ comments within the source code, where developers utilise the comment to 
disregard a sonar warning suggested for the same line. The approach may be unreliable, as it does not consider whether the developer 
has ignored the warning in accordance with any accepted standard or guideline. Furthermore, the dataset was neither manually 
verified by the authors nor used in any other existing studies. Consequently, the dataset is deemed untested for further analysis. Vu and 
Vo [31] used a dataset for their study that was also used by Ngo et al. [32] consisting of 6,620 warnings from 10 popular open-source 
C/C++ programs. The dataset comprised two categories of vulnerability types: Buffer Overflow and Null Pointer Dereference. 
Additionally, Tanwar et al. [9] created a dataset of 10 CWE categories and labelled them using commit history analysis. Koc et al. [33] 
used two datasets to train their models. The first is the OWASP benchmark, and the second is a dataset of warnings generated by the 
FindSecBugs SCA tool for 14 real-world programs. The first dataset is synthetic, while the second consists of bugs labelled manually. 
Furthermore, Lee et al. [34] employed 9,871 alarms, which were either resolved or labelled as false-positives at Samsung Electronics. 
The dataset included warnings from in-house static analysis checkers, comprising six types such as Resource Handle Leak, Double Free, 
and Null Pointer Dereference After Null.
Evaluating the outcomes above, the quality of the datasets utilised to build ML models for identifying false-positive SCA warnings in 
previous studies was inadequate. Several studies employed synthetic datasets with limited diversity [16,33], while others utilised 
automatically generated datasets that lack manual validation [10,26]. Moreover, some datasets used to train ML models were not 
diverse; they involved only a limited range of warnings and did not cover a wide range of source code quality dimensions [2]. As a 
result, the reliability of the findings produced by existing studies remains questionable. Therefore, it is emphasised that constructing 
ML models using manually annotated datasets that encompass various aspects of source code quality has the potential to yield 
generalised results, which is the focus of this study.
2.3. SCA toolsâ€™ rules, the applicable standards for these rules and the gaps between SCA toolsâ€™ rules and established standards
This subsection explored the efforts made to identify the rules of SCA tools, the standards applicable to these rules, and the gaps 
between the rules of SCA tools and established standards. Fatima et al. [35] conducted a comparative study on a few SCA tools that are 
used to analyse C/C++ source code. They evaluated those SCA tools based on twenty-eight checks to rank tools and identify the best 
SCA tools. Although they do not identify all the SCA toolâ€™s rules, they have identified that twenty-eight checks are available in the tool 
as rules. However, they only evaluated some SCA tools for C/C++ source code and did not check the rules against any source code 
4 https://samate.nist.gov/SARD/test-suites/112
L. Deshapriya et al.                                                                                                                                                                                                    
Science of Computer Programming 252 (2026) 103470 
4 
quality standards. Additionally, no false-positive checks were carried out in this study. Ramler et al. [36] identified 42 PMD rules 
which is related to Java Junit test cases. However, they did not identify any possible source code quality standard or false-positives 
generated by PMD rules. Ashfaq et al. [37] conducted a comparative analysis on Java SCA tools, including PMD. They identified 
supported rule types (e.g., Style, General, Concurrency, etc.) from each SCA tool. However, they did not identify specific rules that SCA 
tools supported, nor did they establish any potential source code quality standards relevant to the SCA toolsâ€™ rules.
Novak and Krajnc [38] created a taxonomy of SCA tools using several attributes of SCA tools, including rule types that the SCA tools 
supported. However, they did not study the individual SCA rule level and did not consider whether these rules are aligned with source 
code quality standards. Lenarduzzi et al. [39] identified the rule types (e.g. Syntax, Bugs, etc) each SCA tool (including PMD and 
SonarQube) generated warnings for, the number of rules generated warnings, and the number of warnings generated. They identified 
the top ten generated warnings from SCA rules.
Charoenwet et al. [40] studied eight CWE5 vulnerabilities using several SCA tools, including CodeChecker, Codeql, and Flawfinder. 
However, they evaluated only a few types of vulnerabilities. A similar study was conducted by Ozturk et al. [41] using the top 10 
OWASP6 vulnerabilities. Alqaradaghi and Kozsik [42] evaluated several Java SCA tools against 70 CWEs, validating these CWEs using 
OWASP. However, they do not conduct a comprehensive analysis of all the SCA rules available in the SCA tools and their applicable 
standards.
Software quality models, such as ISO/IEC 9126 and ISO/IEC 25010, are defined to evaluate the quality of software [43,44]. Some 
efforts were taken to map the quality characteristics mentioned in these quality models with the SCA rules to classify these rules. 
Forouzani et al. [44] mapped PMD rules with the relevant quality characteristics according to the definition of quality characteristics 
from ISO/IEC 25010. Some of the quality characteristics mentioned in the software quality models are Performance, Reliability, 
Security and Maintainability, and these characteristics are further divided into subcategories such as Availability, Fault Tolerance and 
Compliance [43,44]. BÂ´ansÂ´aghi et al. [43] conducted a similar work for PMD and FxCop SCA toolsâ€™ rules with both ISO/IEC 9126 and 
ISO/IEC 25010. However, these works did not assess the validity of SCA toolsâ€™ rules in terms of quality, and they categorised rules 
based on the quality characteristics defined in the standard.
According to the existing studies discussed in this sub-section, several efforts have been made to identify rules available in SCA 
tools. However, these efforts were not comprehensive as they did not identify all the rules available in the SCA tools and the established 
standards applicable to those rules. Although several authors have utilised software quality models to categorise the rules available in 
SCA tools, none of the studies identify all the rules in these tools, applicable standards for the rules, or gaps between these rules and 
established standards.
2.4. Summary
Existing studies have developed ML models using datasets created through various methodologies. Some datasets were collected 
and annotated manually [33,43], while others were gathered and annotated using commit history from GitHub [10,18,20]. Certain 
datasets were also generated using real-world code repositories [10,18,20]. However, some datasets were developed using synthetic 
code databases, such as OWASP benchmarks and Juliet test suites, offering distinct advantages and disadvantages compared to other 
types of datasets [12]. Furthermore, datasets discussed in this section are summarised with all the available details in Table 1.
The main benefit of automated labelling systems is possessing a substantial quantity of data [13]. However, the datasets generated 
through automatic methods, such as analysing GitHub commit history, experienced quality issues, whereas those created using synÂ­
thetic code datasets lacked data diversity [11,13]. Additionally, recent studies have shown that ML models were constructed using only 
a limited number of code quality violation types; primarily, only warnings related to bugs were utilised in the creation of these models 
[14,15]. However, several dimensions of source code quality recommended by previous work [2] were not addressed in the existing 
studies, leading to a lack of generalisability to the many aspects of code quality, which needs investigation.
Moreover, several studies were conducted to identify rules available in SCA tools [35,36]. However, these studies did not 
comprehensively study on all the rules available in SCA tools. Furthermore, only a few studies tried to map the available rules with 
CWE and OWASP coding standards [40â€“42]. Several studies mapped quality characteristics of software quality models, such as 
ISO/IEC 9126 and ISO/IEC 25010, with rules of SCA tools [43,44]. However, the purpose of these models is to categorise the available 
rules according to the quality characteristics.
To address the limitations, we manually created four vulnerability datasets, that cover various aspects of source code quality, as 
explained in Section 3.4. We annotated samples from each vulnerability dataset according to established standards identified in 
Section 3.4 to determine whether those warnings were true-positives or false-positives. These four vulnerability datasets were created 
using two publicly available code datasets and two popular SCA tools, as outlined in the Section 3.6.
3. Methodology
This section outlines the research questions of our study, and the methodology employed to create the datasets and analyse the 
data. In reviewing existing studies in Section 2, it is observed that there were no studies that examined static analysis tools (including 
PMD and SonarQube) in terms of their rules, the applicable standards for these rules, false-positive warnings generated by these tools 
5 These CWEs are maintained by Mitra, and we selected this as a source code quality standard in the section 3.4.
6 OWASP was also identified as a source code quality standard in section 3.4.

and the gaps between SCA toolsâ€™ rules and established standards. Furthermore, existing studies employed datasets of low quality and 
limited diversity, rendering the outputs generated by these studies unreliable and ungeneralizable. Thus, four research questions were 
formulated to address these gaps, and four datasets were created to address those research questions, as detailed below.
3.1. Research questions
SCA tools check common software source code defects, producing many warnings depending on the source code size. Developers 
use a large amount of their development effort to address these warnings, and the complexity of that task increases as SCA tools also 
produce false alarms [1]. SCA tools check source code using defined rules that evolve over time7,8. Developers of SCA tools create, 
modify, or remove existing rules based on current requirements by continuously evaluating changes in the software engineering inÂ­
dustry9. In this regard, SCA tools often introduce new rules to detect source code defects while retiring some existing rules when they 
are no longer relevant. However, limited previous studies have investigated the rules that are prone to false-positives in SCA tools and 
established standards relevant to them. Consequently, our first Research Question (RQ) addresses this opportunity:
RQ1: What are the rules and standards of SCA tools that generate warnings for specific source code datasets?
RQ1 was created to identify the current rules available that generated warnings for our source code datasets, in particular SCA tools 
(PMD and SonarQube), as well as the related established standards. In addition, this research question allows us to evaluate the 
applicability of established standards to SCA rules and the categories of rules which report warnings for our datasets.
Existing studies have utilised several approaches to develop SCA warning datasets, including automatic annotation methods [10,
18] and the use of synthetic code datasets like OWASP benchmarks and Juliet test suites [12]. However, these methodologies generate 
low-quality datasets, and it is recommended that researcher create SCA warning datasets by manually annotating them [11]. 
Therefore, we have created four datasets through manual annotation following established standards. We observed that only a few SCA 
rules produced false-positive warnings, and it is crucial to identify these rules, as none of the existing studies have focused on this gap. 
Thus, the second research question is dedicated to this opportunity:
RQ2: Which SCA rules are prone to false-positives?

RQ2 was created to identify the rules that generate a significant amount of false-positive violations. Identifying those rules makes 
fixing them possible and reduces the overall false-positive rate of the SCA tool, thereby reducing practitionersâ€™ workload to sift through 
false-positives.
As with the identification of false-positives, recognizing the causes of false-positive warnings generated by SCA rules is essential. 
However, limited current studies investigate the reasons behind false-positive warnings identified by SCA tools. Therefore, the third 
research question addresses this opportunity:
RQ3: What are the reasons for reported false-positives by SCA tools?
RQ3 was developed to identify the reasons for generating false-positives for each rule in SCA tools. Understanding the causes of 
false-positive warnings simplifies the process of recognising these warnings in an unlabelled warning dataset. It also provides insights 
for SCA Tool Developers to enhance the rules that generate a substantial number of false-positive warnings, reducing practitionersâ€™ 
overhead.
Previous studies have not used established standard/s to annotate SCA warnings. Consequently, no potential gaps have been 
assessed between the rules of SCA tools and established standards. This gap is addressed by our fourth research question:
RQ4: Are there any gaps in code violation classification between selected SCA tools and established standards?
RQ4 was created to understand discrepancies between the description of SCA rules and established standards. There can be misÂ­
matches and gaps between SCA rules and established coding standards. The gaps may arise mainly because SCA tools have defined 
their rules based on the experience of the software engineering community and their preference for coding styles10. In contrast, the 
established coding standards are factually defined, with firm evidence from standard organisations [45,46]. Additionally, SCA tools 
may violate their own standards if they wrongly identify code violations â€“ we investigate this issue.
3.2. SCA tool selection
A systematic mapping study incorporating grey literature was conducted using existing research published between 2013 and 2025 
on SCA tools, and 52 blog posts that were returned from Google search results. The study aimed to identify popular SCA tools within 
the software engineering community and academia. Fig. 2 is extracted from the systematic mapping study, where it is shown that the 
most popular SCA tools used to analyse Java source codes are SonarQube and PMD in academia and industry. Accordingly, for our 
analysis, we used PMD version 6.55.0 and SonarQube version 10.2.1 to analyse Stack Overflow and Apache Tomcat datasets, which are 
described in Section 3.3, using these SCA tools to generate warning suggestions.
3.3. Source code selection
PMD and SonarQube SCA tools were selected for our study, and two publicly available source code datasets were chosen for 
analysis with the selected SCA tools. Having two separate code datasets will enable us to ascertain the generalisability of our outcomes. 
The first dataset is the Stack Overflow dataset collected by Meldrum et al. [2], and the second dataset is the Apache Tomcat source code 
downloaded from GitHub on 8th December 2023, referred to as the Apache Tomcat dataset. These two code datasets were used in our 
study as they were widely used in academia to evaluate software source codes, and these datasets contain two unique sets of Java codes 
[47â€“55], providing evidence for variable code lengths and potential quality. Stack overflow dataset contains source code snippets 
while Apache Tomcat contains full-length source code.
The first dataset comprises 8,010 Java files collected from code snippets found in posts on the Stack Overflow website11 which is a 
question-and-answer website for software engineering, utilised by developers of varying experience levels. In this source code dataset, 
the number of lines in a file ranges from 1 to 355. Furthermore, five Java files contained only class definitions with no code inside them. 
Irrespective, those Java files were also utilised for the analysis.
The code datasets should be compiled to scan datasets with SonarQube. However, there were some compilation issues with the 
Stack Overflow code dataset. In this code dataset, there were some files with conflicting file names. For example, there were two 
â€œEmployeeâ€ classes in two files. In such scenarios, the conflicting class name was modified by adding a number after the class name 
(â€œEmployee1â€). Additionally, when the class was modified with the â€œpublicâ€ modifier, but the file name did not match the class name, 
the â€œpublicâ€ modifier was removed. We did not modify the file name as we needed to keep references to the original code dataset. 
Moreover, we added some library import statements where necessary.
The second dataset is the Apache Tomcat source code downloaded from GitHub on the 8th December 202312. The code dataset 
comprises 2,749 Java files, all of which are compilable. The number of lines in each file ranges from 20 to 6,285, including comment 
lines. Furthermore, only the Java files were utilised for our study.
It is reported that the code snippets found in Stack Overflow are of low quality [2]. In contrast, the Apache Tomcat dataset is 
developed by a software engineering community that reviews the source code regularly13. Therefore, it should be of higher quality. 
Consequently, we have selected two datasets at different maturity levels.
The objective of this study is to create warning datasets generated by PMD and SonarQube. However, the actual datasets used is not

3.4. Identify standards for individual rules
Existing studies have used several approaches to annotate SCA warnings [13]. According to Lin et al. [13], existing studies have 
used automatic labelling frameworks and manual labelling methodology to create warning datasets, where automatic labelling was 
seen to have a higher probability of incorrect labelling than manual labelling. Thus, manual labelling was done by the researchers, 
albeit they did not use any standards/guidelines [28,33]. Therefore, to annotate the datasets in the current study, the standards listed 
in Table 2 were used. Using established standards ensures that the labels are consistent and adhere to existing standards.
In identifying relevant standards, we referred to the official documentation for each rule in PMD and SonarQube to determine 
whether the authors used any standards to define their rules, where some standards were identified from the documentation. OWASP 
was added to the list because it was used in existing studies [56,57], and the Java official documentation is also used as a standard. 
Finally, there were some papers (ID: 10 and 11 in Table 2) mentioned in some PMD rules as a further reference. Since those papers were 
acceptable studies, those standards were also selected.
These standards were used to validate the SCA toolâ€™s rules, as these standards have been widely adopted by the software develÂ­
opment industry and are considered reliable [56â€“58]. However, SonarQube and PMD introduce new rules based on their experience, 
and they also modify rules based on community feedback14,15. These rules are typically not yet mature enough to be presented as 
standards, and in fact some rules contradict others16. For example, the â€œAtLeastOneConstructorâ€ rule in PMD says that â€œEach non-static 
class should declare at least one constructor. Classes with solely static members are ignored, refer to UseUtilityClassRule to detect 
those.â€ However, this rule contradicts the rule â€œUnnecessaryConstructorâ€ in PMD. Therefore, rules in SonarQube and PMD cannot be 
considered standards. Consequently, we evaluate generated warnings for our datasets against more established standards.
The approach used to identify false-positive warnings is documented in Table 3. As mentioned in Table 3, if the SCA rule was 
aligned with the existing standards, SCA warnings were checked manually according to the standards, where warnings were deterÂ­
mined as true-positive or false-positive. However, when the SCA rules were against the existing standards, alarms reported under those 
rules were removed, and the alarms reported under those rules were considered false-positives. Those rules are mentioned in Table 4. 
Additionally, some SCA rules did not align with or contradict the standards. SCA warnings reported under those rules were checked 
manually according to the rulesâ€™ description and the default parameters mentioned on the official website of the SCA tools. AddiÂ­
tionally, identifying or defining standards for those rules is an open research area, as those rules are created based on the practices 
followed by the software engineering Practitioner Community.
Additionally, Deprecated rules, Rule Templates, and Beta rules were removed from the SonarQube rules list, as the SonarQube 
development community does not recommend using them17,18. Those rules are reported in Table 4. When analysing the Java code with 
PMD, the "rulesets/internal/all-java.xml" ruleset was used, which contains all non-deprecated rules. Therefore, the report had no 
warning suggestions related to deprecated rules.

3.5. Statistical analysis for estimating population false-positive percentage
Warnings were manually labelled and the False-Positive (FP) percentage for each dataset was calculated, multiplying the number of 
false-positives by 100 and dividing the result by the sample size. To estimate population-level uncertainty from the observed samples, 
95% Confidence Intervals (CIs) for each FP percentage value were computed using the Wilson score interval method, which provides 
more accurate bounds for binomial proportions than the normal approximation [65]. The CI for a proportion p with sample size n was 
calculated as:
