I. INTRODUCTION
Rapidly developed software has become vital for the modern
industry. Y et, its growing complexity and attack surface have
outpaced the human capacity to reason about every line of
code [1]. Static Application Security Testing (SAST) has
long been the developerâ€™s first line of defence: tools such
as SonarQube, CodeQL, and SnykCode integrate seamlessly
into continuous-integration pipelines, flagging defects before
The associate editor coordinating the review of this manuscript and
approving it for publication was Dominik Strzalka
.
they ever reach production, and are trusted by more than seven
million developers across 400,000 organisations worldwide.
Recent empirical studies nevertheless reveal a persistent
gap, while a single state-of-the-art analyser can highlight
vulnerabilities in roughly half of real-world, vulnerability-
contributing commits, false-positive noise, and rule coverage
limitations continue to hamper day-to-day adoption. Concur-
rently, the remarkable rise of large language models (LLMs)
has opened a new branch of code intelligence. Industry
surveys chart a rapid uptick in LLM pilots across engineering
teams. The research community has begun to fine-tune these
models for vulnerability detection with promising results:

early experiments report competitive F-scores against graph-

analyses on emerging model: GPT-4-class systems, Mistral-
Large, DeepSeek V3, and othersâ€”suggest that LLMs can
reason across larger contexts and identify subtle data-flow

Y et, enthusiasm must be tempered with caution. The

This paper undertakes the first systematic comparison

and SnykCode, and three cutting-edge LLMs, available
on GitHub: GPT-4.1, Mistral-Large, and DeepSeek V3,
evaluated on a standard benchmark suite spanning multiple
projects and vulnerability classes. We measure classical
accuracy metrics (precision, recall, F1), as well as developer-
centric costs, such as inspection effort per true positive, time-

Our contributions consist of:
â€¢ Unified benchmark and protocol. We form a diverse
dataset of real-world vulnerable functions, pair each
with ground-truth labels, and release an open evaluation
harness suitable for rule-based and generative systems.
â€¢ Comprehensive quantitative evaluation. We show where
LLMs already rival, and occasionally surpass, specialist
analysers in recall, while highlighting scenarios in which
deterministic rules remain indispensable for suppressing
false alarms.
â€¢ Qualitative insight. Through thematic analysis of model
rationales and tool reports, we surface strengths (e.g.,
data-flow reasoning across files) and weaknesses (e.g.,
inconsistent CWE mapping) unique to each paradigm.
â€¢ Guidance for practitioners and researchers. We distil
our findings into recommendations on tool choice,
prompt engineering, and future benchmarks that capture
emerging threat vectors.
II. STATE OF THE ART
Static code analysis represents an essential component within
modern software development processes. Early detection of
software defects, which, according to various studies, can
lead to a significant reduction in the cost and impact of
subsequent corrections [2], [3]. Furthermore, it simplifies the
code review process by helping developers identify potential
issues early, thereby reducing the time and effort required for
manual code reviews [4]. It is worth noting that the utility of
static analysis is not limited to professional and commercial
use. Academic research highlights its educational value.
A large-scale study analysing more than 500 student-
developed software projects illustrates that regular static code
analysis tools can significantly improve code quality and
student learning outcomes [5]. With the increasing integration
of artificial intelligence into the software development
lifecycle, the role and application of static code analysis are
also poised to evolve. AI-powered development tools are a
way of reinventing traditional programming practices and
introducing new possibilities. This approach will enhance
the effectiveness of static analysis techniques and redefine
their function, enabling more contextualised, personalised,
and proactive code evaluation processes.
A. HOW STATIC CODE ANAL YSIS WORKS
Static source code analysis involves examining the source
code without executing it to detect potential bugs and
weaknesses. The code is analysed for defined patterns
or rules that indicate undesirable behaviour. Typical tools
use control, data flow analysis, and pattern matching to
known error signatures [6]. Static scanners can detect, for
example, SQL Injection or code injection vulnerabilities
through taint analysis, but typically only if such patterns
have been predefined in their rules. In industry practice, rule
sets are constantly expanded to include new bugs. Due to
the multiplicity of use cases, they have been divided into
categories [7], such as:
â€¢ Naming â€“ Issues related to inconsistent, misleading,
or nonstandard naming conventions for identifiers.
â€¢ Style â€“ Violations of code formatting or stylistic
guidelines can affect readability.
â€¢ Concurrency â€“ Problems arising from incorrect han-
dling of parallel execution or shared resources.
â€¢ Exceptions â€“ Improper use or handling of exceptions
and error conditions.
â€¢ Performance â€“ Inefficiencies or bottlenecks that could
degrade the systemâ€™s performance.
â€¢ Interoperability â€“ Compatibility problems between
different systems, platforms, or APIs.
â€¢ Security â€“ Vulnerabilities that could be exploited to
compromise the systemâ€™s integrity or data.
â€¢ Maintainability â€“ Code complexity or structure issues
that make future modification or understanding more
difficult.
â€¢ General â€“ Broad or uncategorised issues that do not fit
neatly into other specific groups.
B. FORMAT OF RESUL TS
Static code analysis tools are often integrated into other
software development processes. The analysis results are
typically a crucial element before the final implementation
of the system under development.
SARIF (Static Analysis Results Interchange Format) was
introduced in 2020 [8] as a standardised and extensible
format for exchanging results produced by static analysis
tools, enabling consistent interpretation, comparison, and

C. LIMITATIONS OF TRADITIONAL CODE ANAL YSIS
Despite their widespread use, static approaches face sig-
nificant challenges. First, designing a good analyser is
time-consuming and difficult; each new type of defect
requires the development of an appropriate rule. As a result,
typical tools are limited to predefined defect patterns and
may fail to recognise new or unusual problems [11]. Another
limitation may be the lack of ability to fully understand the
context of the analysed code, as shown by the authors of the
paper [12]. This shortcoming underscores the need for more
adaptive and intelligent approaches and methods to fill the
gap between recognising a known pattern and deep semantic
understanding.
D. USE OF LARGE LANGUAGE MODEL
In recent years, numerous works have examined large
language models in the context of industry code quality [13],
[14]. Models trained on massive collections of code and
text demonstrate the ability to understand the context of a
program and suggest corrections. This raises the question of
whether they can take over the role of classic static analysers
in bug detection. An essential advantage of LLMs is the
lack of rigidly defined rules - the model can potentially
catch an error based on its â€˜â€˜understandingâ€™â€™ of the context,
even if the pattern is not explicitly programmed. Research
shows that LLMs can detect certain defects without the need
for a complete set of tests or rules, due to their ability
to infer from the context of the code. The comparative
potential of large language models and traditional static
analysis tools has been explored in studies such as [12],
which analysed the performance of GPT-3.5 Turbo and GPT-
4o in relation to SonarQube. This work is extended by
additional static analysers, including CodeQL and SnykCode,
as well as a broader set of large language models such as
GPT-4.1, DeepSeek V3, and Mistral Large, enabling a more
comprehensive evaluation of their capabilities in the detection
of defects in the source code.
III. METHODS
Ensuring code quality and reliability is crucial in modern IT
systems. Static analysis tools typically identify vulnerabilities
based on predefined patterns or rule sets. The effectiveness of
such tools in improving software quality and their efficiency
in minimising code defects has been demonstrated in the
existing literature [15].
A. OVERVIEW OF EVALUATED TOOLS
For this work, three widely recognised static analysis tools
have been selected for evaluation: SonarQube, SnykCode and
CodeQL.
SonarQube is an open-source tool used for static code
analysis, created in 2006 [16]. It is designed to automatically
detect errors, security vulnerabilities, and issues related to
code quality and technology debt. Over the course of almost
20 years on the market, it has evolved to support over 30 pro-
gramming languages [17] and features a built-in interface
with comprehensive dashboards and detailed reports. This
tool is used by more than 400,000 organisations [18]. When
choosing SonarQube, you can select one of two options to
utilise this solution.
The user can self-host the Community version, which is
open-source and can be used initially at no cost. In that
case, it is in the consumerâ€™s interests to ensure the safety
of processed data. The second option is to choose one
of the two paid versions provided by SonarSource, which
are Team and Enterprise [19]. The first version costs
65$ per month (as of 2025), and the cost of the higher
tier is determined individually after contacting the sales
department. SonarSource guarantees compliance with the
EU General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) and the
California Consumer Privacy Act to ensure the privacy of
its usersâ€™ data [20]. Due to its long existence on the market,
SonarQube is a very mature and proven tool.
CodeQL is an engine created and developed by GitHub.
Its main goal is to discover security vulnerabilities and bugs
in the analysed source code. The distinguishing feature of
this tool over others is that it allows users to write custom
queries using a specialised domain-specific language named
QL. CodeQL is part of the GitHub Advanced Security
platform and can be used with the most popular programming
languages, such as C++, Java, and Python [21]. CodeQL,
as part of GitHub Code Security, also offers two pricing
levels: Team for the price of 4$ per month for each user
and Enterprise starting at 21$ per month for each user [22].
GitHub processed personal data according to the declaration
of respect for the GDPR and other applicable laws [23].
SnykCode is a static application security testing tool
created by the Snyk company. Unlike traditional SAST
tools, SnykCode uses machine learning algorithms to detect
issues in the source code [24]. This tool focuses mainly
on security vulnerabilities such as SQL injection, cross-
site scripting (XSS), and authentication-related issues. The
first version was officially released in 2020 [25]. SnykCode
is also available in two pricing plans, Team for 25$ per
month for each contributing developer and Enterprise, where
the price is determined individually after contacting the
sales department, similar to SonarQube [26]. To ensure data
privacy, Snyk leads a global program designed to align with
the requirements of the GDPR and other privacy laws [27].
Before using each static analysis tool, it is crucial to be
familiar with the license and data privacy arrangements.
Another important aspect is to conduct a cost analysis. Key
elements were visualised with Table 1 to facilitate a better
comparison of each tool. All three solutions comply with data
privacy regulations and offer multiple pricing tiers, but differ

B. LARGE LANGUAGE MODELS IN CODE ANAL YSIS
The use of large language models can significantly improve
code quality assessments, as they can analyse predefined
rules, vulnerabilities, and contextual aspects of the code under
review [12]. For this work, three large language models from
leading companies have been selected for evaluation: GPT
4.1, DeepSeek V3, and Mistral Large.
GPT 4.1, developed by OpenAI, is known for its extensive
context window of 1,047,576 tokens, significantly enhancing
its ability to handle complex tasks, such as analysing large
codebases or extensive documents. The price is set at $2 per
million input tokens and $8 per million output tokens [28].
Regarding data privacy, user interactions with GPT 4.1 in
consumer products can be used to train OpenAI models, but
users can opt out through settings. For business products,
data is not used for training by default [29]. The declared
knowledge cut-off date is June 2024 [30].
DeepSeek V3 offers a cost-effective alternative with a
context window of 64,000 tokens, attractively priced at
$0.27 per million input tokens and $1.10 per million output
tokens [31]. DeepSeekâ€™s privacy policy specifies that the
model may collect user inputs, uploaded files, and network
metadata such as IP addresses and device identifiers. This
reflects a broader trend among commercial LLM providers,
where the scope of data collection and retention policies
varies depending on the vendor[32]. The declared knowledge
cut-off date is July 2024 [33]. It was created by the Chinese
company DeepSeek, founded in 2023. The model has gained
popularity due to its competitive capabilities in relation to the
cost of its exploitation.
Mistral Large, from Mistral AI, features a balanced context
window of 32,000 tokens and costs $2 per million input
tokens and $6 per million output tokens [34]. Its data privacy
policy states that user data is not utilised for training except in
specific cases, such as free-tier usage without explicit opt-out,
feedback provision, or content moderation purposes [35].
Before integrating LLM into practical workflows, it is
essential to understand its licensing terms, data privacy
policies, and associated costs. These factors are critical in
selecting a model that aligns with organisational require-
ments. Key aspects were visualised with a Table 2 to
compare each LLM better. Each of the selected models has
distinct advantages and limitations. GPT 4.1 excels with its
unparalleled context capacity, which is essential for complex
tasks, such as analysing a large codebase, but it has higher
pricing. DeepSeek V3 offers significant cost benefits, but at
the expense of increased data privacy risks. Mistral Large
presents a similar pricing and approach to data privacy to GPT
4.1, but is slightly more cost-effective.
The effective use of large language models for static
analysis requires a structured approach to data preparation
and result handling. This section covers the process of
selecting and preparing software projects, describes the
SARIF format used to represent results, and presents the tool
created to perform the analysis. For projects exceeding the
modelâ€™s context window, the source code was automatically
segmented into coherent, dependency-aware units and pro-
cessed in parallel. This strategy follows recent best practices
in large-scale LLM evaluation [36], [37], ensuring that long
repositories can be analysed without truncation or loss of
semantic context.

For the purpose of generating reports in SARIF format, the

output location, providing a machine-readable summary of
the modelâ€™s findings. C# was chosen as the programming
language to develop the analyser due to its native and
officially supported capabilities for interacting with the API
used in this project [40].

IV. RESULTS
A set of standardised ML model performance metrics was
utilised for each static analysis tool and the large language
model under consideration to evaluate all the projects
prepared. Specifically, the evaluation measured the execution
time, the number of detected vulnerabilities, and the number
of true positive identifications. These indicators form the
basis for a more in-depth and comparative analysis.
A. DEFINITION OF EVALUATION METRICS
The total number of identified vulnerabilities was determined
by counting the number of entries present in the Results sec-
tion of the SARIF reports generated by the analysis tools [10].
Each entry in this section represents a distinct issue identified
during the analysis process, and the aggregate count serves as
a quantitative indicator of detection capabilities.
Each reported vulnerability was individually reviewed and
compared with a reference dataset of known vulnerabilities
for the given project to determine the number of true positive
results. Only findings that accurately matched a real problem
were counted as true positives. The only exception to this
rule was the location region of the results produced by the
large language models. The rationale behind this exception is
explained in detail in the Discussion section.
VOLUME 13, 2025 198415
[Page 7]
D. Gnieciak, T. Szandala: Large Language Models Versus Static Code Analysis Tools
Listing 2. Prompt sent used for analysis.
The number of false positive results was determined by
subtracting the number of confirmed true positives from the
total number of vulnerabilities identified by each tool or
model. A false positive is defined as a reported vulnerability
that does not correspond to any real or known problem in the
reference data set for the analysed project.
The F1 score is a standard evaluation metric used to
assess the overall effectiveness of a classification model
by combining precision and recall into a single harmonic
mean. In the context of vulnerability detection, it pro-
vides a balanced view of how well a tool or model
identifies true vulnerabilities while minimising incorrect
detections. To fully understand and calculate the F1 score,
it is essential to introduce the individual metrics on
which it depends, including false negatives, precision, and
recall, which together determine the overall value of the
score.
False negatives are calculated by subtracting the number
of true positive results from the total number of known
vulnerabilities in the reference data set for each project.
False Negatives
= Total Known Vulnerabilities âˆ’ True Positives.
Precision is defined as the proportion of correctly
identified vulnerabilities (True Positives) among all reported
vulnerabilities and is calculated as:
Precision = True Positives
True Positives + False Positives .
Recall, on the other hand, measures the proportion of
actual vulnerabilities that were correctly identified by the tool
and is given by:
Recall = True Positives
True Positives + False Negatives.
198416 VOLUME 13, 2025
[Page 8]
D. Gnieciak, T. Szandala: Large Language Models Versus Static Code Analysis Tools
The F1 score is then calculated as the harmonic mean of
precision and recall, providing a single measure that balances
both:
F1 Score = 2 Â· Precision Â· Recall
Precision + Recall .
This metric is handy when comparing tools with varying
balances of precision and recall, as it offers a comprehensive
view of detection performance. All F1 scores reported in this
work were calculated based on manually verified true positive
results.
Finally, the execution time was systematically measured
for each run of the static analysis tools and the implemented
analyser. These measurements were recorded in seconds,
maintaining a precision of three floating-point decimal
places, to support accurate performance comparisons and
detailed evaluation.

compares the effectiveness of each tool using the F1 score.
The FP ratio highlights the effectiveness of a tool in isolation.
Still, the F1 score provides a more comprehensive measure
that balances both the precision of correct detections and the
completeness of the tool in recognising issues.

Figure 5 and Figure 6 show that SnykCode performs better
than other traditional static analysis tools in the F1 score
and competes with systems based on large language models,
further validating the effectiveness of its hybrid analysis
strategy. The tool created by Snyk Company achieved the
highest average F1 score of 0.55; however, it should be noted
that it has two outliers for projects S04 and S10, which can be
easily seen earlier, in Figure 5. In contrast, although strong
in precision as shown earlier, SonarQube and CodeQL have
more limited recall, leading to greater variance and lower
medians in their F1 score distributions.
GPT-4.1, Mistral-Large and DeepSeek V3 achieve higher
F1 scores than traditional tools such as SonarQube and
CodeQL. Despite its high false-positive rate, DeepSeek V3
performs well in terms of F1 score, suggesting that this
compensates for its lower precision shown in Figure 3. It is
worth mentioning that with the use of large language models,
outliers can also be observed for Mistral-Large and DeepSeek
V3 in the S04 project. These can be observed in Figure 7.

VI. DISCUSSION, LIMITATIONS, AND FUTURE WORK
One of the fields found in the SARIF schema is region, which
reports the location of vulnerabilities found with line and
column precision in a given file[10]. All of the large language
models tested were unable to determine it correctly. All
results correctly identified the file, but the incorrect location
was always reported. Upon further analysis, no correlation
was found in these errors. They are likely caused by one of the
steps the text undergoes before processing: BPE tokenisation,
which transformer-based models use [41]. This is a known
and common problem. It can be a major limitation in building
systems that require precisely determining error locations.
CodeQL achieved the worst results among all the static
code analysis tools tested, in terms of the time required for
analysis. This may be due to the intended use of this tool,
which was designed for professional applications that use
many predefined rules that the user can define. The need to
load them into memory and process them can be a potential
reason for these results.
A well-known problem that occurs when using large
language models is hallucinations. Is it a situation where
the generated response is deviated, based neither on training
data nor input from the user [42], [43]. Such an answer
only appears to be correct, but it contains false information.
Table 14 contains examples of such findings. In each case,
the latest available versions of the libraries are used in the
analysed projects, but the models consider them obsolete.
This situation cannot occur with classical code analysis tools,
as they typically maintain a list of deprecated dependencies
that is updated regularly.
When analysing the results, false positives and false
negatives were considered. From the end userâ€™s point of
view, false negatives are more dangerous, as they result
in overlooking real vulnerabilities that could impact the
systemâ€™s functioning. However, it is worth noting that false
positive results also have negative effects. The primary one
is that developers pay less attention to the results of the
analysis. As a consequence, this can lead to the ignored real
issues [44]. False positives not only affect tool precision
but also influence developer experience. Frequent, inaccurate
alerts may erode trust in automated analyses and increase
cognitive load, causing developers to overlook genuine
warnings, an effect particularly relevant when deploying
LLMs in continuous feedback environments.
198420 VOLUME 13, 2025
[Page 12]
D. Gnieciak, T. Szandala: Large Language Models Versus Static Code Analysis Tools
TABLE 14. Hallucinated findings by project and model.
Each LLMâ€™s output was manually reviewed to assess
developer effortâ€”the time and number of steps required to
verify a true positive. GPT-4.1 and Mistral-Large typically
produced concise, human-readable rationales (2â€“4 lines) that
accelerated validation, while DeepSeek V3 often produced
verbose or speculative messages, increasing review time.
In contrast, CodeQL requires developers to manually trace
rule identifiers through documentation, resulting in higher
verification overhead.
Beyond metric-level performance, the practical deploy-
ment of LLM-based vulnerability detection requires careful
integration into existing CI/CD environments. In practice,
organisations can incorporate LLM scanners as an early triage
stage, automatically generating SARIF-compatible reports
and human-readable rationales, before traditional SAST tools
perform deterministic verification. Such a setup reduces
missed vulnerabilities while containing false-positive over-
head. Cost-benefit considerations depend on token volume,
model pricing, and review effort, and should be balanced
against the latency and precision of conventional tools.
In hybrid pipelines, the qualitative explanations generated
by LLMs can further assist human reviewers by providing
justifications that enhance trust calibration and decision-
making.
A. FUTURE WORKS
Although this thesis provides a comparative analysis of
traditional static analysis tools, such as SonarQube, CodeQL,
and SnykCode, and the large language models GPT-4.1,
Mistral Large, and DeepSeek V3, in the context of vulner-
ability detection, several directions remain open for further
exploration and development. One aspect worth exploring is
prompt engineering, i.e. manipulating the content of queries
that are sent to the models and their impact on the results
received.
Another direction could be an attempt to create a hybrid
solution that uses both classical tools and language models.
These approaches can be used to prioritise and verify vulner-
abilities found. This could help mitigate the weaknesses of
both methods.
VII. CONCLUSION
After analysing all projects using the selected static code
analysis tools and large language models, conclusions can be
drawn. Large language models perform well in detecting code
vulnerabilities, as seen from comparing the F1 score values
shown in Figure 7. The ability to analyse the entire context of
the code, as opposed to traditional tools that rely on defined
patterns, can be considered the reason. It is also worth noting
that the increased probability of reporting false positives
comes with the greater ability to detect vulnerabilities. This
is shown in Figure 4. Another vital factor to consider when
using large language models as code analysis tools is their
inability to pinpoint the exact location of the vulnerabilities
they identify. When developing more elaborate code analysis
systems, the failure to provide location information when
using the SARIF format may preclude the use of large
language models.
In conclusion, classical tools for static code analysis are
recommended in situations requiring reliability and precision,
such as software audits, which are necessary for systems that
must be reliable and used in critical sectors. In such situations,
defining specific patterns is often required. Solutions based
on large language models have a higher sensitivity, but
generate more false-positive results. They can be used during
the development process to ensure that developers working
on the system are aware of defects.

Usage of Deep Learning (DL) methods is ubiquitous. It is common in the DL/Artiï¬cial Intelligence domain 
to use 3rd party software. TensorFlow is one of the most popular Machine Learning (ML) platforms. Every 
software product is a subject to security failures which often result from software vulnerabilities. In this 
paper, we focus on threats related to 6 common types of threats in TensorFlow implementation. We iden- 
tify them using Common Weakness Enumeration. We analyze more than 100 vulnerability instances. We 
focus on vulnerabilitiesâ€™ severity, impact on conï¬dentiality, integrity and availability, as well as possible 
results of exploitation. We also use Orthogonal Defect Classiï¬cation (ODC). The results show that a ma- 
jority of vulnerabilities are caused by missing/incorrect checking statements, however some ï¬xes require 
more advanced algorithmic changes. Static Analysis Tools tested in our study show low effectiveness in 
detecting known vulnerabilities in TensorFlow, but we provide some recommendations based on the ob- 
tained alerts to improve overall code quality. Further analysis of vulnerabilities helped us to understand 
and characterize different vulnerability types and provide a set of observations. We believe that these 
observations can be useful for the creators of new static analysis tools as a source of inspiration and to 
build the test cases. We also aim to draw the programmersâ€™ attention to the prevalence of vulnerabilities 
in deep learning applications and a low effectiveness of automatic tools to ï¬nd software vulnerabilities 
in such products.

1. Introduction 
Artiï¬cial Intelligence (AI) and Deep Learning (DL) play a cru- 
cial role in digital transformation through automation of decision- 
making process. Although the beneï¬ts of these technologies are 
signiï¬cant, so are the concerns. In the domain of AI, new security 
threats appear. The AI threat landscape is very diï¬ƒcult to map, as 
it involves many advanced methods and complex pipelines. Also, 
AI products often use 3rd party platforms. TensorFlow is one of 
the most popular such platforms ( Abu Daoud et al., 2021 ), or even 
the most popular ( Pang et al., 2020 ). It used by the technology gi- 
ants such as PayPal or eBay ( TensorFlow, 2021 ). The same as for 
every other software product, it is a subject to security failures of- 
ten resulting from software vulnerabilities (a ï¬‚aw resulting from 
a mistake in software speciï¬cation, implementation or conï¬gura- 
tion ( Committee et al., 1990 )). Under some conditions faulty code 
execution can impact Conï¬dentiality, Availability, or Integrity (CIA 
triad) of a system ( Corallo et al., 2020 ). 
âˆ— Corresponding author. 
E-mail addresses: kï¬lus@iitis.pl (K. Filus), joanna@iitis.pl (J. Doma Â´nska) . 
To improve security, organizations such as MITRE and OWASP 
provide guidelines (e.g. OWASP Secure Coding Practices Guide 
( OWASP Secure Coding Practices Quick Reference Guide, 2021 )) and 
conduct standardization activities. The most common standards 
are MITREâ€™s Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVE) ( CVE - 
Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures, 2021 ) and Common Weak- 
ness Enumeration (CWE) ( CWE - Common Weakness Enumera- 
tion, 2021 ). Such standards facilitate weakness identiï¬cation, mit- 
igation, as well as prevention. Also, rankings are created to raise 
awareness regarding the most dangerous weaknesses, e.g. CWE 
TOP25 ( CWE Top 25 Most Dangerous Software Weaknesses, 2021 ). 
Moreover, it is recommended to use tools, e.g. Static Analysis Tools 
(SATs) to analyse software and ï¬nd potential vulnerabilities. 
Despite the fact that a lot of work is being done to improve se- 
curity, vulnerabilities are still extremely common. The most com- 
mon and dangerous vulnerabilities are those related to C/C++ lan- 
guages (According to Veracodeâ€™s report ( Veracode, 2020 ) and CWE 
TOP25 ranking ( CWE Top 25 Most Dangerous Software Weak- 
nesses, 2021 )). They offer high control and eï¬ƒciency, which come 
with a cost - high severity threats. Due to their eï¬ƒciency, C and 
C++ are used to build high-level numerical libraries (e.g. Tensor-

Flow or Caffe). Although there are many other (dedicated) threats 
in AI applications, it is essential to focus on these known vulner- 
abilities, as those are often forgotten in the battle against the AI- 
centred security threats. 
Our paper aims to characterize six different CWE types of soft- 
ware vulnerabilities in TensorFlow implementation (104 CVE in- 
stances): related to memory management issues, integer over- 
ï¬‚ow, improper input validation and NULL pointer dereference. To 
achieve this, our study consists of four complementary direc- 
tions: 
1. Analysis of metadata available on CVEDetails.com: statistics re- 
garding Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS) scores, 
impact on CIA triad and results of exploitation. 
2. Analysis of vulnerabilities and their ï¬xes in TensorFlow based 
on commits regarding these ï¬xes with Orthogonal Defect Clas- 
siï¬cation (ODC). 
3. Analysis of SAT alerts obtained with CppCheck, FlawFinder and 
Visual Code Grepper for vulnerable and neutral ï¬les (before and 
after ï¬x). 
4. Analysis of descriptions of vulnerabilities and their ï¬xes avail- 
able on CVE Details.com and TensorFlow github Advisory and 
code changes. 
Our contribution: The outcome of the study is an analytical 
study regarding the TensorFlow vulnerabilities along with the set 
of observations and the main ï¬ndings regarding these vulnerabili- 
ties. We describe vulnerabilities at the CWE type level along with 
examples from the TensorFlow implementation. We have compiled 
a comprehensive knowledge base regarding main causes of differ- 
ent CWE types, their results and exploitation ways. We also fo- 
cused on the ways to avoid/minimize the exploitation chance. We 
analyzed a larger number of CWE types than other works in the 
literature (they usually analyze one or two CWE types at once). 
Moreover, our work seems to be the ï¬rst one analyzing a DL li- 
brary itself and not its dependencies. We used our main ï¬ndings 
to create a checklist. The checklist includes the characteristic for 
the numerical libraries functionalities and cases, in which there is 
a high chance of introducing security vulnerabilities. We hope that 
our work will help the developers of numerical libraries to spot 
the parts of the code being developed that can become potential 
security hot-spots. When it comes to developers of static analysis 
tools - we believe that our insights can be used to create new rules 
in the rule-based systems, and also to build test cases for such so- 
lutions. Also, we could not ï¬nd any work testing the usefulness of 
SATs for detecting vulnerabilities in deep learning products, there- 
fore we decided to test 3 freely available SATs. Our concise eval- 
uation (mainly the qualitative one but with some quantitative re- 
sults) and discussion of different SATs can serve as a guide for se- 
lecting free tools to assess code quality. We hope that our paper 
will raise awareness regarding Tensorï¬‚ow and related security is- 
sues. Although the described vulnerabilities are well-known, they 
are still a major threat to C/C++ software products, therefore rais- 
ing awareness of these issues should be an ongoing effort - espe- 
cially in the domain of AI and Deep Learning, in which algorithms 
are often treated as miraculous black box machines for solving a 
plethora of problems. 
The rest of the paper is organized as follows: Section 2 ex- 
plains the term â€œsoftware vulnerabilitiesâ€ and describes methods 
that can be used to detect them. It also shortly outlines the AI vul- 
nerability landscape and introduces a clear division of â€œhigh-levelâ€
AI-dedicated and â€œlow-levelâ€ traditional threats - characteristic for 
C/C++ products (we focus on these vulnerabilities in our study). We

of the code ï¬les taken into consideration in our study. Section 7 fo-

ï¬les of known vulnerabilities. Section 8 concludes the paper. In 
Appendix A , we provide our checklist regarding the security threats 
and how to avoid them. 
2. Background and related work 
2.1. Software vulnerabilities 
Vulnerability is deï¬ned by ISO/IEC 270 0 0:2018 
( ISO/IEC 270 0 0:2018, 2018 ) as a â€œweakness of an asset or con- 
trol that can be exploited by one or more threatsâ€. Undetected 
vulnerabilities ultimately entail signiï¬cant maintenance costs 
( Zhioua et al., 2014 ) and can cause potential violation of security 
policies ( Shin et al., 2010 ). CWE and CVE are two of the most 
important standards used to identify vulnerabilities. CWE deï¬nes 
vulnerability types (not speciï¬c instances) and CVE deï¬nes speciï¬c 
instances within a product or a system. 
A typical example of a CWE can be CWE-476 - NULL 
Pointer Dereference. Its instance in TensorFlow is CVE-2021-37638 
(in ï¬le tensorï¬‚ow/core/kernels/ragged_tensor_to_tensor_op.cc). A 
missing check results in a NULL pointer dereference when 
â€œrow_partition_types_â€ is empty and the code tries to access its 
ï¬rst element. Below, we present a ï¬x of this vulnerability (a yellow

2.2. Vulnerabilities regarding artiï¬cial intelligence 
Due to complexity, large scope and constant development of the 
AI domain, the AI threat landscape is still not completely deï¬ned 
and diï¬ƒcult to map. It is also impossible to predict all of the future 
scenarios, especially when DL algorithms are applied to solve prob- 
lems that are troublesome for humans. Some of the threats dedi- 
cated to AI include compromising AI inference, model poisoning 
and sabotage, data poisoning (malicious actors inject false train- 
ing data to corrupt the learned model ( Steinhardt et al., 2017 )) and 
tempering, as well as manipulation of data labelling. Models can 
also be tricked using adversarial examples ( Responsible AI prac- 
tices Google AI, 2021 ). 
Abstracting from these dedicated threats, which we cannot fully 
combat, there are other signiï¬cant threats that are often over- 
looked in the AI threat research papers - compromises of model 
frameworks and 3rd party provider failures. Many companies use 
external (often open-source) machine learning libraries to power 
their solutions. This 3rd party software itself can (and probably 
does) contain many software vulnerabilities, especially those using 
C/C++ for speed and high resource control. They are no less signif- 
icant than threats crafted speciï¬cally against AI. Moreover, these 
are the threats that we know and are able to handle and imple- 
ment some mitigation strategies. That is why, in this study we fo- 
cus on these particular vulnerabilities.

2.3. Vulnerability detection 
The approaches to software vulnerability detection can be di- 
vided into two main groups: Static Analysis and Dynamic Anal- 
ysis ( Ghaffarian and Shahriari, 2017 ). Dynamic analysis requires 
an executable version of a product and is usually very time- 
consuming, as it needs to test a suï¬ƒcient number of test cases 
( Zhioua et al., 2014 ). Static analysis can be applied directly to 
source code, thus we use it to examine the TensorFlow imple- 
mentation. Programs checking the source code ï¬les (based on a 
set of predeï¬ned rules ( Pereira et al., 2021b )) are called Static 
Analysis Tools (SATs). A compilation of static analysis products 
with a description of supported languages, availability and a brief 
characterization can be found on the OWASP organizationâ€™s web- 
site ( Source Code Analysis Tools - OWASP ). Alternatively, one can 
use a list provided by The National Institute of Standards and 
Technology (NIST) ( Source Code Security Analyzers - NIST ). The 
examples of such programs dedicated for C/C++ are CppCheck 
( CppCheck, 2021 ), FlawFinder ( FlawFinder, 2021 ) and Visual Code 
Grepper ( Visual Code Grepper, 2022 ). These tools are commonly 
used in the literature Croft et al. (2021) ; Kaur and Nayyar (2020) ; 
Khaled and Abdelbaki (2020) ; Li et al. (2018) ; Pereira et al. (2021a) ; 
Riom et al. (2021) ; Zhao et al. (2021) to examine general-purpose 
products. In this study, we use them to examine their ability to 
ï¬nd known and potentially unknown issues in TensorFlow. 
2.4. Related work 
ML-based Vulnerability Detection Some recent works use ML 
methods to ï¬nd vulnerabilities. In Medeiros et al. (2020) , differ- 
ent ML-based vulnerability detection methods have been tested. In 
Filus et al. (2021) , metrics generated via SonarQube and CCCC tool 
were used (with ML models) to detect resource management error 
vulnerabilities (CWE-399) and buffer error vulnerabilities (CWE- 
119). The study showed that the detection effectiveness depends 
on the CWE type. In Filus et al. (2020) , the system based on neu- 
ral networks and mixed features (text and from SonarQube) was 
tested to detect CWE-399 vulnerabilities ( Filus et al., 2020 ). In 
Li et al. (2018) , VulDeePecker was proposed - a vulnerability de- 
tection DL system - and tested on CWE-119 and CWE-399 vulner- 
abilities. 
Using SATs for vulnerability detection Although the ML mod- 
els are widely used in the area of vulnerability detection, 
the traditional rule-based Static Analysis Tools are still com- 
monly used. In Pereira et al. (2021b) , Buffer Overï¬‚ow Vulner- 
abilities (CWE-119) have been analyzed using ODC and two 
SATs. In Arusoaie et al. (2017) , eleven C/C++ SATs were bench- 
marked based on the Toyota test suite ( Shiraishi et al., 2015 ) (it 
was also used in Nong et al. (2021) , in which different tools 
were tested to ï¬nd memory-related vulnerabilities). Also works 
Croft et al. (2021) ; Kaur and Nayyar (2020) ; Khaled and Abdel- 
baki (2020) ; Riom et al. (2021) ; Zhao et al. (2021) aim to bench- 
mark different SATs. Their ï¬ndings showed us the potential of 
three SATs in the context of vulnerability detection: CppCheck, 
FlawFinder and Visual Code Grepper. We use these ï¬ndings as 
a guideline and test the effectiveness of these SATs in terms of 
ï¬nding known vulnerabilities in the TensorFlow implementation. 
Nevertheless, software developers can also reach for other alter- 
native products. A compilation of static analysis products with a 
description of supported languages, availability and a brief charac- 
terization can be found on the OWASP organizationâ€™s website along 
with the important selection criteria ( Source Code Analysis Tools - 
OWASP ). Alternatively, one can use a list provided by The National 
Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) ( Source Code Security 
Analyzers - NIST ). It is also worth mentioning a different kind of 
a static analysis tool, which can be used along with the described 
products - code clone detectors. Such tools aim to ï¬nd fragments 
of code copied and pasted within/between software products. The 
example of such a product is VUDDY ( Kim et al., 2017 ), which iden- 
tiï¬es code clones of known CVEs (exact and renamed clones in 
particular). Such tools can be effective in ï¬nding copied parts of 
vulnerable code, however, they show low effectiveness in ï¬nding 
restructured and semantic clones of such vulnerabilities ( Kim et al., 
2017 ). In fact, restructured and semantic clones are excluded from 
the VUDDY clone detection ( Kim et al., 2017 ). On contrary, the 
ï¬ndings presented in our work, do not focus on the code clones, 
but aim to summarize the semantic meaning of code, near which 
vulnerabilities are often introduced. As a result, our main ï¬nd- 
ings provide a more general description of potential security hot- 
spots. Nevertheless, tools such as VUDDY can be helpful, when 
programmers reuse some parts of code from the open-source 
libraries. 
Vulnerabilities in AI products Although numerous works regard 
software vulnerability detection based on Deep Learning models 
( Fang et al., 2019; Filus et al., 2020; Li et al., 2021; 2018; Pechenkin 
and Demidov, 2018 ), works on vulnerabilities in AI products them- 
selves are very limited. One work that we were able to ï¬nd, 
Xiao et al. (2018) , discusses security risks in DL frameworks (Ten- 
sorFlow, Caffe and Torch). However, they examine vulnerabilities 
mainly in their dependencies (i.e. NumPy for TensorFlow, opencv 
for Caffe/Torch) - and not directly in DL frameworks code. Given 
the ubiquity of DL models in a variety of applications, this is a 
large gap in the literature. 
Limitations of the related works Besides the lack of a thorough 
analysis of vulnerabilities in ML products, another limitation of 
the existing works is that they analyze vulnerabilities regardless 
of their CWE type or a very limited number of vulnerability types. 
Moreover, they do not focus on their signiï¬cance and severity. 
Our work in relation to the available literature With respect to 
the works present in the literature, our work can be embedded 
closest to that of Pereira et al. (2021b) in terms of methodology 
and Xiao et al. (2018) in terms of subject matter. Our work aims 
to ï¬ll the gap between them. First of all, we aim to focus on the 
implementation of a deep learning framework itself, and not on 
its dependencies, as in work ( Pereira et al., 2021b ). In terms of 
methodology, work ( Xiao et al., 2018 ) provides a systematic anal- 
ysis of CWE-119 issues (Improper Restriction of Operations within 
the Bounds of a Memory Buffer). Authors examined three C/C++ 
applications: Linux Kernel, Xen and Mozilla. In contrast to these 
old products, we examine a relatively new product in which at 
least some changed programming practices can be expected (al- 
though the development of Linux Kernel, Xen and Mozilla is con- 
tinuous, they have never been rewritten from scratch). Moreover, 
the numerical libraries, such as TensorFlow, mostly rely on math- 
ematical operations using arrays. Here, the root causes of vulnera- 
bilities can be different - e.g. they can result from an insuï¬ƒcient 
knowledge of the mathematical methods to be implemented (as- 
sumptions, boundary conditions, etc.). We aim to identify speciï¬c 
root causes of different CWE types. We take into consideration 
three types of memory issues: not only a generic memory-related 
type - CWE-119, but also its â€œchildrenâ€: Out-of-bounds Read and 
Write. We also analyze problems related to NULL Pointer Derefer- 
ence (CWE-476) and Integer Overï¬‚ow or Wraparound (CWE-190) 
- other common C/C+ issues that are critical for numerical opera- 
tions and dealing with dynamic data structures. We also analyze 
issues related to Improper Input Validation (CWE-20) - as one ex- 
ample of a language-independent CWE group. Work ( Pereira et al., 
2021b ) shows that SATs lack rules to detect most examined vul- 
nerabilities, however the can effectively ï¬nd some memory-related 
vulnerabilities in traditional products. Therefore, we aim to exam- 
ine whether free SATs can be used to improve the security of a 
different product kind - a modern numerical library.

3. Approach to analysis 
In our study, we aim to analyze different types of software vul- 
nerabilities in terms of their severity, impact on conï¬dentiality, in- 
tegrity and availability, as well as possible results of exploitation. 
We also analyze the characteristics of different vulnerability types 
and determine speciï¬c situations, in which these particular types 
can be introduced. We test three static code analysis tools to ex- 
amine their effectiveness in ï¬nding known software vulnerabilities. 
We use three sources of data: CVE Details, CWE TOP25 rank- 
ing and GitHub. We use CVE Details to ï¬nd known instances of 
vulnerabilities in TensorFlow. CVE instances are connected with a 
speciï¬c CWE type. We use this knowledge along with information 
from CWE TOP25 to ï¬nd the most prevalent and severe vulnera- 
bilities. This way we consider TensorFlow as an individual product 
(a numerical library) as well as an example of a modern C/C++ ap- 
plication. Then, we use CVE Details for the second time - to ï¬nd 
CVE instances under a speciï¬c CWE group and gather metadata re- 
garding those vulnerabilities. We take into consideration only those 
CVE pages that provide a single GitHub commit ï¬xing a speciï¬c 
vulnerability. We download vulnerable (before a ï¬x) and neutral 
(after a ï¬x) ï¬les. We inspect the ï¬les manually (with ODC) and 
via static code analyzers. As a results, we provide some numer- 
ical results regarding the effectiveness of SATs and statistics re- 
garding the examined vulnerabilitiesâ€™ metadata. We also provide 
a set of insights regarding different types of vulnerabilities and a 
list, in which we include speciï¬c situations, in which programmers 
can introduce security issues. We present this list in a form of a 
checklist for programmers of numerical libraries, programmers of 
applications using such libraries, as well as creators of SATs (they 
can use it to create new rules or to determine test cases for their 
solutions). In Fig. 1 we present the overview of the steps of our 
analysis. 
3.1. Selection of CWE types and CVE instances 
To choose the CWE types we considered the number of avail- 
able TensorFlow CVE instances per CWE type and its position in 
the 2021 CWE TOP25 ranking ( CWE Top 25 Most Dangerous Soft- 
ware Weaknesses, 2021 ). This way, we take into consideration 
three different aspects of different vulnerability types: their preva- 
lence and severity in software products in general, as well as their 
prevalence in Tensorï¬‚ow. CVE Details provides us with information 
regarding the occurrence of known vulnerability types in Tensor- 
Flow. CWE TOP25, on the other hand, takes into consideration not 
only the prevalence of different vulnerability types in diverse ap- 
plications, but also the severity of these vulnerabilities and their 
impact on the system in the case of exploitation. This allows us to 
treat TensorFlow individually and also as an example of a modern 
C/C++ application. 
Eventually, we included 6 CWE types ( CWE - Common Weak- 
ness Enumeration, 2021 ) (104 CVE instances in total). In Table 1 , 
we gathered all the examined CWE types along with the number 
of their instances in TensorFlow and their rank in the CWE TOP25 
ranking. The examined vulnerabilities seem to be adequate from 
a security point of view for a numerical library. Such libraries of- 
ten rely on mathematical operations using arrays. Although lan- 
guages such as C or C++ offer speed calculations, they do not 
provide built-in protection against memory access/overwriting or 
checks regarding buffer bounds. Our analysis includes a more 
generic memory-related CWE type - CWE-119, but also its â€œchil- 
drenâ€: CWE-125 and CWE-787 as more speciï¬c types of memory 
issues. We also analyze different problems characteristic for nu- 
merical operations and dealing with dynamic data structures: re- 
lated to NULL Pointer Dereference (CWE-476) and Integer Overï¬‚ow 
or Wraparound (CWE-190). We also analyze issues related to Im- 
proper Input Validation (CWE-20) - as one example of a language- 
independent CWE group affecting all kinds of applications. 
3.2. Retrieval of metadata for selected CVE instances and collection of 
source code ï¬les 
We used CVE Details page to ï¬nd the CVE metadata and links 
to github commits with the source code. On the particular CVE 
page, information on CVSS Score, impact on CIA triad (three levels 
are used: None, Partial and Complete) and potential exploitation

(vulnerable ï¬les are versions before the ï¬x, whereas the neutral 
ï¬les include the ï¬x). 
3.3. Orthogonal Defect Classiï¬cation 
Orthogonal Defect Classiï¬cation ( Chillarege et al., 1992 ) is a sys- 
tematic approach developed by IBM, used to classify and analyze 
software defects by transforming semantic information into a mea- 
surement ( Pereira et al., 2021b ). The approach is frequently used in 
software root-cause analysis ( Pereira et al., 2021b ). Full analysis in- 
volves describing the defect before and after a ï¬x with a series of 
8 attributes (with predeï¬ned values). The following attributes can 
be used: activity, trigger, impact (attributes regarding an opened 
defect), target, defect type, qualiï¬er, source and age (attributes re- 
garding an opened defect). To examine vulnerabilities in our study, 
we use two attributes: defect type and qualiï¬er (the others do not 
include any additional relevant information regarding the charac- 
teristics of a particular vulnerability ( Pereira et al., 2021b )). 
Attribute defect type is used to represent the semantics of 
the ï¬x (it captures the meaning of the ï¬x, thus the nature 
of the particular issue)( Chillarege et al., 1992 ). Eight values can 
be assigned to this attribute. We exclude two of them from 
our analysis (build/package/merge and documentation, as we fo- 
cus only on the source code ï¬les). Based on deï¬nitions from 
Chillarege et al. (1992) and Bridge and Miller (1998) , we can de- 
ï¬ne the defect types in the following way: 
â€¢ Assignment/Initialization - problems related to no/incorrect 
assignment of the variable value. 
â€¢ Checking - problems related to conditional logic (incorrect, 
missing conditions). When multiple checking statements have 
to be added/corrected it can belong to type Algorithm/Method. 
â€¢ Timing - problems related to serialization of shared resources. 
â€¢ Algorithm/method - problems related to implementation (gen- 
erally no design ï¬x should be necessary). 
â€¢ Function - problems related to no or incorrect implementation 
of some signiï¬cant capability, end-user interfaces or global data 
structures (generally, it does require a design change). 
â€¢ Interface - problems related to communication issues between 
subsystems, components, device drivers etc. 
Types above have been described in more detail in work 
Bridge and Miller (1998) . 
Qualiï¬er is used to capture what had to be done to ï¬x a par- 
ticular vulnerability in terms of code changes: 
â€¢ Missing - to ï¬x the issue, new code had to be added. 
â€¢ Incorrect - to ï¬x the issue, some code had to be adjusted. 
â€¢ Extraneous - to ï¬x the issue, some code had to be removed. 
We can say, that it extends the semantic information provided 
via a defect type. It provides us with insights on whether a partic- 
ular defect resulted from an omission or rather from some kind of 
a programming mistake. 
Using these two attributes, allows us to associate a vulnera- 
bility with particular activities of different stages of software de- 
velopment and faults in this process ( Chillarege et al., 1992 ). They 
provide us with the causal information regarding an analyzed vul- 
nerability. The resulting insights describe the nature of different 
vulnerability types in a systematic and easy to interpret way. 
In our analysis, we select appropriate attribute values based on 
the changes occurring during the patch of a given vulnerability. 
The changes can be easily inspected via github - by displaying the 
corresponding commit. 
The ODC is a manual classiï¬cation, so similarly to work 
( Pereira et al., 2021b ), two researchers conducted the analysis for 
greater independence and fault tolerance. First, we performed the 
discussion, set the classiï¬cation criteria and analyzed the ï¬rst sev- 
eral examples together. We separately analyzed all of the remain- 
ing CVE instances, and at the end, discussed the non-overlapping 
results and found a common consensus - this is how the ï¬nal re- 
sults have been obtained. 
3.4. Running SATs and analysis of the alerts 
We used three commonly used static code analyzers: CppCheck 
(version 2.6), FlawFinder (version 2.0.19) and Visual Code Grepper 
(version 2.2.0.0). We decided to use only SATs that can be used for 
free - as those SATs can be used by everyone. We chose these par- 
ticular SATs as they showed superior performance over the other 
analyzers tested in the works ( Croft et al., 2021; Kaur and Nayyar, 
2020; Khaled and Abdelbaki, 2020; Riom et al., 2021; Zhao et al., 
2021 ). In work Riom et al. (2021) , 9 SATs were tested. Cppcheck 
was reported to produce very few false positive alerts and special- 
ize in ï¬nding undeï¬ned behaviours. Also in work Kaur and Nay- 
yar (2020) , it was shown that CppCheck was able to ï¬nd the max- 
imum number of the examined vulnerabilities out of the tested 
5
[Page 6]
K. Filus and J. Doma Â´nska Computers & Security 124 (2023) 102948 
tools. In work Khaled and Abdelbaki (2020) , the results showed 
that although the Visual Code Grepper SAT gives a relatively large 
number of false positive alerts, it was able to report all the ex- 
amined vulnerabilities (false negative rate equaled zero). In work 
Zhao et al. (2021) , Flawï¬nder signiï¬cantly outperformed another 
tested traditional SAT in terms of ï¬nding CWE-119 memory-related 
issues and F1 Score. Also in work Croft et al. (2021) , Flawï¬nder was 
able to produce the highest recall values out of all tested SATs. 
We ï¬rst ran the analysis on vulnerable ï¬les corresponding to 
the chosen CWE group, and then we analyzed the respective neu- 
tral ï¬les. We did this for all the examined CWE groups. Dif- 
ferent levels of granularity can be used in the process of soft- 
ware vulnerability detection: among others package-level, ï¬le- 
level, function-level and line-level ( Kluban et al., 2022 ). Usually, 
at least a function-level is recommended, as it provides suï¬ƒcient 
information regarding a code functionality - unlike separate lines 
of code ( Kluban et al., 2022 ). While the Machine Learning models 
built to detect vulnerabilities usually operate on a function-level 
(e.g. works Russell et al. (2018) ; Wei et al. (2021) ), the ï¬le-level 
seems to be the most suitable in our case, as we aim to perform 
the overall assessment of adequacy of different warnings per ï¬le. 
We take into consideration not only a particular vulnerability, but 
also the warnings regarding the qualitative improvements, which 
can reduce the chance of introducing new vulnerabilities in the fu- 
ture. We believe that such an evaluation will be the most useful 
for those who would like to use these static code analyzers to ï¬nd 
security issues and to improve the overall quality of their code. 
When the ï¬les were analyzed for a speciï¬c CWE group, we an- 
alyzed the alerts in terms of their CWE ID (when given), accuracy 
of ï¬nding lines regarding the examined CVE instances (we used the 
information regarding the lines for which SATs found issues, found 
them in ï¬les regarding speciï¬c vulnerabilities on GitHub and com- 
pared with true lines that were responsible for some vulnerability). 
We also analyzed whether the given alerts should be considered 
(we chose alerts that can be used to improve the quality of Tensor- 
Flow code and described the potential issues and improvements). 
We also compared the results obtained for corresponding vulnera- 
ble and neutral versions of ï¬les. In the case of VCG, which offers 
an analysis of comments (to ï¬nd potentially unï¬nished fragments 
of code), we chose two example ï¬les and examined how many 
â€œTODOâ€ instances are found by VCG and how many instances of 
such comments truly are in a particular ï¬le (we used a Visual Stu- 
dio Code search engine for this purpose and simply typed â€œTODOâ€). 
We computed the number of false positives (false alarms - when 
a comment is just an explenation of the code) and false negatives 
(when a clear â€œTODOâ€ can be found and it was not reported by 
VCG). 
3.5. Analysis of text descriptions of vulnerabilities and source code 
elements 
After our primary analysis of information on CVE Details and 
ODC, we focused on the vulnerability descriptions regarding all of 
the examined CVE instances available on CVE Details and corre- 
sponding TensorFlow advisories, as well as code implementations 
(if necessary) to ï¬nd common causes and results of vulnerabili- 
ties occurrence and exploitation. We deï¬ned possible exploitation 
strategies of the users of application using TensorFlow background 
and possible ways to avoid their exploitation in a form of a check- 
list 
4. Analysis of information from CVE Details 
Using information gathered from CVE Details, we have exam- 
ined metadata regarding the examined CVEs: Common Vulnerabil- 
ity Scoring System (CVSS) scores and the impact on Conï¬dential-

ity, Integrity and Availability (CIA triad) of a system when a vul- 
nerability is exploited. Common Vulnerability Scoring System mea- 
sures the severity and characteristics of software vulnerabilities. A 
score ranges from 0 to 10. CVSS is considered to be a standard 
measurement system for organizations, governments and in indus- 
try, as it provides consistent and accurate vulnerability severity 
scores (according to National Institute of Standards and Technology 
- NIST ( National Vulnerability Database (NVD), 2021 )). CIA traid, on 
the other hand, refers to the fundamental elements of information 
systems: Conï¬dentiality, Integrity and Availability ( Samonas and 
Coss, 2014 ). Three categories are used to describe the impact on 
each CIA triad part: none, partial and complete ( Toloudis et al., 
2016 ). 
To gather our metadata, we used the CVE details searching en- 
gine (â€œVulnerability Searchâ€) and typed Tensorï¬‚ow in the â€œProd- 
uctâ€ box. We exported all available data to a csv ï¬le and processed 
it. We calculated average, standard deviation, minimum and max- 
imum values of the CVSS scores for different types of examined 
vulnerabilities. We also counted the CVE instances from each CWE 
group belonging to different categories of the CIA triad impact (for 
all parts of CIA triad separately). We used these values to compute 
the percentage of these impact categories per each CWE type. The 
results can be observed in Fig. 2 and Tables 2 and 3 . CWE groups 
in Fig. 2 have been sorted in the descending order of the average 
CVSS score. 
It can be observed that the highest values of CVSS score have 
been obtained for memory-related issues (CWE-787, CWE-119 and 
CWE-125) - 7.5 (they usually impact all of the CIA triad elements). 
These vulnerabilities are also the most diversiï¬ed in terms of pos- 
sible exploit results (overï¬‚ows, bypasses, code executions, memory 
corruptions and DoS - see Table 2 ). CWE-190 group (Integer Over- 
ï¬‚ow or Wraparound) obtained the lowest CVSS values on aver- 
age (they usually impact only Availability - see Table 3 ). CWE-190 
vulnerabilities result in overï¬‚ows and DoS. The examined CWE- 
20 examples (Improper Input Validation) obtained higher average 
and maximum values than CWE-190 vulnerabilities (also, the high- 
est standard deviation - suggesting the most varying CVSS scores). 
These vulnerabilities have an impact mainly on Availability of sys-

CWE-476 vulnerabilities are similar to those obtained for CWE-20 
in terms of statistics of CVSS scores (almost the same mean, std 
and the same minimum and maximum values). Also these vul- 
nerabilities impact mainly Availability, but in contrast to CWE-20 
vulnerabilities, almost 50 percent of them can also impact Conï¬- 
dentiality or Integrity. For the majority of the examined CVE in- 
stances, the exploitation results were not classiï¬ed to any of the 
given groups, but some of the vulnerability instances can result in 
bypasses, denials of service and code execution.

6.2. CppCheck 
For all of the CWE groups, the results were exactly the same

Generally, the great majority of warnings were of type CWE-398

outer argument, reducing the scopes of some variables and the

and changes could be applied. This prompted us to include one of 
the suggestions that can be used to improve the code quality. For 
ï¬les ( Commit ï¬xing CVE-2021-29566 vulnerability (2021) ) related 
to CVE-2021-29566 (CWE-787), CppCheck returned the following 
warning: â€œLocal variable â€™dâ€™ shadows outer argument (CWE-398)â€: 
It is not a good practise to redeï¬ne a function argument and 
use it as a counter in a loop - it should be ï¬xed. A different vari- 
able should be used here to obtain better code quality. A comment 
shows that it is planned to write a multi-thread implementation of 
this function and potentially const CPUDevice& d will be used there 
(which is now shadowed). Similar issues were found, e.g. variable 
â€œiâ€ in ï¬le tensorï¬‚ow/core/kernels/save_restore_v2_ops.cc. It can of- 
ten be tempting to use variables such as â€iâ€, â€dâ€ or other single 
letters as loop counters, but it should always be checked whether 
this variable is not already taken - this, even if it does not cause 
problems at the moment, may introduce problems in the future 
(e.g. when the code is rebuilt by another programmer). 
6.3. Visual Code Grepper 
Unfortunately, Visual Code Grepper does not provide Com- 
mon Weakness Enumeration IDs in its reports. It only provides 
warnings with different tags (e.g. â€œpotentially unsafeâ€, â€œsuspicious 
commentâ€, â€œcriticalâ€). The highest severity of a warning was â€œhighâ€
- no cases with â€œcriticalâ€ warnings were observed. Besides analyz- 
ing code, VCG also processes comments and analyzes its contents 
via text analysis (e.g. it searches for terms such as â€œTODOâ€). In 
some cases it can be useful - e.g. see Section 6.2 for an example of 
a planned functionality. It also ï¬nds StrCat and memcpy instances 
and suggests replacing them with different functions, as those 
functions appear in Microsoftâ€™s banned function list. VCG returns 
warnings when it ï¬nds multiple deletes for a particular variable 
or when it cannot ï¬nd a delete for a new (in the cases examined 
by us manually, these were false positives - they regarded the

situations, in which a pointer was created inside a function and

What is the accuracy of the VCG text analysis performed 
for comments? We manually analyzed the reported alerts and 
the corresponding source code ï¬les for two example ï¬les (before

In 2 cases for cuda_dnn.cc, and in 6 cases for optimized_ops.cc,
