7. Analysis of descriptions, advisories and source code 
Our manual analysis resulted in the identiï¬cation of common 
effects of exploitation of different CWE types: 
â€¢ CWE-787 : heap buffer overï¬‚ows (writes and reads), segfaults, 
corruptions of the memory. Chained with other types can result 
in more advanced exploits and can trigger undeï¬ned behavior 
by null pointer dereference. 
â€¢ CWE-20 : access to data outside the bounds of heap allocated 
data, segmentation faults, assertion failures, DoS (by query-of- 
death vulnerability, â€˜SIGABRTâ€˜ signal raised by the operating 
system or â€˜CHECKâ€˜-failure), data corruption and undeï¬ned be- 
haviors. 
â€¢ CWE-190 : dereferencing invalid pointers - which can cause 
memory allocation problems and denials of service (via 
â€˜CHECKâ€˜-fail). 
â€¢ CWE-1 19 : read from outside the bounds of the heap buffer al- 
located buffers, segmentation faults, data corruption (by access- 
ing data out of bounds), a heap buffer overï¬‚ow (by accessing 
data out of bounds), undeï¬ned behaviors and DoS (via out of 
memory allocation). 
â€¢ CWE-125 : reads/writes outside of bounds of heap allocated 
data (and disclosure of the contents of process memory), seg- 
mentation faults, undeï¬ned behaviors due to binding to nullptr, 
uninitialized memory accesses and DoS. 
â€¢ CWE-476 : segmentation faults, read from/write to memory out- 
side the bounds of heap allocated data, undeï¬ned behavior, 
crashes and DoS. 
7.1. CWE-787 - Out-of-bounds Write 
CWE-787 vulnerabilities can be caused by no/incomplete/invalid 
validation of input parameters and include wrong types (e.g. CVE- 
2021-37650 - implementation assumes that all records in the ex- 
amined dataset are strings), wrong values (e.g. CVE-2021-29571 - 
implementation assumes using correct values whereas an incor- 
rect value can be passed) and empty variables as arguments (e.g. 
CVE-2021-29535 - it is assumed that input arguments are valid 
scalars and their numeric values are accessed directly. In the case 
of empty tensors, accessing the index 0 results in overï¬‚ow). An- 
other source is no/incomplete/invalid validation of the values calcu- 
lated inside the function , e.g. CVE-2021-29540 - the computed size 
of the ï¬lter is not validated and used instead of the number of 
ï¬lter elements during convolutional ï¬lter backpropagation, which 
can result in an overï¬‚ow when the computed size is too large. 
Another source can be no validation for empty data structures or 
no validation whether the examined data structure has enough ele- 
ments for some operation (e.g. backpropagation) - e.g. CVE-2021- 
29578 - it is not checked whether the pooling sequence arguments 
have enough elements for the required shape. Also, when more 
than one tensor is used in the operation, the source can be lack 
of shape compatibility validation of the tensors (e.g. CVE-2021-29609 
- it is not validated whether the second dimensions of sparse ten- 
sors used in the operation match). Last but not least, the issue can 
be connected to no/improper validation of ML models and specially 
crafted models can cause the vulnerability exploitation (e.g. CVE- 
2021-29603 - for TFLite). 
9 
[Page 10]
K. Filus and J. Doma Â´nska Computers & Security 124 (2023) 102948 
How to exploit? - specially crafted inputs, models, - using func- 
tion arguments with wrong values, wrong types and empty 
variables, - using empty structures or the incompatible ones for 
the operation (both one- and multi-tensor ones) 
7.2. CWE-20 - Improper Input Validation 
Main sources of CWE-20 vulnerabilities are no/improper/ 
insuï¬ƒcient checks whether examined data structures are not empty or 
have a proper dimension (shape) and lack of handling of these oc- 
curences (e.g. CVE-2020-15190 based on the boolean value, one of 
the tensors is the input tensor and the other one should be empty. 
The eager runtime traverses all output tensors, hence when the 
second tensor is examined, a reference to â€˜nullptrâ€˜ is bind. Vulnera- 
bilities can occur, because sometimes the implementation depends 
on the default values of axes, some quantities of the examined data 
structures are used to create different structures (it should be val- 
idated whether the original data structures shapes are proper for 
the new ones - e.g. CVE-2020-15199 - no validation whether the 
examined tensor has the minimum number of elements - required 
for the operation. This quantity is used to initialize a different data 
structure. which needs at least one element to not be â€˜nullptrâ€˜.). 
The improper shape of one structure can entail the risk of another 
structure becoming a null pointer. Another issue can be that all 
assumptions of a method are not satisï¬ed (e.g. CVE-2021-37674 - 
input tensors in this particular method have to be 4-dimensional, 
but it is not checked). Also, some external methods can be not pre- 
pared to operate with empty data structures - e.g. CVE-2020-26270 
- running an LSTM/GRU model where the LSTM/GRU layer receives 
an input with results with 0 elements. The result is a CHECK fail- 
ure when CUDA backend is used. 
How to exploit? - wrong values of parameters and shapes of 
data structures, - empty structures, - using null pointers 
7.3. CWE-190 - Integer Overï¬‚ow or Wraparound 
One source of CWE-190 vulnerabilities can be using implementa- 
tions and unsafe functions , e.g. â€œInitDimsâ€ instead of â€œAddDimWith- 
Statusâ€ (or â€œBuildTensorShapeBaseâ€ in a tensor constructor), which 
can result in â€˜CHECKâ€˜-failures in the presence of overï¬‚ows. This 
function is still used by some APIs, e.g. in ï¬le mkl_util.h (tensor- 
ï¬‚ow/tensorï¬‚ow/core/util/) - it is a potential vulnerability. Other 
source can be no/improper validation of tensorsâ€™ and modelsâ€™ sizes - 
simple operations (e.g. concatenation - CVE-2021-29601) used with 
large models in TFLite can cause overï¬‚ows (even more frequently 
than in traditional TensorFlow, as in this implementation int32 in- 
stead of int64 is often used). The example can be CVE-2021-29605 
(TFLite code used for array allocation is vulnerable to an integer 
overï¬‚ow - a special large model can be crafted such that the â€˜sizeâ€˜ 
multiplier returns the value that overï¬‚ows the â€œintâ€ datatype and 
becomes negative. This negative value is given to â€œmallocâ€ and as 
a result an invalid pointer is dereferenced. The other example can 
be CVE-2021-41198 - the number of elements in the output ten- 
sor is too large for â€œint64_tâ€, overï¬‚ow occurs and is detected via a 
â€œCHECKâ€ statement (and process is aborted). 
How to exploit? - using large inputs and demanding large out- 
puts, - using speciï¬c APIs that still use â€˜AddDimâ€˜ instead of â€˜Ad- 
dDimWithStatusâ€˜, - using specially crafted (also large) models, - 
building tensors without dimension bounds 
7.4. CWE-119 - Improper Restriction of Operations within the Bounds 
of a Memory Buffer 
Main sources of CWE-119 vulnerabilities are no/incomplete/ 
improper validation of input parameters of a function used to ac- 
cess and process the data structures (CVE-2020-15205 - one of 
the arguments lacks validation, thus values can be passed that 
can cause heap overï¬‚ow error/leak of contents of memory, which 
can contain return addresses and can be used to defeat the Ad- 
dress Space Layout Randomization - ASLR). Other issue can be 
no/incomplete/improper validation of values calculated to use for ac- 
cessing and processing the data (also when validation is imple- 
mented for the debug mode, but not for the release mode). Here, 
problems related to mimicking Pythonâ€™s indexing with negative val- 
ues can be considered - e.g. CVE-2020-15207 - to mimic Pythonâ€™s 
indexing with negative values, TFLite converts negative values to 
positive ones. The only check of the converted index is present 
in the debug builds. In the release mode, code execution contin- 
ues with a negative index. Also, no/incomplete/improper validation 
of indexes obtained using double indexing pattern can be problem- 
atic (e.g. accessing the values of gradients in the reversed order - 
CVE-2020-15195). The next issue is no/incomplete/improper valida- 
tion of shapes of examined tensors . Issues often occur when data 
structures are processed in parallel - (e.g. when more than one 
tensor is used in the operation and their shapes have to be equal 
and fully speciï¬ed - e.g. CVE-2020-15198 - no validation whether 
the tensor with weights has the same shape as the data. Weights 
are accessed in parallel with the data, and since there is no val- 
idation, passing fewer weights than the data values can cause an 
out-of-bound read). Another problem is no validation whether val- 
ues given as parameters are not too large for the types used in the 
function and for memory allocation - e.g. CVE-2020-15266 - when 
one of the arguments is very large, the CPU kernel implementa- 
tion reads it as a C++ â€˜nanâ€˜ ï¬‚oating point value. Operation on this 
variable can cause an undeï¬ned behavior and a segfault. The last 
issue found in the analysis regards no/incomplete/improper checks 
whether the initialized values are created properly . 
How to exploit? - using large values of parameters, - using val- 
ues (as indexes) not in the proper range of data, both positive 
and negative ones (also using operations based on reverse in- 
dexing), - using data structures with mismatched shapes when 
these structures are processed in parallel 
7.5. CWE-125 - Out-of-bounds read 
CWE-125 vulnerabilities can be caused by no/incomplete/ 
improper validation of user given parameters . These issues can re- 
gard to axis values (e.g. CVE-2020-15265 - invalid axis value can be 
passed, resulting in accessing a dimension outside the tensor rank), 
no checks of validity of strings (e.g. representing format - see CVE- 
2020-26267), no tensor bounds checks for tensor operations (nega- 
tive numbers, numbers exceeding the size), no checks whether pa- 
rameters used for a speciï¬c data structure speciï¬cation are correct for 
its type (e.g. CVE-2021-29559 - implementation assumes that the 
given parameters specify a valid sparse tensor.). Other issues re- 
gard no/incomplete/improper validation of user given data structures 
(usually arrays): empty checks (e.g. CVE-2021-41219 - sparse matrix 
multiplication was vulnerable to binding a reference to â€œnullptrâ€
when tensors with dimensions 0 or less were used). The ï¬x has 
been introduced in the newest version of TensorFlow - 2.7.0. Also, 
no/incomplete/improper validation of compatibility of data structures 
can introduce vulnerabilities when they are all used together in 
the operation (also in parallel). Incompatibility can often result 
in binding a reference to a null pointer (e.g. CVE-2021-37655). 
Also, very large values of parameters and tensors can cause integer 
overï¬‚ows resulting in an out-of-bounds read and disclosure of the 
process memory contents - CVE-2018-21233. The problem can be 
caused by a missing check of correctness of array ranks . Issues can 
be caused by no control regarding incrementation of pointers and 
trying to access data (e.g. CVE-2021-29532) or using one variable 
10 
[Page 11]
K. Filus and J. Doma Â´nska Computers & Security 124 (2023) 102948 
for indexing two separate arrays in parallel and also using the debug 
checks (e.g. CVE-2020-15208 - when determining the common di- 
mension size of two examined tensors, â€œDCHECKâ€ is used - no-op 
outside of the debug mode. Attackers can use a larger tensor as the 
ï¬rst argument to trigger the attack.) Also, no/incomplete/improper 
validation of models used in the operations can cause vulnerabilities 
(e.g. CVE-2021-29606 - a specially crafted TFLite model can cause 
OOB read). The last issue speciï¬ed in the analysis is improper con- 
trol of the program ï¬‚ow (e.g. CVE-2021-29551 - the implementation 
fails to terminate kernel execution if one validation condition fails 
and only returns from a function). 
How to exploit? - specially crafted input parameters (e.g. 
shapes out of correct bounds), - using large data structures and 
values of parameters (also negative ones), - using empty struc- 
tures as input parameters, - using tensors with different dimen- 
sions when the same dimension is a condition of a mathemat- 
ical operation, - using incompatible values of parameters and 
input data structures in operations 
7.6. CWE-476 - NULL pointer dereference 
CWE-476 vulnerabilities are often caused by problems with ses- 
sion (no validation of availability of a session state, old TF ver- 
sions do not set this state - e.g. CVE-2020-15204), no/incorrect val- 
idation of tensor type (conversion from a Python array to a C++ 
array is vulnerable to a type confusion - CVE-2021-29513) and 
no/improper validation of tensor shape (e.g. CVE-2021-41215 - the 
shape inference function assumes that the tensor has a positive 
rank and that the last dimension is correct). The problems can be 
introduced by no/improper/incomplete validation whether input ten- 
sors are not empty or exist (e.g. CVE-2021-41217 - the control ï¬‚ow 
graph building can cause null pointer exception when nodes can- 
not be paired). Problems can occur when no/improper validation 
of input arguments in terms of their availability and correctness is 
provided (e.g. CVE-2021-37639 - restoring tensors using raw APIs, 
TF can be tricked into dereferencing a null pointer if the tensor 
name is not provided). The next cause can be no/improper valida- 
tion of corner cases and all of the constraints of the operator (e.g. 
CVE-2021-29616 - an undeï¬ned behavior can be triggered due to 
a dereference in corner cases that result in optimizing a no-input 
node). Yet another cause can be improper control of the programme 
ï¬‚ow (e.g. CVE-2021-37648 after unsuccessful validation kernel ex- 
ecution was not terminated, because it only exits a current func- 
tion). Also, using unmaintained APIs can introduce vulnerabilities 
(e.g. CVE-2021-41208 - unmaintained boosted trees). The problem 
can be planned and not implemented validation (e.g. CVE-2021- 
29565 - missing validation under a â€œTODOâ€). 
How to exploit? - using tensors of non-numeric types, using 
empty tensors, - using parameters of the operation not satis- 
fying the constraints of the operation (also corner cases), - us- 
ing specially crafted models, - using one empty tensor and the 
other one/ones valid in multi-tensor operations, - using tensors 
with incorrect shape for the operation 
8. Conclusions 
While dedicated AI threats are undoubtedly extremely impor- 
tant and need to be addressed, we donâ€™t yet know to effectively 
combat them. That is why, in our study we focus on threats caused 
by standard C/C++ vulnerabilities in TensorFlow implementation. 
We analyze 6 common vulnerability types by summarizing meta- 
data regarding various vulnerabilities. We use Orthogonal Defect 
Classiï¬cation, manual code analysis, and descriptions of speciï¬c 
CVEs to characterize their causes and results. 
Though Tensorï¬‚ow is a relatively new product, numerous se- 
curity vulnerabilities regarding this framework have been found 
and potentially many more are still undetected. Some vulnerabil- 
ities considered in this study are very recent and they were only 
patched in the latest version of the product. The results show that 
the majority of TensorFlow vulnerabilities are not entirely different 
from issues regarding general-purpose products written in C/C++. 
However, they can be more diï¬ƒcult to ï¬nd as it often requires 
deep semantic interpretation and good understanding of mathe- 
matical methods used. This seems to be the most likely cause of 
virtually zero effectiveness of examined SATs in detecting known 
vulnerabilities. Only one reported warning was included in one of 
the examined vulnerability ï¬xes. Nevertheless, we ï¬nd that some 
of the warnings can be used to improve the code quality and re- 
duce the chance of introducing new issues. Potentially, some com- 
mercial SATs can be more effective (e.g. they can include more 
rules), however in our study we decided to use only freely avail- 
able SATs that can be used by every researcher/programmer. 
Since automated analysis is failing, it is up to developers to fo- 
cus more on preventing the introduction and ï¬xing existing vul- 
nerabilities. Based on the results of our analysis in Appendix A , we 
provide a checklist for developers/users of TensorFlow (and other 
numerical and DL libraries) that can be used to check their source 
code and potentially eliminate some common programming mis- 
takes (we do not claim that these remarks are groundbreaking, 
however, the issues they relate to are still common and promi- 
nent). This list can also be used by programmers of non-AI plat- 
forms along with other secure programming guidelines, as the ma- 
jority of the described issues also applies to general-purpose appli- 
cations written in C/C++. We also believe that our checklist can be 
useful for the creators of new SATs (especially those that aim to be 
effective for the numerical libraries) - as a source of inspiration for 
new rules and to build the test cases. Here, we would like to en- 
courage other researchers to use these insights to create tools that 
would aim to improve the security of numerical libraries - since 
this type of software is widely used and its security is becoming 
critical. It is vital to provide automatic tools that would be able to 
ï¬nd at least some of the vulnerabilities in such products. We also 
aim to build such a tool in our future work based on the ï¬ndings 
presented in the current paper. We would also like to encourage 
other researchers to examine different vulnerability types in Ten- 
sorFlow (and possibly other numerical libraries) to describe even 
more thoroughly the threat landscape in these types of libraries.

Appendix A. Vulnerability Checklist 
Based on the results of our analysis presented in the article, we 
provide a checklist for developers and users of TensorFlow library 
(and other numerical and DL libraries written especially in C/C++) 
that can be used to check their source code and potentially ï¬nd 
and eliminate some common programming mistakes. This list can 
also be used by programmers of non-AI platforms along with other 
11
[Page 12]
K. Filus and J. Doma Â´nska Computers & Security 124 (2023) 102948 
guidelines - the majority of the issues also applies to general- 
purpose C/C++ applications. We also encourage creators of new 
static analysis tools to use this checklist as a source of inspiration 
for creating new rules and for building their test cases. 
What can developers of DL libraries and TensorFlow do? 
â–¡ use SATs to improve the quality of source code (be sure alerts 
are only false positives - e.g. memcpy usages) and use good 
programming practises to facilitate work of future program- 
mers. 
â–¡ cover important parts (e.g. validation) with code and not 
â€™TODOâ€™s. 
â–¡ when dealing with C/C++ arrays (1) : 
â–¡ empty checks. 
â–¡ proper shape checks (dimensionality, number of necessary 
elements, they should be clearly described in the speciï¬ca- 
tion). 
â–¡ type checks. 
â–¡ checks for overï¬‚ows regarding large data structures. 
â–¡ compatibility check when more than one array is used in an 
operation 
â–¡ check all the arrays - do not assume correctness by 
checking only some of them. 
â–¡ be careful when accessing arrays in paralell with one in- 
dex - be sure that it is safe. 
â–¡ be careful when you use reverse indexing 
â–¡ when dealing with pointers: 
â–¡ nullpointer checks. 
â–¡ when pointer is used to access array elements, check 
whether it is possible (e.g. pointer incrementation). 
â–¡ when dealing with variables in general (2) : 
â–¡ check whether they are assigned. 
â–¡ use type checks. 
â–¡ use format checks (e.g. when strings are given as an input). 
â–¡ use value checks 
â–¡ check limits for the type (to prevent overï¬‚ows). 
â–¡ check assumptions of the method (they should be clearly 
described in the speciï¬cation). 
â–¡ check compatibility with other arguments (e.g. when 
variable is used as an index). 
â–¡ do not use obsolete functions and replace them with safer 
alternatives (e.g. use â€˜AddDimWithStatusâ€˜ instead of â€˜Ad- 
dDimâ€˜) (3) . 
â–¡ do not shadow the variables used in the functions - this can 
make future developersâ€™ work more diï¬ƒcult and potentially 
lead to vulnerabilities. 
What can developers of DL applications using TensorFlow do 
(or other similar libraries)? 
For developers of external applications, the same advice as in 
(1) and (2) applies. They should validate the parameters and data 
structures passed to tensorï¬‚ow. They do not have control over the 
implementation of tensorï¬‚ow, e.g. over pointer incrementation or 
the use of obsolete functions - see (3), but in the second case they 
do have control over what APIs they use and here a risk assess- 
ment should be performed whether it is worthwhile to use an API 
that uses a particular function that may cause vulnerabilities. 
Additionally, an extension of the above list can be introduced 
for developers of external applications using DL libraries: 
â–¡ when it does not require to create very advanced method, bet- 
ter create your own solutions - this way you know what EX- 
ACTLY is implemented and even when the failure happens, you 
can easily correct them (no waiting for a 3rd party library ï¬x 
required). 
â–¡ use only maintained APIs, check for alternatives, when the de- 
sired API is unmaintained or create your own one.

Detection in Codebase

Abstract
In this research paper, a detailed investigation presents the utilization of the BiT5 Bidirectional NLP model for detecting vulnerabil-
ities within codebases. The study addresses the pressing need for techniques enhancing software security by effectively identifying
vulnerabilities. Methodologically, the paper introduces BiT5, specifically designed for code analysis and vulnerability detection,
encompassing dataset collection, preprocessing steps, and model fine-tuning.
The key findings underscore BiT5â€™s efficacy in pinpointing vulnerabilities within code snippets, notably reducing both false
positives and false negatives. This research contributes by o ffering a methodology for leveraging BiT5 in vulnerability detection,
thus significantly bolstering software security and mitigating risks associated with code vulnerabilities.

1. Introduction
In the world of software systems ensuring security is a crucial concern. The presence of weaknesses, in software
codes, poses a risk to the stability and safety of these systems. The seriousness of these threats cannot be overstated, in
sectors like finance, healthcare, and infrastructure. These vulnerabilities serve as potential gateways for cyber threats,

BiT5: A Bidirectional NLP Approach for Advanced Vulnerability
Detection in Codebase
Prabith GSc,a,âˆ—, Rohit Narayanan M d,a, Arya A e,a, Aneesh Nadh R f,a, Binu PK g,b
aDepartment of Computer Science and Engineering, Amrita School of Computing, Amrita Vishwa Vidyapeetham, Amritapuri, India

Abstract
In this research paper, a detailed investigation presents the utilization of the BiT5 Bidirectional NLP model for detecting vulnerabil-
ities within codebases. The study addresses the pressing need for techniques enhancing software security by effectively identifying
vulnerabilities. Methodologically, the paper introduces BiT5, specifically designed for code analysis and vulnerability detection,
encompassing dataset collection, preprocessing steps, and model fine-tuning.
The key findings underscore BiT5â€™s efficacy in pinpointing vulnerabilities within code snippets, notably reducing both false
positives and false negatives. This research contributes by o ffering a methodology for leveraging BiT5 in vulnerability detection,
thus significantly bolstering software security and mitigating risks associated with code vulnerabilities.

1. Introduction
In the world of software systems ensuring security is a crucial concern. The presence of weaknesses, in software
codes, poses a risk to the stability and safety of these systems. The seriousness of these threats cannot be overstated, in
sectors like finance, healthcare, and infrastructure. These vulnerabilities serve as potential gateways for cyber threats,
1877-0509 Â© 2024 The Authors. Published by Elsevier B.V .
This is an open access article under the CC BY -NC-ND license (http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-nc-nd/4.0/)
Peer-review under responsibility of the scientific committee of the 5th International Conference on Innovative Data Communication Technologies
and Application.
2 Prabith GS et al. / Procedia Computer Science 00 (2024) 000â€“000
enabling data breaches and unauthorized access that can wreak havoc, causing substantial financial losses, compro-
mising the confidentiality of sensitive information in sectors like finance and healthcare, and disruptive breakdowns
in critical infrastructure. The gravity of these threats cannot be overstated; they hold the potential to induce profound
societal and economic repercussions, emphasizing the criticality of a robust approach to identifying and mitigating
these vulnerabilities.
Vulnerabilities in software systems come in forms such as buffer overflows, injection attacks, and logical flaws.
Each type of vulnerability brings its set of challenges by exploiting weaknesses that compromise the confidentiality
and integrity of information. Additionally, with cyber threats evolving rapidly, it is essential to take an approach to
identify these vulnerabilities.
1.1. Emerging Need for Advanced NLP Techniques
The convergence of Natural Language Processing (NLP) and code analysis brings hope to vulnerability
detection[1]. NLP techniques provide an understanding of the language structures embedded in code going beyond
the limitations of syntax based analysis. Directional NLP models, like BiT5 introduce an approach by capturing con-
textual information from both preceding and succeeding code segments[2].
The intricate relationship between software vulnerabilities the challenges faced by detection methods and the rise
of NLP techniques sets the stage for an evolutionary step, towards safeguarding software systems[3, 4].
For instance, models like CodeT5+ showcase an advanced understanding of code structures, allowing accurate
identification of vulnerabilities across various programming languages. This capability surpasses traditional syntax-
based approaches, enabling nuanced context comprehension and precise vulnerability pinpointing within code snip-
pets. The robustness of these models in capturing contextual information from preceding and succeeding code seg-
ments further exemplifies their potential to fortify software security measures, marking a pivotal advancement in
safeguarding against cyber threats[2].
1.2. Introduction to BiT5: A Bidirectional NLP Model
The BiT5 modelâ€™s strengths encompass its Transformer-based architecture with self-attention mechanisms, facil-
itating robust relationship capture within code snippets by considering the token context. Its distinctive bidirectional
nature allows holistic comprehension of code semantics across subsequent segments[5, 6, 7], enhancing contextual
understanding within code segments. Moreover, leveraging token embeddings, BiT5 transforms raw code sequences
into dimensional representations, adeptly capturing syntax, and semantic structures, crucial for precise vulnerability
detection[8]. However, potential limitations might involve computational resource intensiveness due to its transformer-
based architecture and a need for substantial labeled data for effective fine-tuning, restricting applicability in scenarios
with limited labeled datasets.
1.2.1. Application Scope in Vulnerability Detection
BiT5 possesses capabilities that make it an invaluable asset, in the field of code analysis especially when it comes
to identifying vulnerabilities within software systems[9]. The models ability to analyze bidirectionally gives it an
advantage allowing it to recognize patterns and subtle cues that indicate vulnerabilities. By considering the context
of both preceding and succeeding parts of code BiT5 captures the essence of code segments comprehensively greatly
improving vulnerability detection accuracy.
Additionally BiT5s proficiency in handling transformations that preserve the meaning of code addresses a standing
challenge in vulnerability detection[10]. These transformations are often used to hide vulnerabilities. Have proven
difficult for methods. However thanks to its understanding of code semantics BiT5 is able to navigate through these
transformations reducing the risks associated with false positives or negatives.
The adaptability of BiT5 across programming languages further enhances its effectiveness. Its architecture is not
dependent on syntax intricacies allowing it to transcend language barriers and serve as a tool for vulnerability detec-
tion, in various codebases.

2. Literature Review
2.1. Traditional Methodologies for Vulnerability Detection
When it comes to software security there have been methods, like Dynamic analysis which observe code behavior
during execution but may not cover all scenarios comprehensively, Pattern matching and signature-based detection
rely on predefined patterns, which can limit their effectiveness against emerging or new threats that aim to find vul-
nerabilities in codebases. Static analysis examines code structure without execution, potentially missing complex
runtime issues. Dynamic analysis observes runtime behavior but may struggle to cover all scenarios. Pattern matching
and signature-based detection rely on predefined patterns, making them less effective against new threats.
2.2. Limitations of Conventional Approaches
Traditional approaches in vulnerability detection often grapple with overfitting, constraining their adaptability to
diverse code structures and languages. Their inherent inflexibility with programming languages hampers their ef-
fectiveness across environments. Real-time deployment complexities restrict their efficiency in dynamic software
systems. Scalability concerns further limit their capacity to comprehensively detect vulnerabilities, especially within
extensive codebases or large-scale systems.
Traditional approaches, like pattern matching, struggle to adapt to evolving threats. For instance, signature-based
detection relies on predefined patterns, making it less effective against new attack variations. In contrast, NLP-based
models, such as BiT5, excel in understanding nuanced code semantics, enabling the detection of vulnerabilities beyond
predefined patterns. Additionally, traditional methods often face scalability issues when handling extensive codebases,
limiting their comprehensive vulnerability detection across large-scale systems. In contrast, NLP techniques leverage
advanced models like BiT5 to efficiently analyze diverse codebases, enhancing scalability and adaptability in dynamic
software ecosystems.
2.3. Recent Advancements in NLP-Based Vulnerability Detection
Lately there have been advancements, in using NLP models to find weaknesses in codebases. BiT5 and CodeT5+
[11] are examples of NLP models that have shown skills in understanding the meaning of code and putting it into
context[11]. They outperform vulnerability detection methods by uncovering connections, within code snippets, which
improves their ability to identify vulnerabilities accurately and precisely.
2.4. Comparative Analysis of NLP-Driven Techniques
Comparing approaches, in Natural Language Processing (NLP) requires scrutinizing performance metrics like ac-
curacy, precision, recall, and F1 score across various models to assess their effectiveness in detecting vulnerabilities.
Our evaluation, spanning diverse codebases and programming languages, provides insights into the strengths and lim-
itations of each model, helping us identify areas of excellence and opportunities for improvement in their adaptability
and robustness when dealing with code structures.
2.5. Current Challenges and Future Directions
Although there have been advancements, in NLP based vulnerability detection there are still challenges that need to
be addressed. One of the obstacles is ensuring that models can effectively handle diverse codebases as this is crucial,
for their overall performance. Another challenge lies in language diversity as models often struggle to overcome
limitations when dealing with programming languages[3]. Additionally the real time applicability of these models
is hindered by demands making it difficult to seamlessly integrate them into software environments. For instance,
a model trained on Python might struggle when faced with C++ code due to syntactic and semantic disparities.
Moreover, ensuring real-time applicability of these models remains a challenge, given the demands for seamless
integration into dynamic software environments. This hurdle involves balancing computational demands with the
need for swift and accurate vulnerability detection within live systems.

3. Methodology
In the domain of identifying vulnerabilities, in software systems the process of acquiring and preparing datasets
plays a role in training Natural Language Processing (NLP) models[12]. This section explores the methods used to
gather and refine datasets thatâ€™re indispensable for vulnerability detection tasks.
3.1. Dataset Collection and Preparation Techniques
The search for datasets begins with an approach that involves various sources and careful curation methods.
Repositories such as the Software Assurance Reference Dataset (SARD) BigVuln, National Vulnerability Database
(NVD) and platforms like GitHub serve as resources offering a range of code snippets that encompass diverse
vulnerabilities[12].
SARD- A Goldmine of Vulnerabilities: SARD is renowned for its compilation of software flaws and vulnera-
bilities providing an abundance of real world code snippets. This repository is meticulously curated by the National
Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST). Covers vulnerabilities, in programming languages and domains. Lever-
aging SARD enhances the dataset with a variety of vulnerabilities enabling a training set with content.
BigVuln- Augmenting Diversity and Scale: The BigVuln dataset complements the effort by providing a col-
lection of code snippets that address vulnerabilities. This compilation includes advanced vulnerabilities expanding
the datasets depth and breadth. By including BigVuln we enhance the diversity and complexity, within the dataset
ensuring that the NLP model can effectively comprehend vulnerabilities.
NVD and GitHub Repositories- Real-World Insights: The National Vulnerability Database (NVD) and GitHub
repositories are resources that offer a real world view of vulnerabilities. NVD is known as a repository of vulnerability
related information encompassing vulnerabilities reported in software products thus providing an understanding of
real world vulnerabilities. GitHub, being a hub for codebases contributes up to date information on vulnerabilities
observed in actively developed projects.
For instance, SARD encapsulates vulnerabilities such as buffer overflows, SQL injections, and cross-site script-
ing (XSS) attacks. BigVuln, on the other hand, extends this diversity by including more sophisticated vulnerabilities
like zero-day exploits or race conditions, augmenting the datasetâ€™s complexity. Moreover, repositories like NVD and
GitHub contribute by providing insights into real-world vulnerabilities observed in software products and actively
developed projects, covering instances such as directory traversal, command injection, or code injection attacks, thus
exposing NLP models to a wide spectrum of vulnerabilities prevalent across various domains and programming lan-
guages, essential for comprehensive vulnerability detection.
The amalgamation of datasets from various repositories, coupled with meticulous preprocessing techniques, be-
queaths a robust foundation for training advanced NLP models. This curated dataset, rich in diversity and qual-
ity, forms the linchpin for enhancing the efficacy of vulnerability detection using Bidirectional NLP models like
BiT5[13, 14].
3.2. Preprocessing Techniques for Dataset Refinement
3.2.1. Data Cleaning for Uniformity
Standardizing Code Snippets:
Aligning code snippets to a structure is a step in achieving uniformity across the dataset. This process involves remov-
ing variations in coding styles, indentation and formatting ensuring that the dataset presents a representation of code
logic to enhance the models understanding of code semantics.
Removal of Redundant Elements
It is crucial to eliminate comments, excessive whitespace or non executable code segments within the snippets. By
doing we can streamline the snippets. Focus on essential code segments that are relevant to vulnerability detection
enabling the model to accurately identify vulnerabilities[13, 15, 14].
3.2.2. F ormatting and Labeling
Code Tokenization
The process of dissecting code snippets into units or tokens, aids in enhancing our comprehension of their syntactic and

Balancing the Dataset
Another important aspect is to balance the dataset[16, 17]. Itâ€™s essential to have a representation of both non vulner-
able instances. Imbalanced datasets can introduce biases and negatively impact model learning. Techniques such, as
oversampling or undersampling can be employed to achieve a distribution, which promotes unbiased model training.
3.3. BiT5 Architecture and Suitability for Vulnerability Detection
3.3.1. BiT5 Architecture Overview
Bidirectional Transformer Framework
Self Attention Mechanisms: The core element of BiT5 lies in its self attention mechanisms, which allow the model
to simultaneously weigh and contextualize parts of the code snippet. By utilizing head attention layers BiT5 assesses
dependencies among code tokens bidirectionally enabling a comprehensive understanding of the context in which the
code operates.
Encoder-Decoder Paradigm: BiT5 employs an encoder decoder architecture that facilitates processing. This ar-
chitecture not captures the sequence relationships within the code but also incorporates a decoding mechanism to
generate meaningful representations that encompass both directions of the codebases context.
3.3.2. Bidirectional Code Processing
Contextual Embeddings: excels at generating embeddings for code tokens by encoding syntactic and semantic in-
formation bidirectionally. This approach enables a nuanced comprehension of the aspects in the code. By considering
both directions this bidirectional encoding strategy enhances the models ability to capture patterns and nuances in
code semantics.
Semantic Understanding: Through its integration of processing BiT5 achieves an understanding of code semantics
by considering relationships between different segments in both directions. This holistic interpretation allows for an
analysis of factors such as code structure, functions and interactions, between variables, methods or classes.
3.3.3. Suitability for Vulnerability Detection
When it comes to identifying vulnerabilities BiT5 excels due, to its ability to understand the nuanced connections
and dependencies present in code snippets. This comprehensive understanding allows the model to uncover vulnera-
bilities that may be hidden within code structures or disguised by variations, in semantics.
Handling Diverse Codebases BiT5 possesses the ability to handle codebases effectively. It can easily accommodate
syntaxes, semantics and programming languages which helps overcome the challenges associated with code diversity
that exist in real world software systems[3].
3.4. Applicability of BiT5 in Vulnerability Detection
3.4.1. Bidirectional Understanding of Code Structures
Comprehensive Contextualization: Thanks, to its nature BiT5 can grasp code structures comprehensively by plac-
ing code snippets in their contexts. It captures dependencies and relationships within the code identifying nuances that
may indicate vulnerabilities.
6 Prabith GS et al. / Procedia Computer Science 00 (2024) 000â€“000
Semantic Context Analysis: By considering context BiT5 understands the implications of different parts of code. It
recognizes the multifaceted relationships between these elements allowing it to identify vulnerabilities that might go
unnoticed by models.
3.4.2. Addressing Traditional Method Challenges
Overcoming Overfitting: Through its processing approach BiT5 reduces overfitting problems by taking into account
context instead of relying solely on isolated code segments. This improves model robustness. Enables generalization
across diverse codebases.
Handling Language Diversity: BiT5s bidirectional nature allows it to transcend language barriers and adapt to
syntaxes and semantics across programming languages. It possesses an understanding of code regardless of language
constraints giving it a significant advantage, over traditional methods.
3.4.3. Enhanced NLP Capabilities
Advanced Semantic Understanding: BiT5 possesses natural language processing capabilities allowing it to com-
prehend the semantics of code more deeply. This enables an analysis of code structures and enhances the accuracy of
detecting vulnerabilities.
Contextualized Vulnerability Identification: By conducting analysis BiT5 contextualizes potential vulnerabilities,
within the larger code context reducing the occurrence of false positives and negatives. This contextual understanding
ensures a identification of vulnerabilities.
3.5. Fine-Tuning BiT5 for Vulnerability Detection
3.5.1. Initialization of BiT5 Model
Model Configuration for Vulnerability Detection Configuring the trained BiT5 model for vulnerability detection
tasks is a crucial step during the initialization phase. One key aspect is modifying the models output layer to cater to
classification, where it distinguishes between non vulnerable code segments. This entails adjusting the output layer
structure to align with the requirements of identifying vulnerabilities.
3.5.2. Fine-Tuning Process
Training Methodology: The tuning process aims to optimize BiT5s performance in vulnerability detection by
utilizing a dataset specifically prepared for this task[18, 18]. Through training the model adapts its weights and pa-
rameters to effectively identify vulnerabilities within code snippets.
Loss Function Selection: To guide the tuning phase a binary cross entropy loss function is employed. This func-
tion is selected due to its effectiveness in facilitating the learning process for classification tasks. It enables BiT5s
parameters to be optimized accurately classifying code segments as either vulnerable or non vulnerable.
Hyperparameter Tuning: Optimizing hyperparameters plays a role in tuning. Parameters such, as learning rate
batch size and number of training epochs are adjusted meticulously to achieve optimal model performance. By ad-
justing these hyperparameters we can ensure that converges reducing loss and improving accuracy, in vulnerability
detection.
Weight Optimization Strategies: To tune the models weights we employ techniques such as gradient descent
based methods, regularization and adaptive learning rates. These approaches help refine BiT5s weights through a
process ultimately enhancing its capability to accurately detect vulnerabilities, in code snippets.

4.2.2. Precision and Recall Trade-offs

compared to Code T5. LineVul achieves a F1 Score of 90% demonstrating a balance, between precision and recall
albeit with a slight trade off.
The comparative assessment reveals differences in vulnerability detection models. Code T5 demonstrates perfor-
mance by balancing precision and recall. DeepWukong prioritizes recall, while LineVul strikes a balance but leans
slightly towards precision. In conclusion Code T5 is chosen as the model for research in this field due to its overall
performance.

5. Conclusions
The research contributes to the field of cybersecurity and software development in several key ways:
Advanced Vulnerability Detection: By employing state-of-the-art transformer-based models and leveraging large-
scale datasets, the study advances the sophistication and accuracy of vulnerability detection methodologies.
Optimized Model Training: The experiments provided insights into fine-tuning models, showcasing techniques to
enhance accuracy while minimizing false positives in vulnerability identification.
The research efforts were focused on optimizing vulnerability detection using transformer-based models like
CodeT5+. Through meticulous fine-tuning, the CodeT5+ model exhibited remarkable enhancements in accuracy,
showcasing a significant increase from 94% to 97.47%, and recall, rising from 93% to 98%. These improvements
were pivotal in ensuring the modelâ€™s adeptness at precisely identifying vulnerabilities within code snippets. While
the study emphasizes the positive advancements in vulnerability detection methodologies by leveraging transformer-
based models and augmented datasets, it is crucial to acknowledge potential limitations. Transformer-based models
might still face challenges in handling semantic-preserving code transformations or nuanced vulnerabilities embedded
within complex code structures. Moreover, ensuring the scalability of these models to accommodate diverse codebases
across multiple programming languages remains an ongoing challenge.

CodeEnhancer: LLM-generated Python code enhancement through SAST 
integration and fine-tuning
Jongmin Lee a
 ,âˆ—, Khang Mai a,b,c
 , Nakul Ghate d
 , Tomohiko Yagyu d
 , Razvan Beuran a
 , 
Yasuo Tan a
a Japan Advanced Institute of Science and Technology, 1-1 Asahidai, Nomi, Ishikawa, 923-1211, Japan
b University of Information Technology, Ho Chi Minh City, Viet Nam
c Vietnam National University, Ho Chi Minh City, Viet Nam
d NEC Corporation, Shiba 5-7-1, Minato-ku, 108-8001, Tokyo, Japan
A R T I C L E  I N F O
Keywords:
Large Language Models (LLMs)
Syntax checking
Vulnerability detection
Functional correctness
Static application security testing
LLM fine-tuning
 A B S T R A C T
Despite the rapid adoption of Large Language Models (LLMs) for automatic code generation, their output 
often exhibits syntax errors, security vulnerabilities, and functional inconsistencies. To address these issues, 
we present CodeEnhancer, a two-stage framework that tightly integrates LLMs with static application security 
testing (SAST) tools and targeted fine-tuning. The goal is to produce more secure and functionally correct 
Python code. In the first stage, our iterative validation pipeline couples LLM-generated code with tools such as 
Pylint and Bandit. These tools automatically identify and remediate issues through structured feedback loops. 
When applied to the GPT-4o model, this process eliminated 82.8% of the initial vulnerabilities and resolved 
all the detected functional correctness issues when tested on the LLMSecEval dataset. In the second stage, we 
fine-tune the LLMs using two types of secure code examples: expert-written samples and code refined by our 
framework. Comparative experiments demonstrate that the framework-tuned model outperforms the baseline 
and expert-tuned models. The framework-tuned model generates only 18.4% vulnerable code snippets on the 
LLMSecEval dataset, whereas the baseline and expert-tuned models produce 43.6% and 54.7% vulnerable code 
snippets, respectively. The framework-tuned model reduces final vulnerability rates to 6.7% on LLMSecEval 
and 3.5% on the SecurityEval dataset. Our results highlight the synergistic effect of integrating static analysis 
with feedback-informed fine-tuning. They also reveal limitations in current evaluation metrics and dataset 
representativeness. These findings suggest a scalable, robust approach to achieving more secure, trustworthy, 
and practical AI-assisted code generation.
1. Introduction
The rapid advancement of Large Language Models (LLMs), such as 
GPT-4 [1], Code Llama [2], and Codex [3], is revolutionizing software 
development. For example, via GitHub Copilot, LLMs are integrated 
into daily programming workflows. LLMs generate code from natural-
language descriptions, accelerating development cycles and automat-
ing complex tasks [1,3]. This offers substantial potential for boosting 
developer productivity and efficiency.
However, this transformative potential is tempered by critical con-
cerns regarding the quality and reliability of the code generated by 
LLMs, particularly with regard to security vulnerabilities. While these 
models can produce functional code snippets, they often generate code 
with syntactic errors, stylistic inconsistencies, and critical security vul-
nerabilities that can lead to severe real-world consequences [4,5].

Empirical studies have confirmed that code generated by popular LLMs 
often contains weaknesses listed in the MITRE Common Weakness 
Enumeration (CWE) Top 25. These weaknesses include command in-
jection (CWE-78), SQL injection (CWE-89), path traversal (CWE-22), 
and insecure use of cryptography (CWE-327) [6,7].
Furthermore, ensuring that the generated code precisely implements 
the functionality specified in the natural language prompt, a prop-
erty often referred to as functional correctness or prompt adherence, 
remains a notable hurdle. Although execution-based evaluations on 
standard coding benchmarks [3] can verify correctness against pre-
defined test cases, they may overlook subtle deviations in nuanced 
free-form prompts. Previous research has demonstrated that LLMs can 
generate code that seems plausible or even passes certain tests yet con-
tains logical errors or fails to align with the userâ€™s intended behavior,

resulting in functional bugs [6]. Automatically evaluating this align-
ment is difficult. Metrics designed primarily for code similarity, such 
as CodeBLEU [8], CodeBERTScore [9] and CodeScore [10], measure 
structural or semantic resemblance to reference code. However, they 
cannot inherently verify behavioral equivalence or guarantee that the 
code accurately fulfills the promptâ€™s specific functional goals. This gap 
highlights the ongoing challenge of automatically validating the true 
functional correctness and prompt fidelity of LLM-generated code.
To comprehensively address these multifaceted issues, this paper 
proposes a novel two-stage framework named CodeEnhancer that im-
proves the security, correctness, and quality of LLM-generated Python 
code. The framework integrates automated validation with targeted 
model improvement through fine-tuning. As a contribution to the re-
search community, we provide the full implementation of the CodeEn-
hancer framework on GitHub.1
The first stage of CodeEnhancer consists of an iterative validation 
and refinement pipeline. This pipeline couples the LLMâ€™s code gener-
ation capabilities with established Static Application Security Testing 
(SAST) tools. Specifically, it uses Pylint [11] to check for syntax is-
sues, and Bandit [12] to detect security vulnerabilities. When the LLM 
generates an initial code snippet based on a natural language prompt, 
these SAST tools are used to analyze it. Any detected issues trigger 
a structured feedback mechanism that provides the LLM with specific 
details, such as the type, location, and severity of the issue, which are 
necessary to revise the code. The generate-validate-refine loop then 
iterates, progressively improving the code until it passes all checks or 
reaches a predefined iteration limit.
While this iterative validation pipeline is effective for post-generation 
correction, it has limitations when relied on solely. The process can be 
computationally intensive and may struggle with complex vulnerabil-
ities that require a deeper understanding of security. Additionally, it 
does not improve the LLMâ€™s inherent ability to proactively generate 
secure code. The LLM remains reactive, depending entirely on external 
tool feedback.
Therefore, the second stage of our framework introduces a targeted 
fine-tuning methodology to enhance the LLMâ€™s intrinsic security aware-
ness and code generation capabilities. This stage adapts the base LLM 
(GPT-4o) using specialized datasets containing secure coding exam-
ples. In particular, fine-tuning is done with one of the following: (1) 
an existing dataset comprising expert-written secure code examples, 
representing best practices and an idealized security standard [13], 
and (2) a novel dataset curated from the framework-refined code 
outputs produced by the first stage (the validation pipeline) of our 
own framework. Thus, we can explore whether LLMs benefit more 
from learning idealized secure patterns or from learning the practical 
process of transforming potentially flawed code into secure, validated 
code via automated feedback loops. We hypothesize that fine-tuning 
on framework-refined data will better prepare the LLM to handle real-
world coding scenarios and generate more robust, secure code from the 
beginning.
The synergy between these two stages is crucial. The fine-tuned LLM 
produces better initial code, reducing the workload and the number of 
iterations required in the validation pipeline. At the same time, the 
validation pipeline can generate better, more refined code examples 
that could be used for further stage of model improvement, creating 
a virtuous cycle.
The primary contributions of this paper are:
1. The design and implementation of a comprehensive, two-stage 
CodeEnhancer framework integrating an iterative LLM-SAST 
validation pipeline and a subsequent targeted LLM fine-tuning 
methodology to enhance Python code security.
1 https://github.com/cyb3rlab/CodeEnhancer
2. A rigorous evaluation demonstrating the frameworkâ€™s effective-
ness using the LLMSecEval benchmark [13] to validate the first 
stage and the LLMSecEval and SecurityEval benchmarks [14] to 
assess the performance of the fine-tuned models in the second 
stage. In particular, the evaluation compares the effectiveness 
of fine-tuning with datasets derived from expert-written secure 
examples and those generated by the automated refinement pro-
cess. The results highlight the benefits of the integrated approach 
and the superiority of leveraging framework-refined data for 
fine-tuning. Notably, this approach outperformed expert-written 
examples in terms of model performance and proved to be more 
cost-effective.
3. An analysis provides insights into the synergistic benefits of 
combining automated validation with model adaptation. This 
contributes to the development of more trustworthy and secure 
AI-assisted coding practices.
The remainder of this paper is structured as follows: Section 2 
provides a background and motivation for the research, and Section 3 
reviews related work in LLM-based code generation, security vulnera-
bility detection, static analysis, and fine-tuning approaches. Section 4 
details the proposed methodology, elaborating on both the real-time 
validation pipeline and the fine-tuning extension. Section 5 outlines the 
experiment setup, including datasets, models, and evaluation metrics. 
Section 6 presents and analyzes the experimental results, comparing the 
performance of the baseline and fine-tuned models. Section 7 discusses 
the limitations of the current work and suggests directions for future 
research. Finally, Section 8 concludes the paper by summarizing the 
key findings and contributions.
2. Background and motivation
The advent of LLMs is a significant milestone in artificial intelli-
gence that has had a profound impact on various domains, including 
software engineering. Models such as Mistral [15], GPT-4 [1], and 
DeepSeek-R1 [16] are trained on vast datasets containing billions of 
lines of code and natural language text. This extensive training en-
ables these models to discern complex patterns, syntax, and common 
programming idioms across multiple languages. Consequently, these 
models can generate code directly from natural language prompts, 
offering substantial potential to accelerate software development [17]. 
Integrated tools, such as GitHub Copilot, leverage these capabilities 
by automating routine coding tasks, allowing developers to focus on 
higher-level system design and problem-solving and boosting produc-
tivity [4].
Alongside the rise of AI-driven code generation, Static Application 
Security Testing (SAST) has become integral to modern secure software 
development practices. SAST tools analyze application source code, 
bytecode, or binary code without executing it, aiming to detect po-
tential bugs, style inconsistencies, and security vulnerabilities early in 
the development lifecycle [18]. SAST tools employ techniques such 
as pattern matching, data flow analysis, and control flow analysis to 
identify deviations from coding standards, such as using Pylint [11] 
to check for compliance with Pythonâ€™s PEP 8, and common security 
pitfalls such as those cataloged by OWASP or MITRE. Security-focused 
SAST tools like Bandit [12] for Python or the more general-purpose 
CodeQL [19] specifically target known vulnerability patterns, including 
SQL injection, cross-site scripting (XSS), hardcoded secrets, and inse-
cure API usage. Early detection through SAST is crucial for reducing 
the cost and effort required for remediation compared to finding flaws 
later in testing or after deployment.
Despite their impressive code generation capabilities, LLMs are 
not infallible. A growing body of evidence highlights significant con-
cerns about the quality and security of the code LLMs produce [4â€“6]. 
LLM-generated code frequently contains:
Knowledge-Based Systems 342 (2026) 115925 
2 
[Page 3]
J. Lee et al.
1. Syntax Errors: Recent work [20] has revealed that syntax er-
rors account for most faults in LLM-generated Verilog code. 
Addressing these errors alone achieved a 98.5% fix rate using 
retrieval-based prompting in the study, highlighting syntax cor-
rection as a critical step toward improving the reliability of 
machine-generated code.
2. Security Vulnerabilities: LLMs often replicate insecure coding 
patterns that are present in their vast training data, generating 
code susceptible to exploits such as command injection, path 
traversal, and improper cryptographic function handling [6,7].
3. Functional Correctness Issues: Ensuring that the generated 
code accurately reflects the userâ€™s intent, as specified in the 
prompt, remains a critical challenge [6]. LLMs may misinter-
pret requirements, overlook edge cases, or produce code with 
subtle logical flaws, leading to incorrect behavior even if it is 
syntactically valid [21].
These shortcomings necessitate robust mechanisms to validate and 
improve LLM-generated code before integrating it into software projects. 
However, relying solely on LLMs to iteratively fix or refine their own 
code often yields suboptimal results. This approach suffers from a 
form of model bias, wherein the same reasoning flaws that led to the 
initial issues may persist or compound during self-revision. A recent 
study [22] has demonstrated that LLMs frequently struggle to detect 
or correct nuanced logical or security flaws in their own outputs, espe-
cially in the absence of structured external feedback. Previous research 
found that LLMs often fail to self-correct reasoning errors without 
external input, and in some cases, their performance degrades after 
self-correction. Similarly, another study highlighted that self-correction 
without external guidance can lead to overfitting to syntactic patterns, 
which limits the modelâ€™s ability to ensure functional correctness or 
robust security guarantees [23].
Other researchers also have shown that fine-tuning large language 
models on carefully constructed code datasets can improve their ability 
to generate more secure and functional code. Training on examples that 
reflect secure coding practices reduces the likelihood of introducing 
vulnerabilities while improving the syntactic and semantic quality of 
the outputs. These findings suggest that fine-tuning is an effective 
mechanism for aligning LLMs with practical coding standards and 
expectations in real-world development settings [24,25].
Therefore, this paper addresses the limitations of relying solely on 
LLM code generation, post-hoc SAST analysis, or isolated fine-tuning 
efforts. There is a clear need for a more holistic approach. We propose 
and evaluate a comprehensive, integrated framework that combines 
the strengths of LLMs and SAST tools synergistically. Our framework 
establishes a virtuous cycle in which an iterative validation pipeline 
integrates SAST feedback to refine generated code. Simultaneously, a 
targeted fine-tuning methodology leverages these refined outputs to 
enhance the LLMâ€™s ability to generate secure, functionally correct code 
from the outset. The overarching goal is to create a more robust and 
trustworthy pathway for leveraging LLMs in software development by 
addressing syntax, security, and functional correctness in a unified, 
multi-stage process.
3. Related work
Research efforts to improve the quality and security of LLM-genera
ted code span several areas, including direct code generation im-
provements, automated code repair, the use of SAST tools, specific 
evaluation methodologies, and fine-tuning techniques. Table  1 provides 
a comparative overview of representative approaches based on their 
primary focus and the specific aspects of code quality they address, 
contextualizing our proposed integrated framework.
3.1. LLM-based frameworks for code generation, validation, and repair
Recent advances in LLM-based code generation have led to a diverse 
array of frameworks that aim to improve the quality, correctness, 
and security of generated code. As summarized in Table  1, these 
approaches differ in their primary focus, tool integration, and treatment 
of validation or repair tasks.
Early work by Chen et al. [3] introduced Codex, a fine-tuned 
GPT-3 model trained on code data, which was demonstrated to be 
capable of generating functional code from natural language prompts. 
However, Codex did not explicitly address code repair or security 
validation, despite achieving high pass rates on benchmark tasks such 
as HumanEval.
In contrast, Alrashedy et al. [26] presented a framework that in-
tegrates LLMs with SAST tools to automatically patch security vul-
nerabilities in source code. Their system leverages SAST tool output 
to generate prompts for LLM-based repair and is one of the earliest 
pipelines to combine static analysis and generation in an automated 
feedback loop.
Pearce et al. [27] further investigated the zero-shot repair capabil-
ities of Codex on vulnerable code snippets. Although no fine-tuning or 
external validation tools were used, the study revealed the potential 
and limitations of prompting alone in addressing security-related issues.
More recent work has shifted toward improving the intrinsic ability 
of LLMs to produce secure code through fine-tuning. For example, Li 
et al. [24] conducted an empirical study on fine-tuning models using 
security patch commits and demonstrated measurable improvements 
in vulnerability reduction. Similarly, Weyssow et al. [25] explored 
parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) methods for code generation, 
however, their study focused more on syntax and structural quality 
than on vulnerability mitigation.
Separately, Keltek et al. [28] proposed LSAST, a hybrid system in 
which SAST tools, such as Bearer, are paired with LLMs to enhance vul-
nerability detection coverage. Although LSAST is not explicitly aimed 
at code generation or repair, it exemplifies the complementary use of 
LLMs for security analysis and code validation.
Building on these advancements, research published in 2024 and 
2025 has scrutinized the efficacy of autonomous self-correction in 
LLMs. For example, Olausson et al. [30] demonstrated that relying 
solely on an LLMâ€™s intrinsic self-repair capabilities without robust ex-
ternal feedback often yields diminishing returns or introduces new 
errors. To overcome this limitation, the field is rapidly shifting toward 
iterative optimization frameworks. Ridnik et al. [29] introduced flow 
engineering approaches that use test-driven validation to refine code 
iteratively, while Kumar et al. [31] explored reinforcement learning 
methods to train models specifically for self-correction.
Unlike prior studies that intentionally prompt the model to generate 
insecure code by using artificial inputs, focus on isolated aspects such 
as generation and repair, or struggle with the limitations of intrinsic 
self-correction, our framework integrates all these components into a 
unified pipeline that employs natural, real-world prompts. By combin-
ing iterative static validation with fine-tuning on both expert-written 
and framework-refined code, our approach systematically bypasses the 
unreliability of autonomous self-repair highlighted in recent literature. 
It addresses syntax errors, functional correctness, and security vulner-
abilities cohesively, firmly positioning our work within the rapidly 
evolving domain of automated, feedback-driven code optimization.
3.2. Code evaluation using SAST tools
SAST tools are standard instruments for security assessment. For 
Python, Bandit [12] targets common security flaws, and Pylint [11] 
checks for code smells, style issues, and syntax errors. More sophis-
ticated tools like GitHubâ€™s CodeQL adopt semantic analysis to detect 
complex vulnerabilities across multiple languages [19]. Researchers

3.3. Functional correctness evaluation
Validating that generated code behaves according to the intention 
expressed in the prompt is crucial yet challenging. Metrics such as 
CodeBLEU [8] and CodeBERTScore [9] measure code similarity by 
directly comparing the reference code and the target code. Execution-
based testing using benchmarks such as HumanEval [3] or The Mostly 
Basic Programming Problems (MBPP) [36] measures functional correct-
ness by checking pass rates against predefined unit tests [37]. While 
valuable, this approach might not fully cover the promptâ€™s specification. 
To address this issue, newer metrics aim for better alignment without 
relying solely on reference code. CodeScore [10] trains a model to 
predict execution outcomes. ICE-Score [38] uses an LLM itself to assess 
LLM-generated code against the given input prompt. SBC-Score [39] 
employs a novel reverse-generation technique, inferring requirements 
from the generated code and comparing them back to the original 
prompt using semantic similarity, lexical overlap, and completeness 
measures. Our framework incorporates a functional validation step 
using LLM reasoning based on prompt-derived specifications.
4. CodeEnhancer methodology
CodeEnhancer improves the security and quality of LLM-generated 
Python code with a two-stage approach: (1) a code generation & valida-
tion and refinement pipeline that integrates LLMs with SAST tools, and 
(2) a fine-tuning methodology that improves the LLMâ€™s secure coding 
capabilities. Fig.  1 provides an overview of this integrated architecture.
4.1. Stage 1: Code generation & validation and refinement pipeline
The first stage focuses on generating code and iteratively improving 
it based on immediate feedback from SAST tools. This pipeline con-
sists of several key steps designed to address syntactic, security, and 
functional correctness progressively, thus being in alignment with a 
structured quality assurance process.
4.1.1. Code generation with structured prompt template
LLMs often produce syntactically correct yet structurally inconsis-
tent or incomplete code when prompted with free-form instructions. 
To address this, our framework adopts a structured prompt template 
that demonstrates the desired output format and enforces a consistent 
generation template across diverse tasks.
The process begins with a natural language prompt provided by the 
user that describes the desired code functionality. To enhance clarity 
and facilitate subsequent validation, we employ a structured prompt 
template. This template instructs the LLM to generate functional code 
and a detailed docstring that restates the userâ€™s request, specifies the 
codeâ€™s purpose, and describes the steps to achieve the intended func-
tionality. The LLM then processes this structured input to generate an 
initial Python code snippet with an embedded docstring that serves as 
a functional specification.
The core idea is to guide the LLM to include a module-level doc-
string with three required fields at the top of each Python file.
1. Input Prompt â€” a restatement of the original user request.
2. Intention â€” the purpose or goal of the function.
3. Functionality â€” a precise description of how the function
achieves that goal.
This docstring improves the code and enables automated down-
stream evaluation. For example, our functional correctness validation 
leverages LLM reasoning to compare the functionality described in the 
docstring with the actual code logic.
4.1.2. Multi-faceted code validation
The Code Validation component iteratively improves the quality 
and security of LLM-generated code by detecting and correcting errors 
across multiple dimensions. This process integrates LLMs with SAST 
tools using three validation components, as follows:
1. Syntax Error Validation: The framework incorporates Pylint to 
validate the syntactic correctness and structure of the generated 
code. This includes identifying missing or misplaced elements 
such as parentheses, indentation inconsistencies and improper 
use of reserved keywords. Identified issues are logged, and cor-
rective prompts are sent to the LLM, which iteratively refines 
the code to align with these standards. This ensures that the 
generated code is both executable and adheres to basic syntac-
tic conventions. Fig.  2 provides an example of a syntax issue 
detected by Pylint, illustrating the type of feedback used for 
iterative correction.
2. Vulnerability Validation: To ensure security, the framework 
integrates Bandit, a SAST tool specifically designed for Python. 
Bandit scans the code for vulnerabilities, such as command
