efficiency of vulnerability detection. VSGFuzz is modeled as a Markov 
decision process, employing a reinforcement learning algorithm to 
direct superior mutation operations for generating higher-quality seed 
inputs. This approach optimizes the fuzzing process, making it more 
effective in identifying vulnerabilities in binary programs. VSGFuzz 
also leverages the RL algorithm to guide the mutation of input seeds 
with a higher likelihood of reaching vulnerable code segments. Unlike 
the equal seed mutation strategy commonly used by existing coverage-
based fuzzers, VSGFuzz emphasizes triggering crashes or attaining 
higher seed values. This approach capitalizes on the strengths of vul-
nerability prediction and coverage while mitigating their respective 
limitations. The contributions of this paper are summarized as follows:
(1) A novel fuzzing method is proposed to enhance coverage effi-
ciency and reduce runtime overhead. The fuzzing process is modeled 
as a Markov decision-making process, with a Reinforcement Learning 
mechanism designed to guide seed mutation, thus improving fuzzing 
efficiency and reducing overhead.
(2) Design a new metric for assessing the quality of seed files 
that not only evaluates vulnerability probability but also considers 
path weight and HugeScore to characterize the probability of program 
crashes.
(3) VSGFuzz has been demonstrated to detect more vulnerabilities 
in both general datasets and real-world programs compared to other 
methods. We implemented VSGFuzz on the LAVA-M dataset as well 
as several real-world programs to evaluate its fuzzing performance on 
binary programs. The results illustrated that VSGFuzz identified more 
vulnerabilities than state-of-the-art methods.
2. Related work
Fuzzing techniques have become integral for software testing and 
vulnerability discovery [5]. In this section, we have compiled some 
research in fuzzing to build upon existing work.
2.1. Fuzzing
Fuzzing techniques originated in the 1980s when Barton Miller and 
his colleagues first introduced the concept of fuzz testing, applying it 
to UNIX systems [6]. In the early 2000s, the mutation-based fuzzing 
approach emerged, involving a random or semi-random mutation of 
input data to generate test cases [7]. In 2005, the book â€˜â€˜Fuzzing for 
Software Security Testing and Quality Assuranceâ€™â€™ by Takanen, DeMott, 
and Miller provided a comprehensive overview of fuzzing techniques 
in software security testing [8]. The year 2006 saw the introduction of 
the SAGE (Scalable Automated Guided Execution) fuzzing framework, 
enabling automated fuzz testing in large-scale programs [9]. In 2010, 
TaintScope [10] employed dynamic taint analysis and symbolic execu-
tion to test x86 binary programs. The next year, SimFuzz [11] utilized 
test case similarity metrics to explore program semantics deeply.
A significant advancement occurred in 2013 with the release of 
American Fuzzy Lop (AFL) [12], which employed coverage-based
strategies and intelligent input mutation to discover program vul-
nerabilities. Dowser [13], a guided fuzzier, integrates taint tracking, 
program analysis, and symbolic execution to detect buffer overflow 
and underflow vulnerabilities. By 2016, the integration of symbolic 
execution and fuzzing gained popularity, enhancing the accuracy and 
efficiency of fuzz testing [14]. QuickFuzz [15] leveraged existing 
Haskell libraries to test various file formats without manual specifica-
tions in 2017 efficiently. Another fuzzier, VUzzer [16], on the other 
hand, utilizes control-flow and data-flow analysis to pinpoint bugs 
in deeper program paths, assigning increased significance to these 
intricate code components. Another strategy entails employing program 
analysis to support fuzzing efforts [17]. V-Fuzz [18] is designed to 
identify a wider array of vulnerabilities than Dowser.
2.2. Learning-based fuzzing
In recent years, researchers have combined machine learning with 
traditional fuzzing techniques, integrating machine learning methods 
into the stages of seed file generation and mutation strategy selection in 
the fuzzing process. Those integrations with different machine learning 
approaches, such as supervised (Regress and Classification), unsuper-
vised (Clustering and Desity estimation), semi-supervised and reinforce-
ment learning, bring in varies features, perspecitves and evolutions on 
fuzzing techniques [19].
In the seed file generation process, SmartSeed [20] utilizes Gen-
erative Adversarial Networks (GANs) to generate new binary samples 
from valid sample data identified by AFL. This approach triggers more 
crashes and execution paths than AFL and other selection strategies. 
REINAM [21] employs a reinforcement learning algorithm to generate 
program input grammar, thereby improving the quality of generated 
variation samples. In addition to traditional seed input in file format, 
software testing engineering encompasses other forms of seed input. For 
instance, Luong et al. [22] employed the Q-Learning algorithm to test 
Android applications. This involved selecting and arranging operations 
to trigger GUI event sequences, resulting in higher code coverage and 
more application errors being triggered. Deng et al. [23] use LLMs 
for black-box fuzzing testing Mutation, proving the effectiveness of 
pre-trained LLMs not only for seed generation but also for mutation. 
Cheng et al. [24] introduces a generative model built on a recurrent 
neural network (RNN) framework to provide high-quality sequences for 
PDF-based program targets. She et al. [25] proposed using a gradient-
guided input generation scheme and procedural smoothing techniques, 
in which the neural network learns smooth approximations. Scott 
et al. [26] leverages multi-agent RL guidance to improve SMT solver 
performance. The core idea revolves around training a single or a 
group of agent explorers to maximize reward signals that indicate the 
effectiveness of the generated inputs, particularly in achieving high 
code coverage or identifying bugs.
In selecting mutation strategies, researchers have been exploring 
integrating reinforcement learning techniques to enhance fuzz-ing ef-
ficiency. Bottinger [27] and colleagues utilized the Deep Q Network 
(DQN) of reinforcement learning to fuzz the Japanese standard program 
pdftotext. This approach employs strings as the state and six self-
defined mutation methods as actions. Compared to the traditional 
random mutation action selection strategy, this design significantly 
improves the code coverage rate and reduces the running time.FUZZ-
BOOST [28] shares a similar concept. FuzzerGym [29] integrates lib-
Fuzzer [30] and Double Deep Q Network (DDQN) via the Remote 
Procedure Call (RPC) method for target programs libjpeg, libpng, bor-
ingssl, re2, and sqllite. In fuzz testing, libFuzzer is guided to select the 
mutation function through the reinforcement learning algorithm. This 
approach leads to a significant improvement in code coverage com-
pared to the original random selection strategy. Kuznetsov et al. [31] 
also employed the DQN algorithm to select mutation actions, resulting 
in a reduction of approximately 30% in the number of sample muta-
tions required to detect vulnerabilities. Zhang et al. [32] introduced 
two key enhancements to traditional grey-box fuzzing: a multi-player, 
multi-armed bandit model and a non-dominated sorting genetic algo-
rithm for fuzzing. Wang et al. [33] use Deep Neural Network (DNN) 
to optimize the selection strategy of samples and improve the coverage 
of vulnerable paths. Suzzer [34] predicts the vulnerable probability of 
functions based on a deep learning-based model and gives each basic 
block in the vulnerable function a static score. Then, for each input, the 
sum of the static score of all the basic blocks on its execution path is 
calculated, and the inputs are prioritized with higher scores.

3. Overview
This section details the proposed vulnerable state-guided fuzzing 
methodology (VSGFuzz). As depicted in Fig.  2, VSGFuzz architecture 
consists of six steps and is grouped into two main processes: (1) static 
analysis and dynamic analysis.
In the static analysis process, the first step is to formulate binary 
functions into an ACFG data structure, which can used in a graph 
embedding network [35,36] to estimate the vulnerability probability of 
functions within binary programs in the second step. Based on function-
level vulnerability probability analysis, a basic block value calculation 
mechanism is designed to seed evaluation during the fuzzing phase.
An RL-based and vulnerable state-guided fuzzy logic is proposed in 
the dynamic analysis process. The core part of the fuzzer is finding 
effective seeds to point to highly vulnerable areas and cover function 
paths as many as possible. The details of the techniques are introduced 
in Step 4 - Step 6. Using the RL algorithm, the fuzzing process is trained 
to select more effective mutations progressively.
4. Methodology of VSGFuzz
4.1. Step 1: Data preprocessing
Vulnerability prediction at the program level cannot capture the 
nuanced relationship between the program and vulnerable code seg-
ments. This limitation hampers the effective mining of vulnerabilities 
and impedes subsequent mutation processes of the fuzzer. To address 
this, we adopt function-level analysis to assess program vulnerabilities, 
and therefore, we need to characterize the specific features of binary 
functions.
Conventional approaches to binary programs are grouped into three 
methods: (1) converting function contents into byte arrays, (2) col-
lecting information on the type and quantity of identifiers within a 
function, and (3) utilizing program abstract syntax trees, among others. 
However, the former two methods disregard the structural information 
of the function, while the latter sacrifices its statistical information. To 
comprehensively account for both the structure and semantic informa-
tion of functions, based on the third method, we build the Attributes 
Control Flow Graph (ACFG) [35,37â€“39] representation to characterize 
the binary function.
ACFG [35] is a directed graph denoted as 
ð‘” = âŸ¨ð‘‰ , ð¸, ðœ™âŸ© (1)
where ð‘‰  represents a set of nodes, ð¸ represents a set of edges, and 
ðœ™ is a mapping function ðœ™ âˆ¶ ð‘‰ â†’ ð›´ that assigns attribute sets ð›´ to 
the nodes in the graph. The construction of ACFG relies on a control 
flow graph (CFG), which employs diagrams to illustrate all possible 
execution paths within a computer program.
The process of obtaining the ACFG of a binary function is illustrated 
in Fig.  3. Firstly, the binary program is disassembled to derive the 
Fig. 3. Procedure for binary programs to extract the ACFG.
CFG of each function within the program. Subsequently, attribute 
information is extracted from each basic block, and each basic block is 
transformed into a numerical vector. By following these steps, the ACFG 
representation of the function is obtained. These attributes encompass 
essential components such as string and numerical constants, transfer 
and call instructions, arithmetic instructions, and child nodes, all of 
which provide insights into the functionâ€™s behavior. Furthermore, the 
betweenness centrality measure captures the significance of a node 
within the overall graph structure, aiding in the identification of po-
tential vulnerabilities within the function. Both the functionâ€™s statistical 
and structural information are stored as vectors in the nodes, serving 
as attribute vectors for the basic block nodes. Each node in the ACFG 
possesses an attribute vector with eight dimensions, representing the 
function as a collection of eight-dimensional vectors. Subsequently, the 
extracted ACFG of the binary function is utilized as input for the model.

4.5. Step5: Dynamic execution
VSGFuzz is a repetitive process. It maintains a seed pool to store 
high-quality inputs as seeds. Initially, VSGFuzz executes the binary 
program using an initial input provided by the user. Concurrently, 
it utilizes Dynamic Binary Instrumentation (DBI) to track program 
execution information, including basic block coverage. Leveraging ðµð‘‰
and execution information, VSGFuzz calculates a seed score for each 
executed test case (i.e., input). Test cases with higher seed scores are 
considered high-quality inputs and added to the seed bank. Test cases 
that trigger crashes are also included in the seed pool and assigned 
higher seed scores. Next, VSGFuzz generates next-generation test cases 
by mutating the seeds present in the seed pool. The new seeds are also 
stored in the seed pool. Then, we repeat the process to select a seed 
from the pool to run a fuzzing test.
In general, control flow is used to specify path priority and identify 
error-handling blocks, and data flow is utilized to determine the loca-
tion of variation and specific operations. Specifically, AFL is improved 
to give greater weight to paths of interest. Based on analyzing the basic 
block weight calculation in line with Markov properties, we conclude 
that the transfer probabilities between blo-cks are independent, and 
their probabilities are only related to connected blocks, so the inverse of 
the probability is set as the weight. In the paper, error-handling blocks 
are designed with weights set to negative numbers, and the sum of 
the weights of the blocks on the path is defined as the path weights. 
The higher the score, the higher the weight and the higher priority the 
input corresponding to the path is considered to have, and it will be 
preferred for seed mutation and being selected again as the seed file. 
Vuzzer recognizes magic bytes by Pin insertion, and through continuous 
iteration, it matches the information in ð‘ð‘šð‘ and address fetching class 
operation ð‘™ð‘’ð‘Ž with the seed file input and the newly generated inputs 
and finds the magic bytes in the input to find the possible locations of 
magic bytes and mutate them more accurately.
4.6. Step6: RL for fuzzing
4.6.1. Modeling based on RL
This section introduces a methodology for constructing the state, 
action, reward and environment components in reinforcement learn-
ing (RL) problems, which takes inspiration from the operations and 
environment of fuzzing. The Markov property is satisfied by ensuring 
that the systemâ€™s state in the subsequent moment is solely dependent 
on its current state and is not influenced by other states. Within 
the context of fuzzing, the mutation strategy is utilized to select an 
appropriate mutating operation for the current seed. Subsequently, the 
target program processes the mutant seed, and the specific reward is 
computed based on the runtime feedback received.

reward, and environment. To effectively utilize the RL algorithm in 
optimizing the fuzzing process, it is crucial to abstractly model the

will focus on introducing the abstraction and selection process of the 
state, action, and reward elements in the fuzzing problem modeling 
based on RL.
State:. In the context of fuzzing, the effectiveness of testing primarily 
relies on the generation of high-quality seeds, where high-quality seeds 
refer to those that uncover more vulnerabilities in the programâ€™s state.

4.6.2. Strategy selection of reinforcement learning algorithm
To effectively select mutation operations for fuzzing, choosing RL 
algorithms that can handle large state and action spaces is essential. 
In 2014, David Silver et al. proposed the deterministic policy gradient 
(DPG) algorithm, which demonstrated the existence of a deterministic 
policy gradient through mathematical analysis. Subsequently, the deep 
deterministic policy gradient (DDPG) algorithm [41] emerged by com-
bining the DPG algorithm with deep neural networks, enhancing its 
practicality. Given the relatively large mutation operation space and 
input seed state space in the fuzzing process model, we opt for the 
DDPG algorithm to construct the RL model [42].
The DDPG algorithm comprises four neural networks, which are

5. Implementation and settings
5.1. Graph embedding-based vulnerability prediction model
As shown in the previous design, we need to accomplish two parts 
to implement a graph embedding-based vulnerability prediction model. 
Those two parts are (1) an ACFG extractor and (2) a vulnerability 
prediction model. The ACFG extractor was implemented by a plugin 
provided by the widely used disassembly tool IDA Pro [43]. The 
vulnerability prediction model was developed using the popular deep 
learning framework TensorFlow.
Based on the Genius project [35], the ACFG extractor for binary 
program functions was developed. By modifying and enhancing the 
feature extraction method of Genius, we can customize and incorporate 
the specific feature data required for our purposes. The vulnerability 
prediction model takes the ACFG of the function along with its corre-
sponding label as input. Therefore, during model training, we require a 
dataset consisting of functions with known vulnerabilities. This exper-
iment uses the Juliet Test Suite as the training dataset, widely used in 
various vulnerability-related studies. The Juliet Test Suite, published by 
the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST), comprises 
C/C++ language programs, where each function is labeled as â€˜â€˜goodâ€™â€™ 
(indicating â€˜â€˜secureâ€™â€™) or â€˜â€˜badâ€™â€™ (indicating â€˜â€˜vulnerableâ€™â€™).
Our parameter settings are shown in Table  2 based on the training 
data analysis and the modelâ€™s tuning.
In terms of the system platform, we utilized the hardware environ-
ment detailed in Table  3.
5.2. RL based and vulnerable states guided fuzzing
In the paper, we developed a fuzzier VSGFuzz based on VUzzer [16], 
an advanced evolutionary fuzzer designed for binary targets. Each 
fuzzing experiment was performed on a virtual machine running
Ubuntu 20.04 LTS. The virtual machine had a 64-bit single-core Intel 
CPU running at 4.2 GHz and 4 GB of RAM.
RL model training and fuzzing efficiency are closely related to its 
hardware and software environment. For the training model, we set 
the hardware environment in Table  3, and the software environment 
is shown in Table  4. We also use library files such as Tensorflow, 
Keras-RL2, and Gym to build a RL model based on the DDPG algorithm.
6. Evaluation
In this section, we evaluate VSGFuzz through the following two 
aspects: (1) the evaluation results of the vulnerability prediction model 
and (2) the evaluation results of the RL-based fuzzer.
6.1. Graph embedding based vulnerability prediction model evaluation
Evaluation metrics:. Accuracy, loss, ACFG extraction time, and training 
time were used to measure the performance of the vulnerability predic-
tion model. Table  5 summarizes our evaluation results. We use the cross 
entropy loss function to calculate the loss of the model. The VPModel-
evaluation table records the loss rate and accuracy of the model. We 
use the cross-entropy loss function to calculate the loss of the model, 
which quickly drops to a low value, then stabilizes, and the surface 
model rapidly converges. The accuracy curve of the model is more than 
0.995, which means that the model can correctly distinguish between 
positive and negative cases to a large extent.
The figure (Fig.  7) depicts the reward graph generated during 
the training of a fuzzy test model using the Deep Q Network (DQN) 
and DDPG. The orange line represents the reward values obtained by 
DDPG, while the brown line represents the reward values obtained 
by DQN. The graph illustrates that DDPG outperforms the DQN algo-
rithm regarding model training performance. The higher reward values
achieved by DDPG indicate its superior performance in optimizing 
fuzzy test models. The red dashed line at the top of the chart represents 
the maximum reward value attained under the DDPG model, while the 
blue dashed line represents the maximum reward value achieved under 
the DQN model. The reward values are designed to be the seed score 
after the seed is executed.
The abscissa in the figure (Fig.  7) represents the number of execu-
tion steps during the fuzz testing process, and the ordinate represents 
the reward feedback value obtained. The image analysis shows that in 
the early stage of fuzz testing, a higher reward value feedback is not 
obtained each time a new seed file is executed. However, about 700 
steps after triggering, the feedback value suddenly increased signifi-
cantly. It is speculated that it may be because the seed file generated 
by the mutation triggered a certain critical path at this stage, which 
may have been marked as possible in previous predictions. Loopholes. 
Subsequently, it remains stable for some time, possibly because the 
mutations performed during this period were local-scale changes that 
failed to induce substantial or larger-scale path changes. It should be 
emphasized that the changes in the two lines shown in the figure all 
come from changes in path coverage, and there is no program crash 
event. In the later experiments, we also used DDPG to train the model.

6.2. RL based and vulnerable states guided fuzzing evaluation
In this section, we demonstrate VSGFuzzâ€™s ability of discovering vul-
nerabilities on three different datasets: A. LAVA-M Dataset, B. DARPA 
CGC binaries and C. Real-Word Dataset. The results demonstrated that 
VSGFuzz was able to not only precisely evaluate vulnerability proba-
bility to detect more vulnerabilities, but also consume less computation 
time with a promising efficiency.
A. LAVA-M Dataset
Table  6 shows the number of bugs found by VSGFuzz, Vuzzer, 
V-Fuzz, AFL, and Suzzer, respectively. The program vulnerability num-
bers triggered by the LAVA-M program during the fuzz testing process 
are as shown in the following Table  7. Furthermore, VSGFuzz can 
trigger several unlisted bugs and exhibits better performance than V-
Fuzz in this case. VSGFuzz excels in terms of coverage as shown in 
Table  8. Compared to other methods, it can explore a wider range of 
execution paths within the program.
B. DARPA CGC Dataset
We obtained a total of 149 CGC binaries. However, we were unable 
to run VSGFuzz on all of these devices due to the following reasons:
(1) All binaries are interactive by accepting input from STDIN. 
Once launched, many display a menu to select actions, including an 
exit option. Additionally, there are many menus (in different states of 
the program) with varying options for exit. Since VSGFuzz requires 
one step to complete with completely random input, performing such 
input would put the application in a loop looking for valid possibilities, 
including an option to exit, which would cause the application to run 
forever. This is an interface issue, not a fundamental limitation of our 
fuzzing approach.
(2) Some binaries involve interactions with others, which CSGFuzz 
cannot handle.
(3) Since VSGFuzz is based on Pin, we cannot run some binaries 
with Pin.

running the patched version of the binary to observe whether there 
were further crashes. The most important result is the number of inputs 
executed per crash among the three fuzzers. We used it for up to 6 h, 
and the graph (Fig.  9) depicts the number of executions in the case 
where all three fuzzes found crashes (13 times in total), which shows 
that VSGFuzz can significantly reduce the search space compared to the 
other two methods.

C. Real-Word Dataset
We evaluate the performance of VSGFuzz using a real-world dataset 
(djepg/eog, tcpdump, tcptrace, pdf2svg, mpg321, gif2png) and com-
pare with Vuzzer, AFL, and Suzzer, shown in Table  9. The fuzzing 
time for each program was up to 24 h. To highlight the perfor-
mance of VSGFuzz, we also ran AFL, VUzzer and Suzzer on these 
programs(Suzzer [34] predicts the vulnerable probability of functions 
based on a deep learning-based model and gives each basic block in the 
vulnerable function a static score. Then, for each input, the sum of the 
static score of all the basic blocks on its execution path is calculated, 
and the inputs are prioritized with higher scores). The table below 
shows the results of running on real programs regarding the number 
of unique crashes found. VSGFuzz significantly outperforms the other 
two methods.
The figure depicts (Fig.  10) the crashes of 6 programs within 24 h. 
The ð‘¥-axis of each graph shows the cumulative sum of crashes sampled 
every 2 h. For almost every application, VSGFuzz can find crashes in 
continuous iterations of fuzz testing. Compared with the other three 
methods, VSGFuzz can find crashes and detect crashes in less time.
7. Conclusion
This paper presents an innovative fuzzing method named VSGFuzz, 
designed for vulnerability analysis in binary programs. Our approach 
comprises several key steps. Firstly, we develop a vulnerability pre-
diction model to estimate the vulnerability probability of individual 
functions within a binary program. Next, we leverage these vulnera-
bility probabilities and basic block values to compute seed file scores. 
Subsequently, a reinforcement learning model is trained to guide the 
mutation operations applied to the seed file, enhancing both the quality 
and efficiency of the fuzz testing process. Finally, our test results on 
the LAVA-M dataset, DARPA CGC dataset and Real-Word Dataset high-
light the effectiveness of VSGFuzz. Moreover, the training results on 
real programs demonstrate the toolâ€™s usability, especially in enhancing 
program coverage. These findings underscore the effectiveness of our 
approach to identifying vulnerabilities and fortifying the security of 
binary programs.

The security testing of Ethereum smart contracts has become increasingly important with the rise of decentralized 
applications and blockchain technology. This systematic literature review (SLR) aims to provide a comprehensive 
overview of the state-of-the-art techniques, methodologies, tools, and challenges in the security testing of 
Ethereum smart contracts. By synthesizing and analyzing existing research articles, conference papers, and 
other relevant sources, this SLR identiï¬es common trends, gaps, and areas for future research in this domain. 
The review covers various aspects of security testing, including vulnerability detection, testing frameworks, 
automated analysis tools, and best practices. In addition, it explores the impact of security vulnerabilities on 
smart contract ecosystems and proposes recommendations to improve the eï¬€ectiveness and eï¬ƒciency of security 
testing processes. This SLR serves as a valuable resource for researchers, practitioners, and developers interested 
in improving the security and reliability of Ethereum smart contracts.
1. Introduction
Smart contracts are revolutionizing the way agreements and trans-
actions are executed in the digital world. Imagine a real estate trans-
action between Alice and Bob using smart contracts on the Ethereum 
blockchain. Traditionally, this process would involve multiple interme-
diaries, paperwork, and veriï¬cation steps, leading to delays and in-
creased costs. With smart contracts, Alice and Bob can automate the 
entire process [1].
1.1. Background and motivation
The emergence of smart contracts on blockchain platforms like 
Ethereum has ushered in a new era of trustless and eï¬ƒcient transactions. 
These contracts, powered by immutable code and distributed consen-
sus mechanisms, oï¬€er unparalleled security and transparency compared 
to traditional agreements. However, these advantages come with chal-
lenges, particularly concerning ensuring the robustness and security 
of smart contract code. Addressing these challenges through rigorous 
testing, auditing, and continuous research is essential to fully exploit 
the potential of smart contracts and foster the widespread adoption of 
blockchain technology across various sectors [2].

â€¢Increased eï¬ƒciency: smart contracts automate manual processes, 
saving time and reducing costs.
â€¢Improved accessibility: smart contracts are accessible to everyone, 
regardless of their location or background.
In the context of Ethereum, smart contracts play a crucial role in 
creating decentralized applications (dApps). dApps are applications that 
run on the Ethereum blockchain and are not controlled by a single entity. 
They oï¬€er a wide range of services, such as decentralized ï¬nance (DeFi), 
gaming, and marketplaces [3].
1.1.2. Challenges and risks of smart contract security
Despite its advantages, smart contract technology also presents sig-
niï¬cant risks. Smart contracts are complex software that can be suscep-
tible to vulnerabilities. Hackers can exploit these vulnerabilities to steal 
funds, manipulate data, or disrupt the functioning of smart contracts 
[4]. The stakes involved in smart contract security are high. Financial

1.1.3. Need for a systematic literature review (SLR)
Given the challenges and risks associated with smart contract secu-
rity, it is crucial to comprehensively understand the techniques and tools 
available for testing and securing smart contracts. An SLR is a valuable 
tool for addressing this need. An SLR is a rigorous and scientiï¬c method 
for identifying, analyzing, and synthesizing existing research on a given 
topic. In the context of smart contract security, an SLR is necessary to 
provide a comprehensive and up-to-date understanding of this critical 
research area. This SLR will contribute to improving smart contract se-
curity and promoting the adoption of blockchain technology.
Software testing is an essential practice to ensure the quality, relia-
bility, and security of computer applications. In the context of smart 
contracts, where trust and security are paramount, testing takes on 
particular importance. Security testing aims to identify potential vul-
nerabilities in the code of smart contracts and ensure that they function 
as expected, without risks of ï¬‚aws or compromises.
Several aspects of security testing are relevant to smart contracts, 
including:
â€¢Static analysis: this method examines the source code of smart con-
tracts without executing them, identifying potential errors such as 
logic vulnerabilities or security ï¬‚aws.
â€¢Dynamic analysis: in contrast to static analysis, dynamic analysis 
involves executing smart contracts in a controlled environment to 
detect vulnerabilities in real time, such as stack overï¬‚ow attacks or 
denial-of-service attacks.
â€¢Security audits: security audits are in-depth examinations of smart 
contract code conducted by cybersecurity experts. These audits aim 
to identify and correct vulnerabilities before deploying smart con-
tracts on the blockchain.
By integrating rigorous security testing practices into the development 
and deployment of smart contracts, developers can reduce the risks of 
exploitation by malicious actors and enhance user conï¬dence in the 
smart contract ecosystem [8].

1.3. Research methodology
SLRs are a cornerstone of research in many ï¬elds, including soft-
ware engineering. They oï¬€er a comprehensive and objective way to 
evaluate existing research on a speciï¬c topic. This section explores a 
well-established approach for conducting SLRs: the Kitchenham method.
1.3.1. The Kitchenham method
The Kitchenham method [9] is a rigorous and well-established ap-
proach for conducting SLRs in the ï¬eld of software engineering. It oï¬€ers 
several advantages:
â€¢Rigor and reproducibility: the Kitchenham method is based on 
scientiï¬c principles and provides a clear and documented process 
to ensure the rigor and reproducibility of the SLR.
â€¢Comprehensiveness and accuracy: the methodology aims to iden-
tify and analyze all relevant primary studies for the SLR topic, min-
imizing the risk of bias and omissions.
â€¢Transparency and evaluation: the Kitchenham method encour-
ages detailed documentation of each step of the SLR, allowing for 
transparent assessment of the quality and validity of the research.
1.3.2. Stages of the Kitchenham methodology
The Kitchenham methodology consists of the following stages:
1. Planning the review
â€¢Deï¬ning the objectives and research questions of the SLR.
â€¢Developing a review protocol that describes the methodology 
and inclusion/exclusion criteria.
â€¢Identifying potential sources of research (databases, libraries, 
etc.).
2. Conducting the review
â€¢Identifying and selecting relevant primary studies.
â€¢Extracting data from the selected studies.
â€¢Analyzing and synthesizing the extracted data.
3. Reporting the review
â€¢Presenting the results of the SLR in a clear and concise man-
ner.
â€¢Discussing the implications of the results and the limitations 
of the research.
â€¢Formulating conclusions and recommendations for future re-
search.
1.3.3. Details of key stages
â€¢Deï¬ning research questions and inclusion/exclusion criteria
â€“ The research questions should be clear, precise, and relevant 
to the topic of the SLR.
â€“ Inclusion/exclusion criteria should be deï¬ned to identify rel-
evant primary studies and exclude those that are not.
â€¢Identifying and selecting primary studies
â€“ The search for primary studies should be conducted in multi-
ple sources of research.
â€“ Primary studies should be selected based on the deï¬ned in-
clusion/exclusion criteria.
â€¢Data extraction and analysis

â€“ Relevant data should be extracted from the selected primary

The Kitchenham methodology provides a robust framework for con-

2.4.1.1. Fuzzing testing Fuzzing, also known as fuzz testing, is an au-
tomated software testing technique that involves providing invalid, un-
expected, or random inputs to a computer program [11,13]. The goal is 
to detect bugs and vulnerabilities that traditional testing methods might 
not identify.
â€¢How it works
A fuzzing tool generates random or semi-random data that 
matches the format expected by the input of the program to be 
tested. It then injects these data into the program and monitors its 
behavior. If the program crashes, hangs, or exhibits unexpected be-
havior, it may indicate the presence of a bug or vulnerability.
â€¢Advantages
â€“ Automation: fuzzing allows for the automated testing of a 
large number of input cases, which is especially useful for 
complex programs with many possible inputs.
â€“ Eï¬€ectiveness: fuzzing can identify bugs and vulnerabilities 
that traditional testing methods, such as unit testing or inte-
gration testing, might not detect.
â€“ Code coverage: fuzzing can explore code execution paths that 
are not always reached by traditional testing methods, which 
can help improve code coverage.
â€¢Disadvantages
â€“ False positives: fuzzing can generate input cases that do not 
cause real bugs, which can lead to false positive alerts.
â€“ Execution time: fuzzing can be time-consuming, especially 
for complex programs with many possible inputs.
â€“ Required skills: setting up and using fuzzing tools can require 
speciï¬c skills.
â€¢Types of fuzzing
â€“ Black-box fuzzing: this approach does not require any knowl-
edge of the source code of the program to be tested. The 
fuzzing tool generates random or semi-random data based on 
the format expected by the programâ€™s input.
â€“ White-box fuzzing: this approach uses information from the 
programâ€™s source code to generate more precise input cases.
â€“ Mutation-based fuzzing: this approach generates input cases 
by modifying existing valid input cases.
â€¢Fuzzing tools
â€“ Generic fuzzers: these tools can be used to test diï¬€erent types 
of programs.
â€“ Speciï¬c fuzzers: these tools are designed to test speciï¬c types 
of programs, such as web browsers or web applications.
2.4.1.2. Symbolic execution Symbolic execution [28] is a static soft-
ware analysis technique that explores the diï¬€erent execution paths of 
a program by using symbolic values instead of concrete values. Unlike 
concrete execution, which only follows one possible path, symbolic ex-
Blockchain: Research and Applications 7 (2026) 100314 
4 
[Page 5]
M. Mnasri, A.J. MaÃ¢lej and M. Jmaiel 
ecution explores all possible paths, considering the diï¬€erent values that 
variables can take.
â€¢How it works
Symbolic execution works by instrumenting the programâ€™s 
source code and simulating it step by step. At each step, the val-
ues of the variables are represented by symbolic expressions. The 
program instructions are then interpreted, and the symbolic expres-
sions are updated according to the operations performed.
â€¢Advantages
Symbolic execution has several advantages over other static anal-
ysis techniques:
â€“ It can test all execution paths of the program, including those 
that are rarely taken.
â€“ It can detect bugs that are not detectable by concrete execu-
tion, such as buï¬€er overï¬‚ows and divisions by zero.
â€“ It can be used to prove properties of the program, such as 
termination or correctness.
â€¢Limitations
Symbolic execution also has some limitations:
â€“ It can be time-consuming and resource-intensive because it 
explores all execution paths of the program.
â€“ It can be diï¬ƒcult to implement for complex programs.
â€“ It may not be able to detect all bugs.
â€¢Additional information
â€“ Symbolic execution is a powerful tool for ï¬nding bugs in soft-
ware, but it is not a silver bullet. It should be used in conjunc-
tion with other testing techniques to ensure that software is 
as bug-free as possible.
â€“ Symbolic execution is a research area, and new techniques are 
being developed all the time to improve its eï¬€ectiveness and 
eï¬ƒciency.
2.4.1.3. Mutation testing Mutation testing [34] is a software testing 
technique that involves the intentional injection of modiï¬cations, called 
â€œmutationsâ€, into the source code of a program. The goal is to determine 
whether existing tests are capable of detecting these mutations and en-
suring the robustness of the code.
â€¢How it works
1. Mutant generation: speciï¬c tools generate mutants by mod-
ifying the source code in diï¬€erent ways. Mutations can be 
simple, such as changing a constant value or a logical opera-
tor, or more complex, such as deleting a condition or a loop.
2. Test execution: existing tests are then executed on the origi-
nal program and on each mutant.
3. Result analysis: mutation testing is considered successful if 
all mutants are detected by at least one test. If a mutant is not 
detected, it means that there is a missing test case and that 
the code is vulnerable to an error.
â€¢Advantages
â€“ Improved test coverage: mutation testing helps identify 
parts of the code that is not suï¬ƒciently tested and ï¬lls cover-
age gaps.
â€“ Detection of hard-to-ï¬nd bugs: mutation testing can iden-
tify bugs that are not detected by other testing techniques, 
such as unit tests or integration tests.
â€“ Improved code quality: mutation testing encourages devel-
opers to write more robust and error-resistant code.
â€¢Limitations
â€“ High cost: mutation testing can be expensive in terms of time 
and resources, as it requires the generation and execution of 
a large number of mutants.
â€“ Diï¬ƒcult to interpret results: it can be diï¬ƒcult to deter-
mine whether an undetected mutant represents a real bug or 
a harmless mutation.
â€“ Not applicable to all types of programs: mutation testing is 
more eï¬€ective for programs whose source code is accessible 
and easy to modify.
Example
Suppose we have the following Python code:
function(x):
if x > 0:
return x
else:
return
 -x
A mutation testing tool could generate the following mutants:
â€“ Mutation 1: Change the > operator to >=.
â€“ Mutation 2: Change the == operator to !=.
â€“ Mutation 3: Delete the else condition.
If the existing tests do not detect all of these mutants, it reveals a 
gap in test coverage, indicating that the test suite may be incomplete 
or insuï¬ƒciently robust. This exposes the code to potential errors 
similar to the undetected mutants.
2.4.1.4. Metamorphic testing MT [33] is a property-based software test-
ing technique that can be an eï¬€ective approach to solving the test oracle 
problem and the test case generation problem.
â€¢Principle
MT is based on the idea that certain properties (called metamor-
phic relations (MRs)) must be satisï¬ed by the system regardless of 
the input dataset.
Example
Consider a program that implements the sine function with a 
precision of 100 signiï¬cant digits. An MR for the sine function is:
sin(ðœ‹âˆ’ð‘¥)=sin( ð‘¥) (1)
â€¢Process
1. Deï¬ne MRs: identify the properties that the system must sat-
isfy after a transformation of the input data.
2. Generate test cases: apply MR transformations to existing 
test cases or generate new test cases.
3. Execute test cases and compare results: compare the ob-
tained results with the expected results based on the MRs.
4. Analyze results: if the results do not match, it may indicate 
a defect in the system.
â€¢Advantages
â€“ Reduces the need for test oracles.
â€“ Helps to generate more eï¬€ective test cases.
â€“ Detects that might not be detected by other testing techniques.
â€¢Limitations
â€“ Depends on the ability to identify meaningful MRs.
â€“ Can be diï¬ƒcult to automate.
In conclusion, MT oï¬€ers a valuable approach to software testing, 
particularly when dealing with challenges like test oracles and case gen-
eration. While it requires identifying meaningful MRs, the beneï¬ts of 
reduced oracle dependence, improved test case eï¬€ectiveness, and de-

2.4.2. Static security testing
2.4.2.1. Formal veriï¬cation Formal veriï¬cation [35] is a rigorous 
method used in software and hardware development to prove or dis-
prove a systemâ€™s compliance with formal speciï¬cations, which are math-
ematically deï¬ned properties. Unlike traditional testing methods, which 
check the proper functioning of a system through speciï¬c scenarios, for-
mal veriï¬cation examines all possible states of the system to ensure it

[Page 6]

meets the given properties. Two of the most commonly used techniques 
in formal veriï¬cation are model checking and theorem proving.
a. Model checking:
Model checking is an automated method of formal veriï¬cation 
that involves exhaustively exploring the state space of a system 
model to check whether it satisï¬es certain speciï¬ed logical proper-
ties, often expressed in terms of temporal logic, such as computation 
tree logic or linear temporal logic.
â€¢Process: the model checking process involves three main el-
ements:
â€“ Modeling: the system to be veriï¬ed is represented as 
a formal model, such as a ï¬nite automaton, Petri net, 
or state transition system.
â€“ Speciï¬cation: the properties to be veriï¬ed are spec-
iï¬ed as logical formulas.
â€“ Veriï¬cation: a model checking algorithm systemati-
cally explores the modelâ€™s state space to determine if 
the speciï¬ed properties are satisï¬ed. If a violation is 
found, a counterexample is provided, indicating the

â€¢Advantages:
â€“ Exhaustiveness: it veriï¬es all possible states, ensur-
ing complete coverage.
â€“ Counterexamples: in case of a violation, it provides

â€¢Limitations:
â€“ State space explosion: the number of states can 
grow exponentially with the systemâ€™s size, making 
veriï¬cation challenging for complex systems.
b. Theorem proving:
Theorem proving is another formal veriï¬cation technique, based 
on using mathematical logic to prove that speciï¬ed properties of a 
system are satisï¬ed. Unlike model checking, which is automated and 
veriï¬es a model through exhaustive exploration, theorem proving

â€¢Process:
â€“ Modeling: the system is described by mathematical

â€“ Speciï¬cation: system properties are expressed as 
theorems to be proven.
â€“ Proof: the theorem proving tool, sometimes assisted

semi-automatic deduction of new formulas until the 
theorem is proven or refuted.
â€¢Advantages:
â€“ Expressive power: capable of handling systems 
with inï¬nite states or complex properties that model 
checking cannot address.
â€“ Precision: allows for very detailed veriï¬cation of sys-
tems, down to the level of mathematical logic.
â€¢Limitations:
â€“ Complexity: may require signiï¬cant expertise to cor-
rectly formulate theorems and to guide the proving

â€“ Less automation: the process is often less automated 
than model checking, making it longer and more 
complex.
Formal veriï¬cation is a powerful tool for ensuring that critical sys-
tems adhere to essential properties for their proper functioning. 
Model checking and theorem proving are two complementary tech-

2.4.2.2. Static code analysis
a. Abstract interpretation
Abstract interpretation is a static analysis technique that trans-

â€¢Process:
â€“ Deï¬ne abstractions: identify and abstract key con-

â€“ Eï¬ƒciency: allows for the analysis of code properties

D) SAILFISH

â€“ The SDG overestimates read-write accesses to stor-

â€“ If the query result is an empty set, the contract is cer-
tainly not vulnerable; otherwise, a counter-example 
is generated. The REFINER module validates coun-
terexamples returned by the EXPLORER.
â€“ It performs contract-wide value summary analysis to 
mitigate potential issues arising from path conditions

examined.
â€¢Advantages

â€¢Limitations

â€“ Wide applicability: the toolâ€™s generic deï¬nition of

â€“ Insights into vulnerability prevalence: by analyz-

â€¢Limitations
â€“ Potential for misuse: while teEther can assist secu-

â€“ Reliance on binary analysis: the use of binary byte-

F) DefectChecker
DefectChecker [32] is a defect detection tool for Ethereum smart 
contracts, primarily based on bytecode analysis. Here is a summary 
of the main points:
â€¢Main features
â€“ Modular architecture: the tool comprises four mod-
ules: bytecode input, control ï¬‚ow graph generation, 
feature detection (such as money calls and payable

â€“ Bytecode analysis: utilizes the Geth API to disas-

â€“ Defect detection: identiï¬es vulnerabilities such as

â€“ Symbolic execution: executes bytecode instruction

â€“ Detected features: the tool identiï¬es speciï¬c fea-
tures like â€œMoney Calls,â€ inï¬nite loops, and payable

â€“ Private bytecode support: can analyze contracts

â€¢Advantages of DefectChecker
â€“ In-depth bytecode analysis: DefectChecker can ana-
lyze Ethereum smart contract bytecode, even without 
the source code, allowing for security veriï¬cation of 
deployed contracts on the blockchain.
â€“ Detection of speciï¬c vulnerabilities: the tool can 
identify common vulnerabilities such as reentrancy, 
inï¬nite loops, and unsecured external calls, enabling 
rapid identiï¬cation of security risks.
â€“ Modular architecture: its modular design allows 
easy adjustments or expansions to integrate new 
checks or adapt them for speciï¬c use cases.
â€“ Symbolic execution: using symbolic execution with 
an SMT solver enables more precise analysis of exe-
cution paths and control conditions, improving test 
coverage.
â€“ Support for private bytecode: the tool can analyze

â€¢Limitations
â€“ Dependence on bytecode: the tool can only analyze

â€“ Lack of support for certain defect types: while ef-

â€“ Limited dynamic security analysis: DefectChecker 
primarily relies on static bytecode analysis. Dynamic

â€“ Integration complexity: while the tool is modular,

â€“ Performance on large contracts: symbolic analysis

â€¢Future work
â€“ Integration with SMT solvers: a key direction for 
future work is to explore combining DefectCheckerâ€™s

â€“ Identifying code patterns causing errors: research-
ers could investigate speciï¬c code patterns that lead

â€“ Enhancing eï¬ƒciency: another direction for future

â€“ Broader application: DefectChecker could be ex-

3.4. Test metamorphic
MT is not a speciï¬c tool but rather a methodological approach used

and leveraging MRs, which are fundamental properties of the software 
that enable the generation of additional test cases or the validation of 
results in various contexts.
Although this approach is highly eï¬€ective, it is typically imple-
mented through third-party tools or integrated into more comprehensive 
testing frameworks. Therefore, this article does not focus on MT itself, as 
our primary objective is to present and analyze speciï¬c tools. Nonethe-
less, we acknowledge the value of this methodology and its signiï¬cant 
potential to enhance testing strategies.

Classifying vulnerabilities plays a key role in strengthening the se-
curity of smart contracts by providing developers, auditors, and re-
searchers with a clear reference framework. This classiï¬cation helps to 
target the most dangerous ï¬‚aws, develop more eï¬€ective detection tools,

This presentation aims to explore two approaches to vulnerability 
classiï¬cation in smart contracts: exploitable vulnerabilities and those 
cataloged by the open smart contract vulnerabilities (OpenSCV) taxon-
omy. The main objectives are as follows:
â€¢Examine exploitable vulnerabilities: this category covers weak-
nesses that are actively exploitable by attackers and often unde-

smart contract security.
â€¢Analyze the OpenSCV framework: widely recognized in the indus-

vulnerabilities, though it may lack certain emerging or context-
speciï¬c ï¬‚aws recently discovered.
This comparison will provide insight into how these classiï¬cations con-

strategies suited to todayâ€™s blockchain challenges.
4.1. Exploitable vulnerabilities
Exploitable vulnerabilities [37] in smart contracts are weaknesses 
that allow attackers to manipulate or compromise the functioning of 
these contracts for malicious purposes. These ï¬‚aws, often subtle and 
complex, enable critical attacks that jeopardize funds and compromise 
the reliability of dApps. Although numerous audit and security tools 
have been developed to detect these vulnerabilities, many of them evade 
existing detection mechanisms, making identiï¬cation challenging and 
prevention essential.
These vulnerabilities are termed â€œexploitableâ€ because they provide 
attackers with tangible attack vectors that can be leveraged to gain 
unauthorized privileges or beneï¬ts. Unlike minor errors or inconsequen-
tial bugs, an exploitable vulnerability presents a real and immediate 
breach in contract security, which can be used to cause ï¬nancial dam-
age, distort transactions, or alter contract behavior.
4.1.1. Methodology for classifying exploitable bugs in smart contracts
The article â€œDemystifying Exploitable Bugs in Smart Contractsâ€ is 
based on a systematic empirical analysis of 516 unique vulnerabili-
ties found in deployed smart contracts between 2021 and 2022. This 
methodology comprises several key steps, each contributing to an in-
depth understanding of exploitable bugs.
â€¢Data collection: the authors gathered information on real-world 
vulnerabilities, focusing on incidents that led to signiï¬cant ï¬nancial 
losses. This comprehensive dataset, drawn from multiple sources, 
oï¬€ers a broad perspective on exploitable vulnerabilities in practical 
scenarios and their ï¬nancial impacts.
â€¢Exploitability analysis: each vulnerability was assessed to deter-
mine its potential to be exploited by attackers. The authors speciï¬-
cally focused on weaknesses that escape conventional analysis tools, 
highlighting gaps in current auditing practices. This step was crucial 
in identifying the most dangerous vulnerabilities for smart contracts.
â€¢Categorization by type: the identiï¬ed vulnerabilities were grouped 
into seven distinct types based on their characteristics and ex-
ploitability. This classiï¬cation involves analyzing the root causes of 
each vulnerability, their distribution across various contracts, and 
the challenges associated with their auditing. The goal of this clas-
siï¬cation is to facilitate understanding and management of these 
vulnerabilities.
â€¢Impact assessment and mitigation strategies: for each type of 
vulnerability, the authors examined the potential consequences of 
exploitation and proposed remediation strategies. This analysis in-
cludes possible ï¬nancial impacts and provides developers with best 
practices to mitigate risks in future smart contract deployments.
â€¢Abstraction of bug patterns: whenever possible, the authors gen-
eralized each type of vulnerability into bug patterns. These ab-
stractions enable the identiï¬cation of similar weaknesses in other 
contracts and support the automation of future detection processes, 
allowing developers and security auditors to proactively identify and 
ï¬x these vulnerabilities.
This empirical analysis and structured classiï¬cation framework 
provide a valuable tool for understanding and managing exploitable 
vulnerabilities in smart contracts, contributing to improved security 
in the blockchain ecosystem.
4.1.2. Types of exploitable vulnerabilities identiï¬ed
4.1.2.1. Price oracle manipulation Description: this vulnerability occurs 
when an attacker manages to inï¬‚uence the price values provided by 
oracles for personal gain by manipulating the information transmitted 
to smart contracts. This can lead to economic imbalances and signiï¬cant 
losses for users. Attack mechanism: the attacker manipulates the price 
of assets by exploiting the dependency of contracts on external oracles. 
This manipulation allows altering ï¬nancial transactions in the attackerâ€™s 
favor, often at the expense of other participants.
4.1.2.2. Privilege escalation Description: this type of vulnerability hap-
pens when an unauthorized user gains access to normally restricted 
functions or privileges, enabling unintended actions such as accessing 
funds or modifying sensitive data. Attack Mechanism: The attacker ex-
ploits ï¬‚aws in permission management or gains indirect access to certain 
functions, achieving a higher level of control than what should be per-
mitted. This ï¬‚aw can be used to divert funds or take control of sensitive 
contract functions.
4.1.2.3. Atomicity violations
â€¢Description: this atomicity issue occurs when sequences of transac-
tions, which are supposed to be executed as an indivisible unit, are 
interrupted, leading to inconsistencies in the contractâ€™s state.
â€¢Attack mechanism: by inserting transactions during critical opera-
tions, an attacker can disrupt the logical sequence of operations and 
compromise the integrity of data or funds, resulting in inconsisten-
cies or losses.
4.1.2.4. ID uniqueness violations
â€¢Description: these violations involve errors in generating or manag-
ing unique identiï¬ers, which can lead to traceability issues or data 
collisions.
â€¢Attack mechanism: by exploiting weaknesses in the generation or 
veriï¬cation of identiï¬er uniqueness, an attacker can create conï¬‚icts 
in identiï¬cation, potentially allowing unauthorized access or modi-
ï¬cation of resources tied to those identiï¬ers.
4.1.2.5. Inconsistent state updates
â€¢Description: this type of vulnerability arises when state updates are 
not properly synchronized, creating contradictions in the informa-
tion stored by the contract.
â€¢Attack mechanism: by disrupting the logical ï¬‚ow of state update 
operations, an attacker can introduce inconsistencies into the data. 
This can lead to unexpected behaviors, such as incorrect fund trans-
fers or execution errors.
4.1.2.6. Contract implementation speciï¬c bugs
â€¢Description: these vulnerabilities result from errors or ï¬‚aws spe-
ciï¬c to the internal logic of a contract, inherent to the individual 
implementation of a contract.
â€¢Attack mechanism: attackers exploit logical weaknesses or cod-
ing errors speciï¬c to a contractâ€™s implementation. These errors may 
include ï¬‚aws in calculating critical values, handling certain trans-
action types, or missing security checks.

4.1.2.7. Erroneous accounting
â€¢Description: accounting errors occur when the contract fails to 
properly record ï¬nancial information or accounting states, which 
can lead to payment errors or improper allocation of funds.
â€¢Attack mechanism: by manipulating or exploiting errors in the con-
tractâ€™s ï¬nancial records, an attacker can alter the distribution of 
funds or create accounting inconsistencies, leading to ï¬nancial loss 
for users or the contract owner.
These seven types of vulnerabilities are critical because they provide 
direct exploitation opportunities for attackers, especially if they are not 
detected before contract deployment. Each of these vulnerabilities has 
the potential to cause signiï¬cant ï¬nancial loss or disruptions in the func-
tioning of smart contract platforms.
4.2. The OpenSCV taxonomy
4.2.1. Analysis methodology
Smart contracts form the cornerstone of blockchain systems, facil-
itating transactions among entities. Despite their pivotal role, smart 
contracts, like conventional software, are susceptible to defects, includ-
ing critical security vulnerabilities.
A) Addressing vulnerabilities: research initiatives and classiï¬ca-
tion frameworks
Various research endeavors aim to detect and mitigate vulnera-
bilities in smart contracts, leading to the development of specialized 
vulnerability detection tools. While classiï¬cation frameworks like 
DASP and SWC have emerged to categorize these vulnerabilities, 
their relevance has diminished over time due to evolving threats 
and advancements in smart contract technology.
B) Introducing OpenSCV: a novel taxonomic approach
To address the shortcomings of existing classiï¬cation schemes, 
OpenSCV [38], a novel hierarchical taxonomy of smart contract 
vulnerabilities, has been devised. Unlike its predecessors, OpenSCV 
remains open to community contributions and is designed to evolve 
alongside emerging threats and technological advancements.
C) Constructing OpenSCV: methodology and rigor
The development of OpenSCV involved a meticulous analysis 
of existing vulnerability classiï¬cations and an extensive examina-
tion of 49 research works on vulnerability detection. The taxonomy 
comprises 76 vulnerabilities meticulously organized into a coherent 
hierarchical structure, ensuring comprehensive coverage of poten-
tial risks.
D) Flexibility and practical utility
OpenSCV stands out for its adaptability and practical utility. 
With a dedicated support infrastructure on GitHub, it welcomes con-
tinuous feedback and updates from the community. Moreover, each 
vulnerability entry is accompanied by a concrete code example, en-
hancing clarity and facilitating understanding.
E) Advancements and signiï¬cance
OpenSCV represents a signiï¬cant leap forward in smart con-
tract vulnerability research, oï¬€ering a dynamic and comprehensive 
classiï¬cation framework. By addressing the limitations of outdated 
schemes and embracing the ever-evolving nature of smart contract 
technology, OpenSCV serves as an indispensable resource for re-
searchers, developers, and security professionals alike, empowering 
them to better understand, prevent, and mitigate smart contract vul-
nerabilities.
After detailing the analysis methodology used to assess the smart 
contract vulnerabilities and presenting the OpenSCV taxonomy along 
with its beneï¬ts, we showcase these concepts through Table 2. This table 
lists various security vulnerabilities of smart contracts, providing details 
on each vulnerability category, as well as relevant research works that 
have studied or addressed these speciï¬c issues.

4.3.1. Reentrancy (1.1)
Calling external contracts introduces a signiï¬cant risk as the control 
ï¬‚ow can be hacked. This vulnerability, known as a reentrancy attack 
or recursive call attack, occurs when a malicious contract initiates a 
callback to the calling contract before the initial function invocation is 
ï¬nished. Consequently, this can result in unintended and undesirable 
interactions between multiple invocations of the function [39]. Fig. 4
presents a scenario of two contracts interacting with each other, contract 
A and contract B [40]. 
In this situation, contract A invokes a function called B() in contract 
B. However, it is important to note that contract B possesses a vulner-
ability known as reentrancy. The reentrancy vulnerability occurs when 
a contract B, upon being called by contract A, permits contract A to 
recursively invoke function B() before completing its initial execution. 
This creates a loop where function B() can be repeatedly called before 
its execution is fully completed. This situation can result in undesirable 
outcomes. For instance, letâ€™s consider a scenario where function B() car-
ries out a funds transfer operation. If the reentrancy vulnerability is not 
adequately addressed, an attacker can exploit the callback loop to ex-
ecute multiple fund transfers before contract B has an opportunity to 
update the balance or implement necessary security measures [41].

From a historical perspective, the reentrancy attack stands out as 
one of the most devastating attacks in the realm of Solidity smart con-
tracts. This particular attack has resulted in substantial ï¬nancial losses, 
amounting to hundreds of millions of dollars over the past few years. 
We can cite:
â€¢ The DAO hack: a reentrancy attack on the DAO in 2016 stole 3.6 
million Ether ($60 million) and forced Ethereum to fork into two 
chains: Ethereum Classic and Ethereum [42].
â€¢ dForce: a hacker stole $25 million in bitcoin and ether from dForceâ€™s 
lending protocol, leaving it with less than 1% of its assets [43]. In 
fact, a hacker used the combination of ERC777 tokens and DeFi 
smart contracts to perform a reentrancy attack. Thanks to the call-
back mechanism, he was able to issue and withdraw ERC777 tokens 
repeatedly, taking advantage of the delay in balance updates [44].
â€¢ Grim Finance: a hacker stole approximately $30 million in tokens 
from the DeFi Grim Finance project by exploiting a reentrancy ï¬‚aw 
in the safeTransferFrom function of the smart contract. This func-
tion was not updating its internal state before transferring tokens to 
an external contract, which could call the function back and cause 
errors [45].
Itâ€™s worth noting that the reentrancy vulnerability is divided into two 
subcategories:
â€¢unsafe credit transfer (1.1.1): reentrancy is a critical vulnerability 
in smart contracts, brought to light after the DAO attack in 2016. It 
allows attackers to manipulate balances by executing credit transfers 
before the completion of a previous call. In short, this vulnerability 
enables unintentional fund transfers, facilitating malicious attacks. 
The various designations, â€œReentrancyâ€ [46], â€œReentrancy with bal-
ance changeâ€ [47], â€œSWC-107 reentrancyâ€[48].
â€¢unsafe system state changes (1.1.2): this vulnerability is similar 
in nature to 1.1.1, with the main diï¬€erence being that no credit is 
involved and therefore, there is no impact on usersâ€™ funds. Due to 
the way the contract is coded, a call that reaches the vulnerable 
contract before a previous one has ended may allow an attacker to 
place the program in an unexpected state, leading to various eï¬€ects 
depending on the type of contract involved, including performance 
or availability issues. This vulnerability is also known in the litera-
ture as â€œReentrancyNoETHâ€ [49], â€œReentrancyâ€ [50], â€œReentrancy 
without balance changeâ€ [47], or â€œSWC-107 reentrancyâ€ [48]. These 
two subcategories illustrate diï¬€erent ways in which reentrancy can 
be exploited for malicious attacks in smart contracts.
4.3.2. Delegatecall to untrusted callee (1.6)
The use of the delegateCall function to invoke untrusted contracts is 
a dangerous practice. It exposes the calling contract to multiple vulner-
abilities. The called contract can potentially modify sensitive variables 
of the calling contract, such as msg.data (the function arguments) and 
msg.sender (the address that initiated the call).
â€¢A striking example: the Parity hack
The Parity hack in 2018 perfectly illustrates the dangers of this 
practice. By exploiting a ï¬‚aw in the delegateCall function of the 
Parity multi-signature wallet contract, attackers were able to take 
control of usersâ€™ wallets. They achieved this by calling a malicious 
contract via delegateCall, which allowed them to override the in-
tended functionality and reset the ownership and usage parameters 
of usersâ€™ wallets, leading to signiï¬cant ï¬nancial losses.

4.3.3. Incorrect use of event blockchain variables for time (5.1.1)
Smart contracts are susceptible to a critical security ï¬‚aw when they 
rely on speciï¬c details within a block (like timestamp, miner address, 
block number, mining diï¬ƒculty, or gas limit) to control the sequence of 
events. This vulnerability allows miners, who have some control over 
block creation, to potentially manipulate the contractâ€™s behavior.
â€¢Multiple Names, One Problem
This issue has been recognized and documented under various 
names in research papers:
â€“ Block state dependence [46], [15]: this term directly high-
lights the contractâ€™s dependence on the state of the block for 
its logic.
â€“ Time restrictions [58]: this name emphasizes the vulnerabili-
tyâ€™s connection to using timestamps for controlling events.
â€“ Blockchain eï¬€ects time dependency [59]: this term focuses on 
how the timing of events on the blockchain is aï¬€ected by this 
dependency.
â€“ Timestamp dependence [60,55] and many others: this is a spe-
ciï¬c example where the contract relies solely on timestamps 
for control.
â€¢Additional terminology
Several other terms describe this vulnerability with a speciï¬c 
focus:
â€“ Block number dependence [51,61]: this term highlights the 
reliance on the blockâ€™s position in the chain.
â€“ Race condition [18]: this term describes a situation where the 
outcome depends on the order in which transactions are pro-
cessed, which miners can inï¬‚uence.
â€¢Other relevant concepts
â€“ BlockTimestamp [62]: this is another way of referring to 
timestamp dependence.
â€“ Time dependency [62]: this is a broader term encompassing 
both timestamp and potentially other time-related dependen-
cies.
â€“ Event-ordering (EO) bugs [63]: this term emphasizes the is-
sueâ€™s impact on the intended order of events within the con-

â€“ SWC-116: block values as a proxy for time [48]: this refers to 
a speciï¬c coding weakness documented in security standards 
for smart contracts.
By understanding these various names and related concepts, de-
velopers and auditors can better identify and address this critical 
vulnerability in smart contract design.
4.3.4. Integer underï¬‚ow (6.1.1)
The integer underï¬‚ow attack is a common vulnerability in Ethereum 
smart contracts and other computer systems that manipulate integers. 
This vulnerability occurs when the result of a subtraction leads to a 
number less than zero, and that number is then used in calculations, 
operations, or conditions unexpectedly.
In the context of Ethereum smart contracts, this vulnerability can 
have serious consequences. For example, if a smart contract uses a vari-
able to track an account balance and that variable is subtracted without 
adequate veriï¬cation, an integer underï¬‚ow could result in a negative 
balance, potentially allowing an attacker to withdraw funds from the 
contract unauthorized.
This vulnerability was one of the causes of the notorious attacks 
against Ethereum smart contracts between 2016 and 2018, highlighting 
the importance of addressing these security issues in blockchain [5].

5. RQ4: What metrics are used to evaluate the quality and 
eï¬€ectiveness of security testing for Ethereum smart contracts?
Several metrics are used to assess the eï¬€ectiveness of security testing 
methods for Ethereum smart contracts.
â€¢Detection capability
â€“ Precision: this metric reï¬‚ects the percentage of identiï¬ed is-
sues that are actual vulnerabilities. High precision ensures the 
focus is on genuine security risks [11].
â€“ Recall: this metric represents the proportion of actual vul-
nerabilities that the testing method successfully detects. High 
recall indicates a comprehensive ability to ï¬nd security ï¬‚aws 
[11].
â€“ True positives (TP): the number of correctly identiï¬ed vul-
nerabilities. High TP indicates successful detection of real is-
sues [13].
â€“ False positives (FP): the number of identiï¬ed issues that are 
not actual vulnerabilities. Low FP reduces wasted time inves-
tigating non-existent threats [13].
â€¢Eï¬ƒciency and performance
â€“ Time: measured in seconds or minutes, it reï¬‚ects how long 
it takes to test a contract. Faster testing allows for quicker 
security assessments [14].
â€“ Test cases generated: the number of test cases created during 
fuzzing. Higher numbers increase the likelihood of exploring 
diverse scenarios and uncovering vulnerabilities [13].
â€“ Coverage: this metric can refer to:
* Branch coverage: the percentage of code branches 
executed during testing. Higher coverage suggests a 
more thorough exploration of the code [13].
* Instruction coverage: the percentage of instructions 
executed during testing. High coverage implies a 
deeper examination of the contractâ€™s logic [14].
â€¢Real-world impact
â€“ Number of vulnerabilities found: the total number of vul-
nerabilities identiï¬ed in real-world smart contracts. This 
demonstrates the toolâ€™s eï¬€ectiveness in practical situations 
[11].
â€“ Vulnerability types: the speciï¬c types of vulnerabilities de-
tected (e.g., reentrancy, delegation ï¬‚aws). A wider range of 
vulnerability detection indicates a more robust testing ap-
proach [11].
â€¢Additional considerations
â€“ Memory usage: excessive memory consumption can hinder 
the testing process. Tools with eï¬ƒcient memory management 
are preferred [14].
â€“ Ease of use: a user-friendly interface and clear documentation 
simplify the testing process for developers.
5.1. Evaluation of fuzzing testing tools
In order to evaluate the performance of smart contract fuzzing tools, 
we conducted a comprehensive analysis of several popular tools, includ-
ing xFuzz, IR-Fuzz, ItyFuzz, SMARTIAN, DEPOSafe, Ethrolic, GasFuzzer, 
Magic Mirror, RLF, Harvey, and ConFuzzius. We extracted relevant pa-
rameters and evaluation results from research papers and oï¬ƒcial doc-

vulnerability detection, and overall performance.
â€¢FunFuzz is an advanced tool for detecting vulnerabilities in smart 
contracts, surpassing existing fuzzers in both eï¬ƒciency and eï¬€ec-
tiveness. It targets speciï¬c vulnerabilities such as reentrancy, block 
dependency, and gasless send, providing a more focused approach to 
fuzz testing. By reducing the scope of exploration to high-risk func-
tions, FunFuzz eï¬ƒciently identiï¬es critical vulnerabilities that might 
be missed by traditional fuzzers. Extensive testing on 170 real-world 
smart contracts has demonstrated its ability to uncover serious se-
curity ï¬‚aws, making it an invaluable tool for ensuring the safety of 
DApps.
â€¢xFuzz demonstrates exceptional precision and recall, particularly 
for reentrancy, delegation, and tx-origin vulnerabilities. It signiï¬-
cantly outperforms sFuzz in terms of time savings and vulnerability 
detection.
â€¢IR-Fuzz exhibits high precision for all vulnerability types, identify-
ing over 485 vulnerable contracts with minimal false positives. It

â€¢ItyFuzz excels in instruction coverage, surpassing SMARTIAN on

â€¢SMARTIAN enhances fuzzing eï¬€ectiveness through static and dy-

tiï¬es various vulnerability types.
â€¢DEPOSafe achieves 100% precision in identifying vulnerabilities 
related to false deposits in ERC-20 smart contracts. Its high recall

â€¢Ethrolic proves eï¬€ective in identifying a wide range of vulnerabili-

Randomness (BR), Re-entrancy (RE), Locked Ether (LE), Unhandled

â€¢GasFuzzer surpasses ContractFuzzer in detecting Exceptions Disor-

â€¢Magic Mirror utilizes constraint solving, state exploration, and com-

â€¢RLF outperforms Mythril and SmarTest in terms of vulnerability 
detection eï¬ƒciency, identifying 98% of vulnerabilities within 30

â€¢Harvey signiï¬cantly reduces the time required to detect bugs and

â€¢ConFuzzius achieves superior code coverage compared to ILF and

vulnerability types, including Assertion Failure, Integer Overï¬‚ows, 
Reentrancy, and Unsafe Delegatecall.

6. RQ5: What are the current challenges and limitations in the 
ï¬eld of security testing for Ethereum smart contracts?
Introduction to challenges and limitations: smart contracts on the 
Ethereum blockchain are seeing increased adoption across various sec-
tors, but their security remains a major concern. Code errors can lead 
to ï¬nancial losses and security breaches, posing challenges such as the 
growing complexity of contracts, diverse usage scenarios, and the need 
for robust security standards. Understanding and addressing these chal-
lenges is crucial to ensuring the reliability of Ethereum smart contracts.
â€¢Speciï¬c challenges in security testing for Ethereum
â€“ Immutability: one of the major challenges in the develop-
ment and security testing of smart contracts lies in the im-
mutability of the blockchain. This characteristic implies that 
everything recorded on the blockchain is permanent and can-
not be altered. Consequently, any vulnerability or program-
ming error that goes undetected before contract deployment 
becomes diï¬ƒcult, if not impossible, to rectify without compro-
mising the systemâ€™s integrity and trust. Unlike traditional soft-
ware development, where iterations and corrections are pos-
sible throughout the process, smart contracts have limitations 
in terms of modiï¬cations post-deployment. This means devel-
opers must exercise extreme vigilance during security testing 
to identify and resolve all vulnerabilities early in the devel-
opment stages, as these vulnerabilities can transform into po-
tential exploits once the contract is active on the blockchain. 
Thus, security testing must be comprehensive and thorough 
prior to deployment to minimize the risks of vulnerabilities 
and future exploits, while also considering the limitations of 
iterative development to make necessary corrections early in 
the process [67].
â€“ The complexity and obscurity of the Solidity language se-
mantics [68]:
The complexity and obscurity of Solidityâ€™s semantics con-
tribute to several challenges and potential vulnerabilities in 
the development and security of smart contracts. Hereâ€™s how 
this manifests:
* Partial understanding: solidity is a language spe-
ciï¬c to the Ethereum blockchain, designed for writ-
ing smart contracts. Its syntax and concepts can be 
challenging to grasp for developers not familiar with 
decentralized programming. As a result, even experi-
enced programmers may have a partial understand-
ing of how certain features or structures in Solidity 
actually work.
* Risk of design errors: the obscurity of the semantics 
can lead to design errors. For example, a developer 
might misinterpret how a function or variable oper-
ates, leading to logical errors in the smart contract.
* Security vulnerabilities: ambiguities or subtleties in 
Solidityâ€™s semantics can open doors to security vul-
nerabilities. For instance, a misunderstanding of per-
mission management or fund transfer functions could 
result in security ï¬‚aws such as reentrancy attacks, ca-
pacity overï¬‚ows, or trap contracts.
* Contract complexity: complex smart contracts writ-
ten in Solidity can be challenging to audit and test 
thoroughly due to the complexity of their semantics. 
This can result in gaps in security testing and leave 
potential vulnerabilities undiscovered.
* Language evolution: as Solidity is an evolving lan-
guage, new features and changes in semantics may 
occur. This necessitates ongoing updates to knowl-
edge and development practices, which can be a chal-
lenge for developers. In summary, Solidityâ€™s obscure 
semantics make understanding and developing smart 
contracts more complex, increasing the risk of design 
errors and security vulnerabilities. Developers must 
therefore exercise great caution and use best devel-
opment practices to mitigate these risks as much as 
possible.
â€“ Scalability [69]: How to eï¬€ectively test thousands of 
deployed smart contracts. The scalability challenge of 
Ethereum refers to the networkâ€™s ability to process a large 
number of transactions eï¬ƒciently and quickly while main-
taining reasonable transaction costs. Ethereum, as a public 
blockchain, faces scalability challenges due to its original 
design, which prioritizes decentralization and security over 
speed and scalability.
Here are some of the main scalability challenges that 
Ethereum faces:
* Limited throughput: Ethereum is limited in terms of 
transactions per second (TPS). Its current capacity is 
approximately 15 to 30 TPS, which is insuï¬ƒcient to 
support large-scale applications.
* Variable transaction costs: during network conges-
tion, transaction fees can signiï¬cantly increase, mak-
ing microtransactions or frequent transactions im-
practical.
* Conï¬rmation time: the time required for a transac-
tion to be conï¬rmed on the Ethereum blockchain can 
vary depending on network load, leading to delays in 
transactions.
* Resource management: Ethereum nodes must man-
age a signiï¬cant amount of data to stay synchronized 
with the blockchain, which can be challenging for 
low-performing nodes or individual users.
* Complex smart contracts: complex smart contracts 
and resource-intensive operations can increase net-
work load and reduce its ability to process new trans-
actions quickly.

one another, complicating tests
