* Multiple interactions: smart contracts can interact 
with each other in complex ways, calling and being 
called by other contracts in scenarios where multiple 
contracts are involved simultaneously. Attack Risks: 
Interactions between smart contracts open the door 
to attack risks, where malicious contracts can be de-
signed to exploit vulnerabilities in other contracts or 
induce unexpected behaviors.
* Prediction diï¬ƒculty: it is often challenging to pre-
dict how multiple contracts will interact with each 
other, especially when these interactions can be trig-
gered by external events or variable data.
* Global understanding: understanding the full scope 
of possible interactions between multiple smart con-
tracts is a challenge in itself, as it requires a deep 
analysis of dependencies, data ï¬‚ows, and triggering 
conditions for interactions.
* Security implications: interactions between smart 
contracts can lead to security issues such as data 
leaks, overï¬‚ow attacks, unexpected reentrancies, etc.
â€¢Limitations in Ethereum security testing [71]
â€“ Incomplete test coverage:
Even thorough testing cannot guarantee 100% code cov-
erage. Gaps may exist in untested areas or unexpected input 
scenarios. Reliance on unit tests and fuzzing may limit the 
detection of more complex issues related to the interaction 
between diï¬€erent contracts or race conditions.
â€“ Diï¬ƒculty in identifying logical ï¬‚aws:
Certain logical ï¬‚aws, such as reasoning errors or inconsis-
tencies in business rules, may be hard to detect by automated 
testing. Formal veriï¬cation can aid in identifying these ï¬‚aws, 
but requires expertise and a precise formal speciï¬cation of the 
contract.
â€“ Evolving threat landscape:
New vulnerabilities and attack vectors emerge constantly, 
making it challenging to update tests to keep up with the 
evolving threat. Tests must be continuously updated and 
adapted to ensure they remain eï¬€ective against the latest 
threats.
â€“ Cost and time:
Thorough security testing, especially formal veriï¬cation, 
can be expensive and time-consuming. A balance must be 
found between testing rigor and the resources available for 
contract development and maintenance.
â€“ Human factors:
Human errors in writing tests or interpreting results can 
compromise the eï¬€ectiveness of security testing. Close com-
munication and collaboration between developers, testers, 
and security auditors are crucial. In summary, smart contract 
security testing is essential to protect dApps from vulnerabili-
ties and attacks, but it has limitations that must be considered. 
It is important to adopt a multi-layered approach that com-
bines diï¬€erent testing techniques and ensures tests are contin-
ually updated and adapted to the evolving threat landscape.
7. Discussion
Our literature review has identiï¬ed several security testing tech-
niques used to evaluate Ethereum smart contracts. These techniques 
include fuzzing, symbolic execution, mutation testing, and MT. Fuzzing, 
which represents a signiï¬cant portion of research and development ef-
forts, involves providing invalid, unexpected, or random inputs to a 
program to detect bugs and vulnerabilities. Symbolic execution explores 
all possible execution paths of a program using symbolic values, thereby 
detecting bugs that are not detectable by concrete execution. Mutation 
testing deliberately injects modiï¬cations into a programâ€™s source code 
to evaluate whether existing tests can detect these mutations and ensure 
code robustness. Finally, MT relies on MRs to validate system behavior 
after transformations of input data.
Each of these techniques has speciï¬c advantages and limitations. 
Fuzzing oï¬€ers eï¬ƒcient automation and code coverage, but can gener-
ate false positives and be time-consuming. Symbolic execution allows 
for in-depth analysis of program execution paths, but can be resource-
intensive. Mutation testing improves test coverage and code quality but 
can be challenging to interpret. Finally, MT reduces reliance on test ora-
cles and detects defects not detectable by other techniques, but requires 
the identiï¬cation of meaningful MRs.
The analysis methodology used to evaluate vulnerabilities in the 
Ethereum smart contracts, along with the introduction of the OpenSCV 
taxonomy, has provided valuable insights into the most common vulner-
abilities and areas requiring further research. The most studied vulner-
abilities include reentrancy attacks, delegateCall to unreliable callers, 
and incorrect use of the blockchain event variables for time, highlighting 
their signiï¬cant impact on the smart contract security. These vulnera-
bilities have historical examples, such as The DAO hack and the Parity 
hack, highlighting the real consequences of these security ï¬‚aws.
Additionally, the analysis has identiï¬ed less studied or unstudied 
vulnerabilities, underscoring the need for targeted research and col-
laboration eï¬€orts within the OpenSCV community. Recommendations 
to address these gaps include creating a centralized database, devel-
oping tools for vulnerability identiï¬cation and correction, and promot-
ing collaborative research among security experts. The adoption of the 
OpenSCV taxonomy promises better risk communication, improved pri-
oritization of security eï¬€orts, and enhanced collaboration to strengthen 
smart contract security in the blockchain ecosystem.
Several criteria are used to evaluate the quality and eï¬€ectiveness of 
security tests for Ethereum smart contracts. These criteria include de-
tection capability, eï¬ƒciency and performance, real-world impact, and 
other considerations such as memory usage and ease of use. To evaluate 
fuzzing tools, criteria such as code coverage, vulnerability detection, and 
overall performance were analyzed for tools like xFuzz, IR-Fuzz, ItyFuzz, 
SMARTIAN, DEPOSafe, Ethrolic, GasFuzzer, Magic Mirror, RLF, Har-
vey, and ConFuzzius. These tools exhibit varied performance in terms 
of accuracy, code coverage, and vulnerability detection, with speciï¬c 
strengths and weaknesses for each tool. For the evaluation of mutation 
testing tools, SuMo was used to assess its ability to generate and detect 
mutants in speciï¬c dApp projects. The results showed that SuMo was 
eï¬€ective in detecting a majority of mutants, with mutation scores indi-
cating its ability to identify potential vulnerabilities. Regarding symbolic 
execution tools like SMARTEST, RA, SAILFISH, and WANA, criteria such 
as vulnerability detection, execution time, accuracy, and ability to iden-
tify unknown vulnerabilities were evaluated. These tools demonstrated 
positive performance in detecting various vulnerabilities, although some 
may require improvements to optimize eï¬ƒciency and analysis speed. In 
summary, the evaluation of these tools highlights their diversity and 
varied performance in detecting vulnerabilities in Ethereum smart con-
tracts, emphasizing the importance of choosing tools tailored to the 
speciï¬c security needs of developers and smart contract auditors.
The article highlights several major challenges and limitations in the 
ï¬eld of security testing for Ethereum smart contracts on the Ethereum 
blockchain. One of the main challenges lies in the immutability of the 
blockchain, which makes rectiï¬cation after deploying a smart contract 
diï¬ƒcult, if not impossible, without compromising system integrity. This 
characteristic demands extreme vigilance during testing to identify and 
correct all vulnerabilities early in the development stages, as an unde-
tected ï¬‚aw can turn into an exploitable loophole once active on the 
blockchain.
Another signiï¬cant challenge lies in the complexity and opacity of 
the Solidity language syntax used to write smart contracts. This com-
plexity makes understanding Solidityâ€™s features and structures diï¬ƒcult 
for developers, leading to design errors and security vulnerabilities. 
Furthermore, Solidityâ€™s constant evolution requires frequent updates

to development practices to adapt to new changes and reduce risks. 
Ethereumâ€™s scalability also poses a major challenge, with limitations in 
terms of TPS, variable transaction fees, and variable conï¬rmation times. 
This limitation can hinder the deployment of large-scale applications on 
the Ethereum blockchain, necessitating innovative solutions to improve 
scalability while maintaining security and decentralization.
The complexity of interactions between smart contracts represents 
another obstacle, with potential risks of malicious attacks and unex-
pected behaviors. The diï¬ƒculty in predicting these interactions and un-
derstanding their overall impact makes security testing more complex, 
requiring in-depth analysis of dependencies and data ï¬‚ows between con-
tracts.
Finally, limitations of security testing itself, such as incomplete code 
coverage, diï¬ƒculty in identifying logical ï¬‚aws, and the costs associated 
with rigorous testing, underscore the need for a multi-level approach 
to ensure Ethereum smart contract security. This approach should com-
bine diï¬€erent testing techniques, be adaptable to evolving threats, and 
encourage close collaboration between developers, testers, and security 
auditors.
8. Future works
Future work in this ï¬eld could focus on several aspects to enhance 
the security of Ethereum smart contracts:
â€¢Diversiï¬ed case studies: enriching case studies by including a 
wider range of smart contracts across various sectors such as ï¬nance, 
healthcare, education, etc. This will help understand sector-speciï¬c 
vulnerabilities and adapt best security practices accordingly.
â€¢Exploring new blockchains: besides Ethereum, exploring other 
blockchains like Binance Smart Chain, Polkadot, and Cardano to 
understand diï¬€erences in security protocols and identify the best ap-
proaches to securing smart contracts on these alternative platforms.
â€¢Improving testing techniques: developing more advanced testing 
techniques, such as integrating artiï¬cial intelligence and machine 
learning for automated vulnerability detection, enhancing code cov-
erage, and reducing false positives in security test results.
â€¢Securing sensitive data: focusing on safeguarding sensitive data 
stored in smart contracts using advanced encryption techniques and 
strengthening key management protocols to mitigate risks of privacy 
breaches.
â€¢Development of specialized security tools: designing and devel-
oping specialized security tools for smart contract developers, such 
as automated security scanners, vulnerability simulation platforms, 
and sandbox test environments for more secure contract evaluation.
â€¢Enhancing collaboration and awareness: encouraging collab-
oration among researchers, developers, and security auditors to 
share knowledge, best practices, and lessons learned. Raising fur-
ther awareness among developers about secure programming best 
practices for smart contracts.
â€¢Adoption of security standards: promoting the adoption of spe-
ciï¬c security standards for Ethereum smart contracts by develop-
ing guidelines and recommendations to ensure optimal security in 
contract development and deployment. By combining these various 
research and development aspects, it is possible to signiï¬cantly en-
hance the security of Ethereum smart contracts and strengthen user 
trust in the blockchain ecosystem.
9. Conclusions
Research on Ethereum smart contract security highlights a diverse 
range of techniques and methodologies aimed at ensuring the reliability 
and security of smart contracts. Among the main techniques discussed 
are fuzzing, symbolic execution, mutation testing, and MT.
Fuzzing, as an automated testing technique, is highly eï¬€ective in 
identifying bugs and vulnerabilities by providing unexpected inputs to 
smart contracts. It oï¬€ers automation, code coverage exploration, and 
bug detection capabilities, but may suï¬€er from false positives and exe-
cution time issues.
Symbolic execution, a static analysis technique, explores all possible 
execution paths of a program, thereby detecting bugs that traditional 
methods may miss. While powerful, it can be resource-intensive and 
challenging to implement for complex contracts.
Mutation testing involves injecting mutations into the source code to 
evaluate the robustness of existing tests. It improves test coverage and 
code quality, but can be costly and challenging to interpret results.
MT, based on deï¬ning MRs, oï¬€ers an eï¬€ective approach to testing 
smart contracts by reducing reliance on test oracles and generating more 
eï¬€ective test cases. However, it depends on identifying meaningful re-
lations and may be diï¬ƒcult to automate fully.
By combining these techniques and tools, developers can enhance 
the overall quality and reliability of their smart contracts, thereby re-
ducing the risk of vulnerabilities and ensuring a more secure blockchain 
ecosystem.
The analysis of security testing tools and frameworks for smart con-
tracts reveals that fuzzing is a predominant technique, with several 
specialized tools available for grey-box testing, reï¬‚ecting the industryâ€™s 
emphasis on automated testing with random input data.
On the other hand, mutation testing tools are less prevalent, indicat-
ing that this approach might not be as widely adopted or prioritized in 
the context of smart contract security testing.
Symbolic execution tools are represented, but to a lesser extent com-
pared to fuzzing, suggesting a more selective use of this technique pos-
sibly due to its resource-intensive nature and complexity in analyzing 
all possible execution paths.
MT, while essential for verifying transformations of input data, is 
relatively less common, with only one tool listed for grey-box testing. 
This could imply a need for further development or awareness of this 
approach within the smart contract security testing community.
In conclusion, the availability and usage of diï¬€erent testing tech-
niques vary, with fuzzing being the most prominent, followed by sym-
bolic execution, mutation testing, and MT. The choice of tools and tech-
niques should align with the speciï¬c requirements and complexities of 
the smart contract being tested, highlighting the importance of informed 
decision-making in security testing practices.
The detailed analysis methodology used to assess smart contract vul-
nerabilities, along with the presentation of the OpenSCV taxonomy and 
its beneï¬ts, provides a comprehensive framework for understanding and 
addressing security challenges in smart contracts.
The results of the vulnerability analysis oï¬€er a visual representation 
of the research eï¬€orts dedicated to each vulnerability category between 
2020 and 2023, helping to identify critical areas in smart contract secu-
rity and shedding light on under-researched vulnerabilities that deserve 
increased attention.
By leveraging the OpenSCV taxonomy and prioritizing research ef-
forts based on identiï¬ed vulnerabilities, the smart contract community 
can enhance security practices, mitigate risks, and foster a more secure 
and trustworthy smart contract ecosystem.
The evaluation of various security testing tools for Ethereum smart 
contracts provides valuable insights into their eï¬€ectiveness in identi-
fying vulnerabilities and improving overall security. These evaluations 
showcase the diversity of tools available for smart contract security, 
each with its strengths and capabilities.
Combining these tools and leveraging their unique features can sig-
niï¬cantly enhance the reliability, robustness, and trustworthiness of 
Ethereum smart contracts, ultimately contributing to a more secure 
blockchain ecosystem.
These overall conclusions provide a comprehensive overview of the 
challenges and opportunities in the ï¬eld of Ethereum smart contract 
security, emphasizing the importance of an integrated and balanced ap-
proach to testing and security techniques to ensure trust and security in 
the smart contract ecosystem.

Performance and  interpretabilit y analysis  of  code  generation  large  language  
models
Vishnu S.  Pendyala  
âˆ—

H I G H L I G H T S
âˆ™ Interpretability analysis  uncovers  prompt  sensitivity  in  Code-Generating  LLMs.
âˆ™ A detailed  analysis  of  the  reliability  of  LLMs  shows  that  some  open-source  LLMs  inherently  possess  superior  performance  in  code  generation.
A R T I C L E I N F O
Communicated by  W.  Luo
Keywords:
Transcoding 
Code conversion  
Model explainability
A B S T R A C T
As Large  Language  Models  (LLMs)  are  increasingly  getting  integrated  into  software  development  workflows,  un -
derstanding their  reliability,  error  patterns  and  interpretability  in  real-world  development  scenarios  is  crucial  for  
establishing their  practical  utility.  This  study  evaluates  and  interprets  the  performance  of  15  open-source  LLM  
models, including  Code  LLaMa,  Granite  Code,  DeepSeek-Coder-V2,  and  Yi-Coder  on  code  translation  and  genera -
tion from  requirements  using  the  Rosetta  Code  dataset  across  diverse  programming  languages  and  tasks.  Syntactic  
correctness and  code  quality  are  quantified  using  metrics  such  as  CodeBLEU,  chrF,  and  METEOR.  Interpretability  
is explored  through  Feature  Ablation  and  Shapley  Value  Sampling  to  elucidate  prompt  processing  mechanisms.  
Results indicate  high  syntactic  correctness  and  quality  scores  for  models  such  as  DeepSeek-Coder-V2  and  Yi -
Coder, alongside  observed  sensitivities  to  specific  prompt  components.  This  research  provides  quantitative  and  
qualitative insights  into  the  capabilities  and  limitations  of  open-source  code-generating  LLMs,  informing  model  
selection and  the  understanding  of  LLM-generated  code.
1. Introduction
Automated code  translatio n, a  crucial  aspect  of  software  engineer -
ing, has  streamlined  the  tedious  process  of  converting  code  from  one  
language to  another,  thereby  enhancing  efficiency  and  scalability  with  
minimal effort.  It  facilitates  seamless  integration  of  diverse  projects  us -
ing different  languages,  reducing  manual  effort  and  the  potential  for  
human errors.  As  stated  by  Ech everria et  al.  [ 6], automated  code  trans -
lation has  been  valuable  for  modernizing  legacy  s ystems since  it  has  
lowered costs  by  minimizing  reliance  on  multilingual  developers  and  has  
fostered collaboration  in  open-source  communities.  It  has  also  supported  
the development  of  cross-platform  technologies,  enabling  the  flexible  
migration of  functionality  between  different  platforms.  Automating  code  
translation thus  aids  in  the  maintainability  and  scalability  of  large  and  
complex projects.  Traditional  translation  tools  rely  on  established  syn -
tax rules  to  convert  code,  which  provides  speed  and  predictability  for
straightforward tas ks but  has  been  less  effective  with  nuanced  contexts.  
In contrast,  methods  that  incorporate  Artificial  Intelligence  (AI)  use  con -
textual understanding  capabilities  of  Large  Language  Models  (LLMs)  for  
more accurate  and  adaptable  translations.
This study  evaluates  15  open-source  LLMs  for  code  translation  
tasks, focusing  on  two  key  selection  criteria:  instruction-tuned  models  
with fewer  than  ten  billion  parameters  and  compatibility  with  efficient  
deployment frameworks.  The  selected  models  span  two  architectural  
categories: those  based  on  the  LLaMa  architecture  by  Touvron  et  al.  
[7] (such  as  Yi-Coder  by  Wang  [ 8], Granite  Code  by  Mishra  et  al.  
[9], and  DeepSeek-Coder  by  Guo  et  al.  [ 10]) and  models  with  distinct  
architectures like  Qwen2  by  Yang  et  al.  [ 11], Gemma  by  Mesnard  et  
al. [ 12], and  DeepSeek-Coder-V2  by  Zhu  et  al.  [ 13] (which  employs  a  
Mixture-of-Experts approach  developed  by  Dai  et  al.  [ 16]). All  models  
were deployed  using  4-bit  quantization  to  significantly  reduce  memory
âˆ—

usage and  accelerate  inference,  which  enabled  deployment  and  testing  
on resource-constrained  devices.
This study  leverages  Rosetta  Code  by  Rosetta  Code  [ 17], a  compre -
hensive coding  chrestomathy  website,  to  construct  a  robust  translation  
dataset. The  sampled  dataset  covers  17  everyday  programming  tasks  
with implementations  across  seven  programming  languages:  C,  C+ +, 
Golang, Java,  JavaScript,  Python,  and  Rust.  This  approach  generated  42  
translation pairs  per  task,  serving  as  reference  translations  and  covering  
diverse programming  domains  such  as  bitwise  operations,  integer  oper -
ations, string  manipulations,  and  file  operations.  This  resulted  in  a  total  
of 714  translations  for  each  LLM.
LLM performance  was  evaluated  through  multiple  evaluation  met -
rics. Primary  metrics,  which  included  CodeBLEU  by  Ren  et  al.  [ 18], chrF  
by PopoviÄ‡  [ 19], METEOR  by  Banerjee  and  Lavie  [ 20], and  BLEU  by  
Papineni et  al.  [ 21], measured  translation  accuracy.  Additionally,  sup -
plementary metrics  were  developed  to  evaluate  code  extractability  and  
syntactic correctness.  The  unbiased  Pass@k  metric  introduced  by  Chen  
et al.  [ 22] was  also  calculated  for  evaluating  the  functional  correctness  
of code  generated  by  LLMs.  Advanced  techniques  like  Feature  Ablation  
from Merrick  [ 24] and  Shapley  Value  Sampling  from  Mitchell  et  al.  [ 25] 
were used  to  understand  the  LLMâ€™s  interpretative  capabilities.  The  exper -
imental protocol  also  incorporates  an  error  correction  mechanism.  When  
an LLM  generates  code  with  errors,  the  error  feedback  is  provided  within  
the same  conversation,  instructing  the  model  to  explain  and  rectify  the  
issue. This  approach  allows  assessment  of  the  LLMsâ€™  capacity  for  self -
improvement through  iterative  prompting.  Furthermore,  the  reasoning  
behind these  corrections  is  analyzed  to  identify  common  error  patterns  
across different  programming  languages.
Various prompts  were  developed  to  address  different  types  of  
LLMs, programming  languages,  and  experimental  stages.  The  regular  
expression-based code  extraction  methodology  demonstrated  a  99.4  %  
success rate  across  10,710  translations  evaluated  from  multiple  LLMs.  
The LLM-generated  translations,  formatted  using  language-specific  code  
formatters, compile  successfully  or  demonstrate  syntactical  correctness  
in approximately  62.75  %  of  instances  with  DeepSeek-Coder-V2  and  Yi -
Coder achieving  syntactically  correct  code  generation  in  more  than  80  %  
of the  translation  pairs.
These results,  along  with  interpretability  and  explainability  results,  
contribute towards  answering  the  following  research  questions.
â€¢ RQ1 - How effectively  can  the  process  behind  LLMs  translating
software in  one  programming  language  to  another,  or  generating  
software code  from  natural  language,  be  explained?
The dependency  of  translated  code  generated  by  LLMs  in  transla -
tion settings  on  the  source  code  is  analyzed  utilizing  interpretability  
methods, including  Feature  Ablation  and  Shapley  Value  Sampling.  
The visualization  of  interpretability  scores  as  heatmaps  reveals  
crucial insights  into  the  code  translation  process  and  illuminates  
potential methodologies  for  controlling  this  process.  These  find -
ings contribute  significantly  to  the  understanding  of  the  underlying  
mechanisms that  govern  LLM-based  code  translation.
â€¢ RQ2 - What do  the  findings  from  the  explanations  reveal  about  the
reliability and  accuracy  of  the  code  conversion  task  accomplished  by  
the foundation  models?
The code  translated  by  the  LLM  occasionally  generates  errors  dur -
ing compilation  or  syntax  verification  processes.  When  the  LLM  is  
presented with  these  errors  and  instructed  to  explain  the  error  and  
produce corrected  code,  this  research  initiative  examines  whether  
the subsequent  code  successfully  resolves  the  identified  errors.  It  also  
examines what  insights  the  LLMâ€™s  reasoning  reveals  regarding  com -
mon mistakes  made  by  LLMs  across  various  programming  languages.  
The analysis  of  these  error  correction  patterns  provides  valuable  per -
spectives on  the  underlying  limitations  and  corrective  capabilities  of  
LLMs in  the  context  of  code  translation  tasks.
Existing studies  primarily  focus  on  functional  correctness  in  com -
petitive programming  problems  or  standard  library  usage.  There  is  not
much insight  into  the  types  of  errors  LLMs  make  across  various  pro -
gramming paradigms  or  specific  software  development  tasks  like  code  
conversion. Studies  often  evaluate  proprietary,  black-box  models  such  
as Codex,  making  it  difficult  for  the  broader  research  and  developer  
community to  replicate  findings,  understand  internal  mechanisms,  or  
contribute to  their  improvement.  There  is  a  lack  of  systematic  evaluation  
of how  LLMs  handle  multiple  programming  languages  and  different  task  
types, such  as  direct  code  translation  vs.  generation  from  high-level  re -
quirements, within  a  controlled  environment.  This  makes  cross-language  
comparisons difficult.
Studies by  Pendyala  and  Kim  [ 1] have  shown  that  merely  using  eval -
uation metrics  without  the  backing  of  explainability  analysis  can  be  risky  
in some  domains.  While  some  studies,  such  as  the  work  of  Pendyala  
and Hall  [ 2], explore  LLM  interpretability  in  natural  language  tasks,  
its application  to  code  generation  is  less  common  and  often  less  gran -
ular. Understanding  why  an  LLM  generates  a  particular  piece  of  code,  
or which  parts  of  a  prompt  it  attends  to  most,  is  crucial  for  debugging,  
improving prompt  engineering,  and  building  trust.  This  study  addresses  
these gaps  in  the  current  literature.  The  key  contributions  of  this  paper  
are:
1. A comprehensive  study  of  LLM  performance  on  code  transla -
-
-
tion tasks  from  Rosetta  Code,  which  includes  translation  to  and  
from JavaScript,  a  language  often  underrepresented  in  translation  
datasets and  benchmarks,  utilizing  recent  LLMs.
2. A practical  guide  on  interpreting  the  translated  code  generated  by
LLMs in  comparison  to  the  source  code  and  interpretability-driven  
methodologies to  direct  the  LLM  output  toward  desired  outcomes.
3. A detailed  analysis  of  the  reliability  of  LLMs  with  and  with
out follow-up  prompting  when  the  models  produce  errors  in  the  
generated code.
4. Research artifacts  which  include  the  selected  tasks  and  their  im
plementations in  seven  coding  languages,  along  with  automation  
scripts and  all  intermediate  results  generated  by  the  LLMs.
This research  represents  the  first  initiative  to,
1. utilize Rosetta  Code  as  a  code  translation  benchmark,  analyz -
-
-
ing translation  tasks  through  both  translation  metrics  and  inter -
pretability methods.
2. evaluate translations  to  and  from  JavaScript  in  a  comprehen
sive manner  against  other  popular  programming  languages  like  
C, C+ +, Golang,  Java,  Python,  and  Rust.
3. provide interpretability  insights  into  the  LLM-driven  code  transla
tion process.
2. Background  and  related  work  
2.1. Automated  code  translation
Code translation  has  been  a  fundamental  task  in  software  engineer -
ing. It  involves  transforming  source  code  from  one  programming  lan -
guage to  another  while  preserving  the  original  functionality.  It  is  essen -
tial for  modernizing  legacy  systems,  cross-platform  compatibility,  and  
enhancing software  performance.  Automated  code  translation  reduces  
maintenance efforts,  improves  reliability,  and  boosts  non-functional  
properties like  security  and  performance.  It  has  enabled  seamless  in -
tegration between  diverse  projects,  reduced  reliance  on  multilingual  
developers, and  fostered  open-source  collaboration.
Traditionally, code  has  been  translated  using  rule-based  source-to -
source compilers,  which  rely  on  hard-coded  rules  and  program  analysis  
to convert  code  between  languages.  However,  these  tools  have  been  
costly to  develop  and  have  been  limited  to  specific  language  pairs,  often  
failing to  produce  code  that  aligns  with  idiomatic  expressions  of  the  tar -
get language.  In  contrast,  LLMs  have  presented  a  promising  alternative  
for code  translation,  offering  the  potential  to  understand  and  generate
Neurocomputing 656 (2025) 131461 
2 
[Page 3]
V.S. Pendyala  and  N.B.  Thakur
code in  multiple  languages  through  prompt  engineering  without  the  
need to  make  extensive  model  parameter  adjustments.
2.2. LLMs  in  software  engineering
LLMs have  been  utilized  in  software  engineering  for  code  generation,  
code development,  software  testing,  quality  assurance,  requirements  en -
gineering, code  translation,  and  program  repair  (debugging  and  bug  
detection), with  prompt  engineering  proving  crucial  for  enhancing  their  
accuracy and  controlling  their  output.  LLMs  have  required  techniques  
such as  iterative  prompting,  feedback,  and  program  analysis  to  address  
some of  their  limitations  in  software  engineering  tasks.  Code  LLMs  have  
been explicitly  trained  on  code  data,  which  renders  them  more  effec -
tive at  code  generation  and  translation  compared  to  general  LLMs.  On  
the other  hand,  general  LLMs  have  been  trained  on  a  broader  range  of  
text and  code  data  and  thus  have  demonstrated  greater  proficiency  with  
natural language  instructions  but  exhibit  less  robustness  in  core  cod -
ing tasks.  Both  categories  of  models  benefit  from  the  implementation  of  
prompt engineering  techniques  aimed  at  improving  code  quality.
The field  of  automated  code  generation  has  witnessed  significant  
breakthroughs with  the  introduction  of  interactive  and  self-improving  
methodologies. Fakhoury  et  al.  [ 60] proposed  TiCoder,  an  interactive  
workflow that  uses  LLM-generated  tests  to  clarify  user  intent  and  im -
prove code  generation  accuracy  by  45.97  %  through  guided  intent  
clarification. Adnan  et  al.  [ 61] developed  automated  debugging  strate -
gies that  enable  LLMs  to  identify  and  fix  code  flaws  using  intelligent  
debugging mechanisms  rather  than  relying  on  preemptive  test  case  
generation. Complementing  these  developments,  Zhang  et  al.  [ 62] intro -
duced a  sophisticated  approach  that  combines  backtracking  algorithms  
with program  analysis  techniques.  This  methodology  allows  models  to  
revise and  refine  generated  code  iteratively,  resulting  in  more  robust  
and accurate  code  output  that  better  meets  developer  specifications.
The automation  of  software  testing  has  experienced  substantial  
innovation through  the  application  of  large  language  models,  with  
researchers developing  comprehensive  frameworks  that  address  mul -
tiple aspects  of  the  testing  life  cycle.  Sherifi  et  al.  [ 63] presented  an  
agent-oriented framework  that  represents  a  holistic  approach  to  test  
automation. This  framework  integrates  LLMs  to  generate  unit  tests,  vi -
sualize call  graphs,  and  automate  test  execution  and  reporting  with  
high test  coverage,  significantly  reducing  the  manual  effort  required  in  
traditional testing  workflows.
Security considerations  have  become  increasingly  important  in  soft -
ware development,  leading  to  innovative  applications  of  LLMs  in  vul -
nerability detection  and  security  analysis.  FuzzCoder  by  Yang  et  al.  [ 64] 
proposed using  fine-tuned  large  language  models  to  guide  fuzzing  test  
mutations by  formulating  the  entire  process  as  sequence-to-sequence  
modeling, where  LLMs  learn  to  predict  optimal  mutation  locations  and  
strategies in  byte  sequences  to  trigger  program  crashes  and  vulnera -
bilities. The  approach  demonstrates  significant  improvements  in  crash  
detection across  various  file  formats  compared  to  traditional  heuristic  
fuzzing methods  like  AFL,  showing  that  LLMs  can  enhance  automated  
vulnerability discovery  in  software  testing.  Similarly,  LProtector,  pro -
posed by  Sheng  et  al.  [ 65], demonstrates  an  automated  vulnerability  
detection system  that  leverages  LLMs  to  identify  security  vulnerabilities  
in code  through  pattern  recognition  and  static  analysis.  This  approach  
represents a  significant  advancement  in  proactive  security  measures,  en -
abling organizations  to  identify  potential  security  issues  earlier  in  the  
development process.
The output  format  of  code  LLMs  is  not  always  consistent  and  can  
include natural  language  text,  comments,  or  code  in  unexpected  formats,  
which may  require  post-processing  to  extract  the  code.  This  variability  in  
output has  affected  the  reliability  of  evaluation  metrics  and  the  practical  
use of  the  generated  code.  Research  from  the  likes  of  Abukhalaf  et  al.  
[26], Jiang  et  al.  [ 27], White  et  al.  [ 28], Zhuo  et  al.  [ 29] shows  that  
LLMs have  also  struggled  with  understanding  the  overall  task  and  have  
acted like  â€œnext-token  predictorsâ€,  often  requiring  adequate  context  via  
prompt crafting.
2.3. Evaluation  of  LLMs  in  code  generation  scenarios
The evaluation  of  LLMs  for  code  generation  involves  several  key  
metrics that  assess  their  performance  beyond  merely  confirming  the  
functional correctness  of  the  generated  code.  Functional  correctness,  
which ensures  that  the  produced  code  generates  the  expected  output  for  
given inputs,  has  often  been  measured  using  test  suites.  This  measure -
ment is  done  with  metrics  such  as  Pass@k,  which  evaluates  whether  at  
least one  of  the  top  k  code  samples  passes  all  tests,  and  Computational  
Accuracy (CA)  for  code  translation,  which  assesses  whether  a  trans -
formed function  yields  the  same  output  as  its  source  counterpart.  
Efficiency is  evaluated  by  measuring  the  runtime  performance  of  the  
generated code,  utilizing  metrics  such  as  average  normalized  runtime,  
and considering  how  well  the  generated  code  performs  in  compari -
son to  that  produced  by  other  users  on  platforms  such  as  LeetCode.  
Adherence to  coding  standards  is  evaluated  to  determine  if  the  gen -
erated code  adheres  to  best  practices,  thereby  ensuring  its  readability  
and maintainability.  Furthermore,  code  quality  metricsâ€”such  as  valid -
ity, maintainability,  and  the  absence  of  code  or  security  â€œsmellsâ€  â€“  are  
deemed essential  for  ensuring  the  overall  quality  of  the  generated  code.  
In the  context  of  code  translation,  translation  accuracy  metrics,  includ -
ing CodeBLEU,  chrF,  METEOR,  and  BLEU,  have  measured  the  quality  of  
the translation.  However,  these  text-based  metrics  have  been  found  to  
be misleading,  indicating  that  it  is  preferable  to  assess  the  functionality  
of the  code  through  execution.
2.4. Interpretability  and  explainability  of  LLMs
Interpretability in  LLMs  is  essential  for  understanding  their  output  
generation and  decision  making,  which  helps  to  build  trust,  debug,  and  
identify biases.  Kokhlikyan  et  al.  [ 30] highlighted  that  interpretability  
involves methods  like  attribution  algorithms,  categorized  into  primary,  
neuron, and  layer  attributions,  which  highlight  the  importance  of  input  
features. These  methods  can  be  gradient-based  (e.g.,  Saliency,  Integrated  
Gradients) or  perturbation-based  (e.g.,  Feature  Ablation,  Shapley  Value  
Sampling). The  Captum  library  supports  these  interpretability  methods,  
offering implementations  for  various  PyTorch  models.  Miglani  et  al.  [ 31] 
showed that  it  allows  flexibility  in  defining  attribution  features  and  tar -
get outputs  (most  likely  decoded  token  sequences  or  a  user-specified  
sequences), benefiting  the  evaluation  of  specific  outcomes.  Wang  et  al.  
[32] showed  that  explanations  generated  by  LLMs  alongside  code  pro -
vide insights  into  the  modelâ€™s  reasoning  process,  which  is  crucial  for  
understanding how  the  LLM  arrived  at  a  particular  solution  or  identi -
fied a  bug.  Palacio  et  al.  [ 33] showed  that  this  interpretability  allows  
users to  assess  the  reliability  and  accuracy  of  the  code,  going  beyond  
simple functional  correctness  to  evaluate  the  logic  and  approach  used.
2.5. Related  works
Non-LLM code  translation  techniques  use  rule-based  source-to -
source compilers,  like  C2Rust  by  Immunant  [ 14] and  CxGo  by  Transpile  
[15], which  convert  code  by  analyzing  it  into  an  abstract  syntax  tree  
(AST) before  translating  it  to  the  target  languageâ€™s  AST.  Other  methods  
include statistical  learning  approaches  like  those  presented  by  Nguyen  
et al.  [ 34,35], and  neural  networks  that  employ  attention  mechanisms  
in the  work  done  by  Chen  et  al.  [ 36]. As  Roziere  et  al.  [ 37] pointed  
out, LLM-based  methods  utilize  large  language  models  trained  on  ex -
tensive code  datasets  and  require  prompt  engineering  to  get  the  best  
results. LLMs  can  produce  inconsistent  output,  require  post-processing,  
and struggle  with  complex  dependencies  and  API  mappings,  potentially  
introducing bugs.
A study  of  1700  code  samples  in  five  programming  languages,  by  
Pan et  al.  [ 38], identified  15  categories  of  translation  bugs,  primarily  
due to  syntax  and  semantic  challenges.  These  issues  often  stem  from  
language differences,  incorrect  data  types,  missing  library  imports,  and  
API mismatches.  Manual  analysis  is  often  needed  to  identify  these  bugs,  
which can  be  time-consuming.  The  study  found  that  LLMs  struggle  with  
real-world projects  due  to  complex  dependencies  and  language-specific
Neurocomputing 656 (2025) 131461 
3 
[Page 4]
V.S. Pendyala  and  N.B.  Thakur
features, with  many  errors  arising  from  incorrect  input  parsing  and  a  
lack of  understanding  of  program  data  flow.
The BESTER  study  by  Song  et  al.  [ 39] explored  an  iterative  process  
for improving  code  generated  by  LLMs.  Initially,  the  LLM  creates  code  
from a  natural  language  description,  which  is  then  tested.  If  the  code  
fails, the  LLM  uses  self-reflection  to  identify  errors,  review  its  output,  and  
utilize test  results  to  guide  revisions.  This  cycle  of  generating,  testing,  
reflecting, and  correcting  continues  until  a  successful  solution  is  found  
or a  maximum  number  of  iterations  is  reached.
Prompt engineering  is  crucial  for  effective  code  generation  with  
Large Language  Models  (LLMs),  as  the  design  of  prompts  can  greatly  
influence the  output  formatâ€”whether  code  appears  directly,  wrapped  
in backticks,  or  mixed  with  natural  language  as  shown  by  Macedo  et  al.  
[40]. Pan  et  al.  [ 38] also  showed  that  adding  context  like  stack  traces  
and error  messages  helps  the  LLM  learn  from  past  mistakes  and  improve  
code generation,  especially  for  error  correction.  Feng  and  Chen  [ 41] 
showed that  techniques  like  chain-of-thought  prompting  encourage  the  
LLM to  analyze  problems  before  coding,  enhancing  output  quality.
3. Methodology  
3.1. Large  language  models
Many LLMs  are  openly  available  for  code  generation  tasks  on  the  
HuggingFace platform  by  Wolf  et  al.  [ 42]. Each  of  these  LLMs  has  
different architectures,  parameters,  context  lengths,  capabilities,  and  
performance. Specifically  for  this  study,  instruction-tuned  versions  of  
the code  generation  LLMs  are  used  since  these  models  are  fine-tuned  
to follow  prompted  instructions.  Since  LLMs  can  have  a  varying  num -
ber of  parameters,  and  the  resources  required  for  working  with  LLMs  
scale with  the  number  of  parameters  in  the  model,  only  LLMs  with  
less than  10  billion  active  parameters  were  chosen.  The  list  of  se -
lected LLMs,  along  with  their  details,  is  summarized  in  Table 1 . The  
LLMs were  selected  based  on  three  principles:  LLM  should  be  fine -
tuned for  code  generation,  its  weights  and  architecture  should  be  
open-source, and  the  number  of  parameters  should  be  below  10  billion.  
Since LLMs  require  many  resources,  efficient  deployment  frameworks  
like llama.cpp  by  Gerganov  [ 43] and  Ollama  by  Morgan  and  Chiang  
[44] are  important  in  ensuring  LLMs  can  be  run  efficiently  on  any  
hardware and  operating  system.  Hence,  an  additional  constraint  was  
put in  place  to  ensure  that  the  selected  LLMs  are  not  only  compati -
ble with  HuggingFace  but  also  with  llama.cpp  and  Ollama  frameworks.  
This ensures  that  these  LLMs  can  be  easily  deployed  and  used  in  
not only  research  applications  but  also  in  the  software  engineering  
industry.
The LLMs  selected  for  this  study  can  be  grouped  into  two  dis -
tinct categories  based  on  the  architecture  â€“  LLaMa  and  its  deriva -
tives, and  other  architectures  like  Qwen2  and  Gemma.  Categorizing  by
architecture reveals  shared  characteristics  and  potential  performance  
similarities derived  from  the  same  foundational  model.  A  significant  
portion of  the  models,  including  Yi-Coder  (both  sizes),  Granite  Code  
(both sizes),  DeepSeek  Coder,  Magicoder  by  Wei  et  al.  [ 45], and  Code  
LLaMa by  RoziÃ¨re  et  al.  [ 46] utilize  the  â€œLLaMaâ€  architecture.  Models  
like CodeQwen1.5  by  Q.  Team  [ 47], Qwen2.5-Coder  by  Q  Team  [ 48] 
(both sizes)  utilize  the  Qwen2  architecture.  Models  like  StableCode  by  
Pinnaparaju et  al.  [ 49], DolphinCoder  by  Hartford  [ 50], CodeGemma  
by Zhao  et  al.  [ 51] and  CodeGeeX4  by  y  Hartford  (2024),  CodeGemma  
by Zhao  et  al.  (2024)  and  CodeGeeX4  by  Zheng  et  al.  [ 52] have  their  
own distinct  architectures.  DeepSeek-Coder-V2  is  different  from  other  
models selected  in  the  study  since  it  uses  a  Mixture  of  Experts  (MoE)  ar -
chitecture called  DeepSeekMoE,  introduced  by  Shazeer  et  al.  [ 53], which  
means that  the  total  number  of  model  weights  that  are  actively  used  dur -
ing decoding  is  significantly  smaller  than  the  total  number  of  parameters  
in the  LLM.
3.2. Quantization
Quantization is  a  technique  used  to  compress  LLMs  and  make  them  
more efficient  during  execution.  Instead  of  using  very  precise  numbers  
(like 32-bit  floating  point  numbers)  to  represent  the  weights  and  ac -
tivations of  LLM,  quantization  uses  lower  precision  numbers  like  8-bit  
integers as  shown  by  Dettmers  et  al.  [ 54] in  LLM.int8().  This  reduces  
the memory  footprint  of  the  model,  making  it  faster  to  load  and  run,  
and reducing  the  power  consumption.  Liu  et  al.  [ 55] introduced  4-bit  
quantization, which  makes  it  possible  to  run  powerful  LLMs  on  de -
vices with  limited  resources.  All  the  models  used  in  this  study  were  
quantized to  4-bit  integer  precision  using  llama.cpp  with  the  Q4_K_M  
quantization preset  and  deployed  using  Ollama.  Q4_K_M  is  a  specific  
quantization format  within  GGML  specification  by  Gerganov  et  al.  [ 56] 
that uses  4  bits  per  weight,  and  the  128-weight  block  is  a  common  
unit for  processing.  This  strategy  preserves  critical  layer  precision  while  
achieving substantial  compression  ratios,  typically  reducing  model  size  
by approximately  3.3x  compared  to  16-bit  precision  models.  However,  
quantization can  lead  to  a  slight  decrease  in  model  accuracy  due  to  
the loss  of  information  from  reduced  precision  of  the  weights,  which  
is often  an  acceptable  trade-off  to  ensure  that  larger  high-performance  
LLMs can  be  run  on  consumer-grade  hardware.  Empirical  evaluation  
on the  WikiText-2  dataset  by  Chen  et  al.  [ 57] demonstrated  that  4-bit  
quantization using  Q4_K_M  resulted  in  perplexity  increases  of  8â€“15  %  
compared to  16-bit  models,  while  maintaining  85â€“92  %  of  original  per -
formance on  downstream  tasks  such  as  MMLU  (accuracy  dropping  from  
approximately 65  %  to  55  %  for  7B  parameter  models).  Kim  et  al.  
[58] found  that  complex  reasoning  tasks  requiring  multi-step  chain-of -
thought showed  greater  sensitivity  to  quantization,  with  performance  
degradation of  10â€“20  %,  compared  to  single-token  prediction  tasks  
which exhibited  minimal  impact.  The  trade-off  analysis  revealed  that

3.3. Programming  languages
To evaluate  the  capabilities  of  the  Large  Language  Models,  each  
LLM was  asked  to  execute  each  code  conversion  task  in  the  following  
languages: C,  C+ +, Golang,  Java,  JavaScript,  Python,  and  Rust.  These  
languages were  chosen  to  represent  a  range  of  programming  paradigms,  
levels of  abstraction,  and  technological  trends.  The  languages  can  be  
broadly categorized  into  two  groups  â€“  System  Programming  Languages  
and Application-Focused  Languages.  System  Programming  Languages  
(C, C+ +, Golang,  Rust)  prioritize  performance  and  low-level  system  ac -
cess, while  Application-Focused  Languages  (Java,  JavaScript,  Python)  
are typically  used  for  higher-level  applications.  A  summary  of  these  
programming languages  is  provided  in  Table 2 .
These languages  represent  diverse  challenges  from  an  LLM  perfor -
mance perspective.  They  encompass  varying  syntax  complexity,  from  
Câ€™s minimalist  approach  to  Pythonâ€™s  readability  and  Rustâ€™s  complex  type  
system, thus  testing  an  LLMâ€™s  adaptability.  They  also  represent  differ -
ent programming  paradigms,  like  procedural  (C),  object-oriented  (Java),  
and functional  (Rust),  along  with  varying  levels  of  abstraction,  from  
low-level system  languages  to  high-level  scripting  languages.  Fayyad  et  
al. [ 69] highlighted  that  these  languages  also  reflect  key  technological  
trends, such  as  the  increasing  focus  on  memory  safety  and  performance,  
the growth  of  cloud-native  and  distributed  computing,  the  expansion  of  
web and  cross-platform  technologies,  and  the  rising  importance  of  data  
science and  machine  learning  ecosystems.
3.4. Code  translations
Since there  are  seven  languages  (C,  C+ +, Golang,  Java,  JavaScript,  
Python, and  Rust)  against  which  the  LLMs  are  evaluated,  42  valid  com -
binations of  code  translations  are  possible  for  each  task  selected  from  
the Rosetta  Code  dataset.  The  LLM  is  asked  to  convert  the  code  from  
a source  to  a  target  language  along  with  a  task  description  to  ensure  
proper clarity  on  its  code  conversion  task.  This  process  tests  the  LLMâ€™s  
understanding of  diverse  syntax,  data  structures,  memory  management  
models (where  applicable),  and  standard  programming  paradigms  when  
implementing the  same  algorithm  or  concept.
3.5. Dataset
Rosetta Code  by  Mol  [ 70] is  a  programming  chrestomathy  website  
that collects  solutions  to  a  variety  of  tasks  in  hundreds  of  different  
programming languages.  The  website  presents  a  task,  for  example,  
â€œImplement the  Bubble  Sort  algorithmâ€,  and  invites  programmers  to  
contribute solutions  in  their  chosen  language.  The  Rosetta  Code  dataset  
provides a  valuable  resourc e for  evaluating  code  generation  LLMs  for  
several reasons.  First,  its  diverse  range  of  over  745  tasks,  spanning  
simple exercises  to  complex  algorithmic  problems  and  data  structure  im -
plementations, allows  for  comprehensive  evaluation  of  LLM  capabilities  
across various  computational  problems  and  programming  paradigms.  
Second, the  inclusion  of  solutions  in  379  programming  languages
enables assessment  of  how  well  LLMs  handle  the  nuances  and  id -
ioms specific  to  each  language.  Furthermore,  the  presence  of  multiple  
solutions for  each  task  in  different  languages  provides  reference  im -
plementations. These  reference  solutions,  developed  and  refined  by  a  
community of  programmers,  ensure  a  high  standard  of  quality  and  cor -
rectness, facilitating  robust  evaluation  of  the  correctness  and  quality  
of LLM-generated  code.  Finally,  while  Rosetta  Code  solutions  are  gen -
erally smaller  than  real-world  applications,  they  often  represent  core  
functionalities crucial  to  larger  projects.  Nanz  and  Furia  [ 71] stated  that  
this focus  on  core  functionality  makes  Rosetta  Code  a  suitable  bench -
mark in  terms  of  quality,  performance,  and  reliability  of  these  essential  
components, and  by  proxy,  for  evaluating  LLMs.
3.6. Tasks
The tasks  included  in  the  Rosetta  Code  dataset  cover  many  different  
aspects. One  such  aspect  is  Basic  Language  Learning,  which  focuses  on  
problems and  tasks  that  help  in  learning  a  programming  language  and  
which can  be  combined  to  make  more  complex  applications.  This  study  
covers two  main  categories  of  programming  fundamentals  from  Rosetta  
Code that  help  demonstrate  an  LLMâ€™s  code  generation  capability:  Basic  
Data Operations  and  File  System  Operations.  Basic  Data  Operations  can  
also be  divided  into  two  further  categories  â€“  Bitwise,  Logical,  and  Integer  
Operations, and  String  Operations.

is essential for modern software development. Through this structured 
approach, the tasks effectively assess both an LLMâ€™s understanding of 
programming fundamentals and its ability to generate practical code 
across different domains.
3.7. Prompt templates
Two prompt templates are utilized in this study for the initial trans-
lation task. One for LLMs which come with a default system prompt, 
and one for LLMs which donâ€™t come with a default system prompt, 
as shown in the Table 3. If a default system prompt is provided for 
the LLM, then that system prompt is preserved. If it is not provided, 
the system prompt is given as â€œYou are a helpful code conversion as-
sistantâ€. The user-prompt remains the same for both cases. SRC_LANG 
refers to the language in which the source code is provided, TGT_LANG 
refers to the language in which the source code must be converted, 
TASK_DESCRIPTION refers to the description of the task that the source 
code represents, and SRC_CODE refers to the code written in SRC_LANG
that implements the TASK_DESCRIPTION. The System Prompt and User-
Prompt are then plugged directly into the Chat Template prescribed by 
the authors of each LLM used in the experiments.
In the later sections, scenarios are discussed where the LLM is asked 
a follow-up prompt if the code generated by the LLM in response has 
compilation or syntax issues. The LLM is then provided with this error 
and asked to explain the error and fix it. Table 4 describes the chat 
structure used to structure the follow-up prompt. The System Prompt 
and first User-Prompt are the same as Table 3. The Assistant Prompt 
contains the entire response generated by the LLM, which contains the 
code with mistakes. The following User-Prompt contains the instructions 
for the LLM to explain the error and then fix it. It also contains additional 
response formatting instructions for the LLM to structure the output.
3.8. Translation metrics
To evaluate the code translations quantitatively, the study uses three 
metrics, Code Extraction Rate (CER), Code Correctness Rate (CCR) and 
Pass@K. CER represents how successfully a piece of code can be ex-
tracted from the response generated by LLM for a particular translation 
task. CCR captures the â€œcorrectnessâ€ of code extracted from the LLM 
and reflects the reliability of the LLM. CCR does so by checking whether 
the generated code compiles successfully (C, C+ +, Go, Java, Rust) or 
has correct syntax (Python, JavaScript), depending on the programming 
language.
Pass@K is a critical evaluation metric for quantitatively assessing 
the functional correctness of Large Language Models in code genera-
tion tasks, where K represents the number of code samples generated 
per programming problem. The metric measures the probability that at 
least one of the top K generated code samples for a given problem suc-
cessfully passes all associated unit tests, fundamentally differing from 
traditional text-similarity metrics by focusing on executable correctness 
rather than syntactic resemblance to reference solutions. Originally in-
troduced in the evaluation of OpenAIâ€™s Codex model by Chen et al. 
[22], Pass@K demonstrated that repeated sampling significantly im-
proves problem-solving capability, with Codex achieving 28.8 % success 
on Pass@1 but 70.2 % success on Pass@100 for the HumanEval bench-
mark. The metric addresses limitations of binary assessment approaches 
by enabling evaluation across multiple attempts, though recent research 
by Yeo et al. [23] has highlighted the need for more granular accu-
racy measures beyond the all-or-nothing nature of traditional Pass@K 
implementations.
Code translation quality assessment presents unique challenges 
compared to natural language translation evaluation. While Rosetta 
Code provides reference implementations across multiple languages for 
benchmark comparisons, traditional natural language metrics may not

adequately capture  code  translation  quality  due  to  strict  syntax  require -
ments and  emphasis  on  semantic  preservation  over  lexical  similarity  in  
programming languages.
Common natural  language  translation  metrics  include  BLEU  by  
Papineni et  al.  [ 72], which  calculates  n-gram  precision  with  a  brevity  
penalty, and  ROUGE  by  Lin  [ 73], which  measures  n-gram  overlaps  
and longest  common  subsequences.  However,  these  metricsâ€™  reliance  on  
surface-level text  matching  makes  them  suboptimal  for  code  evaluation,  
as they  cannot  assess  algorithmic  equivalence  or  recognize  semantically  
identical solutions  with  different  syntactic  implementations.  More  so -
phisticated metrics  like  METEOR  by  Banerjee  and  Lavie  [ 74] incorporate  
semantic similarity  measures  like  stemming,  synonyms,  paraphrase  de -
tection and  word  order  sequencing.  WER  by  Morris  et  al.  [ 75], which  
quantifies required  edit  operations  between  generated  and  reference  
text, may  be  more  applicable  to  code  translation  due  to  well-defined  
word boundaries  and  syntactic  constraints  of  programming  languages.  
However, these  metrics  still  fail  to  capture  the  fundamental  requirement  
of preserving  program  functionality  across  different  implementation  
approaches.
CodeBLEU by  Ren  et  al.  [ 76] is  a  specialized  metric  for  evaluat -
ing code  generation  that  addresses  BLEUâ€™s  limitations  by  incorporating  
four key  components:  traditional  n-gram  matching  from  BLEU,  Abstract  
Syntax Tree  (AST)  matching  (identifying  structural  equivalence),  data  
flow analysis  (capturing  variable  relationships),  and  semantic  matching  
(recognizing functionally  similar  implementations).  While  BLEU  only  
considers surface-level  token  similarity,  CodeBLEUâ€™s  additional  compo -
nents enable  it  to  recognize  functionally  equivalent  code  even  when  
written differently.  This  makes  CodeBLEU  significantly  more  suitable  
for evaluating  generated  code,  as  it  can  appropriately  score  correct  
implementations that  use  different  variable  names,  control  structures,  
or coding  styles.  chrF  by  PopoviÄ‡  [ 77] is  a  character-level  metric  for  
evaluating machine  translation  quality  that  computes  F-scores  based  on  
character n-grams  instead  of  word  n-grams.  Recent  studies  by  the  likes  
of Evtikhiev  et  al.  [ 78] have  shown  that  chrF  is  much  closer  to  human -
level assessments  of  code  translations  compared  to  traditional  metrics  
like BLEU  and  CodeBLEU.
Hence, for  this  study,  metrics  like  CodeBLEU,  chrF,  BLEU-METEOR,  
ROUGE and  WER  are  used  to  evaluate  the  translations  produced  by  the  
LLMs for  all  the  tasks  and  translation  combinations.
3.9. Interpretability  metrics
An LLMâ€™s  output  is  fundamentally  a  probability  distribution  over  its  
token vocabulary  at  each  step.  This  process  can  be  summarized  as,
1. For each  next  token  that  the  LLM  predicts,  the  model  calculates
probabilities for  every  token  in  its  vocabulary  (which  can  be  10  s  
or 100  s  of  thousands  of  tokens).
2. For example,  if  predicting  the  next  word  after  â€œThe  cat  sat  on  the
___â€, it  might  output:  â€œâ€˜
mat: 0.35
floor: 0.25
chair: 0.20
table: 0.15
[other tokens]:  0.05
â€â€™
3. When generating  text,  the  model  typically  samples  from  this  distri -
-
bution (rather  than  always  picking  the  highest  probability  token)  
to create  more  natural  and  varied  outputs.  The  sampling  can  be  
adjusted via  temperature  and  other  parameters.
4. This process  repeats  for  each  new  output  token,  with  the  previ
ous tokens  (both  from  the  input  prompt  and  previously  predicted  
tokens) providing  context  that  influences  the  next  probability  
distribution.
Thus, changing  any  token  in  the  input  prompt  will  change  the  prob -
ability distribution  of  the  output  token.  So,  given  a  sequence  of  output
tokens, the  LLM  outputs  will  provide  a  probability  distribution  over  the  
entire LLM  token  vocabulary  for  each  output  token.
Perturbation techniques  to  interpret  LLMs  use  the  fact  that  the  out -
put token  probability  distribution  is  conditioned  on  the  input  tokens  and  
compute the  change  in  the  output  token  probability  distribution  as  the  
tokens in  the  input  are  systematically  augmented.  A  token  or  a  sequence  
of tokens  is  removed  from  the  input,  and  the  probability  distribution  of  
each token  in  the  output  is  compared  to  the  corresponding  probability  
distribution of  the  token  in  the  original  output,  and  this  change  in  prob -
ability is  quantified  as  an  interpretability  score  using  various  methods.  
This results  in  an  interpretability  score  being  assigned  to  each  token  or  
sequence of  tokens  in  the  input  that  is  perturbed,  and  each  token  in  the  
original sequence  of  output  tokens.
Feature ablation  is  one  way  of  calculating  this  interpretability  score  
by taking  the  difference  in  the  log  probabilities  at  each  token  position  
of the  original  output.  Similarly,  Shapley  values  also  calculate  this  inter -
pretability score  by  considering  other  factors  like  efficiency,  symmetry,  
and linearity  along  with  the  difference  in  the  log  probabilities  at  each  
token position  of  the  original  output.
3.9.1. Feature  ablation
As stated  by  Merrick  [ 24], feature  ablation  is  a  technique  used  in  
machine learning  to  understand  the  importance  of  different  features  in  
a model.  In  the  case  of  Large  Language  Models  specialized  for  Code  gen -
eration, a  feature  can  be  considered  as  a  set  of  tokens  in  the  input.  Each  
line of  the  input  source  code  is  considered  a  feature  for  the  LLM  in  code  
conversion experiments.  It  involves  removing  or  â€œablatingâ€  features  one  
at a  time  and  observing  the  impact  on  the  modelâ€™s  performance,  and  by  
comparing the  performance  with  and  without  a  particular  feature,  it  pro -
vides an  idea  of  how  important  that  feature  is  for  the  modelâ€™s  predictions.  
Performance in  the  code  conversion  experiments  is  the  log  probability  
of the  output  tokens  generated  by  the  LLM  for  the  input  in  question.
3.9.2. Shapley  value  sampling
Shapley Values  are  a  concept  from  game  theory  that  has  been  
adopted in  machine  learning  to  explain  the  contributions  of  individ -
ual features  to  a  modelâ€™s  prediction.  They  offer  a  way  to  understand  
how much  each  feature  contributes,  positively  or  negatively,  to  the  final  
output, providing  valuable  insights  into  model  behavior.  Shapley  Value  
Sampling by  Mitchell  et  al.  [ 79] involves  calculating  Shapley  Values  for  a  
subset of  possible  feature  combinations  instead  of  exhaustively  evaluat -
ing all  of  them.  This  significantly  reduces  computational  costs  while  still  
providing a  good  approximation  of  feature  contributions.  Like  Feature  
Ablation, each  line  of  the  input  source  code  is  considered  as  a  feature  
for the  LLM,  and  the  Shapley  Values  calculated  reflect  the  importance  
of that  line  with  respect  to  the  output  tokens.
3.10. LLM  explainability
Even though  LLMs  tend  to  be  black  boxes  in  the  sense  that  it  is  
difficult to  accurately  estimate  why  and  how  the  LLMs  generated  the  re -
sponse, interpretability  metrics  like  Feature  Ablation  and  Shapley  Value  
Sampling provide  an  insight  into  the  importance  of  input  features  with  
respect to  the  LLM  output.  Another  way  to  obtain  insights  into  how  an  
instruction-tuned LLM  thinks  is  to  ask  follow-up  prompts  that  instruct  
the LLM  to  explain  its  prior  response.  In  the  case  of  this  study,  when  the  
LLM is  provided  with  a  compiler  error  message  or  syntax  check  issue  
for the  translated  code  it  generated,  it  is  often  helpful  if  the  LLM  can  
explain the  mistake  it  made  and  then  fix  it.  This  improves  the  reliability  
of an  LLM,  where  it  can  not  only  solve  problems  in  zero-shot,  but  also  
improve upon  its  mistakes  when  prompted  with  the  errors  in  the  code.

binations, on  all  17  Rosetta  Code  tasks  for  13  LLMs  fine-tuned  for  code

generation, a  script  was  developed  using  Python  and  the  Ollama  infer -

10,710 code  conversion  tasks.  The  system  prompt  and  user-prompt  are  
then used  together,  along  with  the  specified  chat  template  provided  by

to identify  the  LLM,  Rosetta  Code  task,  source  code  language  and  the  
target language.  Any  failures  are  recorded  separately  to  keep  track  of  
extraction-related issues.
4.2. Code  extraction  from  LLM  response
LLM often  responds  in  the  markdown  format,  where  code  is  enclosed  
inside explicit  code  blocks  marked  by  backticks.  Hence,  the  code  must  
be parsed  from  th e LLM  response  using  Regular  Expressions,  as  exper -
imented with  by  Macedo  et  al.  Since  the  LLM  response  can  contain  
multiple code  blocks,  the  code  blocks  sometimes  represent  alternate  im -
plementations, or  sometimes  the  extra  code  blocks  contain  driver  code  
to execute  the  code.
A two-step  approach  was  adopted  where  a  regular  expression,  as  de -
scribed in  Fig. 1 , was used  to  extract  all  the  code  blocks  from  an  LLM  
response and  manually  process  the  cases  where  there  were  multiple  code  
blocks or  no  code  blocks  detected  in  the  LLM  response.  In  the  case  where  
there was  only  one  code  block  in  the  LLM  response,  it  was  preserved  as  
it is.  This  accurately  reflects  real-life  scenarios  where  developers  often  
must apply  additional  manual  processing  steps  to  obtain  code  from  an  
LLM response.  Despite  some  manual  processing,  out  of  10,710  responses,  
there were  64  responses  from  which  no  code  could  be  extracted,  result -
ing in  a  99.4  %  Code  Extraction  Rate  (CER).  The  distribution  of  CER  
across the  selected  LLMs  in  this  study  is  shown  in  Table 7 .
4.3. Formatting  extracted  code  using  code  formatters
To reliably  evaluate  the  translated  code  generated  by  LLMs  against  
the reference  implementations  provided  in  the  Rosetta  Code  dataset,  
language-specific code  formatters  were  used  to  format  both  the  trans -
lated code  and  reference  code.  Code  formatters  for  each  language  along  
with their  versions  are  summarized  in  Table 5 . Code  formatters  nor -
malize superficial  variations  in  code  style,  enabling  metrics  to  focus  on  
semantic differences  rather  than  formatting  choices.  They  also  enforce  
standardization between  the  LLM  translated  code  and  reference  trans -
lations. Without  standardization,  the  same  logically  correct  translation  
might receive  different  similarity  scores  solely  due  to  formatting  vari -
ations. Code  formatters  also  help  isolate  actual  translation  errors  from  
style differences.  By  applying  consistent  formatting  rules,  the  metrics  
more accurately  reflect  meaningful  differences  in  translation  quality,  
rather than  focusing  on  simple  formatting  variations.
4.4. Compilation,  syntax  check  and  execution  of  generated  code
Validating the  syntax,  compilation  and  execution  of  code  generated  
by LLM  serves  as  an  important  quality  metric  for  assessing  the  practical  
usability of  LLM  in  software  development.  This  validation  process  across  
multiple programming  languages  in  this  study  provides  quantifiable  data  
about how  often  the  LLM  translated  code  meets  basic  correctness  re -
quirements without  human  intervention.  Code  Correctness  Rate  (CCR)  is  
a metric  devised  to  keep  track  of  the  â€œcorrectnessâ€  of  the  code  generated
by LLM.  Pass@1  measures  the  reliability  of  automated  code  translation  
by indicating  whether  the  first  generated  solution  is  correct,  which  is  
essential for  truly  autonomous  systems  that  cannot  rely  on  multiple  at -
tempts or  human  verification.  The  compilers  and  runtimes  used  for  each  
programming language  are  described  in  Table 6 .
4.4.1. Results
A summary  of  the  results  obtained  from  evaluating  the  correctness  of  
translated code  for  each  LLM  in  this  study  is  shared  in  Table 7 . Pass@1  
scores shown  in  this  table  are  averaged  across  all  the  tasks  and  possi -
ble translation  pairs  for  each  LLM.  CCR  scales  with  the  total  number  
of parameters  in  the  LLM.  All  the  LLMs  followed  the  prompt  instruc -
tions closely,  and  CER  for  all  the  models  is  almost  1.0  for  all  the  LLMs.  
DeepSeek Coder  V2,  a  Mixture  of  Experts  model  with  2.4  B  active  pa -
rameters and  15.7  B  total  parameters,  was  the  best  LLM  with  a  CCR  
of 0.840395  and  Pass@1  of  0.684873,  while  StableCode,  with  a  CCR  
of 0.213783  and  Pass@1  of  0196078,  was  the  most  underperforming  
LLM. Yi-Coder  and  CodeGeeX4,  with  nearly  9B  active  parameters,  were  
the next  best  models  with  a  CCR  of  nearly  0.8  and  very  similar  Pass@1  
score of  0.65.  Barring  CodeLLaMA  and  Granite  Code  [8B],  there  is  a  
clear trend  of  increasing  CCR  with  the  total  number  of  parameters  in  
the model.  There  seems  to  be  a  general  trend  where  Pass@1  scales  with  
the number  of  parameters  in  t he LLM,  but  there  are  exceptions  like  Code  
Gemma and  Code  Llama  which  perform  much  worse  despite  high  param -
eter counts,  or  CodeQwen1.5,  which  crossed  the  0.6  threshold  despite  
having half  the  number  of  parameters  as  DeepSeek  Coder  V2.

4.5.1. Results
Based on  the  summary  of  translation  metrics  presented  in  Table 8 , 
on average,  all  the  LLMs  performed  quite  like  each  other.  Just  using  
translation metrics  is  not  enough  to  distinguish  between  LLMs,  but  may  
prove to  be  effective  in  distinguishing  between  Rosetta  Code  tasks.  To  
identify any  distinguishing  features  between  different  LLMs  and  tasks  in  
the study,  the  distribution  of  translation  metrics  is  visualized  in  Fig. 2 . 
It shows  KDE  plots  for  the  distribution  of  each  metric  with  respect  to  
LLMs and  tasks.  The  distribution  of  individual  LLMs  for  each  metric  has  
the same  shape  and  density  variations,  indicating  that  none  of  the  LLMs  
performed better  than  the  others  based  on  the  translation  metrics  alone.  
The peaks  and  spread  of  KDE  plots  for  each  LLM  also  align  closely  with  
the mean  and  standard  deviations  from  Table 8 .
However, it  seems  that  individual  Tasks  from  Rosetta  Code  had  dif -
ferent distributions  on  each  translation  metric.  Each  Task  has  a  distinct  
KDE plot  across  all  the  metrics  except  WER,  indicating  that  these  trans -
lation metrics  can  be  used  to  analyze  the  differences  between  individual  
tasks and  highlight  the  complexity  and  the  quality  of  reference  trans -
lations of  each  task.  The  Logical  Operations  task  (represented  as  Red  
lines) was  easily  translated  by  LLMs  and  closely  matched  the  reference  
translations from  Rosetta  Code.  Its  KDE  plot  for  METEOR  metric  is  com -
pletely different  and  has  a  clear  peak  towards  0.9,  compared  to  other  
tasks whose  peaks  lie  below  0.8.
Based on  the  results,  the  token-overlap  metrics,  BLEU,  ROUGE-1,  
METEOR, and  chrF  mostly  moved  together.  This  is  expected  because  
they all  reward  n-gram  matches.  CodeBLEU  includes  a  BLEU  term,  so  as  
expected, it  is  substantially  correlated  with  that  cluster  of  token-overlap  
metrics. It  shows  extra  spread  owing  to  its  syntax/semantic  sub-scores.  
On the  other  hand,  word-error-rate  (WER)  moves  in  the  opposite  di -
rection because  higher  WER  means  worse  performance,  yielding  strong  
negative correlations  with  every  other  metric.
Code-specific metrics  leverage  the  unique  properties  of  programming  
languages to  provide  a  more  accurate  and  meaningful  evaluation.  For  in -
stance, CodeBLEU,  by  adding  abstract  syntax  tree  (AST)  and  data-flow  
matching, captures  structural  correctness.  CodeBLEUâ€™s  AST-matching
