4.6. Interpretability  of  LLM  responses  using  captum
To interpret  the  responses  generated  by  the  LLMs  in  this  study,  an  
experiment was  conducted  using  the  version  of  LLM  weights  hosted  on  
Huggingface, and  the  Captum  library  by  Kokhlikyan  et  al.  [ 80], similar  
to the  efforts  made  by  Miglani  et  al.  [ 81] while  interpreting  the  responses  
made by  LLaMa  2  in  Captum  [ 82]. Since  there  are  42  translation  com -
binations for  each  Rosetta  Code  task,  the  best  LLM  was  chosen  based  on  
CER, CCR  and  Pass@1,  which  was  Yi-Coder  [9B].  Feature  Ablation  and  
Shapley Value  Sampling  were  chosen  as  the  perturbation  techniques  for  
evaluating the  interpretability  of  LLMs.
For each  combination  of  translation,  interpretability  was  calculated  
using the  entire  prompt  and  the  output  code  generated  by  the  Yi-Coder  
model. Only  the  source  code  section  in  the  prompt  was  perturbed  for  cal -
culating the  Feature  Ablation  and  Shapley  Value  Sampling  scores.  At  the  
end, for  each  combination,  the  per-line  interpretability  and  summarized  
interpretability were  saved  along  with  the  output  tokens  from  the  target  
language. These  data  have  been  visualized  and  analyzed  in  Sections 5.1  
and 5.2.
4.7. Explainability  of  LLM  responses
It is  understood  that  the  translations  generated  by  LLMs  will  not  
be accurate  all  the  time.  The  code  generated  by  the  LLM  might  have  
syntax or  semantic  errors  or  might  suffer  from  hallucinations,  which  ig -
nore the  translation  instructions  and  generate  code  completely  different  
from the  task  description.  Since  all  the  LLMs  included  in  this  study  are  
instruction-tuned and  support  a  chat  interface,  it  opens  an  avenue  to  in -
vestigate whether  the  LLM  can  explain  and  fix  the  errors  in  its  code,  if  
provided with  an  error  message  from  the  target  language  compiler  or  
syntax checker.  The  first  step  in  this  process  is  to  identify  all  the  code  
translations across  all  the  LLMs  and  tasks  from  Rosetta  Code  that  either  
failed to  compile  or  had  incorrect  syntax.  The  experiment  then  continues  
the chat  conversation  from  Section 4.1  with the  same  LLM  that  generated  
the incorrect  translation  and  asks  a  follow-up  prompt  to  the  LLM.  The  
follow-up prompt  consists  of  instructions  indicating  whether  the  fail -
ure was  due  to  compilation  or  syntax  check,  the  error  generated  by  the  
compiler or  syntax  checker,  and  instructions  to  explain  and  correct  the  
code. Once  the  LLM  responds,  the  next  steps  are  like  the  ones  discussed  
in Sections 4.2 â€“4.4, where a  regular  expression  is  used  to  extract  cor -
rected code  from  the  LLM  response,  and  it  is  then  parsed  and  analyzed  
to understand  how  well  the  LLM  can  improve  upon  the  errors  in  the  code  
it generated.  The  analysis  performed  in  this  stage  of  the  experiment  is  
discussed in  Sections 6.1  and 6.2.
5. RQ1  - how  effectively  can  the  process  behind  LLMs  translating  
software in  one  programming  language  to  another  or  generating  
software code  from  natural  language,  be  explained?
5.1. Investigation  strategy
LLM responses  in  this  study  were  interpreted  using  perturbation  tech -
niques as  described  in  Section 3.9 . To  calculate  the  interpretability  of  
LLM responses,  the  input  tokens  are  grouped  based  on  lines  of  source  
code in  the  input  prompt,  and  only  perturb  the  lines  of  source  code  
present in  the  input  prompt  that  need  to  be  converted  to  a  target  lan -
guage. Running  feature  ablation  method  on  the  Yi-Coder  [9B]  model  
for the  Logical  Operations  task  from  Rosetta  Code  to  translate  code  
from C  to  C+ +, the  interpretability  scores  obtained  are  shown  in  the  
first image  of  Fig. 5 . In  the  figure,  on  the  y-axis  are  the  code  lines  
from the  original  C  code  to  solve  the  Logical  Operations  task,  while  on  
the x-axis  are  the  code  lines  from  the  translated  C+ + code  that  were  
generated by  Yi-Coder  [9B]  previously  as  a  response  to  the  original  
prompt.
Letâ€™s take  the  first  line  from  the  C  code  â€œ void  print_logic(int  
a, int  b)  {  â€,  and  the  first  line  from  translated  C+ +  â€œ include  
<iostream> âˆ– nâ€. It  has  a  score  of  âˆ’2.2.  This  means  that  the  proba -
bility of  the  first  line  from  the  translated  C+ + code  was  smaller  by  a  
factor of  2.2  when  the  ``void  print_logic(int  a,  int  b)  {''  line  
was present  in  the  source  as  compared  to  when  the  line  was  removed  
from the  input.  This  means  that  the  line  ``void  print_logic(int  a,  
int b)  {''  has  a  negative  influence  on  the  probability  of  the  first  trans -
lated C+ + code  line.  Letâ€™s  take  the  same  first  line  from  the  source  code,  
and the  fourth  line  ``void  print_logic(bool  a,  bool  b)  { âˆ–  n â€ from  
the translated  C+ + code.  It  has  a  score  of  +5.3.  This  means  that  the  
probability of  the  fourth  line  in  the  translated  C+ + code  was  bigger  
by a  factor  of  5.3  when  the  first  line  was  present  in  the  source  code,  
as compared  to  when  the  line  was  removed  from  the  source  code.  This  
means that  the  first  line  in  the  input  has  a  positive  influence  on  the  
probability of  the  fourth  line  in  the  translated  C+ + code.
The numbers  imply  the  magnitude  of  effect  the  source  code  line  has  
on the  translated  code  line,  whereas  the  sign  indicates  the  type  of  effect  
it has;  positive  values  mean  positive  effect,  while  negative  values  mean  
negative effect.  A  positive  effect  means  that  the  presence  of  that  set  of  
tokens in  the  input  increases  the  probability  of  the  corresponding  set  of  
tokens in  the  output,  thus  increasing  the  chance  of  those  tokens  being  
selected in  the  same  order  during  the  sampling  stage  of  the  LLM  decoder  
output (as  described  in  Section 3.9 ). A  negative  influence  means  that  
it decreases  the  probability  of  the  output  set  of  tokens,  which  in  turn  
reduces the  chance  of  output  tokens  being  selected  in  the  same  order  
during the  sampling  stage.
Since the  number  of  tokens  generated  by  the  LLM  will  change  as  the  
target language  varies  for  conversion,  itâ€™s  not  possible  to  compare  how  
the source  code  lines  affect  the  translated  code  across  different  target  
languages. Instead,  the  entire  interpretability  score  is  summarized  by  
taking the  sum  of  interpretability  scores  row-wise,  essentially  assigning  
an overall  interpretability  score  for  each  line  in  the  source  code.  The  
heatmaps of  these  summary  interpretability  scores  for  Feature  Ablation  
and Shapley  Value  Sampling  are  shared  in  Figs. 3  and 4. These  can  then  
be compared  with  the  summarized  interpretability  for  other  target  lan -
guages as  well.  A  positive  value  in  such  a  summary  context  means  that  
the source  code  line,  on  average,  increases  the  probability  of  translated  
code lines  in  that  target  language  for  the  specific  task.  A  negative  value,  
in turn,  means  that  the  source  code  line  decreases  the  probability  of  the  
translated code  lines  in  that  target  language.
Consider the  Feature  Ablation  interpretability  for  Yi-Coder  [9B]  
for C  source  code  as  seen  in  Fig. 3 .a. Letâ€™s  take  the  first  line  void  
print_logic(int a,  int  b)  as  an  example.  Java  has  the  highest  sum -
mary interpretability  score  of  13.42.  It  means  that  this  input  line  
increases the  confidence  in  the  translated  Java  code  by  a  factor  of  13.42  
on aggregate.  It  also  means  that  this  line  in  C  source  code  increases  
the translation  code  confidence  the  most  for  Java,  followed  by  Python,  
Golang, and  JavaScript.  Also,  the  fourth  C  source  code  line  seems  to  have  
the most  negative  impact  on  the  output  tokens  when  the  target  language  
is Rust.  A  similar  approach  for  summarizing  interpretability  is  also  used  
for Shapley  Value  Sampling.
5.2. Results
From the  summarized  interpretability  heatmaps  from  Figs. 3  and 4, 
the interpretability  scores  of  the  translated  code  tend  to  decrease  with  
the increasing  line  number  of  the  source  code.  In  fact,  the  interpretabil -
ity scores  decrease  so  much  that  the  later  source  code  lines  tend  to  have  a  
negative influence  on  the  translated  code  probabilities  across  all  the  lan -
guages. This  effect  is  observed  across  both  Feature  Ablation  and  Shapley  
Value Sampling.
â€¢ Interpretability scores  seem  to  be  sensitive  to  the  local  scope  of  code,
as observed  in  the  interpretability  of  Rust  source  code  when  translat -
ing to  other  languages.  The  interpretability  scores  appear  to  decrease  
within the  local  scope.

â€¢ Lines in  the  source  code  tend  to  have  a  large  but  sparse  influence  on

and deep  red  colors  in  the  heatmaps,  except  for  Rust.
These findings  suggest  that  LLMs  primarily  leverage  the  initial  con -

code, to  establish  the  fundamental  problem,  language  mapping,  and  ini -
tial structural  elements.  Subsequent  lines  contribute  incrementally  less  
to the  final  output,  implying  a  strategy  where  the  models  prioritize  early  
contextual cues  for  efficiency,  potentially  processing  later  elements  with  
lower computational  cost  or  diminished  attention.  This  phenomenon  
highlights a  key  characteristic  of  how  these  LLMs  process  sequential
code input,  favoring  strong  initial  signals  over  extensive  full-sequence  
dependency.
The study  conducted  an  interpretability  analysis  using  two  meth -

guage in  Feature  Ablation,  then  it  also  has  a  positive  influence  on  the  
translated code  for  the  same  other  language  in  Shapley  Value  Sampling  
as well,  even  though  the  magnitude  of  that  influence  differs  based  on  
the method.
â€¢ The C+ + source  codeâ€™s  first  line  seems  to  have  a  large  positive  in -
fluence on  the  translated  Java  and  Rust  code  in  both  Shapley  Value  
Sampling and  Feature  Ablation.

6. RQ2  - what  do  the  findings  from  the  explanations  reveal  about  
the reliability  and  accuracy  of  the  code  conversion  task  
accomplished by  the  foundation  models?
6.1. Investigation  strategy
This part  of  the  study  follows  a  two-step  process  for  each  trans -
lation task  from  Rosetta  Code.  First,  the  LLM  attempts  to  translate
code from  one  programming  language  to  another,  whose  process  and  
results have  been  discussed  in  Sections 4.4  and 4.5. Then,  after  re -
ceiving compiler  error  and  syntax  check  error  feedback,  the  LLM  gets  
a chance  to  explain  and  correct  its  mistakes.  This  closely  follows  the  
Chain-of-Thought reasoning  process  to  ensure  the  LLMs  donâ€™t  halluci -
nate, since  the  study  prompts  the  LLM  to  first  explain  the  error  and  
then fix  it.
This also  mirrors  the  real-world  process  of  code  development  in  soft -
ware engineering,  where  programmers  often  iterate  based  on  compiler  
and syntax  checker  tool  feedback.  If  the  LLM  made  a  mistake  in  the  code  
it generated,  then  it  is  prompted  again  using  the  prompt  template  shared  
in Section 3.7 . This  prompt  is  tailored  to  provide  the  LLM  with  the  com -
piler error  or  the  syntax  checker  error  and  asks  the  LLM  to  explain  the  
error and  then  fix  it.  Rather  than  just  testing  one-shot  translation  capabil -
ity, this  experiment  examines  how  LLMs  handle  errors  and  improve  their
Neurocomputing 656 (2025) 131461 
13 
[Page 14]
V.S. Pendyala  and  N.B.  Thakur
output. The  feedback  loop  incorporated  as  part  of  this  study  provides  
interesting insights  into  the  reliability  and  accuracy  of  the  LLM.
â€¢ It tests  the  LLMâ€™s  understanding  of  both  the  source  and  target  lan -
guages. To  fix  an  error,  the  model  must  understand  not  just  what  the  
original code  does,  but  also  why  its  translation  failed  to  achieve  the  
same result.
â€¢ It evaluates  the  LLMâ€™s  ability  to  reason  about  code  at  a  meta  level.
The LLM  must  understand  compiler  error  messages  (which  can  be  
quite cryptic)  and  relate  them  back  to  both  the  original  codeâ€™s  intent  
and its  attempted  translation.
â€¢ It simulates  a  realistic  development  scenario  where  initial  code  often
needs refinement  based  on  compiler  feedback.
Since the  LLMs  in  this  study  are  tuned  to  follow  instructions,  they  
are provided  with  the  entire  context  as  a  conversation.  This  means  that  
the feedback/follow-up  prompt  contains  the  following  sections.
1. A system  prompt
2. A user-prompt  â€“  The  original  translation  prompt  which  contains
the task  description,  the  source  language,  the  target  language,  and  
the source  code.
3. An assistant  prompt  â€“  The  original  response  generated  by  the  LLM,
which includes  the  code  the  LLM  generated.
4. A user-prompt  â€“  If  the  code  had  an  error,  then  this  contains  the
error message  along  with  instructions  to  explain  and  fix  the  error.
The code  generated  by  the  LLM  in  response  is  then  extracted,  format -
ted, and  checked  for  correctness  using  the  same  methods  as  described  in  
Sections 4.2 â€“4.5. The  key  metrics  to  assess  here  are  the  Code  Correctness  
Rate (CCR)  and  Pass@1,  since  they  summarize  how  often  the  LLM  is  
generating syntactically  correct  code  and  how  reliably  can  that  code  be  
executed without  runtime  errors.  The  expectation  here  is  that  the  LLM  
should be  able  to  parse  the  compiler  or  syntax  checker  errors  and  fix  
the errors.  This  should  reflect  directly  in  the  increased  CCR  as  well  as  
Pass@1 and  thus  reflect  the  reliability  and  accuracy  of  the  LLMs.
The explanations  and  reasoning  generated  by  the  LLM  in  the  process  
of writing  the  code  were  analyzed  with  respect  to  the  target  program -
ming language.  To  do  so,  all  the  errors  belonging  to  a  particular  language  
were combined  and  then  tokenized  into  individual  sentences.  These  sen -
tences would  contain  the  error  description  and  would  repeat  across  
multiple examples.  These  sentences  were  then  ranked  using  TF-IDF  
and helped  in  isolating  the  most  important  errors  from  the  reasoning  
generated by  the  LLMs.
6.2. Results
After compiling  and  checking  the  syntax  of  code  generated  by  the  
LLMs as  follow-up  to  the  incorrect  code  it  gave  on  the  first  pass,  the  
results showed  that  the  overall  CCR  for  the  study  increased  by  0.1019,  
or in  other  words  the  LLM  gave  correct  code  for  roughly  1090  translation  
tasks out  of  3963  translation  tasks  in  the  Rosetta  Code  dataset  on  which  
they had  previously  made  a  mistake  in  Section 4.5 . This  means  that  by  
asking the  LLM  to  explain  the  error  and  then  fix  its  mistake,  the  LLMs  
were able  to  fix  roughly  25  %  of  the  total  mistakes  across  all  LLMs.  
Thus, prompting  the  LLMs  with  error  feedback  increases  the  CCR  by  
10 %  for  Rosetta  Code  tasks.  Table 9  breaks this  down  further  to  show  
the CCR  Gain  with  respect  to  each  LLM.  Qwen2.5-Coder  (both  sizes)  
and DeepSeek  Coder  had  the  most  improvement  in  their  CCR,  while  
Stable Code,  DeepSeek-Coder-V2  and  Yi-Coder  (smaller  size)  had  the  
least improvement  in  their  CCR.
Upon executing  the  code  generated  by  the  LLMs  on  follow-up  
prompts, the  results  from  Table 10  show that  the  overall  Pass@1  score  
improved by  0.0847,  indicating  that  the  LLMs  were  able  to  correct  run -
time errors  and  mistakes  for  additional  907  translation  tasks.  The  change  
in Pass@1  is  correlated  with  the  change  in  CCR  scores,  as  Qwen2.5 -
Coder [7B]  had  the  highest  gain  in  both  CCR  and  Pass@1,  while  Stable  
Code and  DeepSeek-Coder-V2  had  the  smallest  change  in  CCR  as  well  as  
Pass@1.
A key  insight  here  is  that  having  the  largest  CCR  Gain  or  Pass@1  
gain doesnâ€™t  usually  mean  that  the  LLMs  in  question  had  the  best  
CCR/Pass@1 or  were  the  most  reliable.  When  looking  at  Fig. 6 , the 
top 3  LLMs  after  follow-up  prompts  to  correct  mistakes  were  still  the  
same, DeepSeek  Coder  V2,  Yi-Coder  [9  b]  and  CodeGeeX4.  In  fact,  
DeepSeek Coder  V2,  which  had  the  highest  CCR  after  the  first  translation  
prompts, had  one  of  the  lowest  gains  in  CCR  after  the  follow-up  prompt -
ing. Qwen2.5-Coder  [7B],  with  the  highest  CCR  Gains,  jumped  from  6th  
place to  4th  place  in  the  overall  CCR.  When  inspecting  Fig. 7 , the top  
3 LLMs  in  terms  of  Pass@1  are  still  DeepSeek  Coder  V2,  Yi-Coder  [9  b]  
and CodeGeeX4,  but  their  positions  have  changed  relatively.  Similar  to  
CCR, Qwen2.5-Coder  [7B]  jumped  to  4th  spot  from  7th  after  follow -
up prompting  when  measuring  Pass@1.  Both  the  figures  highlight  that  
smaller models  like  Qwen2.5-Coder  [1.5B]  and  Yi-Coder  [1.5B]  have  the  
ability to  compete  with  larger  LLMs  when  measuring  CCR  and  Pass@1.
These results  highlight  the  accuracy  and  reliability  of  LLMs  when  
translating codes  from  the  Rosetta  Code  dataset.  Larger  LLMs  (with  7â€“9  
billion parameters)  tend  to  have  the  highest  CCR/Pass@1  and  are  thus  
quite accurate  and  reliable  out  of  the  box.  They  become  even  more  
reliable when  given  the  chance  to  explain  the  errors  they  made  and  fix

From Table 11 , the gains  in  CCR  and  Pass@1  across  target  program -

languages benefited  more  from  the  follow-up  prompting.  In  fact,  systems  
programming languages  like  Rust,  Go,  and  C  had  the  most  improve -
ment in  CCR  and  Pass@1  after  follow-up  prompting.  These  languages  
are known  in  the  developer  community  to  have  detailed  error  messages  
during compilation,  which  help  the  LLMs  in  making  corrections  in  the  
code. Languages  like  JavaScript  and  Python,  which  are  not  compiled  
and rely  on  syntax  checkers  to  identify  mistakes  before  execution,  only  
had minor  gains  in  CCR  and  Pass@1  after  follow-up.
But again,  having  a  large  CCR  Gain  or  Pass@1  Gain  doesnâ€™t  mean  
that the  LLMs  are  more  accurate  or  reliable  in  generating  code  in  that  
programming language.  In  fact,  when  looking  at  Fig. 8 , JavaScript and  
Python still  have  the  highest  CCR  after  follow-up  prompting,  being  accu -
rate more  than  90  %  of  the  time  in  translation  tasks.  In  fact,  languages
with the  highest  CCR  gain  still  have  the  worst  CCR  across  the  seven  
programming languages.  This  shows  that  LLMs  tend  to  be  more  reli -
able and  accurate  when  generating  code  in  JavaScript  and  Python.  LLMs  
tend to  make  mistakes  in  systems  programming  languages  like  C,  Rust,  
and Golang  on  the  first  try,  but  tend  to  improve  a  lot  when  prompted  
again with  the  errors  generated  by  the  respective  compilers.  From  Fig. 9 , 
Python had  the  highest  Pass@1  score,  both  before  and  after  follow-up  
prompting. Java  improved  a  lot  on  Pass@1  after  follow-up  prompt,  mov -
ing just  ahead  of  JavaScript  after  follow-up  prompt.  Similar  to  CCR,  
Go, C,  C+ +, Rust  had  low  initial  Pass@1  scores,  but  improved  signif -
icantly after  follow-up  prompts.  In  fact,  Rust  had  the  highest  increase  
in Pass@1  out  of  all  the  target  languages,  indicating  how  detailed  er -
ror messages  generated  by  Rust  compiler  help  in  guiding  the  LLM  code  
towards functional  correctness.
The trends  observed  in  Figs. 8  and 9 for CCR  and  Pass@1  point  
out that  LLMs  tend  to  perform  much  better  on  JavaScript  and  Python  
compared to  compiled  languages  like  C,  C+ +, Go,  Java,  and  Rust.  As  
stated by  Github  Staf  [ 67] and  Stack  Overflow  Developer  Survey  [ 68], 
JavaScript and  Python  have  some  of  the  largest  presences  on  GitHub  
and Stack  OverFlow,  which  translates  directly  to  more  extensive  pres -
ence in  public  LLM  training  datasets,  giving  these  models  substantially  
more examples  to  learn  from.  JavaScript  and  Python  are  frequently  used

for rapid  prototyping,  web  development,  and  data  analysis  tasks  where

richer contextual  examples  during  training,  resulting  in  more  accurate  
and practical  code  generation  capabilities.
The follow-up  responses  generated  by  the  LLMs  contained  code  as  
well as  an  explanation  of  the  error  and  proposed  fix.  Based  on  the  process  
discussed in  Section 6.1 , analyzing the  reasoning  generated  by  the  LLMs  
before fixing  the  issue  reveals  interesting  language-specific  insights  into  
the errors  introduced  by  LLMs.
â€¢ For C  code,  the  most  common  errors  were  missing  header  files,  use  of
functions without  declaring  or  including  the  proper  headers,  missing  
closing parentheses  in  function  calls,  misuse  of  read-only  variables,  
C+ + features  in  C  code,  and  namespace  issues.
â€¢ For C+ + code,  the  most  common  errors  were  missing  header  files,
using features  unsupported  by  the  current  compiler  or  library  ver -
sion, issues  with  using  std::string  vs.  const  char*,  namespace  issues,  
unnecessary parentheses  or  mismatched  types  in  logical  operations,  
incorrect use  of  logical  and  conditional  operators,  and  missing  main  
function.
â€¢ For Go  code,  the  most  common  errors  were  missing  package  dec -
larations, missing  import  statements,  extra  import  statements,  unex -
pected parentheses,  missing  or  misplaced  keywords,  issues  related  to  
unused variables  or  incorrect  variable  types,  type  mismatches,  and  
incorrect usage  of  standard  library  functions.
â€¢ For Java  code,  the  most  common  errors  were  due  to  disabled  pre -
-
view features,  missing  semicolons,  misplaced  parentheses,  missing  
access modifiers,  incorrect  type  usage,  use  of  implicitly  declared  
classes (which  are  disabled  by  default),  modifying  variables  inside  
lambda expressions  that  are  not  effectively  final,  missing  exceptions  
in try-catch  blocks  and  incompatibility  with  the  Java  version  being  
used.
â€¢ For JavaScript  code,  the  most  common  syntax  errors  were  due  to
unbalanced parentheses  or  braces,  issues  related  to  data  type  mis -
matches, and  improper  usage  and  syntax  of  common  functions  like  
Math.sqrt and  Math.trunc.
â€¢ For Python  code,  the  most  common  syntax  errors  were  due  to  un
balanced parentheses,  square  brackets,  indentation  errors,  missing  
components in  expressions,  and  improper  placement  of  operators.
â€¢ For Rust  code,  the  most  common  errors  were  due  to  missing  main
method in  the  code,  incorrect  use  of  â€œletâ€  variables  in  global  context,  
unbalanced or  mismatched  braces  and  parentheses,  compiler  being  
unable to  infer  the  correct  type,  missing  traits  (packages),  and  invalid  
characters in  identifiers.
7. Discussion
The first  key  finding  from  this  study  uncovers  scale  patterns  in  the  
Rosetta Code  dataset.  This  study  reveals  that  the  Code  Correctness  Rate  
(CCR), a  measure  of  how  many  translated  code  samples  generated  by  the  
LLMs were  syntactically  correct  and  compiled  correctly,  scales  with  the  
number of  parameters  in  the  LLM,  with  larger  models  performing  better  
on this  measure  compared  to  smaller  models.  A  similar  phenomenon  
was also  observed  in  Pass@1  metric,  which  measures  the  functional
Neurocomputing 656 (2025) 131461 
17 
[Page 18]
V.S. Pendyala  and  N.B.  Thakur
correctness of  the  generated  code  against  a  set  of  known  test  cases.  
This agrees  with  the  results  from  Code  Llama  research  by  RoziÃ¨re  et  
al. [ 66], which  also  observed  the  same  phenomenon  on  the  HumanEval  
and MBPP  datasets.  The  same  phenomenon  was  also  observed  in  the  
study by  Macedo  et  al.  [ 83] that  evaluated  the  effect  of  output  format  
on LLMs  in  code  translations.  In  the  study,  this  effect  was  observed  on  
the Computational  Efficiency  (CA)  metric  for  the  WizardCoder  family  of  
models, while  this  effect  was  noted  across  all  the  models  considered  in  
the study.  This  can  be  explained  by  the  availability  of  more  parameters  
for the  LLM  to  learn  from  a  greater  number  of  coding  samples,  resulting  
in a  better  CCR.
Contrary to  expectations,  the  second  finding  revealed  that  transla -
tion metrics  like  CodeBLEU,  chrF,  METEOR,  BLEU,  ROUGE-1,  and  WER  
are ineffective  when  it  comes  to  evaluating  machine  translations  on  the  
same set  of  translation  tasks  and  language  pairs.  This  is  in  contrast  to  
the results  obtained  on  natural  language  translation  tasks  from  the  study  
by Huang  and  Liu  [ 84]. The  difference  is  expected,  as  a  code  trans -
lation dataset  is  being  used  in  conjunction  with  LLMs  fine-tuned  for  
code generation.  Instead,  it  was  demonstrated  that  these  metrics  are  
more suitable  for  distinguishing  between  different  translation  tasks  and  
are much  more  representative  of  the  quality  and  quantity  of  reference  
translations available  for  each  task.
The next  findings  showed  that  the  interpretability  of  source  code  
lines with  respect  to  the  translated  code  decreased  with  increasing  line  
number. This  effect  can  be  attributed  to  the  fact  that  the  original  prompt  
contained the  task  description  as  well,  so  the  LLM  relies  even  less  on  the  
later source  code  lines  to  translate  the  code.  The  initial  source  code  lines,  
along with  the  task  description,  provide  enough  context  and  signal  for  
the LLM  to  make  accurate  translations  even  without  the  remaining  lines.  
This phenomenon  was  observed  across  all  the  translation  pairs  and  both  
Feature Ablation  and  Shapley  Value  Sampling  methods.  Based  on  prior  
research, this  is  the  first  time  such  interpretability  studies  have  been  
conducted on  coding  LLMs  for  translation  tasks.
It was  observed  that  the  interaction  pattern  between  source  code  
lines and  translated  code  lines  is  sparse  and  shows  strong  interpretabil -
ity scores  when  they  both  represent  the  same  programming  concept,  
such as  loops,  expressions,  and  logical  flow.  This  is  expected  behavior  
and closely  resembles  human  translation  efforts,  since  human  transla -
tors will  only  change  the  section  of  translated  code  when  the  equivalent  
section is  changed  in  the  source  code.  It  was  also  observed  that  the  
interpretability of  translated  code  lines  decreases  as  the  line  number  
increases with  respect  to  the  source  code  lines.  The  latter  translated  
code lines  depend  less  on  the  source  code  lines.  This  can  be  explained  
by the  context  window  of  LLMs,  where  the  latter  tokens  from  trans -
lated code  would  attend  more  to  the  previously  generated  tokens  than  
the source  code  tokens,  as  the  source  code  tokens  move  out  of  the  
context window.
Based on  the  findings  from  RQ1,  it  is  proposed  that  line-to-line  inter -
pretability heatmaps  can  serve  as  a  valuable  tool  in  guiding  the  output  
code towards  a  desired  outcome.  If  the  translated  code  contains  logi -
cal errors,  it  is  possible  to  analyze  how  the  source  code  lines  influence  
the code  generated  by  the  LLM  and  then  adjust  the  source  code  lines  
with high  interpretability  scores  to  achieve  a  correct  output.  Consider  
the scenario  where  the  source  code  is  heavily  commented.  Since  LLMs  
can understand  natural  language  as  well,  it  is  possible  that  the  trans -
lated code  would  attend  more  to  the  comments  in  a  heavily  commented  
source code.  In  such  scenarios,  the  source  code  comments  that  have  
interpretability with  the  affected  line  could  also  be  tweaked  to  direct  
the translated  code  towards  a  desired  outcome,  along  with  traditional  
prompt engineering  techniques.
The findings  from  RQ2  show  that  LLMs  can  not  only  translate  code  
but also  comprehend  and  explain  their  own  errors  and  then  correct  those  
errors when  presented  with  compiler  or  syntax  checker  feedback.  A  10  %  
improvement on  average  was  achieved  across  all  the  LLMs  on  the  CCR  
metric when  feedback  from  the  compiler  or  syntax  checker  was  provided  
to the  LLM.  An  8  %  improvement  on  average  was  also  achieved  across
all the  LLMs  on  Pass@1  metric  as  well  after  the  follow-up  prompt.  This  
result agrees  with  the  observations  from  the  BESTER  study  by  Ref.  [ 85], 
where they  also  saw  improvement  in  the  Pass@K  metric  for  HumanEval  
and MBPP  datasets  when  the  LLM  was  systematically  prompted  with  
compiler feedback  to  output  correct  code.  The  study  also  revealed  a  sim -
ilar phenomenon,  though  it  differs  from  that  study  with  the  use  of  the  
Rosetta Code  dataset  for  translation  tasks  across  multiple  open-source  
Code Generation  LLMs.
It was  observed  that  the  improvement  in  CCR  and  Pass@1  was  
dependent on  the  target  programming  language.  JavaScript  is  often  un -
derrepresented in  Machine  Translation  studies,  and  it  was  noted  that  
code translated  to  JavaScript  had  a  CCR  greater  than  0.90  even  without  
feedback, increasing  to  0.94  when  feedback  was  provided  by  the  Node  
compiler. Python,  on  the  other  hand  had  the  highest  Pass@1  score  be -
fore any  follow-up  prompt  across  all  the  LLMs  and  tasks.  This  increase  
was the  highest  for  Rust,  which  had  the  lowest  CCR  of  0.4  and  Pass@1  of  
0.3 before  feedback,  but  improved  massively  to  CCR  of  0.61  and  Pass@1  
of 0.46  after  Rust  compiler  feedback  was  given  to  the  LLM  in  follow-up  
prompts. The  BESTER  study  by  Song  et  al.  [ 85], which  implemented  a  
similar setup,  didnâ€™t  provide  any  details  about  the  sensitivity  of  this  phe -
nomenon on  the  target  programming  language.  This  suggests  a  form  of  
systematic error  correction  capabilities  in  LLMs  that  enhances  reliability  
in two  ways.
â€¢ It demonstrates  that  LLMs  can  leverage  concrete  feedback  like
compiler output  to  improve  their  responses,  much  like  human  pro -
grammers do  when  debugging  code.
â€¢ The consistency  of  improvement  across  multiple  LLMs,  program -
ming languages,  and  code  types  indicates  that  this  isnâ€™t  a  random  
occurrence but  rather  a  reliable  pattern  of  behavior.
The observation  that  statically-typed  languages  like  Rust  ex -
hibit more  substantial  improvements  through  feedback  loops,  while  
dynamically-typed languages  such  as  JavaScript  achieve  higher  initial  
correctness rates,  can  be  attributed  to  several  factors  inherent  to  their  
respective paradigms  and  how  LLMs  interact  with  them.  Statically-typed  
languages enforce  rigorous  type  checking  at  compile-time.  Even  minor  
type mismatches,  incorrect  function  signatures,  or  misuse  of  data  struc -
tures result  in  immediate  compilation  errors.  When  an  LLM  generates  
code for  these  languages,  a  single  type  error  can  cascade  into  multiple  
compiler errors,  making  the  initial  raw  correctness  rate  lower.
However, the  explicit  and  specific  nature  of  these  compiler  errors  
provides very  clear,  unambiguous  feedback  signals  to  the  LLM.  This  
precise error  information  allows  the  LLM  to  learn  and  correct  fundamen -
tal structural  and  type-related  issues  more  effectively  during  feedback  
sessions, leading  to  more  significant  jumps  in  correctness.  The  LLM  
essentially gets  highly  informative  hints  on  exactly  where  and  how  it  
deviated from  the  languageâ€™s  strict  rules.
On the  other  hand,  dynamically-typed  languages  defer  type  checking  
to runtime.  Syntactic  validity  often  doesnâ€™t  guarantee  functional  cor -
rectness, as  type  errors  or  attribute  errors  may  only  manifest  during  
execution. This  leniency  means  an  LLM  can  generate  syntactically  valid,  
but semantically  incorrect,  code  that  appears  correct  initially  but  fails  
later. Consequently,  their  raw  correctness  rates  tend  to  be  higher  for  
simple syntactic  checks.  However,  the  feedback  from  runtime  errors  in  
these languages  can  be  less  precise  regarding  the  root  cause  of  the  issue,  
especially for  complex  logical  errors  or  subtle  type  interactions  that  are  
only discovered  during  execution.  The  feedback  loop  might  thus  offer  
less direct  guidance  for  fundamental  structural  corrections,  leading  to  
smaller relative  improvements.
Statically-typed languages  often  require  more  explicit  declarations  
such as  variable  types,  function  return  types,  and  error  handling  mecha -
nisms. This  explicitness  provides  more  surface  area  for  the  LLM  to  learn  
the correct  patterns  and  relationships.  When  an  LLM  gets  it  wrong,  the  
error messages  pinpoint  these  explicit  elements.  Dynamically-typed  lan -
guages rely  more  on  inference  and  convention,  leading  to  more  concise
Neurocomputing 656 (2025) 131461 
18 
[Page 19]
V.S. Pendyala  and  N.B.  Thakur
code. This  brevity  can  mean  fewer  explicit  signals  for  the  LLM  to  latch  
onto for  self-correction  when  errors  occur.
The improvement  through  feedback  can  also  be  explained  based  
on error  propagation  and  debugging  complexity.  In  statically-typed  
languages, errors  often  stop  the  compilation  process  early,  preventing  
deeper, more  complex  runtime  issues.  Fixing  one  compilation  error  can  
resolve several  downstream  issues.  In  dynamically-typed  languages,  an  
error might  only  appear  deep  within  a  programâ€™s  execution  flow,  far  
from its  original  cause,  making  feedback  less  effective  in  pinpointing  
the core  issue  for  an  LLM  to  correct  iteratively.
This differential  impact  of  feedback  highlights  that  while  LLMs  are  
proficient at  generating  syntactically  plausible  code  for  dynamic  lan -
guages, the  structured  and  explicit  nature  of  static  type  systems,  coupled  
with their  precise  compile-time  error  feedback,  provides  a  more  effec -
tive learning  signal  for  LLMs,  enabling  more  substantial  and  systematic  
improvements through  iterative  feedback  mechanisms.  This  suggests  
that for  applications  requiring  high  reliability  and  performance,  guiding  
LLMs with  environments  that  provide  strong,  immediate,  and  explicit  
feedback, such  as  those  found  in  statically-typed  languages,  can  be  
particularly beneficial.
As part  of  RQ2,  it  was  observed  that  LLMs  can  clearly  parse  the  out -
put from  code  compilers  and  syntax  checker  tools,  and  they  can  describe  
those errors  in  natural  language.  The  last  finding  suggests  LLMs  can  ac -
curately identify  language-specific  errors  and  describe  a  fix  for  them  in  
natural language.  This  is  significant  because  it  shows  that  LLMs  have  
a degree  of  metacognition  â€“  they  can  analyze  their  own  output,  under -
stand what  went  wrong,  articulate  their  reasoning  process,  and  fix  the  
errors. This  transparency  in  decision-making  is  crucial  for  explainability,  
as it  helps  in  understanding  how  the  LLM  arrives  at  its  solutions  rather  
than treating  it  as  a  black  box.
Rosetta Code  tasks,  though  not  full  applications,  effectively  assess  an  
LLMâ€™s proficiency  in  handling  fundamental  linguistic,  algorithmic,  and  
translational challenges  in  real-world  software  development.  Even  if  the  
tasks are  smaller,  the  types  of  errors  LLMs  make  are  representative  of  the  
challenges developers  face  in  more  complex  scenarios.  Understanding  
these patterns  in  a  controlled  environment  is  crucial  before  scaling  up.  
In real  applications,  developers  constantly  translate  user  stories,  de -
sign documents,  and  architectural  specifications  into  code.  While  our  
prompts are  concise,  they  capture  the  essence  of  defining  a  problem  and  
expecting a  functional  solution.
Many Rosetta  Code  tasks  are  foundational  components  of  virtually  
every real-world  application,  from  backend  services  to  data  processing  
pipelines and  user  interfaces.  The  ability  of  an  LLM  to  correctly  gen -
erate or  translate  these  core  components  directly  reflects  its  utility  in  
building larger  systems.  The  insights  gained  from  the  controlled  exper -
iments detailed  in  this  study  are  directly  transferable  to  understanding  
LLM behavior  in  more  complex,  practical  coding  scenarios.
8. Limitations
The most  important  limitations  of  this  study  were  the  selection  of  
only seven  programming  languages,  15  LLMs,  and  the  Rosetta  Code  
dataset. The  programming  languages  were  shortlisted  based  on  their  
popularity in  Agarwal  et  al.  [ 86], ultimately  resulting  in  a  selection  
of C,  C+ +, Go,  Java,  JavaScript,  Python,  and  Rust,  as  this  combina -
tion provided  a  representative  mix  of  procedural  versus  object-oriented  
languages, scripting  versus  compiled  languages,  and  systems  versus  ap -
plication programming  languages.  The  selection  of  15  LLMs  was  guided  
by various  factors.  Initially,  the  LLMs  that  were  available  on  both  the  
Hugging Face  and  Ollama  platforms  were  identified.  Subsequently,  mod -
els that  had  been  fine-tuned  for  code  generation  and  optimized  for  
adherence to  instructions  were  selected.  These  models  were  further  fil -
tered to  ensure  they  would  run  on  most  consumer-grade  devices  (1â€“10  
billion active  parameters).
The dataset,  Rosetta  Code,  though  not  as  widely  used  as  CodeNet,  
contained implementations  for  many  programming  tasks  in  a  much
wider variety  of  languages.  From  the  entire  dataset,  only  seventeen  tasks  
were selected  to  represent  the  core  concepts  of  programming  languages,  
specifically bitwise,  integer,  string,  and  file  operations.  The  dataset  was  
specifically chosen  because  it  allowed  for  direct,  homogeneous  compar -
isons of  LLM  performance  across  different  languages  and  task  types  for  
the same  underlying  problem.  This  control  is  often  difficult  to  maintain  
in more  unconstrained,  large-scale  datasets.
It also  allowed  for  focused  interpretability  analysis.  The  structured  
nature of  Rosetta  Code  tasks  facilitated  a  more  precise  application  of  
interpretability techniques,  enabling  us  to  pinpoint  the  influence  of  spe -
cific prompt  elements  without  the  overwhelming  noise  present  in  highly  
varied real-world  code.  Constructing  and  rigorously  evaluating  the  out -
put of  LLMs  on  significantly  larger,  more  diverse  datasets,  especially  
while also  conducting  in-depth  interpretability  analysis,  would  necessi -
tate a  substantially  larger  research  effort,  exceeding  the  current  project  
scope and  computational  resources.  Similarly,  the  experimental  setup  
was focused  on  LLMs  that  can  be  deployed  readily  on  consumer  lap -
tops, so  that  experiments  are  more  accessible  and  easily  reproducible.  
Hence, the  focus  is  on  4-bit  quantization  and  a  limit  on  the  number  of  
parameters. Using  larger  models  would  require  more  resources.  The  ex -
ploration of  larger,  more  complex  datasets  and  larger  models  is  therefore  
a direction  for  future  work.
Another limitation  in  any  study  of  LLMs  has  been  their  non -
deterministic behavior.  To  mitigate  this,  the  LLMs  were  queried  using  a  
constant seed  of  42,  which  is  a  commonly  used  seed  whose  origins  were  
popularized by  Adams  [ 5]. The  study  adhered  to  the  chat  templates  pro -
vided for  each  LLM  to  ensure  clarity  in  the  adherence  to  instructional  
prompts. Additionally,  a  limitation  of  this  study  was  the  lack  of  test  cases  
to support  each  translation  task,  which  could  have  aided  in  analyzing  the  
performance of  code  generated  by  LLMs  at  runtime.  However,  this  was  
not a  concern  since  the  primary  aim  of  this  research  was  to  evaluate  the  
interpretability and  explainability  of  code  generation  LLMs.
The metrics  used  for  this  study,  such  as  BLEU  and  METEOR,  pri -
marily assess  syntactic  and  stylistic  quality  and  not  direct  functional  
correctness. Functional  correctness  evaluation  frameworks  can  be  more  
challenging to  standardize  across  diverse  languages  and  tasks.  Metrics  
like BLEU  and  METEOR  were  selected  to  provide  quantitative  measures  
of code  similarity  and  structure  adherence,  which  are  crucial  precur -
sors to  functional  correctness.  While  not  direct  measures  of  functional  
correctness, a  high  score  in  these  metrics  implies  a  greater  likelihood  
of correct  syntax  and  structure,  making  the  code  more  amenable  to  
debugging and  potential  functional  validation.
Therefore, integration  of  automated  functional  tests  is  the  next  
step for  a  more  comprehensive  evaluation  in  future  studies.  This  be -
comes particularly  pertinent  as  dedicated  testing  frameworks  for  LLM -
generated code  mature  across  diverse  programming  languages  and  
problem types.
9. Conclusion
The use  of  Large  Language  Models  (LLMs)  in  software  engineering  
for code  generation  and  translation  has  become  increasingly  common;  
however, it  remains  critical  to  ensure  both  their  reliability  and  the  in -
terpretability of  the  code  they  generate.  This  study  reveals  that  larger  
models tend  to  achieve  higher  Code  Correctness  Rates  (CCR)  on  the  
Rosetta Code  dataset,  indicating  that  the  ability  to  generate  syntacti -
cally correct  code  scales  with  the  size  of  the  models.  This  study  also  
suggests that  the  effectiveness  of  translation  metrics  like  CodeBLEU,  
chrF, METEOR,  and  BLEU  is  not  effective  in  differentiating  between  the  
quality of  code  generated  by  various  LLMs.  Therefore,  the  application  
of interpretability  methods  such  as  Feature  Ablation  and  Shapley  Value  
Sampling is  crucial  for  gaining  insights  into  how  LLMs  process  code  in  
translation tasks.
Interpretability methods  discussed  in  this  study  show  that  the  ini -
tial source  code  lines,  along  with  the  task  description,  exert  the  most  
significant influence  on  the  translated  code.  These  initial  lines  provide
Neurocomputing 656 (2025) 131461 
19 
[Page 20]
V.S. Pendyala  and  N.B.  Thakur
sufficient context  for  the  LLMs  to  generate  accurate  translations,  with  
later lines  exhibiting  less  impact.  Furthermore,  the  interpretability  of  
translated code  lines  relative  to  the  source  code  decreases  with  the  line  
number, indicating  that  later  lines  in  the  translated  code  are  conditioned  
more on  earlier  translated  lines  than  on  the  source  code  lines.  These  in -
terpretability techniques  are  useful  for  understanding  how  the  model  
generates code  and  can  potentially  be  used  to  guide  the  LLM  towards  a  
desired result.
Moreover, when  LLM  generated  code  produces  errors  on  execution,  
LLMs can  parse  error  feedback  from  compilers  and  checkers  and  artic -
ulate the  errors  in  natural  language.  Analysis  of  these  explanations  and  
corrections provided  by  the  LLM  uncovers  common  language-specific  
errors, such  as  missing  header  files  in  C  or  absent  semicolons  in  Java.  
Prompt engineering  also  plays  a  critical  role  in  obtaining  usable  code  
from LLMs.  Techniques  such  as  iterative  prompting  improve  the  qual -
ity of  code  generated  by  LLMs.  By  providing  additional  context  in  the  
follow-up prompts,  including  error  messages  from  the  compiler,  this  
study demonstrates  that  LLMs  can  often  correct  their  errors  and  produce  
enhanced code  within  the  same  conversation  context.  The  consistency  
of improvement  in  the  follow-up  prompts  across  multiple  LLMs,  pro -
gramming languages,  and  tasks  from  the  Rosetta  Code  dataset  suggests  
that this  is  a  reliable  behavioral  pattern,  thereby  supplementing  prior  
research in  this  area.
Further work  is  still  required  in  the  direction  of  interpretability  and  
reliability of  LLMs  in  Code  Translation  tasks.  Rosetta  Code  is  a  vast  
repository of  coding  tasks  that  have  been  implemented  in  multiple  pro -
gramming languages,  of  which  only  a  subset  of  tasks  and  languages  is  
included in  this  study.  Methods  like  feature  ablation  and  Shapley  value  
sampling are  only  some  of  the  ways  in  which  interpretability  can  be  
measured, and  further  work  is  required  to  extrapolate  the  results  from  
this study  across  other  interpretability  methods.

Quality assurance of LLM-generated code: Addressing non-functional quality 
characteristicsI
Xin Sun
 âˆ—, Daniel StÃ¥hl
 , Kristian Sandahl
 , Christoph Kessler
Department of Computer and Information Science, LinkÃ¶ping University, Sweden
A R T I C L E  I N F O
Keywords:
LLM-generated code
Code generation
Non-functional quality characteristics
Maintainability
Security
Performance efficiency
 A B S T R A C T
In recent years, large language models have been widely integrated into software engineering workflows, 
supporting tasks like code generation. While prior evaluations focus on functional correctness, there is still a 
limited understanding of the non-functional quality characteristics of generated code.
Guided by the ISO/IEC 25010 quality model, this study adopts a multi-methods approach comprising three 
complementary elements: a literature review of 109 papers, two industry workshops with practitioners from 
multiple organizations, and an empirical analysis of patching real-world software issues using three LLMs. 
Motivated by insights from both the literature and practitioners, the empirical study examined the quality of 
generated patches regarding security, maintainability, and performance efficiency, which were identified as 
critical code-level quality attributes.
Our results indicate that existing research primarily emphasizes security, performance efficiency, and main-
tainability, while other quality attributes are understudied. In contrast, practitioners prioritize maintainability 
and readability, warning that generated code may accelerate the accumulation of technical debt. The empirical 
evaluation demonstrates the instability of optimizing NFQCs through prompts in practical software engineering 
settings.
Overall, our findings expose a misalignment between academic focus, industry priorities, and observed 
model behavior, highlighting the need to integrate quality assurance mechanisms into LLM code generation 
pipelines to ensure that future generated code not only passes tests but truly passes with quality.
1. Introduction
The prevalence of large language models for code (LLMs for code) 
has brought new changes to the field of software engineering (Chen 
et al., 2021; RoziÃ¨re et al., 2023). These models are tailored for 
understanding and processing code and can generate functionally cor-
rect outputs under appropriate prompts (Luo et al., 2024; Hui et al., 
2024; Jiang et al., 2023). Currently, these powerful models have been 
integrated into the workflow of software engineering and are used by 
millions of developers worldwide. GitHub Copilot, released by GitHub 
and OpenAI, is an AI pair programmer that is built on Codex, which 
is a family of code LLMs (Chen et al., 2021; GitHub, 2025). Copilot 
can generate code across multiple programming languages from various 
types of prompts, such as natural language descriptions, function sig-
natures, and surrounding code. In some cases, it can produce complete 
applications such as interactive websites or data pipelines from a single 
prompt. As these models continue to evolve rapidly, their potential and

1 In this study, generated code refers to source code generated by LLMs, including both code snippets and code patches.
implications for software engineering remain in flux (The AI Digest, 
2024).
Several carefully curated metrics and benchmarks have been devel-
oped to evaluate the generation capability of code LLMs (Chen et al., 
2021; Jimenez et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2024; Deng et al., 2025; Li 
et al., 2025; Du et al., 2024). Chen et al. (2021) released HumanEval, 
together with GitHub Copilot, to evaluate the ability of code LLMs to 
generate functionally correct code. SWE-bench (Jimenez et al., 2024) 
was introduced to assess the ability of LLMs to solve real-world software 
engineering tasks.
While these benchmarks provide a good basis for evaluating the 
ability of LLMs to generate functionally correct code, they offer limited 
support for assessing the non-functional quality characteristics (NFQCs) 
of generated code. According to the ISO/IEC 25010 quality model (In-
ternational Organization for Standardization, 2023), software quality 
encompasses not only functional correctness but also NFQCs such as 
performance efficiency, maintainability, and security.

X. Sun et al.
Due to the limited assessments of NFQCs in the current evalua-
tion system, code LLMs may produce code with varying quality along 
different NFQCs, which makes the generated code1 unreliable and 
sometimes causes severe faults. For example, Pearce et al. (2022) 
studied the performance of GitHub Copilot in high-risk cybersecurity 
scenarios (MITRE, 2024). In their study of 1689 programs generated 
across 89 scenarios, approximately 40% were found to contain code 
patterns considered vulnerable, illustrating the security weakness in 
generated code.
In particular, it remains unclear how NFQCs of generated code are 
currently conceptualized and assessed in existing research, whether 
these studies align with practitioner concerns, and how they interact 
with each other in concrete code generation settings beyond functional 
correctness.
To address our research goal, we adopt a mixed-method design in 
which each component plays a distinct role, while using the ISO/IEC 
25010 quality model as a common reference to structure and relate the 
investigation of NFQCs.
First, the literature review examines how NFQCs of generated code 
are currently conceptualized and evaluated in existing studies, reveal-
ing both commonly studied attributes and gaps. Secondly, the industry 
workshops provide an independent perspective on NFQCs by capturing 
how practitioners perceive, prioritize, and reason about quality con-
cerns of generated code in real-world development settings. This step 
allows us to contrast research evaluation practices with practitioner 
expectations, rather than assuming their alignment. Finally, informed 
by insights from both the literature and the workshops, the empirical 
study focuses on a set of NFQCs that are consistently highlighted as 
important across research and practice. Rather than evaluating each 
quality characteristic in isolation, the study examines how multiple 
NFQCs are jointly reflected in SWE-bench under different evaluation 
and optimization choices. This design enables us to explore patterns for 
trade-offs among selected NFQCs and to illustrate how current evalu-
ation practices may influence NFQCs when multiple quality concerns 
are considered simultaneously.
Together, the mixed-methods form a complementary design that 
connects conceptual definitions, practitionersâ€™ perspectives, and em-
pirical observations, providing an integrated perspective on NFQCs in 
generated code.
To guide our study, we defined three overarching Research Goals 
(RGs), each addressing a different aspect. The research goals are as 
follows:
â€¢ RG1: Explore how NFQCs in generated code have been addressed 
in existing research, and identify research gaps in this area.
â€¢ RG2: Identify the real-world expectations and pain points that 
practitioners have when integrating generated code in software 
projects.
â€¢ RG3: Characterize the observed behavior of generated code across 
key NFQCs identified in the previous research goals, and ex-
amine how feedback-driven strategies affect these qualities and 
the trade-offs among them in a real-world software engineering 
context.
For each research goal, we further formulated corresponding Re-
search Questions (RQs) to guide the analysis, which are presented in 
the corresponding sections.
The rest of the paper is organized as follows: Section 2 introduces 
the background on code generation and related work. Section 3 outlines 
the structure of the literature review. Section 4 presents the organiza-
tion of the two industry workshops, detailing the participant selection, 
session design, and experience of practitioners. Section 5 summarizes 
the setup of the empirical evaluation, covering dataset selection, ex-
periment configuration, evaluation metrics, and analysis workflow. 
Additionally, we discuss the implications of our findings, highlighting 
challenges and opportunities for future research. We discuss the threats 
to validity in Section 6. Finally, Section 7 concludes the study and 
outlines directions for integrating NFQCs into the quality assurance of 
LLM-generated code in real-world software systems.
2. Background and related work
This section presents the background of LLMs for code generation 
and related works.
2.1. Code generation
Code generation has become a more important application scenario 
since LLMs were first proposed (Manna and Waldinger, 1971; Liventsev 
et al., 2023). Code generation aims to automatically generate code 
given the problem description, high-level specifications, or existing 
code. Before the advent of LLMs, code generation was limited to 
structured methods (Hemel et al., 2008). These methods usually require 
detailed formal specifications and several steps for generation. LLMs 
changed this paradigm by learning from large code corpora, thus elim-
inating the need for formal specifications and allowing code generation 
from natural language prompts (Luo et al., 2024).
The release of GitHub Copilot marked the beginning of integrating 
LLMs into daily software workflows. Since then, numerous code LLMs 
have emerged, demonstrating remarkable performance in generating 
functionally correct and meaningful code across various programming 
languages (RoziÃ¨re et al., 2023; Hui et al., 2024; Jiang et al., 2023; 
Chen et al., 2021; Li et al., 2022, 2023).
By 2025, many AI programming tools have emerged, and a new 
approach called vibe coding has gained prominence (Lovable, 2024; 
Bolt, 2024; Cursor, 2024; Windsurf, 2024). In vibe coding, users do 
not directly engage with the code; instead, they remain entirely at the 
level of natural language, formulating prompts that instruct the code 
LLMs to generate, modify, and deploy components of the software. 
For example, Lovable2 is an AI-driven platform that enables users to 
build full-stack applications using natural language prompts, allowing 
rapid prototyping and deployment without extensive coding knowl-
edge. These advancements have significantly lowered the barrier to 
programming and accelerated software development processes.
2.2. Literature reviews
A review by Wang and Chen (2023) examined LLM code gener-
ation from a different angle. By reviewing 20 existing studies, they 
demonstrated that while using LLMs to generate code has been widely 
studied, the evaluation of LLM-generated code had received relatively 
little attention. The study addressed functional requirements such as 
functional correctness, as well as NFQCs, including security, main-
tainability, and others. It also highlighted key limitations in current 
evaluation practices, such as the use of inadequate evaluation criteria, 
the absence of systematic and quantitative evaluation frameworks, and 
the lack of consideration for human involvement in the evaluation 
process.
Z. Yang et al. (2024) presented a systematic literature review of 146 
studies focusing on NFQCs of code LLMs. They identified and discussed 
six NFQCs beyond functional correctness: robustness, security, privacy,
explainability, efficiency and usability. The study highlighted the vul-
nerability of LLM4Code systems to adversarial attacks, data poisoning, 
and privacy leaks, as well as challenges in explainability and usability. 
To address these issues, they proposed three complementary perspec-
tives, which are data-centric, human-centric, and system-centric, for 
developing more reliable and effective LLM4Code systems in the future. 
This work provided a comprehensive overview for understanding the 
broader implications of adopting LLM4Code in software engineering. 
However, most of the studies included in Z. Yang et al. (2024)â€™s 
literature review focus on evaluating the models themselves, such as 
the architecture, training data, or prompting strategies, rather than the 
quality of the code generated by LLMs. In practice, a model capable of 
2 https://lovable.dev/
The Journal of Systems & Software 238 (2026) 112885 
2 
[Page 3]
X. Sun et al.
producing high-quality code in principle does not guarantee that the 
actual outputs will meet high standards across NFQCs. It is therefore 
essential to acknowledge that, in real-world practice, systematic eval-
uation of generated code is required to ensure the overall quality of 
the software system. This motivates our study, which differs from prior 
work by shifting the perspective from the model to its outputs, and by 
examining to what extent the generated code satisfies NFQCs.
2.3. Empirical studies
Beyond conceptual discussions and literature reviews, a growing 
body of studies has examined the NFQCs of LLM-generated code. Niu 
et al. (2024a) conducted a comprehensive performance study using 
HumanEval and MBPP benchmarks and a set of programming problems 
from LeetCode, an online programming practice platform. They also in-
vestigated generating efficient code using prompt engineering methods. 
Their findings noted that the performance can depend heavily on how a 
prompt is given. If not instructed, LLMs might output a straightforward 
solution that ensures correctness but is not efficient.
Fu et al. (2025a) found that approximately 27.3% of generated code 
contained security weaknesses, spanning 43 Common Weakness Enu-
meration categories, including critical issues like Insufficiently Random 
Values and Cross-site Scripting. The study also explored the effec-
tiveness of Copilot in fixing these vulnerabilities, demonstrating that 
enhanced prompts could resolve up to 55.5% of issues.
In the area of maintainability, Liu et al. (2024a) applied static anal-
ysis tools such as Pylint to assess generated code and reported frequent 
code smells and issues, suggesting the need for human oversight.
Taken together, prior work reveals a growing effort towards under-
standing the NFQCs of generated code. Our study extends that effort by 
integrating evidence from research, practice, and empirical evaluation.
3. Literature review
To be able to achieve RG1 in Section 1, we first conducted a 
literature review to assess the current state of research and potential 
issues in this field. Furthermore, the literature review sought to answer 
the following research questions:
â€¢ RQ 3.1: What trends can be observed in research on NFQCs of 
generated code?
â€¢ RQ 3.2: How have different NFQCs been examined in the existing 
studies, and what challenges and limitations have been identified?
3.1. Research design
LLMs have been utilized across various tasks. In this literature re-
view, we focus especially on code generation. Code generation involves 
producing source code from natural language descriptions or limited 
hints, allowing NFQCs to emerge directly from the generation process. 
As this form of AI assistance is widely used in practice, studying it 
provides a representative context for the quality of generated code.
The search process of the literature review combines a structured
search strategy, clearly defined inclusion and exclusion criteria, and the 
use of snowballing to identify additional relevant literature. We included 
papers that examine code LLMs and AI programming tools or platforms 
that integrate these models, such as GitHub Copilot. To be eligible, 
the selected papers must explore the NFQCs of the code generated by 
these tools or models. To facilitate consistent discussion and compar-
ison, based on the ISO/IEC 25010 quality model, we map the diverse 
quality characteristics mentioned across studies to their corresponding 
terms in the ISO/IEC 25010 software product quality model, thereby 
standardizing terminology for our analysis. The search date is January 
20th, 2026.

Search strategy. We conducted the search on Scopus, chosen for its 
extensive coverage of peer-reviewed publications and inclusion of some 
preprints. Specifically, we limited our search to studies published be-
tween Jan. 2022 and Dec. 2025, as the majority of studies in code 
generation prior to 2022 were based on traditional approaches rather 
than LLMs, which gained major traction with the release of ChatGPT 
in late 2022. Our search query was formulated in two stages. First, we 
identified three core concepts: (1) LLMs, (2) code generation, and (3) 
software quality. Next, we broadened the first and third concepts using 
closely related terms to maximize recall while maintaining precision. 
For example, for LLMs, we included terms like â€˜AIâ€™ and â€˜artificial in-
telligenceâ€™; for quality, we included â€˜performanceâ€™ and â€˜non-functionalâ€™. 
To ensure the included papers focus on code generation, we kept â€˜code 
generationâ€™ unchanged.

The initial results contained many irrelevant studies, so we applied

generation. The language is restricted to English. Applying these filters, 
we initially retrieved 945 papers. Our inclusion and exclusion criteria

Manual screen and snowballing. After the initial retrieval, we conducted

empirical evaluation, systematic analysis, or concrete tooling? Only studies 
that satisfied both screening questions were retained. Following this 
manual screening process, a total of 107 papers were included in the 
dataset. In addition, during the manual screening phase, we applied 
forward and backward snowballing to the included studies to identify

of recent studies still exist as preprints. This growth indicates that 
the research community has shifted from investigations of functionally

several non-functional quality attributes.

model. Security emerges as the most frequently examined attribute, 
accounting for 33.6% of the studies. Performance efficiency (23.3%) 
and maintainability (17.2%) also receive substantial attention. In com-
parison, readability represents 12.9% of the studies, while reliability 
(5.2%) and modularity (1.7%) are addressed far less often. The remain-
ing 6.0% of studies fall into an â€˜â€˜othersâ€™â€™ category, covering quality 
aspects that are either less commonly investigated or do not map 
cleanly to a single ISO/IEC 25010 attribute. The distribution suggests 
that existing research tends to prioritize certain quality attributes over 
others, suggesting a potential research gap for future investigation.
In the results, we examined the distribution of programming lan-
guages evaluated across different NFQCs. Overall, Python is the most 
frequently studied language across all NFQCs, particularly in evalua-
tions of security (44.1%), performance efficiency (60.9%), and main-
tainability (66.7%). Other programming languages are less commonly 
examined in isolation and are more often included alongside Python 
within multi-language evaluation settings. These patterns suggest that 
current evaluation practices are influenced by language availability and 
execution convenience, with Python-centric benchmarks shaping much 
of the existing evidence on LLM code generation.
How NFQCs are examined and the limitations. To answer RQ 3.2, we 
summarized representative studies on the evaluation of NFQCs in gen-
erated code, together with the typical evaluation methods they employ 
and the metrics used to reflect NFQCs, as shown in Table  3.
Taken together, existing studies provide a partial but structured 
view of how NFQCs of generated code are currently evaluated. The 
following paragraphs summarize the state of research across three main 
dimensions.
â€¢ Security A growing body of studies has observed that LLM-
generated code can be functionally correct while containing secu-
rity vulnerabilities (Perry et al., 2023; Khoury et al., 2023; Pearce 
et al., 2022; Elgedawy et al., 2024; Siddiq and Santos, 2022; Asare 
et al., 2023b). Most existing work evaluates security using static 
code analysis tools, such as CodeQL, Bandit, or SonarQube, which 
detect security issues using the presence of predefined vulnerabil-
ity patterns or insecure coding practices (Pearce et al., 2022; Liu 
et al., 2024). Besides the widespread use of static analysis tools, 
several datasets and benchmarks have been introduced to support 
systematic security evaluation, including SecurityEval (Siddiq and 
Santos, 2022), LLMSevEval (Tony et al., 2023) and AI Code 
Generators for security (Natella et al., 2024). These benchmarks 
improve reproducible across studies, but they primarily focus on 
isolated code snippets and a limited set of vulnerability types. As a 
result, security evaluation in the current literature remains largely 
constrained to what can be detected through static analysis at 
the code level. A small set of studies compares the security 
of generated code with human-written code using manual in-
spection (Asare et al., 2023b). These comparisons suggest that 
the generated code is not uniformly worse than human-written 
code in terms of introducing vulnerabilities, but differences are 
observed in the types and severity of issues detected.
Overall, existing studies consistently indicate security concerns 
in generated code, while also reflecting a strong methodological 
reliance on static, code-level evaluation approaches.
â€¢ Performance Efficiency Performance efficiency of generated 
code is mainly evaluated using runtime performance and memory 
usage (Niu et al., 2024a; Singhal et al., 2024; Coignion et al., 
2024b; Huang et al., 2024b; Waghjale et al., 2024; Shypula 
et al., 2024b). The studies measure these properties by executing 
generated solutions on standardized programming tasks, often 
drawn from platforms such as LeetCode. Execution time and 
memory consumption are then compared with human-written 
The Journal of Systems & Software 238 (2026) 112885 
5 
[Page 6]
X. Sun et al.
or reference solutions. Under this setup, many studies report 
that functionally correct generated code achieves performance 
comparable to human-written solutions. In some cases, generated 
solutions even outperform human-written code (Coignion et al., 
2024b). A small number of studies also consider energy con-
sumption (Vartziotis et al., 2024; Solovyeva et al., 2025). These 
studies typically measure power usage during program execution 
and analyze it together with runtime and memory usage. The 
results suggest that LLMs do not optimize for energy efficiency 
by default. Energy improvements are usually observed only when 
energy consumption is explicitly included in the evaluation or 
optimization process.
Overall, current performance evaluations rely on a limited set 
of measurable indicators, mainly runtime and memory usage. 
These evaluations are often conducted on isolated problems. This 
approach supports controlled and reproducible experiments, but 
it also restricts performance analysis to settings where execu-
tion behavior is easy to benchmark. Interactions between perfor-
mance efficiency and other quality characteristics are sometimes 
reported, but they are rarely examined in a systematic manner.
â€¢ Maintainability Maintainability refers to how easily code can 
be understood and modified by developers over time. In the 
literature, maintainability of generated code is most commonly 
evaluated using static analysis tools and predefined metrics. Tools 
such as SonarQube, CodeQL and PMD are frequently used to 
identify code smells, complexity issues, and structural problems 
in generated code (Nguyen and Nadi, 2022b; J. Zheng et al., 
2024; Liu et al., 2024a; Yetistiren et al., 2023). Some studies show 
the reports from static analysis, which report low complexity 
and reasonable structure in generated code (Nguyen and Nadi, 
2022b). However, other studies combined manual review and 
static analysis tools (Liu et al., 2024a); they report that such code 
can still be verbose or poorly organized, which makes it harder 
to maintain in the future. This suggests that static metrics reflect 
only part of maintainability and may overlook issues that affect 
long-term maintenance.
Readability is not an attribute defined ISO/IEC 25010. Existing 
studies evaluate readability using benchmarks or proxy metrics 
derived from static analysis (Weyssow et al., 2025). Their results 
suggest that code generated by GPT-4 is more readable than that 
generated by open-source models, likely due to the well-formatted 
and structured training data. Besides readability, some studies 
also investigate the modularity and structure of the generated 
code. The study also reported that LLMs often generate code with 
poor modularity and structure, making it difficult for developers 
to understand and modify. Kang et al. (2024) questioned the 
traditional assumption that modularity improves code quality for 
LLM-generated code, finding that modular code does not consis-
tently enhance performance and may not be favored by LLMs 
during generation.
Several studies compare maintainability between LLM-generated 
and human-written code using the same analysis tools (Licorish 
et al., 2025; Eltabakh et al., 2024). These comparisons yield 
inconsistent results. In some cases, human-written code is found 
to be more readable and better aligned with coding standards. In 
other cases, generated code appears more structured and better 
documented, particularly for simpler tasks. Overall, these results 
suggest that maintainability outcomes depend strongly on task 
complexity, prompt design, and evaluation method.
Taken together, current results indicate that LLMs can produce 
readable and partially maintainable code, but maintainability is 
not ensured by default. Most evaluations rely on static, code-level 
metrics, and human intervention remains necessary to address 
structural and long-term maintenance issues.
3.3. Discussion of literature review findings
Our analysis of the literature reveals that the research community 
has made some progress in evaluating the quality of generated code. 
However, several challenges and open gaps need to be addressed before 
NFQC evaluation in this context can become systematic and comparable 
across studies.
â€¢ Ambiguity and inconsistency in defining quality character-
istics. Existing studies often use overlapping or loosely defined 
terms to describe quality characteristics, such as using readability, 
maintainability, or code quality interchangeably. While ISO/IEC 
25010 provides a well-established taxonomy for software quality, 
it has not been systematically adapted to the context of generated 
code. As a result, studies redefine quality characteristics based 
on available tools or metrics, rather than on a shared conceptual 
framework. This lack of alignment complicates the interpretation 
of results and makes it difficult to determine whether different 
studies are evaluating comparable aspects of quality, even when 
similar terminology is used.
â€¢ Imbalance in evaluated quality characteristics . The litera-
ture mainly focuses on a small number of NFQCs, most notably 
performance efficiency, security, and maintainability. These char-
acteristics are clearly important in practice, but their frequent 
appearance in research is also linked to the fact that they can 
be evaluated using existing automated, code-level tools. Other 
quality characteristics defined in ISO/IEC 25010 receive much 
less attention. This is not necessarily because they are less im-
portant, but because their evaluation depends on system context, 
runtime behavior, or user interaction, which are difficult to assess 
from isolated code artifacts. As a result, current NFQC coverage 
is influenced by what can be easily measured, and this may lead 
to a skewed view of the overall quality of generated code.
â€¢ Lack of a unified quantitative evaluation framework. Re-
searchers measure the functional correctness of the generated 
code using accuracy or pass@k, which measures how often LLMs 
generate a correct response on its ð‘˜ð‘¡â„Ž attempt for a given prob-
lem. In contrast, NFQC evaluation relies on a heterogeneous set 
of metrics, benchmarks, and tools, often tailored to individual 
studies. This methodological diversity limits comparability and 
reproducibility, as differences in reported results may stem from 
evaluation choices rather than underlying model behavior. More 
importantly, the absence of a common framework prevents joint 
analysis of functional correctness and multiple NFQCs, reinforcing 
a fragmented view of code quality that treats each characteristic 
in isolation.
â€¢ Limited understanding of interactions and trade-offs among 
NFQCs. Most studies assess NFQCs only for code that is al-
ready functionally correct, and some report trade-offs between 
correctness and individual quality characteristics. However, inter-
actions among multiple NFQCs are rarely examined in a system-
atic way. Unlike traditional software engineering, where trade-
offs are largely determined by design decisions and constraints, 
LLM-based code generation introduces new degrees of freedom 
through prompting strategies, model selection, and generation 
workflows. These mechanisms suggest that trade-offs may be 
influenced or steered rather than simply observed. The lack of em-
pirical studies that explicitly investigate such controllability limits 
our understanding of how NFQCs jointly evolve in generated 
code.
In summary, current research on NFQCs in generated code is incon-
sistent in terminology, selective in scope, and inconsistent in evaluation 
methods. Addressing these gaps will require unified definitions, stan-
dardized benchmarks, and comprehensive evaluation frameworks to 
improve understanding of the quality of generated code.
